problem: Un projet public indivisible coûte 6. La valeur privée de A est 3 ou 7 avec probabilités égales; celle de B est 2 ou 5 avec probabilités égales, indépendamment. Le projet est réalisé si et seulement si les deux consentent. Un individu consent exactement lorsque sa valeur couvre sa contribution, y compris à égalité. Calculez le surplus social espéré de la décision efficace et de contributions fixes (3,3). Puis choisissez une contribution fixe x de A et 6-x de B, avec 0<=x<=6, pour maximiser le surplus espéré sous cette règle de consentement. Trouvez tous les x optimaux et prouvez qu'aucun partage fixe ne met en œuvre la décision efficace dans tous les états.
thinking:
Avant de choisir un partage, je dois distinguer efficacité et consentement. Les sommes de valeurs possibles sont 5,8,9 et 12, avec poids 1/4 chacune. La décision efficace rejette seulement le total 5 et donne surplus espéré [(8-6)+(9-6)+(12-6)]/4=11/4. Avec contributions (3,3), A consent dans les deux types et B seulement au type 5. Le surplus espéré est [(8-6)+(12-6)]/4=2.

Pour trouver le partage optimal sans balayer des montants, je dois repérer les seuils. A de valeur 3 consent si x<=3; A de valeur 7 consent pour tout x<=6. B de valeur 2 consent si x>=4, tandis que B de valeur 5 consent si x>=1. Ces quatre inégalités partitionnent la contribution en intervalles économiquement distincts.

Pour 0<=x<1, même le type élevé de B refuse, donc le projet n'est jamais réalisé. Pour 1<=x<=3, tous les types de A consentent et seul B élevé consent; le surplus est 2. Pour 3<x<4, seuls les deux types élevés consentent; le surplus est 6/4=3/2. Pour 4<=x<=6, seul A élevé consent, mais tous les types de B consentent; le surplus est (3+6)/4=9/4. Les égalités suivent la règle de consentement donnée.

Pour conclure globalement, le maximum est 9/4 et tous les partages x dans [4,6] l'atteignent. La perte relative à l'efficacité est 11/4-9/4=1/2. Il s'agit de l'état A faible, B élevé, où le surplus positif vaut 2 mais où A refuse la contribution supérieure à sa valeur. Les taxes n'ont aucun coût réel supplémentaire ici: elles financent simplement le coût 6.

Pour prouver l'impossibilité d'un partage fixe efficace, l'état (3,5) doit être réalisé et impose 1<=x<=3. L'état (7,2) doit aussi être réalisé et impose 4<=x<=6. Ces intervalles sont disjoints. Aucun x ne peut satisfaire les deux contraintes, même si l'on sait que chaque état a une somme de valeurs supérieure au coût.

Un contrôle indépendant part des états acceptés au partage optimal. Quand A=7 et B=2, les gains privés sont 7-x et x-4, dont la somme est 3. Quand A=7 et B=5, leur somme est 6. Pondérer ces deux états par 1/4 donne 9/4. Les consentements rendent chaque gain non négatif et vérifient simultanément la participation et la comptabilité sociale.

General pattern: je dois convertir les consentements en intervalles sur les contributions. Leurs seuils donnent un nombre fini de régimes sans essais numériques; des intersections disjointes prouvent l'impossibilité d'une implémentation fixe, même lorsque chaque décision efficace paraît finançable isolément.
reference_answer:
La décision efficace atteint un surplus espéré de 11/4. Les contributions (3,3) donnent 2. Les partages fixes optimaux sont tous les x dans [4,6], avec surplus 9/4 et perte 1/2.

L'état (3,5) impose x dans [1,3], tandis que (7,2) impose x dans [4,6]. Ces contraintes incompatibles prouvent qu'aucun partage fixe ne réalise la décision efficace dans tous les états.

problem: Un graphe connexe a tous ses sommets de degré pair. Explique pourquoi il possède un circuit eulérien sans ordonner toutes les arêtes à l'avance.
thinking:
Avant de construire une tournée, pars d'un sommet et prolonge une marche en empruntant toute arête inutilisée disponible. On ne peut pas rester bloqué en un sommet autre que le départ: les arêtes incidentes y sont appariées entrée-sortie, et un degré pair laisse une sortie inutilisée après chaque arrivée.

La marche finit donc au point de départ et forme un circuit fermé. Si des arêtes restent, la connexité fournit un sommet du circuit incident à une arête inutilisée; les degrés inutilisés restent pairs, donc une autre marche fermée peut y être construite puis greffée au circuit.

La finitude fait terminer cette procédure après chaque arête utilisée exactement une fois. L'argument de parité locale fournit l'extension; la connexité empêche qu'un composant d'arêtes reste isolé du circuit.

General pattern: l'eulérien se construit en alternant parité et greffe. Une condition locale garantit que les marches se ferment; la connexité permet de fusionner les circuits jusqu'à épuisement des arêtes.
reference_answer: Le graphe possède un circuit eulérien; on le construit par des marches fermées successivement greffées.

problem: A monopolist sells one unit-demand product to a single buyer with inverse demand P=20−Q and marginal cost5. Compare monopoly pricing with a two-part tariff that charges per-unit price equal to marginal cost and extracts consumer surplus as a fixed fee.
thinking:
Under one-part monopoly pricing, marginal revenue is20−2Q. Setting it equal to5 gives Q=15/2 and price25/2, so profit is(25/2−5)(15/2)=225/4.

With a two-part tariff, set the unit price to marginal cost5. The buyer then chooses Q=15 efficiently; consumer surplus is the triangle with height15 and base15, equal to225/2. A fixed fee of225/2 extracts that surplus, leaving the buyer indifferent to not buying.

The tariff raises profit from225/4 to225/2 because the monopoly price otherwise suppresses quantity. The fixed fee transfers surplus without changing the marginal consumption choice; exact extraction assumes the seller knows demand and can exclude nonbuyers.

As a check, at the efficient quantity inverse demand equals5 and quantity is15. Integrating demand above5 gives225/2, which is twice the one-part monopoly profit225/4; both calculations use the same linear demand and marginal cost.

General pattern: A two-part tariff separates the efficient marginal price from surplus extraction. Price each unit at marginal cost to maximize quantity, then use the fixed fee to capture consumer surplus.
reference_answer: One-part monopoly profit=225/4. Two-part tariff uses unit price5, quantity15, fixed fee225/2, and extracts profit225/2.

problem: Can you show how asymmetric information can eliminate trade even when every quality creates gains from trade? Seller quality theta is uniform on[0,1] and known only to the seller. The seller's reservation value is theta; the buyer's value is 3theta/2. A buyer can post any price p>=0, and sellers accept exactly when p>=theta. Find the buyer's expected profit for every price range, the optimal trade outcome, and the efficient surplus under full information. Explain precisely where the gains from trade disappear.
thinking:
Before evaluating an offer, I condition on acceptance because accepted sellers are not a random draw. For0<=p<=1, acceptance means theta<=p, so its probability is p and the accepted mean quality is p/2. The buyer's conditional value is therefore3p/4, below the posted price p; expected profit per potential seller is p*(3p/4-p)=-p²/4.

For p>=1, every seller accepts. The unconditional mean quality is1/2, so the buyer's expected value is3/4 and expected profit is3/4-p, still negative. Thus no positive offer is profitable; p=0 yields zero and no positive-mass trade. The optimal posted-price outcome is no trade, even though the buyer could gain from known high-quality units.

Under full information, trade occurs whenever buyer value exceeds seller value:3theta/2>theta for every theta>0. Total gains from trade are the integral of theta/2 from0 to1, equal to1/4. The entire efficient surplus is lost under the optimal posted offer because any price high enough to attract sellers also attracts low qualities whose conditional mean value is below the price.

As an independent check, at p=1 the accepted pool is the whole population, its buyer value is3/4, and the buyer loses1/4. As p falls below1, the accepted pool's mean quality falls linearly to p/2; multiplying the negative conditional margin by acceptance probability gives the quadratic loss -p²/4. Both calculations confirm that selection, not absence of technological gains, blocks trade.

General pattern: Under hidden quality, evaluate value conditional on the seller's acceptance decision, then multiply by the acceptance probability. The offer changes both price and composition. A positive full-information surplus does not guarantee a profitable posted price when adverse selection worsens the pool.
reference_answer:
For0<=p<=1, expected buyer profit is-p²/4. For p>=1 it is3/4-p. No positive price is profitable, so the optimal outcome is no trade with profit0.

With full information, every theta>0 trades and total surplus is integral from0 to1 of theta/2, equal to1/4. Adverse selection destroys these gains because low-quality sellers are more likely to accept a low offer.

problem: Je cherche la fonction de coût duale d'une technologie Cobb-Douglas. Une firme produit y=K^(1/3)L^(2/3), avec prix des facteurs r=w=3. Pour produire y=12 au coût minimal, trouvez K,L, le coût total et vérifiez la condition de tangence ainsi que la contrainte de production.
thinking:
La firme minimise3K+3L sous production12. Le rapport des productivités marginales est MP_K/MP_L=L/(2K); à l'optimum il égale r/w=1, donc L=2K. Cette tangence transforme le problème à deux choix en une seule inconnue.

En substituant, y=K^(1/3)(2K)^(2/3)=2^(2/3)K. Ainsi K=12/2^(2/3)=6·2^(1/3), et L=12·2^(1/3). Le coût est3(K+L)=54·2^(1/3), environ68,04.

La condition de tangence se voit aussi par les parts de coût: rK=18·2^(1/3), wL=36·2^(1/3), donc le capital prend un tiers et le travail deux tiers du coût, conformément aux exposants. La technologie est à rendements constants, donc le coût minimal est proportionnel à y.

Comme contrôle, K L²=(6·2^(1/3))(12·2^(1/3))²=12³, donc K^(1/3)L^(2/3)=12 exactement. Et MP_K/MP_L=L/(2K)=1=r/w, ce qui vérifie faisabilité et optimalité intérieure indépendamment.

General pattern: La dualité producteur transforme une contrainte de production en minimisation du coût. Pour Cobb-Douglas, la tangence fixe le ratio des facteurs, puis la contrainte donne l'échelle; les exposants deviennent les parts de coût à rendements constants.

problem: Maximize xy subject to x+y=10 and x,y≥0. Give a proof of the maximizer and explain why the endpoints cannot compete.
thinking:
Before differentiating, AM-GM yields xy≤((x+y)/2)²=25, with equality only when x=y. The constraint then forces x=y=5, so the maximum25 is attained.

The endpoints have product0, strictly below25. More generally, positivity and fixed sum make balance optimal; no interior candidate search is needed because the inequality already bounds the entire feasible set.

A square identity gives the same certificate: xy=25−(x−y)²/4. The loss from the optimum is exactly a squared imbalance, so equality and uniqueness are immediate.

General pattern: under a fixed sum, rewrite a symmetric product as a constant minus a square, or invoke AM-GM. The imbalance term measures exactly how far a feasible point lies from the optimizer.
reference_answer: The unique maximum is 25 at (x,y)=(5,5).

problem: Find the exact number of onto functions from a 4-element set to a 3-element set. Please show a compact counting argument instead of listing maps.
thinking:
Before counting onto maps directly, I should count all maps and remove those that miss a target value. There are 3^4 total functions. For each of the three target values, 2^4 maps omit it; adding these exclusions double-subtracts maps whose image has size1, so add back the three constant maps.

Inclusion-exclusion gives 3^4−3·2^4+3·1^4=36. The same result follows by choosing the singleton fiber: pick its target value in3 ways and its unique preimage in4 ways, then map the remaining three domain points onto the other two target values in6 ways, for3·4·6=72—this route overcounts because the singleton target is unique, wait, all onto maps to three targets need exactly one singleton fiber only when the fiber sizes are 2,1,1; but they may be 2,2,0 which is not onto. For a surjection from 4 to3, sizes must be 2,1,1, so there are three choices of doubled target, then choose its two preimages in C(4,2)=6; assign the remaining two points bijectively to remaining targets in2 ways: 36.

The fiber-size route independently yields3·6·2=36 and also explains the combinatorial structure: every onto map has fiber sizes 2,1,1. Agreement with inclusion-exclusion is a useful check because the first route works by excluded images and the second by exact fiber structure.

General pattern: use inclusion-exclusion when forbidden events are 'a value is missing'; use fiber sizes for an independent structural count. A second counting route can expose an accidental overcount before it becomes an answer.
reference_answer: There are 36 onto functions. Inclusion-exclusion and the fiber-size count both give 36.

problem: Find the sum of the reciprocals of the roots of x³−2x²−x+2, without solving for the roots.
thinking:
Before factoring the cubic, use Vieta. For roots r_i, the reciprocal sum is (r₁r₂+r₁r₃+r₂r₃)/(r₁r₂r₃). The pairwise sum is the coefficient of x divided by the leading coefficient, here−1; the product is−2, so the quotient is1/2.

No root can be zero because the constant term is2. This validates the reciprocal expression. The result is a ratio of symmetric coefficients, so individual roots are unnecessary.

As a check, the polynomial factors (x−2)(x−1)(x+1); reciprocals sum1/2+1−1=1/2. The factorization is a check, not the method needed to derive the value.

General pattern: symmetric functions of reciprocals can often be obtained by reversing the polynomial or applying Vieta to elementary symmetric sums. Avoid solving for roots when the requested expression is symmetric.
reference_answer: The reciprocal sum is 1/2.

problem: How can adding firms fail to eliminate market power if the market size is held fixed? Consider n>=1 differentiated products with quasilinear gross utility U=a*Q-[n*sum(qi^2)+m*Q^2]/[2*(1+m)], where Q=sum(qi),qi>=0,m>=0 and a>c>=0. Every firm has cost c*qi and chooses quantity simultaneously. Derive the unique Cournot equilibrium and its aggregate welfare. Compare it with efficient production and joint-profit maximisation. Analyse n tending to infinity with m fixed, and m tending to infinity with n fixed. Evaluate quantities, price, per-firm profit and the welfare efficiency ratio at a=4,c=1,n=4,m=10. Explain exactly what this normalisation holds fixed and why the standard homogeneous Cournot limit cannot be imported blindly.
thinking:
Before taking a firm-count limit, I should inspect how preferences change with n. Inverse demand is pi=a-[n*qi+m*Q]/(1+m). The curvature matrix is[n*I+m*11']/ (1+m), with eigenvalue n in the aggregate direction and n/(1+m) in directions whose quantities sum to zero. It is positive definite for every finite n and m>=0. For a fixed aggregate Q, sum(qi^2)>=Q^2/n, with equality only at equal quantities, so maximal gross utility is a*Q-Q^2/2, independent of n.

For the firm condition, I must include the own effect inside Q before imposing symmetry. Own inverse-demand slope is-(n+m)/(1+m), so the marginal-profit condition is a-c-[n*qi+m*Q]/(1+m)-[(n+m)/(1+m)]*qi=0. Writing s=a-c>0 gives(2*n+m)*qi+m*Q=(1+m)*s. The own second derivative is-2*(n+m)/(1+m)<0, making this condition sufficient when output is positive.

For uniqueness, I should also rule out an inactive firm rather than simply assume symmetry. If an active firm has qi>0, its condition implies(1+m)*s-m*Q=(2*n+m)*qi>0. But the left side is the marginal-profit numerator of every inactive firm at zero output. Such a firm would profitably enter production, so all firms must be active. Their conditions have the same right side, hence all quantities are equal. Solving gives qi=(1+m)*s/[n*(2+m)+m] and Q=n*(1+m)*s/[n*(2+m)+m]. At symmetry pi=a-Q, and pi-c=[(n+m)/(1+m)]*qi.

For welfare, equal quantities make real surplus W=s*Q-Q^2/2. Completing the square gives W=s^2/2-(Q-s)^2/2, so efficient aggregate output is QStar=s and WStar=s^2/2. The efficient allocation is equal across products. Joint revenue at equal quantities is(a-Q)*Q, so joint profit is s*Q-Q^2, maximised at Qmon=s/2. More generally unequal allocations lower utility and joint revenue at any Q because they increase sum(qi^2); therefore equality is also optimal for the planner and joint owner.

A cheaper route to the efficiency ratio is normalising output by s. Let theta=Q/s=n*(1+m)/[n*(2+m)+m]. Then W/WStar=2*theta-theta^2=1-(1-theta)^2. Costs and demand level affect scale but not this ratio within the declared interior model. Consumer surplus is Q^2/2 at symmetry, and total profit is(s-Q)*Q. Their sum reproduces s*Q-Q^2/2 independently.

For many firms at fixed m, Q tends to(1+m)*s/(2+m), price tends to c+s/(2+m), and the efficiency ratio tends to1-1/(2+m)^2. A positive aggregate markup remains. Per-firm profit nevertheless tends to0 because each quantity shrinks with n while its own demand slope grows with n. The count normalisation preserves symmetric aggregate demand p=a-Q; it also changes each variety's demand sensitivity as n changes. A growing count alone therefore does not imply the homogeneous atomic-quantity limit.

For nearly homogeneous products at fixed n, let m tend to infinity. Then inverse demand tends to a-Q, each Cournot quantity tends to s/(n+1), and total output tends to n*s/(n+1). The efficiency ratio tends to1-1/(n+1)^2, the ordinary homogeneous Cournot result. At m=0, instead, each normalised independent product has quantity s/(2*n), so total output remains s/2 and the ratio is3/4 for every n. These limits diagnose what the differentiation parameter, rather than just the firm count, controls.

For a=4,c=1,n=4,m=10, s=3 and the equilibrium has qi=33/58,Q=66/29 and pi=50/29. Profit per firm is[(n+m)/(1+m)]*qi^2=(14/11)*(33/58)^2=693/1682. Efficient output is3, with WStar=9/2. Actual welfare is3*(66/29)-(1/2)*(66/29)^2=3564/841, giving ratio792/841. Joint-profit output is3/2, split3/8 per product, with total profit9/4.

For an independent numerical check, pi-c=50/29-1=21/29 equals(14/11)*(33/58). Consumer surplus is2178/841 and total profit is4*(693/1682)=1386/841; their sum is3564/841. With m=10 held fixed, the many-firm output limit is11/4, the limiting price5/4 and ratio143/144, all below full efficiency in quantity or ratio despite individual profits vanishing.

General pattern: I should identify what a demand normalisation preserves before comparing markets with different numbers of products. Aggregate and zero-sum eigenmodes separate market size from differentiation. Output normalisation and a completed welfare square give efficiency immediately; a many-firm limit must track how each firm's own demand slope changes as well as how its quantity shrinks.
reference_answer:
The unique equilibrium is qi=(1+m)*(a-c)/[n*(2+m)+m], with equal prices p=a-Q. Efficient aggregate output is a-c; joint-profit output is(a-c)/2. Writing theta=Q/(a-c), the welfare ratio is1-(1-theta)^2.

At a=4,c=1,n=4,m=10: qi=33/58,Q=66/29,p=50/29,profit per firm693/1682 and W/WStar=792/841. With fixed m=10 and infinitely many firms, Q tends to11/4,p to5/4 and the ratio to143/144. Fixed symmetric aggregate demand does not hold each variety's own demand slope fixed. In contrast, m tending to infinity at fixed n gives homogeneous Cournot Q=n*(a-c)/(n+1).

problem: A policy's treatment effect is 2 for 40% of people and 5 for the remaining 60%. Find the population average and variance of individual effects, then explain why the average alone hides a distributional fact.
thinking:
Before averaging, treat the effect as a two-point random variable. Its mean is0.4·2+0.6·5=3.8.

The second moment is0.4·4+0.6·25=16.6, so variance is16.6−3.8²=2.16. The mean summarizes total average gain but not heterogeneity; two populations can share the same mean and different variances.

A direct centered calculation gives0.4(2−3.8)²+0.6(5−3.8)²=0.4·3.24+0.6·1.44=2.16. This confirms the moment identity.

General pattern: compute heterogeneity from second moments or centered deviations. Average effects and effect dispersion answer distinct policy questions.
reference_answer: The average effect is 3.8 and its variance is 2.16.

problem:
Help me find the missing assumption in this backward-induction argument: because the game ends at a known date, cooperation must disappear in every period.

Two players play a symmetric stage game with actions C,D,R and payoff pairs: CC:(3,3), CD:(0,5), DC:(5,0), DD:(1,1), RR:(4,4). Every other pair has payoffs(0,0). Actions are publicly observed. There are T>=2 periods, known in advance, with discount factor delta in[0,1], and no outside transfers. A strategy prescribes CC in every period before T while all previous outcomes have been CC. At T it prescribes RR if the entire earlier history consists of CC. Following any other earlier outcome, it prescribes DD for every remaining period, including T. Indifferent players may follow the prescription.

Find all pure stage-game Nash equilibria. For T=2, derive the effective first-period payoff matrix under the prescribed terminal strategies and characterize every pure first-period equilibrium. Determine exactly when the stated cooperation strategy is subgame-perfect for every finite T>=2, using a formula in the number of remaining cooperative periods instead of enumerating histories. Check payoffs and deviations at T=3,delta=3/4. Explain the precise reason finite-horizon unraveling does or does not apply, without claiming that arbitrary finite repeated games permit cooperation.
thinking:
Before applying backward induction, I should identify the terminal alternatives. Against C, D gives5 while C gives3 and R gives0. Against D, D gives1 while C and R give0. Against R, R gives4 while C and D give0. Hence DD and RR are the only pure stage equilibria. CC is not a stage equilibrium. The final period can nevertheless reward a cooperative history with RR and punish a deviation with DD; both prescriptions are credible Nash outcomes.

To compress the two-period game, I add4*delta to each player's current payoff only after CC, and delta after every other outcome. In row and column order C,D,R, the first player's effective payoff matrix is [[3+4*delta,delta,delta],[5+delta,1+delta,delta],[delta,delta,4+delta]]. The second player's matrix is its transpose. Against D, only D is optimal; against R, only R is optimal. Against C, C is optimal exactly when3+4*delta>=5+delta, or delta>=2/3; otherwise D is optimal. Consequently DD and RR remain pure first-period equilibria for every delta, and CC joins them exactly at delta>=2/3. No asymmetric pure pair survives the counterpart's best response.

For an arbitrary horizon, I let m>=1 count cooperative periods including the current one before the final reward. Define S_m=1+delta+...+delta^(m-1), a finite sum valid even at delta=1. Compliance gives V_m=3*S_m+4*delta^m. The best current deviation is D against C, earning5, followed by m remaining punishment periods with payoff1: its value is5+delta*S_m. Deviating to R earns0 with exactly the same punishment continuation, so it is inferior to D. The incentive gap is G_m=(3-delta)*S_m+4*delta^m-5.

To avoid checking every horizon, I search for a recursion in this gap. The identity S_(m+1)=S_m+delta^m gives G_(m+1)-G_m=(3*delta-1)*delta^m. The last cooperative period has G_1=3*delta-2. If delta<2/3, that final cooperative period fails, so the stated strategy cannot be subgame-perfect. If delta>=2/3, G_1>=0 and every successive increment is nonnegative. Thus all earlier cooperation incentives hold as well. This telescoping-gap trick makes the least patient cooperative history the one just before the final reward.

For completeness, every history after a deviation has DD now and forever, which is credible because D is the unique best response to D and a further deviation cannot alter the punishment state. At the final cooperative history RR is a stage equilibrium. These terminal and punishment checks, together with G_m>=0 at every cooperative history, establish subgame perfection by the finite one-period deviation argument. At equality delta=2/3, the last cooperative player is indifferent and may comply. At delta=1, S_m=m and G_m=2*m-1>0, independently confirming that the finite sum avoids a spurious division by zero.

For the numerical check, T=3 and delta=3/4 give m=2 initially. Compliance is3+(3/4)*3+(9/16)*4=15/2. An immediate D deviation gives5+3/4+9/16=101/16, leaving gap19/16. In the second cooperative period, measured from that period, compliance is3+(3/4)*4=6 and deviation is5+3/4=23/4, leaving gap1/4. The recurrence predicts1/4+(3*(3/4)-1)*(3/4)=19/16, matching the direct histories without needing a full tree.

For the missing assumption, a unique stage equilibrium forces the same terminal continuation after every history in the usual unraveling argument. Here terminal equilibrium selection is history-dependent: RR gives4 and DD gives1. That credible payoff difference3 makes present incentives depend on earlier behavior. Backward induction still works and is exactly what verifies the strategy; it does not force identical terminal payoffs when multiple equilibria are available. This example establishes cooperation for the declared strategy and stage game, not a universal exception to finite-horizon reasoning.

General pattern: I inspect terminal equilibrium multiplicity before using an unraveling claim. History-dependent selection among credible equilibria can create a reward even with a known final date. A continuation-value gap and its recursion replace history enumeration, while separate checks at punishment and terminal histories certify credibility.
reference_answer:
The pure stage equilibria are DD and RR. Under the prescribed two-period continuations, DD and RR are always pure first-period equilibria; CC is also one exactly when delta>=2/3.

With m cooperative periods left before the terminal reward, the compliance-minus-best-deviation gap is G_m=(3-delta)*S_m+4*delta^m-5, where S_m=sum of delta^j for j=0,...,m-1. Since G_1=3*delta-2 and G_(m+1)-G_m=(3*delta-1)*delta^m, the stated strategy is subgame-perfect for every finite T>=2 exactly when delta>=2/3. The equality is included.

At T=3,delta=3/4, initial compliance and deviation values are15/2 and101/16; the later cooperative values are6 and23/4. Terminal RR and punishment DD are credible stage equilibria. Multiple terminal equilibria allow history-dependent rewards, so the usual unique-equilibrium unraveling argument does not apply.

problem: Deux variables normales conjointes centrées ont Var(X)=4, Var(Y)=9 et Cov(X,Y)=3. Donnez E[Y|X=2] et Var(Y|X), puis interprétez la variance conditionnelle comme une incertitude résiduelle après projection.
thinking:
La régression conditionnelle normale a pente Cov(X,Y)/Var(X)=3/4. Donc E[Y|X=2]=(3/4)·2=3/2.

La variance résiduelle est Var(Y)−Cov(X,Y)^2/Var(X)=9−9/4=27/4. Elle ne dépend pas de la valeur observée de X dans le cas conjointement normal.

La projection linéaire explique une part de la dispersion de Y, mais ne l'annule pas: R²=Cov²/(VarX·VarY)=9/36=1/4. Les trois quarts de Var(Y), soit27/4, restent conditionnellement incertains.

Comme contrôle, variance expliquée plus variance résiduelle vaut9/4+27/4=9, la variance initiale de Y. La pente3/4 est aussi le coefficient qui minimise l'erreur quadratique de Y−bX.

General pattern: Pour un vecteur normal conjoint, l'espérance conditionnelle est la projection linéaire et la variance conditionnelle est le résidu de variance. La décomposition sépare signal expliqué et incertitude restante.

problem: I have 10 minutes before a meeting. Give me a three-item checklist for preparing.
thinking: The time limit calls for immediately usable actions; the requested item count is exact.
reference_answer:
- Write the one outcome you need from the meeting.
- Open the relevant notes and documents.
- Check the attendees and prepare one question.

problem: A one-period call has strike100. The underlying is100 today and will be120 or80 next period; the risk-free gross return is1.05. Find the no-arbitrage call price by replication and verify it with risk-neutral probabilities.
thinking:
The call pays20 in the up state and0 in the down state. A replicating portfolio holds Δ=(20−0)/(120−80)=1/2 share. To match the down payoff, its bond position must satisfy40+1.05B=0, so B=−800/21.

The portfolio costs50−800/21=250/21 today, approximately11.90. Replication pins down price because identical state-contingent payoffs cannot trade at different values without arbitrage.

The risk-neutral up probability is(1.05−0.8)/(1.2−0.8)=5/8. Discounting its expected payoff gives[(5/8)·20]/1.05=250/21, independently matching replication.

As a check, the replicating portfolio pays60−40=20 in the up state and40−40=0 in the down state. Both state payoffs match the call exactly, so the price is not dependent on investors' actual risk preferences in this complete one-period market.

General pattern: In a complete binomial market, solve state-by-state replication or use risk-neutral probabilities. Both price the same payoff vector and must agree by absence of arbitrage.
reference_answer: The call price is250/21≈11.90. The replicating portfolio is one-half share and a bond position of−800/21.

problem: Express 45 minutes as a fraction of an hour in simplest form.
thinking: An hour has 60 minutes, so reduce 45/60 by their greatest common divisor.
reference_answer: 45 minutes is 3/4 of an hour.

problem: My instrumental-variable estimate is a ratio, and its confidence interval looks strange. Can you explain it rigorously? Population moments A and B obey A=beta*B with B!=0. Their estimators Ahat and Bhat are independent normal variables with means A,B and known variances1,1. The observed values are Ahat=2 and Bhat=1. For a candidate beta, accept the moment restriction when |Ahat-beta*Bhat|<=2*sqrt(1+beta^2). Invert this exact normal test to obtain the confidence set for beta. Compare with the plug-in delta-method interval centred at Ahat/Bhat using the same critical value2. Give a geometric proof of the confidence set, explain its coverage and its disconnected shape, and decide whether beta=-1 and beta=-10 are included. Do not replace the set by a finite interval just because the observed denominator is positive.
thinking:
Before dividing, I should retain the moment restriction. Under the true beta, Ahat-beta*Bhat has mean A-beta*B=0 and variance1+beta^2, because the estimators are independent. Its standardised version is exactly normal. Inverting the test therefore has coverage P(|Z|<=2)=2*Phi(2)-1, about0.9544997, for every fixed admissible A,B,beta. No normal approximation for the ratio itself is needed.

For the observed values, acceptance is|2-beta|<=2*sqrt(1+beta^2). Both sides are nonnegative, so squaring is equivalent: (2-beta)^2<=4*(1+beta^2). Cancellation gives3*beta^2+4*beta>=0, or beta*(3*beta+4)>=0. The roots are-4/3 and0. An upward-opening quadratic is nonnegative outside its root interval, giving(-infinity,-4/3] union[0,infinity). Reversing the inequality would incorrectly keep precisely the excluded middle.

For the geometry, I should seek intersection rather than divide every point in an uncertainty region. The moment line is(a,b)=(beta*b,b). The minimum squared distance from the observed point(2,1) to that line is(2-beta)^2/(1+beta^2). A line intersects the radius2 disk centred at(2,1) exactly when this distance is<=4, reproducing the test inequality. At beta=0 the tangent point is(a,b)=(0,1); at beta=-4/3 it is(4/5,-3/5). Both have b!=0 and hence correspond to admissible ratios.

For any other accepted beta, a line through the origin intersects the disk in a nontrivial segment, so I can choose an intersection with b!=0. The origin is outside the disk because its squared distance from(2,1) is5>4. Thus no accepted point is included solely because a forbidden zero-denominator intersection was allowed. The disk still contains denominator values of both signs, since its b range is[-1,3]; a positive observed Bhat does not establish a positive population B.

For the delta approximation, the ratio map g(a,b)=a/b has gradient(1/b,-a/b^2), evaluated at(2,1) as(1,-2). Its plug-in variance is1+4=5. The resulting interval is[2-2*sqrt(5),2+2*sqrt(5)], approximately[-2.4721,6.4721]. This linearisation assumes locally stable division near the observed denominator; it misses the geometry of a region that reaches and crosses zero denominator values.

For the requested decisions, beta=-1 gives3-4=-1<0, so the exact set excludes it, although the delta interval includes it. Beta=-10 gives300-40=260>0, so the exact set includes it, although the delta interval excludes it. Very large positive or negative ratios can be compatible with moments near a zero denominator. A disconnected unbounded set honestly reports weak denominator information; its gap is not a parsing error to be filled in.

For an independent distance check, the line for beta=-1 has squared distance(2+1)^2/(1+1)=9/2>4. The line for beta=-10 has squared distance12^2/101=144/101<4. These reproduce the algebraic inclusion decisions. The disk's joint coverage for the two-dimensional mean vector is1-exp(-2), not2*Phi(2)-1; the ratio set's stated coverage comes from the one-dimensional distance-to-the-true-line pivot. Confusing point-in-disk coverage with line-intersection coverage would attach the wrong confidence level.

General pattern: I should invert the original standardised moment test when a parameter is a ratio. The sign of the resulting quadratic determines whether the confidence set is bounded, disconnected or unbounded; denominator uncertainty cannot be repaired by forcing a conventional interval. Geometry supplies an independent check and distinguishes simultaneous mean-region coverage from scalar restriction-test coverage.
reference_answer:
The exact confidence set is(-infinity,-4/3] union[0,infinity), obtained from beta*(3*beta+4)>=0. Its coverage is2*Phi(2)-1, approximately95.45%, by inversion of the exact normal moment test.

The delta interval is[2-2*sqrt(5),2+2*sqrt(5)]. It includes beta=-1, which the exact set excludes, and excludes beta=-10, which the exact set includes. The disconnected shape reflects uncertainty spanning both signs of the population denominator. A line's intersection with the radius2 disk, rather than the disk's joint point coverage, proves the exact ratio result.

problem: A monopolist can charge one price or use a two-part tariff. Inverse demand is p=10−q and marginal cost is2, with no fixed cost. Find the uniform-price quantity, price, profit, and consumer surplus. Then find the efficient quantity and the largest entry fee the firm can charge under a two-part tariff while keeping the buyer willing to participate.
thinking:
Under a single price, profit is(10−q−2)q=(8−q)q. Its derivative8−2q vanishes at q=4 and the second derivative is−2, so this is the unique maximum. Price is6 and profit is16. Consumer surplus is the triangle between inverse demand and price: one half times quantity4 times the choke-price gap4, hence8.

With a two-part tariff, set the usage price equal to marginal cost2. The buyer then chooses the efficient quantity where willingness to pay equals cost: 10−q=2, so q*=8. The buyer's gross surplus above usage payments is the triangle one half times8 times8, or32.

A fixed fee up to32 extracts all of that surplus while leaving the buyer just indifferent to participation. Variable profit is zero at marginal-cost pricing, so total profit reaches32, twice the uniform-price profit. The mechanism separates the marginal usage decision from the surplus-extraction decision.

As a check, total surplus at q=8 is the integral from0 to8 of(10−q−2), equal to32. The fixed fee transfers that surplus to the monopolist without changing the efficient quantity; under the single price, profit16 plus consumer surplus8 leaves total surplus24.

General pattern: A two-part tariff can set the per-unit price at marginal cost to implement efficient consumption, then use a fixed fee to extract consumer surplus. Uniform pricing bundles the margin and transfer together, creating a quantity distortion.
reference_answer: Uniform price: q=4, p=6, profit=16, consumer surplus=8. Two-part tariff: usage price2, q*=8, maximum entry fee32 and total profit32.

problem: A regulator believes a case involves fraud with probability 1/10. A diagnostic flag has sensitivity 4/5 and false-positive probability 1/5. The regulator can audit for real cost c=1/4; an audit generates benefit 1 if fraud exists and zero otherwise. Find both posterior fraud probabilities, the optimal audit rule, and expected net benefit with and without the flag. A flag costs 1/100 to obtain: is it worth buying? Characterise the optimal audit rule for general cost c in [0,1], and prove that free information cannot reduce the optimal expected value.
thinking:
Before interpreting the flag, I should calculate joint probabilities with the base rate. Fraud and a positive flag has probability (1/10)*(4/5)=2/25, while no fraud and a positive flag has probability (9/10)*(1/5)=9/50. Positive probability is 13/50, giving posterior fraud probability 4/13. The negative joint fraud probability is 1/50 and the negative probability is 37/50, giving posterior 1/37. Sensitivity is not the positive predictive probability.

For the decision, the conditional gain from auditing is posterior fraud probability minus c. At c=1/4, the positive posterior 4/13 exceeds cost while 1/37 is below it. Thus I audit positive flags and skip negative flags. Without the flag, the prior 1/10 is below cost, so optimal expected gain is zero.

A cheaper expected-value calculation uses joint events directly. Auditing only positives gives fraud benefit 2/25 minus audit cost (1/4)*(13/50), equal to 3/200. This matches (13/50)*(4/13-1/4). Deducting the flag price 1/100 leaves net gain 1/200>0, so buying the flag is worthwhile for this stated decision problem.

To characterise all costs without a grid, the two posterior thresholds are 1/37 and 4/13. Below 1/37 both flags lead to audit. Between them only the positive flag does. Above 4/13 neither does. At either threshold the corresponding decision is indifferent and any randomisation there preserves value. These inequalities give the complete policy correspondence.

To verify the value generally, the optimal expected gain with free information is V(c)=max(2/25-13*c/50,0)+max(1/50-37*c/50,0). Without information it is V0(c)=max(1/10-c,0). The former equals the expectation of max(P(fraud|flag)-c,0). The maximum of a line and zero is convex, and the posterior's mean is the prior, so Jensen gives V(c)>=V0(c). This proof covers every cost and both indifference boundaries.

An independent probability check is the posterior martingale identity. (13/50)*(4/13)+(37/50)*(1/37)=1/10. At c=0 the regulator audits all cases with or without information and obtains 1/10, so the free-information value gain is zero. Information is valuable because it changes a choice, not because every more accurate posterior necessarily raises payoff.

General pattern: I should calculate predictive probabilities from joint events and the base rate, then compare posterior benefits with decision costs. Joint-event accounting checks the expected payoff, and convexity of the optimal value proves the nonnegative value of free information.
reference_answer:
Posterior fraud probabilities are 4/13 after a positive flag and 1/37 after a negative flag. At audit cost 1/4, audit only positives. The free flag yields expected gain 3/200 versus zero without it; buying it for 1/100 leaves gain 1/200.

The policy thresholds are c=1/37 and c=4/13, with indifference at equality. The posterior mean remains the prior, and convexity of max(p-c,0) proves that free information cannot lower optimal expected value.

problem: I need an economic interpretation of this wage decomposition. Group A has mean schooling 12, intercept 2 and return to schooling 3. Group B has mean schooling 10, intercept 1 and return 4. Decompose the mean wage gap A−B using first B's coefficients as the reference, then show how the explained and coefficient components change if A's coefficients are the reference.
thinking:
I write each mean as x_g β_g, with x=(1, schooling), so μ_A=2+3(12)=38 and μ_B=1+4(10)=41. The gap is −3. For B's coefficient reference, add and subtract x_A β_B: μ_A−μ_B=(x_A−x_B)β_B+x_A(β_A−β_B). This is an algebraic identity, not a causal attribution by itself.

The explained component is (12−10)4=8. The coefficient component is (2−1)+(3−4)12=−11. Their sum is −3. With A's coefficients as reference, use (x_A−x_B)β_A+x_B(β_A−β_B): the explained schooling component is 2(3)=6, and the coefficient component is (1−2)+(4−3)10=9. The two components move with the reference, while their sum remains fixed.

The higher mean schooling favors A under either schedule, but its measured contribution is 8 under B's return and 6 under A's return. The coefficient component absorbs intercept and slope differences evaluated at a chosen covariate profile; it is not automatically discrimination or a treatment effect without additional assumptions.

As a check, 8−11=6−9=−3=38−41. The explained component falls by 2 when the reference changes, while the coefficient component rises by 2. This exact offset is a useful algebra check and shows why one component alone cannot be treated as reference-free.

General pattern: Oaxaca-style decompositions split a mean gap by adding and subtracting a counterfactual mean. The total is invariant, but the explained and coefficient pieces depend on reference returns and the evaluation profile, so interpretation requires stating that choice.
reference_answer: Mean wages are μ_A=38 and μ_B=41, so A−B=−3. Using B's coefficients gives explained=8 and coefficient=−11. Using A's coefficients gives explained=6 and coefficient=−9. Both sum to−3.

problem: Two firms choose outputs q1 and q2. Their gross benefits are B1=12q1−q1²/2 and B2=8q2−q2²/2. Production creates a common external damage D=(q1+q2)²/2. Find private outputs, socially efficient outputs, and the per-unit Pigouvian tax that decentralizes the optimum. Compute social surplus at the optimum.
thinking:
Without a tax, each firm equates its marginal benefit to private marginal cost zero: 12−q1=0 and 8−q2=0, so outputs are12 and8. Each ignores that one extra unit raises total damage by q1+q2.

The planner maximizes B1+B2−D. Let E=q1+q2. The first-order conditions are12−q1−E=0 and8−q2−E=0. Adding them gives E=20−2E, so E=20/3; hence q1=12−E=16/3 and q2=8−E=4/3. The objective is strictly concave because its negative quadratic part has a positive-definite Hessian.

A common per-unit tax τ=E*=20/3 makes each firm's private condition B_i'(q_i)=τ coincide with the planner's condition. It decentralizes both quantities. The tax is the marginal external damage evaluated at the efficient aggregate output, not at the unregulated output.

At the optimum, total gross benefit is12(16/3)−(16/3)²/2 + 8(4/3)−(4/3)²/2 = 536/9. Damage is(20/3)²/2=200/9, leaving social surplus=336/9=112/3. Tax revenue is a transfer and is not subtracted again from total surplus.

As a check, each firm's marginal benefit equals20/3 at its assigned output, while aggregate marginal damage is also20/3. This verifies both individual tax incentives and the planner's aggregate externality condition.

General pattern: A Pigouvian tax aligns private and social first-order conditions by charging marginal external damage. For a common damage function, the efficient tax depends on the aggregate activity; count tax revenue as a transfer when computing social surplus.
reference_answer: Private outputs are(12,8). Efficient outputs are(16/3,4/3), aggregate output20/3. Pigouvian tax τ=20/3. Social surplus at the optimum=112/3.

problem: I thought a known final date always prevents cooperation. Help me check the missing assumption. Two players simultaneously choose C,D or R in a stage game. Payoffs are(4,4) at(C,C), (5,0) at(D,C), (0,5) at(C,D), (1,1) at(D,D), and(3,3) at(R,R); every other action pair gives(0,0). The stage game is played twice, with publicly observed first-period actions, independent private randomisation and total payoff u1+delta*u2 for0<=delta<=1. Find the stage Nash equilibria analytically and the lowest discount factor at which some subgame-perfect equilibrium can prescribe(C,C) in period1. Continuations may use pure or mixed stage equilibria. Construct such a strategy, prove its credibility after every history, and explain why backward induction does not force the same stage outcome after every history.
thinking:
Before invoking a finite-horizon theorem, I should check whether the last-period equilibrium is unique. Against opponent probabilities c,d,r, action C gives4*c, D gives5*c+d, and R gives3*r. I can eliminate C with a strict mixed-dominance witness: mix D with probability9/10 and R with1/10. Against C,D,R, its payoffs are9/2,9/10,3/10, each strictly above C's4,0,0. Thus C receives zero probability in any stage Nash equilibrium.

For the remaining D,R coordination game, if the opponent chooses D with probability q, my payoff from D is q and from R is3*(1-q). The indifference threshold is q=3/4. Best responses therefore give the pure equilibria both D and both R, and the interior equilibrium in which each chooses D with probability3/4. There is no asymmetric interior mixture: one player's positive mixing forces the other's probability to the same threshold. Their payoff levels per player are1,3 and3/4 respectively.

To discover the cheapest credible punishment, I should compare equilibrium payoffs rather than stage actions. The mixed equilibrium yields3/4, below the pure both-D payoff1. Its randomness is therefore a more severe credible continuation than pure D. The largest equilibrium reward is3 at both R. All last-period subgames must select one of these stage equilibria, but their selection may depend on the public first-period history.

For a construction, I prescribe C in period1. In period2 I prescribe both R after the history(C,C), and the mixed equilibrium with D probability3/4 for each player after every other history. Compliance against a first-period C gives4+3*delta. Deviating to D gives5+(3/4)*delta, so the incentive inequality is(9/4)*delta>=1, or delta>=4/9. Deviating to R gives only(3/4)*delta and cannot improve upon compliance. Mixed first-period deviations cannot beat the best pure deviation because expected payoff is affine in the deviation distribution.

For credibility, after(C,C), R is a strict best response to R. After any other history, the opponent's D probability3/4 makes my D and R payoffs both3/4, while C gives0. The prescribed independent mixture is thus a Nash equilibrium in every last-period subgame. Each first-period incentive and each last-period best response has been checked, so the whole strategy is subgame-perfect; the punishment is not an unenforceable threat.

For necessity, any equilibrium continuation after cooperation can give at most3 to a player, and any equilibrium continuation after that player's D deviation can give at least3/4. A first-period gain of1 from D therefore requires1<=delta*(reward-punishment)<=delta*(9/4). Hence no subgame-perfect strategy prescribing(C,C) initially can work below4/9. The construction attains this bound, including indifference at equality.

An independent check sets delta=1/2. Cooperation gives4+3/2=11/2, while D deviation gives5+3/8=43/8, smaller by1/8. If I restricted punishment to pure both-D instead, cooperation would require4+3*delta>=5+delta, hence delta>=1/2. The mixed continuation strictly expands the sustainable range, from1/2 down to4/9.

For the theorem's scope, backward induction requires last-period Nash play, but uniqueness would be needed to make its payoff independent of history. Multiple stage equilibria create a credible continuation-payoff spread even with exactly one period remaining. This is an endogenous reward and punishment mechanism, not an infinite-horizon trigger or an added terminal bonus.

General pattern: I should inspect equilibrium multiplicity before applying finite-horizon unraveling. A strict mixed-dominance witness reduces the stage game, and continuation-payoff bounds prove both implementability and the sharp discount threshold. A mixed equilibrium can be a stronger credible punishment than every pure equilibrium.
reference_answer:
The stage equilibria are both D with payoff1 each, both R with payoff3 each, and independent mixtures choosing D with probability3/4, with payoff3/4 each. Action C is strictly dominated by a9/10-D,1/10-R mixture.

The lowest discount factor is4/9. Prescribe C initially, reward(C,C) with both R, and use the mixed equilibrium after any other history. The incentive condition is4+3*delta>=5+(3/4)*delta. All continuations are stage equilibria, and their maximum payoff spread9/4 proves that no smaller delta suffices. A finite horizon alone does not remove history-dependent equilibrium selection.

problem: Can you solve this positive-externality exercise and also check how the subsidy is financed? A representative buyer has gross utility U(q)=q-q^2/2, a competitive producer has cost C(q)=q^2/2, and a third party receives external benefit E(q)=q/2. Quantity is nonnegative and money enters all utilities linearly. Find the unregulated equilibrium, resource-efficient quantity and welfare gain. Find the unit production subsidy implementing efficiency, buyer and seller prices, consumer and producer surplus, and subsidy expenditure. Would an equal unit purchase tax on the same traded quantity finance the subsidy while preserving efficiency? Finally give a nonnegative, budget-balanced lump-sum levy scheme on the three beneficiaries that funds the efficient subsidy and makes each weakly better off than without intervention.
thinking:
Before applying a subsidy, I should distinguish marginal private and social gains. Demand is pc=1-q and competitive supply is pp=q. Without a wedge, q=1/2 and both prices1/2. Resource welfare is U-C+E=(3/2)*q-q^2=9/16-(q-3/4)^2. Thus the unique efficient quantity is3/4. Welfare rises from1/2 to9/16, a gain1/16. The completed square proves the global maximum, including the nonnegative boundary.

For the implementing subsidy s, seller receipts exceed buyer payments by s: pp=pc+s. Substituting the inverse supply and demand gives q=(1+s)/2. Setting q=3/4 requires s=1/2, equal to the marginal external benefit E'=1/2. The buyer pays1/4 and the seller receives3/4. These two prices serve different surplus calculations and should not be conflated.

For the component check, linear demand and supply give CS=q^2/2 and PS=q^2/2. At3/4 each is9/32; external benefit is3/8. Subsidy expenditure is s*q=3/8. Hence CS+PS+E-expenditure=9/32+9/32+3/8-3/8=9/16, agreeing with the primitive welfare calculation. The subsidy changes incentives but its cash payment is not an extra resource benefit.

For self-finance by a purchase tax t on the same base, let P be the underlying transaction price. Buyers pay pc=P+t and sellers receive pp=P+s, giving pp-pc=s-t. Balanced fiscal flows require t*q=s*q; with positive trade, t=s. The net wedge is then zero, so q returns to1/2. An equal purchase tax exactly cancels the subsidy's marginal incentive. At t=s=1/2, P=0, but all-in buyer and seller prices are both1/2; the tax and subsidy each move1/4 through the government.

For an independent welfare check of that paired intervention, quantity1/2 implies the original resource welfare1/2. Tax receipts equal subsidy payments, and both agents face the original effective prices. Thus fiscal balance alone does not preserve the efficient outcome. The subsidy needs a financing instrument that does not reverse its marginal wedge in this model.

For lump-sum finance, baseline CS and PS are1/8 each and baseline external benefit1/4. The efficient subsidy increases CS and PS by9/32-1/8=5/32 each and external benefit by3/8-1/4=1/8. Levy1/8 on each party: the three levies sum3/8, exactly subsidy expenditure. Buyers and producers retain gain5/32-1/8=1/32 each, while the third party retains gain0. Everybody is weakly better off, and total gain remains1/16.

For participation limits, taxing only the external beneficiary cannot fund the full subsidy without making that person worse off: its maximum levy consistent with its own baseline is1/8, below expenditure3/8. The private-market beneficiaries must contribute as well. Their payments are lump-sum, so the quantities still follow pc=1-q,pp=q and pp-pc=1/2. The absence of income effects in the stated quasilinear model makes this separation exact.

General pattern: I should derive the social optimum from primitives and keep buyer payments, seller receipts and public cash flows separate. A correcting subsidy can lose its effect when funded by an equal marginal tax on the same base. Lump-sum finance preserves the wedge, while partywise surplus gains determine whether the financing scheme is voluntarily acceptable.
reference_answer:
Unregulated quantity is1/2 and welfare1/2. Efficiency requires q=3/4 and welfare9/16, a gain1/16. A subsidy1/2 gives buyer price1/4, seller receipts3/4, CS=PS=9/32 and expenditure3/8.

An equal purchase tax balances the budget but cancels the wedge, restoring q=1/2. Instead levy1/8 lump-sum on each of the buyer, producer and external beneficiary. This funds3/8 and leaves gains1/32,1/32,0, proving a weak Pareto improvement without reversing the subsidy incentive.

problem: A sample of10 observations has variance s²=4. For the null hypothesis that a normal population variance equals1, compute the chi-square test statistic and degrees of freedom. State what additional choice is needed to make a rejection decision.
thinking:
Under the null, (n−1)s²/σ₀² follows a chi-square distribution with n−1 degrees of freedom. Here the statistic is9·4/1=36 and the degrees of freedom are9.

A rejection decision still needs a significance level and an alternative direction. A two-sided variance test allocates tail probability to both extremes; an upper-tail test is appropriate only if the alternative specifically asserts greater variance.

This reference law relies on normal sampling. Unlike the sample-mean t statistic, the variance statistic is especially sensitive to nonnormal observations because squared deviations enter directly.

As a check, if the observed sample variance equaled its null value1, the statistic would be9, matching its degrees of freedom. The observed value36 lies far above that center, but formal rejection uses the selected chi-square tail.

General pattern: Under normality, scaled sample variance has a chi-square law with n−1 degrees of freedom. The statistic is not a decision until the alternative and tail rule are specified.
reference_answer: χ²=36 with9 degrees of freedom. A rejection decision additionally requires a significance level and a specified alternative/tail.

problem:
A symbolic solver gave me a positive production quantity and called it optimal. How can I check whether it is actually a maximum, especially when the technology has increasing returns?

A firm uses inputs x,y>=0 with normalized unit prices1 each. For a fixed r>0 its technology is F(x,y)=(x*y)^(r/2). To produce at least q>=0 it minimizes expenditure x+y. There are no fixed costs, capacity limits or financing constraints. After deriving the exact cost function, let the firm take an exogenous output price P>=0 and maximize P*q-C(q) over q>=0. The price is fixed regardless of output; this is not a monopoly with downward-sloping demand.

Prove the global cost minimum without enumerating multiplier solutions. Relate the degree of homogeneity of production to the curvature of cost. Classify the complete profit-maximization problem for0<r<1,r=1 and r>1, including shutdown, indifference and unbounded-profit cases. When an interior stationary point exists, determine whether it is a maximum or minimum and relate its profit to r.

For r=1/2,P=4 give optimal output, both inputs, cost and profit. For r=1 compare P=1,2,3. For r=4/3,P=3 check the solver's q=1/16: give its least-cost inputs, profit and second derivative, then determine the true global outcome. Include an independent scale or square check. Do not infer finite supply merely from a positive first-order-condition solution.
thinking:
Before using the solver, I should exploit the input budget's geometry. Let S=x+y. Since(x-y)^2>=0, xy<=S^2/4. Hence F(x,y)=(xy)^(r/2)<=(S/2)^r because r>0. Producing at least q therefore requires S>=2*q^(1/r). This lower bound is attained at x=y=q^(1/r), so C(q)=2*q^(1/r) globally for every q>=0. The arithmetic-geometric-mean trick provides both the certificate and the unique positive-output input allocation.

For scale, multiplying both inputs by lambda multiplies production by lambda^r. The degree of homogeneity is r, while the degree of homogeneity of cost in output is1/r. At positive q, C'(q)=(2/r)*q^(1/r-1) and C''(q)=(2/r)*(1/r-1)*q^(1/r-2). Thus decreasing returns r<1 produce strictly convex cost, constant returns r1 produce linear cost, and increasing returns r>1 produce strictly concave cost. I should examine this sign before interpreting any marginal-cost equality.

For0<r<1 and P>0, profit is strictly concave. Its derivative P-(2/r)*q^(1/r-1) starts positive near0 and becomes negative at large output. The unique global maximizer is qstar=(P*r/2)^(r/(1-r)). Revenue minus cost tends to negative infinity at large output, so the stationary point cannot be a merely local candidate with a better tail. At P0, every positive quantity has negative profit and the unique optimum is shutdown q0.

For an interior stationary point, I can remember the homogeneity identity q*C'=C/r. Since C'=P there, C=r*P*q and profit=(1-r)*P*q. This simultaneously checks the quantity calculation and tells me whether the stationary profit is positive or negative. Under decreasing returns it is positive, as required for an interior optimum better than shutdown. The identity will also expose the error under increasing returns.

For r1, cost is2*q and profit is(P-2)*q. If P<2, the unique optimum is q0. If P=2, every finite q>=0 gives profit0 and is optimal. If P>2, profit increases without bound and there is no finite maximizing quantity. A solver that divides by1-r would discard precisely this important boundary. Constant returns require a separate linear argument, not a limiting stationary formula.

For r>1 and P>0, profit has strictly positive second derivative at positive q. Its derivative starts negative near0 and tends to P>0 as q grows, so the unique positive stationary point is a minimum. More decisively, profit/q=P-2*q^(1/r-1) tends to P>0 at infinity; profit is unbounded above. There is no finite global maximizer despite the positive stationary solution. At P0 shutdown remains the unique optimum. This unboundedness follows from a fixed output price and no capacity limit; it is not a claim that every increasing-returns monopoly model is unbounded.

For r1/2 and P4, cost is2*q^2 and profit4*q-2*q^2=2-2*(q-1)^2. Thus qstar1, inputs x=y1, cost2 and profit2. The square is an independent global maximum certificate. For r1, prices1,2,3 respectively give unique shutdown, every finite nonnegative output as an optimum, and unbounded profit with no maximizer.

For the solver's r4/3,P3 example, cost is2*q^(3/4). At q1/16 the least-cost inputs are x=y=q^(3/4)=1/8, so cost1/4 and revenue3/16. Profit is-1/16, already below the shutdown profit0. The derivative is3-(3/2)*q^(-1/4), which vanishes there; the second derivative is(3/8)*q^(-5/4), equal to12 there. It is a strict local minimum, not an optimum. Global profit is unbounded above, consistent with the large-output scale argument.

For an independent check of the numerical stationary classification, the homogeneity formula gives(1-r)*P*q=(-1/3)*3*(1/16)=-1/16, agreeing with direct revenue minus input expenditure. The allocated inputs satisfy F(1/8,1/8)=((1/8)^2)^(2/3)=1/16 exactly. Under r1/2 the same formula gives(1-1/2)*4*1=2, matching the profit square. These checks link technological scale, minimal cost and profit curvature rather than treating the first-order condition as a complete solution.

General pattern: I should use an input inequality to certify minimal cost, then connect production homogeneity with cost homogeneity before optimizing output. Marginal-cost equality is sufficient only with the right curvature and a controlled tail. The identity C=r*P*q at a stationary point gives a cheap profit-sign check, while a separate constant-returns argument preserves shutdown, indifference and unbounded cases that a divided formula would miss.
reference_answer:
The globally minimal cost is C(q)=2*q^(1/r), attained by x=y=q^(1/r), because xy<=(x+y)^2/4. Production has degree r and cost degree1/r.

For0<r<1 and P>0, output q=(P*r/2)^(r/(1-r)) uniquely maximizes profit; P0 gives shutdown. For r1, P<2 gives shutdown, P2 makes every finite nonnegative output optimal, and P>2 gives unbounded profit. For r>1 and P>0 the positive stationary point is a minimum and profit is unbounded; P0 again gives shutdown. At any positive stationary point, profit=(1-r)*P*q.

At r1/2,P4, optimal output1 uses inputs(1,1), costs2 and earns2. At r4/3,P3, the proposed q1/16 uses inputs(1/8,1/8), earns-1/16 and has second derivative12. It is a minimum; the true supremum is unbounded. The input inequality, completed profit square and homogeneity identity independently verify these conclusions.

problem: On the cycle graph C_6, find the eigenvalues of its adjacency matrix and identify the smallest one without computing a 6×6 characteristic polynomial.
thinking:
Before expanding a determinant, I exploit translation symmetry: the Fourier vectors with coordinates exp(2πijk/6) diagonalize every cyclic shift. The adjacency operator is shift plus inverse shift, so its eigenvalue at frequency k is 2cos(2πk/6).

Substituting k=0,…,5 gives 2,1,−1,−2,−1,1. The minimum is−2 at the alternating mode k=3, whose signs flip across every edge. The negative eigenvalue is therefore explained by bipartite alternation.

The trace is0, equal to the eigenvalue sum, and the maximum degree is2, so all eigenvalues lie in[−2,2]. These independent checks support the Fourier diagonalization and the extremal value.

General pattern: translation-invariant operators are diagonal in Fourier modes. Replace a large matrix calculation by evaluating its symbol at discrete frequencies, then interpret extremal modes geometrically.
reference_answer: The eigenvalues are 2,1,−1,−2,−1,1; the smallest is −2.

problem: 某经济指标的四次独立观测为 1、3、4、8。假设它们服从 N(mu,sigma2)，其中 mu 和 sigma2 都未知且 sigma2>0。求无约束最大似然估计、无偏方差估计，以及检验 H0:mu=2 的受约束方差估计和似然比 Lambda。给出观测到的 t 统计量平方，证明似然比与 t 统计量的精确关系，并区分有限样本精确分布和渐近分布。不要通过试验许多参数值寻找极大值。
thinking:
计算之前，我应先找平方和分解。样本均值 xbar=4，而 SSE=sum((xi-4)^2)=9+1+0+16=26。对任何 mu，sum((xi-mu)^2)=26+4*(mu-4)^2。交叉项为零，因为 sum(xi-4)=0；这就是投影恒等式，不需要搜索候选均值。

优化时，我先集中掉方差。令 S(mu)=sum((xi-mu)^2)，对数似然除常数外为 -2*log(sigma2)-S(mu)/(2*sigma2)。给定 mu，其唯一极大点是 sigma2=S(mu)/4。代回后只需最小化 S(mu)，因此 muhat=4，sigma2hat=26/4=13/2。无偏方差使用自由度 3，得到 s2=26/3；最大似然方差和无偏方差不能混用。

检验时，我固定 mu=2。平方和分解给出 S0=26+4*(4-2)^2=42，受约束方差估计为 42/4=21/2。在两个方差极大点，指数项都相同；方差比例决定 Lambda=(26/42)^(4/2)=169/441。因此 -2*log(Lambda)=4*log(21/13)，不是使用已知方差的检验统计量。

为寻找更一般的模式，我写 T=(xbar-mu0)/(s/sqrt(n))。本例 T^2=(4-2)^2/((26/3)/4)=24/13。恒等式 S0/SSE=1+n*(xbar-mu0)^2/SSE=1+T^2/(n-1) 给出 -2*log(Lambda)=n*log(1+T^2/(n-1))。似然比检验和双侧 t 检验因这个严格递增关系而使用同样的拒绝顺序。

独立核对时，我用正态投影几何。常数向量方向上的均值投影与三维残差投影正交；正态性让这两部分独立。H0 下，sqrt(4)*(xbar-2)/sigma 是标准正态，SSE/sigma2 服从自由度 3 的卡方分布。它们的比值恰好给出 T~t3，故 T^2~F(1,3)。这不是大样本近似。

解释分布时，我应保留精确与渐近的差别。Wilks 极限把 -2*log(Lambda) 近似为自由度 1 的卡方分布，但 n=4 时精确校准来自 t3 或 F(1,3)。我没有给定显著性水平或临界值，因此应报告统计量与分布，而不是凭空宣布拒绝原假设。

General pattern: 我应先用正交平方和分解消去位置参数，再集中掉尺度参数。有限样本的正态投影给出精确枢轴量；似然比是该枢轴量的单调函数，渐近卡方不能冒充小样本精确分布。
reference_answer:
无约束估计为 muhat=4、sigma2hat=13/2；无偏方差为 26/3。H0 下的方差最大似然估计为 21/2，似然比 Lambda=169/441，观测到的 T^2=24/13。

平方和分解推出 -2*log(Lambda)=4*log(1+T^2/3)=4*log(21/13)。H0 下 T 的精确分布是 t3，T^2 的精确分布是 F(1,3)。自由度 1 的卡方仅是似然比统计量的渐近校准。

problem:
Why can't I just set both prices equal to marginal cost here? Each firm has limited capacity. Please help me check whether a pure equilibrium exists before I start calculating a price.

Two firms simultaneously choose nonnegative prices for a homogeneous good. Demand is D(p)=max(0,1-p). Both have zero marginal cost and an identical fixed capacity K>0; capacity expenditures are already sunk. Use the following specified efficient-rationing allocation rule. The lower-price firm sells min(K,D(its price)). The higher-price firm sells min(K,max(0,1-its price-K)). At equal prices p, each sells min(K,D(p)/2). Profit is price times units sold. This rationing rule, including the equal-price split, is part of the game and may not be replaced by another rule.

Characterize all pure-strategy Nash equilibria as a function of K. Prove that asymmetric price pairs cannot be equilibria, then examine every possible symmetric price region analytically. Explain why sufficient combined capacity to serve demand at price0 does not necessarily make price0 an equilibrium. Do not infer the existence or form of a mixed equilibrium from a failure of pure equilibrium.

Give equilibrium price, quantities and profits for K=1/4 and K=1/3. For K=2/5, evaluate the market-clearing symmetric price p=1-2*K and find the best unilateral upward deviation and its exact profit gain. Generalize that gain for1/3<K<1/2. For K=3/4, find a profitable deviation against a rival price0. Finally check the boundary K=1 and explain what changes when each individual firm, rather than just the pair, can serve the whole market.
thinking:
Before applying the zero-cost Bertrand result, I should use the residual-demand rule. If my rival charges a lower price, it can absorb at most K buyers; my high-price demand is the positive part of1-p-K, capped at K. This can leave profitable residual demand even against a zero-priced rival. The allocation discontinuity at a tie also matters, so a smooth first-order condition alone cannot establish equilibrium.

For asymmetric prices, let p_L<p_H. If p_L=0, the lower-price firm earns0 and can raise its price a little while remaining below p_H, obtaining positive revenue. If0<p_L<1-K, it fills capacity and can again raise its price slightly while staying below both p_H and1-K; sales remain K and profit rises. If p_L>=1-K, the higher-price firm's residual demand is0. It can instead choose a positive price below min(p_L,1), sell a positive quantity and improve on0. This last argument also covers K>=1, when1-K is nonpositive. Hence no asymmetric pair is a pure equilibrium.

For a symmetric positive price p<1, I should compare demand to combined capacity. If D(p)>2*K, both sell K at the tie. Either can raise its price slightly while residual demand still exceeds K, preserving sales and increasing profit. If D(p)<2*K, each tied firm sells D(p)/2<K. An arbitrarily small undercut makes the deviator's sales approach min(K,D(p)), strictly greater than D(p)/2. At p>0, this creates a strict profit improvement for a sufficiently small undercut. Thus any symmetric positive equilibrium must satisfy D(p)=2*K, or p_c=1-2*K. Symmetric prices at least1 yield no sales and admit a profitable positive price below1.

At the clearing candidate, I should check both directions globally. For0<K<1/2, p_c>0 and each firm earns K*(1-2*K). A lower price still sells K, so it lowers profit. At a higher price p>p_c, residual quantity is max(0,1-K-p)<K and positive-profit revenue is f(p)=p*(1-K-p). Its derivative at p_c is1-K-2*(1-2*K)=3*K-1, and f is strictly concave. Therefore every upward deviation is unprofitable exactly when K<=1/3. At K1/3, the derivative is0 at the boundary and f falls strictly above it. For K>1/3, a small upward deviation is profitable.

For symmetric price0, I should check the individual rather than combined capacity. If0<K<1, choose a positive price p<1-K against the zero-priced rival. Residual demand1-K-p is positive, and its cap at K remains positive, so the deviation yields positive profit from a zero baseline. Thus price0 fails even when2*K>=1. If K>=1, the rival alone can serve all demand at0, every higher price sells0, and no negative price is allowed. Then(0,0) is an equilibrium; the previous asymmetric and positive-price arguments make it the only one.

Putting the analytic certificates together, for0<K<=1/3 the unique pure equilibrium is(p_c,p_c)=(1-2*K,1-2*K), with each quantity K and profit K*(1-2*K). For1/3<K<1 there is no pure equilibrium. For K>=1 the unique pure equilibrium is(0,0), with each tied quantity1/2 and profit0. The statements concern pure equilibria only. Discontinuous payoffs require a separate analysis before making claims about mixed strategies.

For the small-capacity checks, K1/4 gives prices1/2, quantities1/4 each and profits1/8 each. K1/3 gives prices1/3, quantities1/3 each and profits1/9. For K2/5, the clearing price is1/5, with profit2/25 per firm. The residual-demand parabola is maximized at p_d=(1-K)/2=3/10, which is indeed above1/5 and yields quantity3/10 below capacity2/5. The deviating profit is9/100, an improvement of1/100. Market clearing does not itself prove unilateral optimality.

For the reusable deviation formula, when1/3<K<1/2 the residual maximizer p_d=(1-K)/2 lies above p_c, and its quantity(1-K)/2 is below K. The gain is(1-K)^2/4-K*(1-2*K)=(3*K-1)^2/4>0. This factorization independently checks the threshold K1/3 and the numerical gain. For K3/4 against price0, p_d1/8 leaves residual quantity1/8 and profit1/64>0. Although combined capacity is3/2, the rival alone can serve only3/4, leaving that deviation available.

For the capacity boundary K1, I should reevaluate the residual instead of extending a formula across regimes. Against price0, every p>0 has max(0,1-p-1)=0, so the profitable deviation disappears. At the tie each firm sells1/2, below its own capacity, but there is no profitable undercut below0. The equilibrium change is caused by each rival's ability to supply the entire zero-price demand, not by a change in marginal cost.

General pattern: I should test allocation rules and unilateral deviations before solving smooth conditions. Capacity can make a price increase profitable despite a cheaper rival, while tie splitting can make undercutting profitable at other prices. Residual-demand concavity and a factored gain identify an existence threshold analytically. Combined supply adequacy differs from a rival's ability to serve the whole market, and absence of pure equilibrium is not a classification of mixed equilibria.
reference_answer:
For0<K<=1/3, the unique pure equilibrium has both prices1-2*K, quantities K each and profits K*(1-2*K). For1/3<K<1 there is no pure equilibrium. For K>=1, the unique pure equilibrium is(0,0), with quantities1/2 each and zero profits.

Asymmetric pairs permit either a price increase by the lower-price seller or a profitable undercut by a zero-sales rival. At a positive symmetric equilibrium, demand must equal2*K. The clearing candidate survives upward deviations exactly when3*K-1<=0; downward deviations reduce profit.

K1/4 gives price1/2 and profit1/8 each; K1/3 gives price1/3 and profit1/9 each. At K2/5, clearing price1/5 is defeated by price3/10, raising unilateral profit from2/25 to9/100. The gain is1/100, or generally(3*K-1)^2/4 for1/3<K<1/2.

At K3/4, a price1/8 against rival price0 sells1/8 and earns1/64. At K1 this residual demand disappears. Sufficient combined capacity therefore does not imply a zero-price equilibrium; sufficient individual capacity does under the stated rule. No mixed-equilibrium conclusion is asserted.

problem:
My intuition says that raising a minimum wage must reduce employment. Can you solve a monopsony example exactly and tell me when that intuition fails?

A single employer sells output competitively. Hiring q>=0 workers produces gross value integral from0 toq of(14-z) dz. Workers have inverse labor supply w_s=2+q. The employer must pay at least a statutory wage floor t>=0 to every worker. If it hires q, the wage is max(2+q,t), so total labor cost is q*max(2+q,t). The employer chooses q to maximize gross value minus this cost. Ignore fixed costs and assume a worker's outside option is already represented by the labor-supply curve.

Find the globally optimal employment and wage for every t, including the exact thresholds and boundary cases. Prove global optimality across the kink where the wage floor begins binding; a first-order condition from only one branch is not enough. Compare with the no-floor monopsony and competitive employment. Compute employer profit, worker surplus and total real surplus at the unregulated outcome, at the efficient floor, and at t=10. Find the floor that maximizes total surplus and separately the floor that maximizes worker surplus. Explain whose surplus changes as the floor rises. Do not try a grid of wage floors.
thinking:
Before differentiating, I split total labor cost at the supply kink. If t<=2+q, the employer pays the reservation wage and cost is(2+q)*q. If t>=2+q, supply at the floor permits q<=t-2 and cost is t*q. Gross value is14*q-q^2/2. Each branch of profit is strictly concave, but the derivative changes at q=t-2, so its sign on each side determines whether the optimum is at a smooth point or the kink.

On the reservation-wage branch, profit is12*q-3*q^2/2 and its unconstrained maximum is q=4, with wage6. This remains feasible whenever t<=6. On the floor-binding branch, profit is(14-t)*q-q^2/2, whose unconstrained maximum is q=14-t. It lies in q<=t-2 exactly when t>=8 and t<=14. Between these regions, for6<t<8, the derivative from the binding side is positive at the kink and the derivative from the reservation-wage side is negative there: profit rises into and falls away from q=t-2. Thus employment is t-2.

For t>14 the binding-branch derivative at zero is already negative, while the reservation-wage branch cannot offer a profitable hire; zero employment is optimal. At t=6 and8 the adjacent formulas meet at q=4 and6 respectively. At t=14 the positive-branch optimum reaches zero. Strict concavity on both branches and the one-sided derivative signs prove the global piecewise solution, not just local stationarity.

The full solution is q=4 for0<=t<=6, q=t-2 for6<=t<=8, q=14-t for8<=t<=14, and q=0 for t>=14. The wage is max(2+q,t). With no floor the employer solves marginal product14-q equal to marginal expenditure2+2q, giving q=4,w=6. Competitive hiring solves14-q=2+q, giving q=6,w=8.

For welfare I remove wage payments because they are transfers. The employer’s no-floor profit is gross value48 minus labor cost24, hence24. Worker surplus is the area under wage minus inverse supply, integral from0 to4 of(6-2-z) dz=8. Total surplus is32. The efficient quantity instead solves14-q=2+q, so q=6 and total surplus is the triangle integral of12-2z from0 to6, equal36. A floor t=8 implements q=6. At that point gross value66, wage bill48, profit18 and worker surplus18.

At t=10 employment is4 and the wage is10. Gross value is48, wage bill40, and profit8. Worker surplus is integral from0 to4 of(10-2-z) dz=24, so total real surplus is32. More generally, real surplus is12*q-q^2, maximized at q=6; this occurs only at t=8. Worker surplus is8 for t<=6, equals(t-2)^2/2 for6<=t<=8, and equals12*q-3*q^2/2 with q=14-t for8<=t<=14. Its maximum occurs at q=4, hence t=10 and worker surplus24. The floor that maximizes worker surplus differs from the one that maximizes total surplus because the latter counts both employer and worker surplus.

General pattern: I split the objective at the policy-induced kink, solve each concave branch, and use one-sided derivatives to select a boundary solution. I then evaluate welfare from marginal social surplus, excluding wage transfers. A wage floor can undo monopsony underhiring, but a stronger floor eventually destroys mutually beneficial employment.
reference_answer:
Employment is4 for0<=t<=6, t-2 for6<=t<=8, 14-t for8<=t<=14, and0 for t>=14. Wage is max(2+q,t). The monopsony outcome is(q,w)=(4,6); competitive and efficient employment is6 at wage8. The efficient floor is t=8.

At no floor, profit24, worker surplus8 and total surplus32. At t=8, employment6, profit18, worker surplus18 and total surplus36. At t=10, employment4, wage10, profit8, worker surplus16 and total surplus24. Total surplus is12*q-q^2, maximized at q=6. Employment is maximized for every floor from6 through8, while welfare is maximized only at8.
