problem:
Je ne comprends pas pourquoi un client accepterait une exclusivité qui empêche une entrée avantageuse. Considère ce modèle complet. Deux clients représentent deux marchés indépendants, chacun avec demande q=max(0,1-p); leur gain est le surplus du consommateur plus toute compensation reçue. L'incumbent a un coût marginal1/5. Un entrant a coût marginal0 et doit payer un coût fixe réel1/5 pour entrer, quel que soit le nombre de marchés accessibles. L'incumbent propose à chaque client le même paiement T>=0 contre une exclusivité exécutoire, payé dès la signature. Les clients choisissent simultanément signer S ou refuser R. L'entrant observe les signatures et choisit d'entrer ou non. Il ne peut servir les marchés exclusifs. En cas d'entrée, l'incumbent est contractuellement tenu d'offrir le prix1/5 sur chaque marché libre; l'entrant peut proposer un prix inférieur ou égal et obtient toutes les ventes à égalité de prix. Sans entrée, l'incumbent fixe son prix de monopole sur chaque marché. Les compensations sont des transferts, pas des coûts réels.

Résous les prix et la décision d'entrée après chaque nombre de refus, puis caractérise tous les équilibres de signature, y compris mixtes, pour tout T>=0. Une offre peut-elle garantir l'exclusion dans tous les équilibres tout en donnant à l'incumbent un profit au moins nul? Pour T=1/25, calcule la probabilité d'entrée, les gains espérés des clients, le profit de l'incumbent, le profit de l'entrant et le bien-être dans chaque équilibre. Compare aussi le bien-être lorsque les deux signent et lorsqu'ils refusent ensemble. Explique pourquoi un refus unilatéral peut échouer alors qu'un refus conjoint améliore les deux clients. Utilise les seuils d'incitation et les identités de bien-être, sans recherche de profils numériques.
thinking:
Avant d'étudier les signatures, je dois résoudre l'entrée. Sur un marché libre, l'entrant maximise p*(1-p) sous0<=p<=1/5. La dérivée1-2*p reste positive, donc il choisit1/5 et vend4/5. Son profit variable par marché est4/25. Avec un seul marché libre, le profit d'entrée serait4/25-1/5=-1/25; avec deux,8/25-1/5=3/25. Il entre donc exactement quand les deux clients refusent. Cette comparaison donne la complémentarité des refus à partir du coût fixe, au lieu de supposer arbitrairement que l'entrée exige deux clients.

Pour l'option sans entrée, le monopole maximise(p-1/5)*(1-p), d'où p=3/5 et q=2/5. Son profit par marché est4/25, et le surplus d'un client est q^2/2=2/25. Avec entrée, chaque client a surplus(4/5)^2/2=8/25. Le gain de concurrence pour chaque client est donc L=6/25. Le coût fixe appartient à l'entrant; je ne dois ni l'omettre du bien-être ni le faire payer directement au client dans son choix de signature.

Pour les incitations, je soustrais le surplus monopolistique commun2/25. Si l'autre signe, mon refus ne rend qu'un marché accessible et ne provoque pas l'entrée. Signer me donne alors un gain supplémentaire T, refuser0. Si l'autre refuse, signer empêche l'entrée et donne T, tandis que refuser permet l'entrée et donne L. Si l'autre signe avec probabilité p, l'avantage de signer est D(p)=T-L*(1-p). Ce seuil affine suffit pour caractériser les équilibres.

Pour0<T<L, signer est strictement optimal contre S et refuser strictement optimal contre R. Les équilibres purs sont donc(S,S) et(R,R). Si l'un mélange strictement, l'indifférence impose p=1-T/L chez l'autre, puis réciproquement; le seul autre équilibre est le mélange symétrique de probabilité de signature p*=1-T/L. Aucune mixture partielle asymétrique n'est possible puisque les meilleures réponses aux actions pures sont strictes. L'exclusivité dommageable et l'entrée avantageuse peuvent ainsi être toutes deux auto-confirmantes.

Pour les limites, T=0 donne D(p)=-L*(1-p). Si l'autre refuse avec une probabilité positive, refuser est strictement optimal; cela ne laisse que(R,R) ou(S,S), ce dernier avec indifférence à un refus unilatéral. À T=L, D(p)=L*p: toute probabilité positive de signature de l'autre impose la signature certaine, mais(R,R) reste possible par indifférence. Les mêmes deux profils purs sont les seuls équilibres à ces deux seuils. Pour T>L, signer domine strictement et(S,S) est unique.

Pour une garantie rentable, exclusion dans tous les équilibres exige T>L=6/25; au seuil T=L, le refus conjoint reste un équilibre. Lorsque tous signent, le profit de l'incumbent est8/25-2*T. Sa non-négativité exige T<=4/25, incompatible avec T>6/25. Il n'existe donc aucune offre de ce type garantissant une exclusion rentable. Une petite compensation peut soutenir un équilibre d'exclusion sans la garantir: je dois distinguer possibilité et implémentation dans tous les équilibres.

Pour T=1/25, le seuil mixte est p*=1-(1/25)/(6/25)=5/6. Dans(S,S), chaque client reçoit2/25+1/25=3/25, l'incumbent gagne8/25-2/25=6/25 et l'entrant0. Dans(R,R), chaque client reçoit8/25, l'incumbent0 et l'entrant3/25. L'entrée a donc probabilité0 ou1 dans les deux équilibres purs. Un client passant seul de S à R perd sa compensation sans déclencher l'entrée; les deux refusant ensemble gagnent chacun8/25-3/25=1/5 par rapport à(S,S).

Pour le mélange, les signatures sont indépendantes. L'entrée exige deux refus, donc sa probabilité est(1/6)^2=1/36. Chaque client est indifférent: refuser lui donne2/25+(1/6)*(6/25)=3/25, la même valeur que signer. Le nombre moyen de signatures est2*(5/6)=5/3. L'incumbent gagne8/25 quand il n'y a pas d'entrée et paie T par signature, d'où profit espéré(8/25)*(35/36)-(1/25)*(5/3)=11/45. L'entrant reçoit3/25 uniquement à l'entrée, donnant profit espéré1/300.

Pour le bien-être réel, sans entrée chaque marché donne bénéfice brut q-q^2/2 moins coût q/5, soit6/25. Les deux marchés donnent12/25, indépendamment des compensations. Avec entrée, chaque marché donne bénéfice brut12/25 et coût marginal0; après le coût fixe1/5, le total est24/25-1/5=19/25. L'exclusion détruit donc7/25 de surplus réel. Au mélange, le bien-être attendu est12/25+(1/36)*(7/25)=439/900.

Pour un contrôle indépendant, les gains des agents doivent retrouver ce total. Sous(S,S), les clients obtiennent6/25 ensemble et l'incumbent6/25, soit12/25. Sous(R,R), les clients obtiennent16/25 et l'entrant3/25, soit19/25. Au mélange, la somme est6/25+11/45+1/300=439/900. Les paiements d'exclusivité s'annulent entre clients et incumbent; le coût fixe d'entrée reste une ressource consommée. Cette identité évite de confondre compensation privée et réduction du dommage collectif.

General pattern: je dois résoudre le seuil d'entrée avant de comparer des contrats. Un coût fixe peut rendre les refus complémentaires: un client isolé ne change pas l'entrée, alors qu'un refus coordonné la permet. Une différence affine donne les équilibres et les limites d'implémentation; les transferts déterminent l'acceptation, mais les ressources déterminent le bien-être.
reference_answer:
L'entrant choisit p=1/5 sur les marchés libres et entre uniquement si les deux clients refusent. Sans entrée, p=3/5. Les surplus par client sont8/25 avec entrée et2/25 sans entrée, soit un gain de concurrence L=6/25.

Pour0<T<L, les équilibres sont(S,S),(R,R) et le mélange symétrique avec probabilité de signature1-T/L. À T=0 et T=L, seuls les deux profils purs restent; pour T>L, seul(S,S) subsiste. Garantir l'exclusion exige T>6/25, mais un profit d'incumbent non négatif exige T<=4/25: aucune garantie rentable n'est possible.

À T=1/25, les valeurs(entrée probable; gain de chaque client; profit incumbent; profit entrant; bien-être) sont(0;3/25;6/25;0;12/25) sous(S,S), (1;8/25;0;3/25;19/25) sous(R,R), et(1/36;3/25;11/45;1/300;439/900) au mélange. Le refus conjoint améliore chaque client de1/5 par rapport à l'exclusion; un refus unilatéral perd seulement la compensation. La perte sociale d'exclusion est7/25, avec les transferts annulés dans le bilan total.

problem: How can I solve a continuous waiting game without guessing a list of waiting times? Two risk-neutral agents compete for a prize of value3 to each. Each chooses a nonnegative concession time. The first to concede loses; the other wins the prize. Both pay waiting cost1 per unit of elapsed time until the first concession. A tie splits the prize equally. Find and verify a symmetric continuous mixed equilibrium, including deviations to any finite waiting time. Calculate expected duration, winning probability and expected net payoff per agent. Compare with immediate coordinated allocation of the prize, and distinguish intended concession time from actual elapsed time.
thinking:
Before choosing a distribution, I should derive the payoff from an arbitrary deterministic waiting time T. Facing an atomless opponent distribution F with density f, winning against concession at t<T yields3-t; losing because the opponent waits beyond T yields -T. Thus U(T)=integral from0 toT of(3-t)*f(t)dt-T*(1-F(T)). This formula accounts for waiting cost on both victory and defeat.

To discover a mixing pattern, differentiate using the product rule. The terms involving T*f(T) cancel, leaving U'(T)=3*f(T)-(1-F(T)). Full-support indifference therefore requires hazard f(T)/(1-F(T))=1/3. The survival equation S'(T)=-S(T)/3 with S(0)=1 gives S(T)=exp(-T/3), so concession times are exponential with mean3. A constant hazard comes from the local balance of prize value and waiting cost.

For all finite deviations, substituting this distribution gives U'(T)=0. Since U(0)=0 against an atomless opponent, U(T)=0 for every finite T>=0. Any probability mixture over those times also gives zero, so the candidate is a symmetric equilibrium. A commitment never to concede would earn3-E[t_opponent]=0 as well if that enlarged action were permitted; it supplies a useful limiting check but is not needed in the stated finite action space.

For duration, the two intended concession times are independent exponentials with survival exp(-t/3). Actual elapsed time D is their minimum, with survival exp(-2*t/3). Hence E[D]=3/2. Each wins with probability1/2 by symmetry and absence of ties, so expected prize receipt is3/2 and expected waiting cost is3/2. Each net payoff is zero.

To verify the resource loss, the contest always allocates a prize worth3 to one person but imposes total waiting cost2*D. Its expected net surplus is3-2*(3/2)=0. Immediate coordinated allocation could deliver the prize without waiting, yielding total surplus3. Symmetric random allocation at time0 would give each expected payoff3/2, but unilateral timing choices in the contest do not enforce that coordination.

An independent check integrates the deviation payoff directly: integral from0 toT of(3-t)*exp(-t/3)/3 dt equals T*exp(-T/3). Subtracting the losing-branch term T*exp(-T/3) gives zero. This validates the differential hazard argument for every finite waiting time, rather than only at a selected candidate.

General pattern: I should express expected payoff as a survival-weighted integral and differentiate to reveal a hazard identity. Mixing equalises all waiting-time deviations through an ODE. The minimum of intended times determines realised cost, so the equilibrium distribution's mean is not the contest's mean duration.
reference_answer:
Each agent independently draws a concession time with survival exp(-t/3). The expected payoff from every finite deterministic waiting time is zero, verifying equilibrium.

Expected intended time is3, but expected actual duration is3/2. Each agent wins with probability1/2 and has zero expected net payoff. Total expected waiting cost3 dissipates the prize value; immediate coordinated allocation would preserve surplus3.

problem: A worker's productivity is1 if low type and3 if high type; the high-type prior probability is1/3. Education e>=0 does not change productivity. Its utility cost is e for a low type and e/2 for a high type. Competitive employers pay expected productivity conditional on observed education. Characterise separating equilibria with low type choosing0, high type choosing E>0, and wage1 at every off-path education level. Then apply this refinement: after an off-path observation, eliminate a type if no wage in [1,3] would improve on that type's equilibrium payoff; if only the high type remains possible, employers pay3. Which separating education level survives? Compare expected worker utility with free revelation of type, and explain why equality in a constraint does not invalidate separation when indifferent workers follow the stated strategy.
thinking:
Before guessing education values, I should use the two incentive bounds. Separation gives wages1 at e=0 and3 at e=E. The low type's deviation to E pays3-E rather than1, so low-type incentive compatibility requires E>=2. The high type's deviation to0 pays1 rather than3-E/2, so its condition is E<=4. Thus the separating range is2<=E<=4, not a single education level determined by arbitrary trial values.

For off-path deviations under the stipulated beliefs, any other e receives wage1. The low type gets1-e<=1. The high type gets1-e/2<=1<=3-E/2 for E<=4. Hence neither gains off path. Beliefs on the two on-path signals are fixed by separation, while the stated pessimistic off-path beliefs support every E in the interval. At E=2 the low type is indifferent about mimicking, and at E=4 the high type is indifferent about choosing zero; prescribed choices still form equilibria.

To discover which signals are credible under the refinement, I compare maximum possible deviation payoffs with each equilibrium payoff. Suppose E>2 and choose an off-path e strictly between2 and E. Even at the largest possible wage3, the low type receives3-e<1, so this type cannot benefit. The high type would receive3-e/2>3-E/2 at wage3, so it remains a possible profitable deviator.

The refinement therefore forces wage3 at that signal. The high type strictly benefits by choosing it, contradicting equilibrium. This eliminates every E>2 in one interval argument. I should not enumerate nearby education values; single crossing orders the incentives and makes an entire range of deviations informative.

For E=2, the high type's equilibrium utility is2. At off-path e>2, even wage3 gives3-e/2<2, so the high type cannot benefit; the low type cannot benefit either because3-e<1. At0<e<2, both types could benefit at wage3, so the refinement does not force a high-only belief. Keeping wage1 there deters both. No forced profitable off-path signal remains, so E=2 survives the specified criterion.

For the welfare comparison, expected wages equal expected productivity: (2/3)*1+(1/3)*3=5/3. At E=2, expected education cost is (1/3)*(2/2)=1/3, giving expected worker utility4/3. Free revelation pays the same type-specific wages with no education cost, so expected utility is5/3. The signaling loss is1/3. The low type's boundary indifference affects selection of its action, not the resource cost paid by the high type.

An independent incentive check at the surviving signal gives low-type truthful utility1 and mimicking utility3-2=1; high-type truthful utility3-1=2 and mimicking-zero utility1. Thus separation satisfies both weak constraints, and only the high type pays education. The cheapest separating signal is pinned down by the low type's constraint, despite education having no productive effect.

General pattern: I should derive a separating interval from single-crossing inequalities, then use the payoff range to eliminate implausible deviators. A refinement can select the least-cost signal by an interval argument, while weak incentive compatibility still requires an explicit choice at indifference.
reference_answer:
With the stated off-path wage1, separating equilibria exist for2<=E<=4. The refinement eliminates E>2: a signal in (2,E) can benefit only the high type, forcing wage3 and a profitable deviation. E=2 survives.

At E=2, expected wages are5/3 and expected education cost1/3, so expected worker utility is4/3 versus5/3 under free revelation. Weak low-type indifference is compatible with the prescribed separating strategy.

problem: A monopolist with linear demand P=40−Q and marginal cost10 must choose quantity before learning whether demand will be high or low. With probability1/2, the inverse demand is50−Q; otherwise it is30−Q. Find the optimal quantity and expected profit, and compare it with the quantity chosen if demand were known first.
thinking:
Without information, expected inverse demand is40−Q. Expected profit is(30−Q)Q, maximized at Q=15 with profit225.

If demand is known first, the firm chooses Q=20 in the high state and Q=10 in the low state, since each state's marginal revenue equals10. State profits are400 and100, so expected profit is250.

The value of perfect demand information is25. The firm can condition quantity on the state, gaining from tailoring output; averaging demand first loses that flexibility even though expected demand is linear.

As a check, the high-state profit curve is(40−Q)Q and the low-state curve is(20−Q)Q. Their maxima occur at20 and10; averaging their peak profits gives250, above the uninformed maximum225.

General pattern: With uncertainty, maximize expected profit for a fixed decision; with information, maximize separately by state and then average. The latter weakly dominates because it expands the feasible decision rules.
reference_answer: Without information choose Q=15 for expected profit225. With perfect information, choose20 or10 by state for expected profit250; information is worth25.

problem: A monopsonist faces labor supply w=10+L and marginal revenue product MRP=100−2L. Find its employment and wage, then compare with the competitive outcome. Why does equating wage to MRP fail for the monopsonist?
thinking:
Before choosing employment, I distinguish the wage paid from marginal labor expenditure. Total payroll is w(L)L=10L+L², so marginal expenditure is10+2L. A monopsonist hires until MRP=10+2L, giving Lm=22.5 and wm=10+22.5=32.5.

Under competition, each firm takes wage as given and hires until MRP=w. Intersecting100−2L=10+L gives Lc=30 and wc=40. Monopsony employment and wage are both lower because the firm internalizes the wage increase imposed on inframarginal workers.

At Lm, MRP=55 while the wage is32.5; the gap is not an inconsistency but the marginal expenditure wedge. Using MRP=w would erase the monopsonist's upward-sloping labor-supply effect.

General pattern: with market power in input procurement, optimize against marginal expenditure, not the posted average wage. Differentiate total payroll w(L)L before setting it equal to marginal revenue product.
reference_answer: The monopsonist hires L=45/2 and pays w=65/2. Competition gives L=30 and w=40.

problem:
Mon solveur oscille entre deux productions. Est-ce qu'il y a plusieurs équilibres, ou est-ce ma méthode qui est mauvaise? Dans un Cournot à n>=2 entreprises identiques, qi>=0, Q=sum(qi), le prix est p=1-Q et les coûts sont nuls. Cette demande linéaire est utilisée sans plancher de prix; des vecteurs d'essai peuvent donc donner un prix négatif. Le profit est(1-Q)*qi. Trouve analytiquement l'unique équilibre, puis étudie la mise à jour simultanée qi'=max(0,(1-sum(qj,j!=i))/2). Montre exactement ce qui se passe depuis le vecteur nul lorsque n>=3, sans chercher l'équilibre par une grille.

Propose ensuite la mise à jour projetée T_eta(q)=[q+eta*(1-Q*1-q)]_+, où1 est le vecteur de uns et la partie positive s'applique coordonnée par coordonnée. Trouve une fonction potentielle, prouve que ses optima correspondent aux équilibres, et détermine pour quels eta>0 cette mise à jour est une contraction globale en norme euclidienne. Trouve le pas qui minimise le facteur de contraction. Pour n=4, donne l'équilibre, le pas optimal, le facteur, les deux premiers vecteurs depuis zéro, et une borne exacte de l'erreur à partir du résidu||T_eta(q)-q||. Quel seuil sur ce résidu suffit pour certifier une erreur euclidienne au plus1/100? Distingue la preuve d'existence, la stabilité d'une procédure et la précision d'un calcul.
thinking:
Avant d'itérer, je devrais résoudre le jeu. La dérivée propre du profit est1-Q-qi, avec courbure-2. Une fonction potentielle exacte est Phi(q)=Q-Q^2/2-sum(qi^2)/2: sa dérivée en qi est précisément1-Q-qi. Sa Hessienne est-H, où H=I+1*1'. Les valeurs propres de H sont n+1 dans la direction commune1 et1 dans les directions de somme nulle. Phi est strictement concave et tend vers moins l'infini quand la norme augmente sur l'orthant; elle possède donc un maximum unique.

Pour relier le maximum au jeu, chaque choix individuel a les mêmes variations de profit que de Phi lorsque les autres quantités restent fixes. Les conditions de meilleure réponse sont qi>=0,1-Q-qi<=0 et qi*(1-Q-qi)=0. Ce sont aussi les conditions suffisantes d'optimalité de la potentielle concave sur l'orthant. Par symétrie et unicité, toutes les quantités optimales sont égales. L'équation1-(n+1)*q=0 donne qi*=1/(n+1), Q*=n/(n+1), p*=1/(n+1) et profit individuel1/(n+1)^2. Le vecteur strictement positif vérifie toutes les conditions globales.

Pour diagnostiquer l'oscillation, je peux suivre la direction commune sans essayer tous les vecteurs. Au vecteur nul, chaque meilleure réponse vaut1/2. Si toutes les entreprises produisent1/2, chaque firme voit une production rivale(n-1)/2. Dès n>=3, sa nouvelle réponse est max(0,(3-n)/4)=0. La procédure alterne donc exactement entre0 et(1/2)*1. Aucun de ces vecteurs n'est l'équilibre. Près de q*, la mise à jour non projetée des meilleures réponses a une valeur propre-(n-1)/2 dans la direction commune et1/2 dans les directions de somme nulle. Les substituts stratégiques ne garantissent pas la convergence simultanée lorsque leurs effets s'additionnent.

Pour trouver une méthode certifiable, je regarde le gradient de la potentielle: grad Phi=1-H*q. La mise à jour proposée est la projection sur l'orthant de(I-eta*H)*q+eta*1. La projection coordonnée max(0,x) est non expansive:|max(0,x)-max(0,y)|<=|x-y|. Le théorème spectral donne donc||T_eta(q)-T_eta(z)||<=rho*||q-z||, avec rho=max(|1-eta|,|1-(n+1)*eta|). Puisque n>=2, les deux modes existent. La contraction exige et est obtenue pour0<eta<2/(n+1).

Pour vérifier la nécessité, je dois regarder un voisinage de l'équilibre positif. La projection y reste inactive pour des perturbations assez petites; la dérivée est exactement I-eta*H. Si une de ses valeurs propres a un module au moins1, aucune constante globale strictement inférieure à1 ne peut majorer toutes les distances locales. Au pas frontière2/(n+1), une petite perturbation commune change de signe sans réduire son amplitude. L'absence de contraction à ce pas n'est pas une nouvelle multiplicité d'équilibres.

Pour accélérer sans chercher les pas, j'équilibre les deux erreurs spectrales extrêmes. Au minimum du maximum,1-eta=-(1-(n+1)*eta), d'où eta*=2/(n+2) et rho*=n/(n+2). Ce pas appartient bien à l'intervalle de contraction. Comme q* est un point fixe, l'erreur après k mises à jour est au plus rho^k fois l'erreur initiale. La preuve est globale, même quand certaines coordonnées de la procédure touchent zéro; elle ne dépend pas de l'hypothèse d'une trajectoire toujours intérieure.

Pour n=4, qi*=1/5 et p*=1/5; le pas optimal est1/3, avec rho=2/3. Depuis0, le premier vecteur est(1/3,1/3,1/3,1/3). Sa somme4/3 donne grad Phi=-2/3 sur chaque coordonnée, donc le suivant est(1/9,1/9,1/9,1/9). Ces valeurs ne sont pas des solutions candidates énumérées: elles vérifient directement la formule de mise à jour et son mode commun, dont la valeur propre est-2/3. Le contraste avec le cycle des meilleures réponses confirme que la difficulté vient de la procédure.

Pour certifier la précision, j'utilise le résidu actuel r=||T_eta(q)-q|| plutôt qu'un nombre arbitraire d'itérations. La triangulation donne||q-q*||<=||q-T_eta(q)||+||T_eta(q)-T_eta(q*)||<=r+rho*||q-q*||. Ainsi||q-q*||<=r/(1-rho). Au pas optimal avec n=4, la borne est3*r: r<=1/300 certifie une erreur au plus1/100. Ce n'est pas une égalité systématique, seulement une garantie globale suffisante. Une petite variation entre itérés sans contraction prouvée ne donnerait pas cette garantie.

Pour un contrôle indépendant, la Hessienne fournit aussi une identité exacte autour de q*: Phi(q*)-Phi(q)=(q-q*)'*H*(q-q*)/2, car le gradient y est nul. Elle est positive hors de q*, confirmant l'unicité sans argument d'itération. Dans le cas n=4, H a les valeurs propres5 et1, donc l'écart de potentielle est compris entre||q-q*||^2/2 et5*||q-q*||^2/2. La preuve économique par meilleures réponses et la preuve géométrique par carrés concordent.

General pattern: je devrais résoudre et identifier la structure avant d'itérer. Une potentielle concave établit l'équilibre; ses modes propres expliquent pourquoi une méthode simultanée peut échouer. Une projection non expansive et un pas équilibrant les modes donnent une contraction globale, puis un résidu apporte un certificat de précision au lieu d'une recherche exhaustive.
reference_answer:
L'unique équilibre est qi=1/(n+1), avec prix1/(n+1). La potentielle Phi=Q-Q^2/2-sum(qi^2)/2 est strictement concave, et ses conditions d'optimalité sont les meilleures réponses. Pour n>=3, leur mise à jour simultanée depuis zéro forme le cycle exact0 puis(1/2)*1 puis0; cela ne prouve pas une multiplicité d'équilibres.

La mise à jour projetée est une contraction globale exactement pour0<eta<2/(n+1), avec facteur max(|1-eta|,|1-(n+1)*eta|). Le meilleur pas est2/(n+2), donnant n/(n+2).

Pour n=4: quantités1/5 chacune, prix1/5, pas1/3 et facteur2/3. Les deux premiers vecteurs sont(1/3)*1 et(1/9)*1. Le résidu r=||T(q)-q|| garantit||q-q*||<=3*r; r<=1/300 suffit donc pour une erreur au plus1/100. L'identité Phi(q*)-Phi(q)=(q-q*)'*(I+1*1')*(q-q*)/2 vérifie indépendamment l'optimalité globale.

problem: Help me check the sign in this deterrence calculation. Relative to lawful conduct, an illegal exclusion gives a firm gain Delta=9 before enforcement. An investigation occurs with probability x and, conditional on investigation, conviction with probability y; take x=y=1/2. An unconvicted firm keeps the gain. If convicted, it pays a nonnegative fine F and returns a fraction gamma in[0,1] of the illicit gain. The firm is risk neutral and chooses lawful conduct at indifference; lawful conduct has incremental payoff0. Write the state payoffs and derive the minimum deterrent fine. Compare complete gain retention and complete disgorgement. A draft instead writes expected gain as Delta-x*y*(F-Delta) and obtains F=45. Can that draft describe any gamma in[0,1] under these assumptions? If gamma is unknown within this interval, what fine guarantees deterrence? Treat these as explicit hypothetical payoff conventions, not statements of current law.
thinking:
Before simplifying, I should write each enforcement state relative to the same lawful baseline. Without conviction, the incremental payoff is Delta. With conviction, the firm retains(1-gamma)*Delta and pays F, giving(1-gamma)*Delta-F. Conviction probability is rho=x*y, because y is conditional on investigation. I should not multiply two unconditional probabilities without that interpretation.

A cheaper route is the state-payoff difference. Conviction reduces payoff by gamma*Delta+F. Thus expected incremental gain is G=Delta-rho*(gamma*Delta+F)=(1-rho*gamma)*Delta-rho*F. For rho>0, deterrence requires G<=0, so F>=Delta*(1/rho-gamma). With Delta=9 and rho=1/4, the exact threshold is Fmin=36-9*gamma. It is nonnegative throughout the declared interval; lawful choice at equality makes the boundary sufficient.

For full retention, gamma=0 gives convicted payoff9-F and expected gain9-F/4. The minimum fine is36. At F=36, the unconvicted payoff9 with probability3/4 balances the convicted payoff-27 with probability1/4:27/4-27/4=0. Retention of the gain means the fine alone must offset the full illicit gain in expectation.

For full disgorgement, gamma=1 gives convicted payoff-F, since the gain is returned. Expected gain is(3/4)*9-(1/4)*F; the minimum fine is27. At F=27, the same state-payoff check gives27/4-27/4=0. Returning the gain reduces the required additional fine by9; it does not increase that fine.

For the draft, Delta-rho*(F-Delta)=(1+rho)*Delta-rho*F. To match the valid state model, -rho*gamma*Delta must equal+rho*Delta, which requires gamma=-1 when rho*Delta>0. The implicit convicted payoff is then2*Delta-F: conviction awards another full gain rather than disgorging any fraction. Therefore the root45 is algebraically correct for the written expression but economically incompatible with the specified gamma range.

For unknown recovery, I should use monotonicity instead of searching candidate conventions. Since dG/dgamma=-rho*Delta<0, expected gain is largest at gamma=0. The robust deterrent fine is therefore36. Any F<36 fails at that admissible endpoint. F=45 also deters, but it exceeds every minimum in the interval[27,36]; it is not the robust minimum. At F=36 and gamma=1 the expected gain is-9/4, an independent check of the monotonicity direction.

For the detection boundary, rho=0 gives G=Delta regardless of any finite F or gamma. A positive gain cannot be deterred with zero conviction probability in this model. Dividing by rho without checking it would conceal this impossibility. If Delta=0, lawful conduct is already chosen at F=0 under the stated tie rule, including rho=0.

General pattern: I should derive enforcement incentives from state payoffs before manipulating expected penalties. Gain retention and gain repayment change the convicted payoff and the fine threshold in opposite ways. A worst-case endpoint gives robust deterrence only after the recovery parameter's monotonicity and the zero-probability boundary are checked.
reference_answer:
The convicted payoff is(1-gamma)*Delta-F, so G=Delta-rho*(gamma*Delta+F). Here rho=1/4 and Fmin=36-9*gamma:36 with gain retention,27 with full disgorgement.

The draft's expression requires gamma=-1, outside[0,1]; it implicitly adds another gain upon conviction. Its root45 is not the minimum under the stated conventions. The fine guaranteeing deterrence for every gamma in[0,1] is36, because no recovery is the worst case. With zero conviction probability and a positive gain, no finite fine works.

problem: Two firms compete in nonnegative Cournot quantities with p=1-q1-q2. Firm 1 has zero marginal cost. Firm 2 privately observes cost c2, equal to 0 or h>=0 with probabilities 1-alpha and alpha, where 0<alpha<1. Firm 1 chooses before learning the realised cost; firm 2 knows it when choosing, and quantities are chosen simultaneously. Derive the full Bayesian equilibrium as a function of h, including the high-cost shutdown regime. At alpha=1/2 and h=9/10 compute quantities by type, expected total output, its variance, expected profits and expected welfare. Explain why substituting expected cost into complete-information Cournot can fail.
thinking:
Before taking an expectation, I should preserve the type-specific nonnegative response. Firm 2 chooses qL=(1-q1)/2 when c2=0 and qH=max(0,(1-h-q1)/2) when c2=h, provided q1<1. Firm 1's expected-profit condition is 1-2*q1-[(1-alpha)*qL+alpha*qH]=0. Its own objective is strictly concave because the opponent's type-contingent strategy is held fixed during a unilateral deviation.

For the regime with both types active, substitution gives q1=(1+alpha*h)/3, qL=(2-alpha*h)/6 and qH=(2-(alpha+3)*h)/6. The high type is active precisely when h<2/(alpha+3). On that range q1<1 and qL>0, so the expressions are feasible. I must verify this inequality before using the interior Bayesian formula.

For the shutdown regime, set qH=0 in the expected condition. Then q1=(1+alpha)/(3+alpha) and qL=1/(3+alpha). The high type's derivative at zero is 1-h-q1=2/(3+alpha)-h, nonpositive exactly when h>=2/(3+alpha). The interior and shutdown expressions agree at the threshold. Thus they form a complete continuous equilibrium across h, with no negative type output.

To check uniqueness beyond these candidates, q1>=1 cannot be optimal: with every opponent output zero, firm 1 would prefer its own monopoly quantity 1/2. On q1<1 the low type is active and the high response is clipped with slope either -1/2 or 0. Substitution in firm 1's condition gives a continuous strictly decreasing left side, with slope between -2 and -3/2. It has at most one zero; the feasible branch solutions therefore give the unique Bayesian equilibrium.

At alpha=1/2, the shutdown threshold is 4/7, below h=9/10. Quantities are q1=3/7, qL=2/7 and qH=0. Total quantity is 5/7 in the low state and 3/7 in the high state, so E(Q)=4/7 and Var(Q)=1/49. Firm 1's expected price is 3/7 and profit is 9/49; firm 2's expected profit is (1/2)*(2/7)^2=2/49.

For welfare, resource costs are zero in the low state and also zero in the high state because the costly type shuts down. Hence E(W)=E(Q-Q^2/2)=4/7-(17/49)/2=39/98. An independent check gives E(CS)=E(Q^2)/2=17/98, and adding expected profits 9/49+2/49 yields the same 39/98. Using E(Q)^2 instead of E(Q^2) would omit the output-variance term.

To expose the expected-cost shortcut, the average cost is 9/20. Complete-information Cournot with that cost would give quantities 29/60 and 1/30. Actual Bayesian expected firm-2 quantity is 1/7, not 1/30. Taking expectation does not commute with the positive-part response, and firm 1 chooses against a distribution of actions rather than a fictitious average-cost firm. After high-type shutdown, equilibrium expected total output is 2/(3+alpha), independent of further increases in h.

General pattern: I should solve type-specific clipped best responses before taking expectations. A threshold separates active and shutdown types, and monotonicity proves uniqueness across the kink. Welfare under uncertainty uses second moments, while an average-cost replacement can erase both corners and information incentives.
reference_answer:
The active-type regime is h<2/(3+alpha), with q1=(1+alpha*h)/3, qL=(2-alpha*h)/6 and qH=(2-(alpha+3)*h)/6. Above the threshold, q1=(1+alpha)/(3+alpha), qL=1/(3+alpha) and qH=0.

At alpha=1/2 and h=9/10, quantities are (3/7,2/7,0); E(Q)=4/7, Var(Q)=1/49, expected profits are (9/49,2/49), and expected welfare is 39/98. Consumer surplus plus expected profits verifies welfare. The average-cost substitute produces different quantities because it removes the type-specific shutdown constraint.

problem: A seller has one buyer with value v uniform on [0,1] and zero reserve cost. What reserve price maximizes expected revenue, and how much is the maximum?
thinking:
Before maximizing expected revenue, note the item sells only when v≥r. Revenue is r with probability1−r, so expected revenue is r(1−r).

Completing the square gives r(1−r)=1/4−(r−1/2)². Therefore r*=1/2 and maximal expected revenue is1/4.

The first-order condition1−2r=0 and negative second derivative−2 confirm the same unique maximum. The reserve balances a higher conditional payment against a lower sale probability.

General pattern: for a single uniform buyer and zero cost, revenue is reserve times sale probability. Completing the square exposes the optimal tradeoff and global maximum.
reference_answer: The optimal reserve is 1/2 and maximum expected revenue is 1/4.

problem: A policy changes an outcome by 6 units. The treated group has 100 observations and control has 100; individual outcome variance is 25 in each independent group. Find the standard error of the difference in means.
thinking:
Before using the pooled sample size, keep the two sample means distinct. Independence gives Var(mean_T−mean_C)=25/100+25/100=1/2.

The standard error is sqrt(1/2)=1/√2, about 0.707. Equal group sizes do not make the variance 25/200; both group mean errors contribute.

A 95% normal interval for the estimated change is 6±1.96/√2, approximately [4.61,7.39]. Its half-width equals critical value times the derived standard error.

General pattern: variances of independent contrasts add with squared coefficients; divide each group variance by its own sample size before taking the square root.
reference_answer: The standard error is 1/√2, approximately 0.707.

problem: A demanda é Q=100−p e a oferta é Q=10+2p. Com um imposto por unidade de 6, encontre os preços pagos e recebidos, a quantidade e a divisão do imposto.
thinking:
Antes de atribuir o imposto ao lado legalmente responsável, escrevo pc−pp=6 e igualo demanda e oferta:100−pc=10+2pp. Isso dá pc=34 e pp=28, com Q=66.

Sem imposto, o preço é30 e a quantidade70. Assim consumidores suportam4 por unidade e produtores2; a quantidade cai4. O lado com oferta menos elástica absorve a parcela maior.

A verificação pelas inclinações dá parcela do consumidor2/(1+2)=2/3 do imposto, isto é4, e parcela do produtor1/3, isto é2. As duas equações de mercado confirmam o novo equilíbrio.

General pattern: resolva simultaneamente o wedge e a igualdade entre quantidades. Em oferta e demanda lineares, as inclinações determinam a divisão econômica do imposto, independentemente de quem o recolhe.
reference_answer: Consumers pay 34, producers receive 28, quantity is 66; burden shares are 4 and 2.

problem: Can you help me solve this voting example and check a hidden turnout assumption? Twenty-one voters have fixed rankings:10 prefer A>B>C,6 prefer B>C>A and5 prefer C>B>A. Compare sincere plurality voting, sincere two-round voting with the two largest first-place totals advancing, all pairwise majority comparisons, and Borda scores(2 for first,1 for second,0 for last). All21 vote in the first round. In a possible A-B runoff, exactly k of the5 C>B>A voters abstain, with integer0<=k<=5; everyone else votes sincerely. A second-round tie favours B. Find the smallest k making A win without trying each turnout count. Does that outcome contradict the statement that a Condorcet loser cannot win a sincere runoff? Keep the distinction between the full electorate and the people actually voting.
thinking:
Before comparing rules, I should identify the electorate behind each score. With all21 participating, first-place totals are A10,B6,C5. Plurality selects A, and the runoff finalists are A and B. In their duel, all6 B>C>A voters and all5 C>B>A voters prefer B, so B wins11 to10. First-place support alone does not tell me a candidate's majority comparisons.

For the pairwise relations, B beats A11 to10 and C beats A11 to10. B beats C16 to5, because the10 A>B>C voters join the6 B>C>A voters. Thus A is the full-electorate Condorcet loser and B the Condorcet winner. The sincere runoff selects B, consistent with excluding a Condorcet loser when the same electorate votes in the final.

For Borda, I can aggregate by group instead of expanding21 ballots. A gets2*10=20. B gets10+2*6+5=27. C gets6+2*5=16. B wins under Borda in this particular profile. That agreement with the Condorcet winner is a property of these rankings, not a proof that Borda always has the Condorcet property.

For turnout, A retains its10 runoff votes while B has11-k. Because a tie favours B, A wins precisely when10>11-k, or k>1. The smallest admissible integer is k=2, yielding A10 and B9 among19 participants. No preference changed; only the participating electorate changed. The other k outcomes follow from the inequality without recounting ballots individually.

For the apparent contradiction, the full21-voter pairwise profile still makes A a Condorcet loser. But with k=2 absent C>B>A voters, the19 participants prefer A to B10 to9 and A to C10 to9; B still beats C16 to3. A is now the participating electorate's Condorcet winner. The theorem about the loser assumes its pairwise comparisons and the runoff use the same electorate. Calling A a loser of the original electorate and a winner of a different turnout does not violate that theorem.

For an independent count check, the full electorate's Borda total is20+27+16=63=21*(2+1+0). At k=2 the runoff total10+9=19=21-2, and every new pairwise count also totals19. These checks distinguish a turnout change from a lost ballot or an inconsistent rank aggregation.

General pattern: I should hold both preferences and the electorate fixed when applying voting criteria. Group counts give pairwise and positional scores directly; a single turnout inequality finds the reversal threshold. A rule's property for one fixed electorate need not compare outcomes across different participation sets.
reference_answer:
Plurality selects A with first-place totals(10,6,5). With full turnout, B wins the A-B runoff11-10. B also beats C16-5; C beats A11-10, so B is Condorcet winner and A Condorcet loser. Borda scores are(A,B,C)=(20,27,16), selecting B.

A wins the reduced-turnout runoff iff k>=2; the smallest case gives10-9 among19 voters. This changes the electorate: A becomes that participating group's Condorcet winner. It does not contradict Condorcet-loser exclusion for a sincere runoff with the same fixed electorate.

problem: Summarize this in one sentence: “The library extended its hours during exam week. More students used the quiet study rooms, while the number of borrowed books stayed about the same.”
thinking: Keep the main change and the two outcomes, while respecting the one-sentence limit.
reference_answer: During exam week, longer library hours brought more students to study rooms, while book borrowing stayed roughly unchanged.

problem: Um mercado competitivo tem procura inversa p=6-q, custo real C(q)=q^2/2 e dano externo d*q, com d desconhecido em [1,3]. O regulador escolhe uma taxa unitária t em [0,6] antes de conhecer d; a receita é devolvida por transferência fixa. Determine a quantidade de mercado e a quantidade eficiente se d fosse conhecido. Compare a política que minimiza o maior arrependimento de bem-estar com a que maximiza o menor bem-estar absoluto. Calcule os piores valores e, sob distribuição uniforme de d, a política de bem-estar esperado e o arrependimento esperado. Prove os resultados sem testar uma lista de taxas ou valores de d, e explique por que os dois critérios robustos escolhem políticas diferentes.
thinking:
Antes de escolher uma taxa robusta, devo reduzir a política à quantidade que implementa. A oferta competitiva exige p-t=C'(q)=q; com p=6-q, resulta q=(6-t)/2. Cada t em [0,6] corresponde a q em [0,3]. O bem-estar de recursos é W(q,d)=(6-d)*q-q^2; as receitas fiscais são transferências, não entram como custo adicional.

Se d fosse conhecido, completo o quadrado: W(q,d)=(6-d)^2/4-(q-(6-d)/2)^2. A quantidade eficiente é qd=(6-d)/2, implementada por t=d. Quando d percorre [1,3], qd percorre [3/2,5/2]. O arrependimento relativamente à política informada é exatamente R(q,d)=(q-qd)^2.

Para minimizar o pior arrependimento, procuro o centro do intervalo de quantidades eficientes. Para qualquer q, a maior distância a um ponto do intervalo é a maior distância aos seus extremos. A desigualdade triangular obriga essa distância máxima a ser pelo menos metade do comprimento1, isto é1/2. O ponto médio q=2 atinge essa cota, logo t=2 e o pior arrependimento é1/4. Esta é uma prova global por geometria, sem enumerar parâmetros.

Para maximizar o menor bem-estar absoluto, observo que dW/dd=-q<=0. O pior estado é sempre d=3 para qualquer quantidade positiva. Nesse estado W(q,3)=3*q-q^2=9/4-(q-3/2)^2. Portanto q=3/2 e t=3 maximizam o mínimo, com valor9/4. A mesma política tem pior arrependimento1 no estado d=1, pois a quantidade eficiente aí seria5/2.

Para comparar de maneira simétrica, a política de menor arrependimento q=2 tem pior bem-estar W(2,3)=2, inferior a9/4. Ela sacrifica1/4 de garantia absoluta para reduzir o pior desvio do ótimo informado de1 para1/4. Os critérios usam referências diferentes: um compara cada decisão ao ótimo do seu próprio estado; o outro protege apenas o nível absoluto no pior estado.

Sob d uniforme em [1,3], E[d]=2 e E[W(q,d)]=4*q-q^2=4-(q-2)^2. A política esperada também escolhe q=2,t=2, mas por uma razão distinta da prova robusta. Como qd=(6-d)/2, a sua variância é Var(d)/4=(1/3)/4=1/12. O arrependimento esperado é(q-2)^2+1/12, igual a1/12 na política ótima.

Uma verificação independente calcula a receita no ponto q=2,t=2: ela é4. O excedente do consumidor é q^2/2=2, o do produtor é q^2/2=2, e o dano é2*d. Somando excedentes, receita e dano negativo dá8-2*d, idêntico a W(2,d). No estado médio d=2 o bem-estar é4; no pior estado d=3 ele é2, em acordo com as duas verificações anteriores.

General pattern: devo escrever a perda relativa como um quadrado antes de escolher uma política robusta. O centro de um intervalo minimiza a pior distância, enquanto a monotonicidade identifica o pior nível absoluto. Coincidência com uma política bayesiana não torna os objetivos equivalentes.
reference_answer:
O mercado produz q=(6-t)/2; com d conhecido, a política eficiente é t=d e q=(6-d)/2. O menor arrependimento máximo escolhe t=2,q=2 e tem perda máxima1/4.

O maior bem-estar mínimo escolhe t=3,q=3/2, garantindo9/4, mas com arrependimento máximo1. A primeira política garante apenas2 de bem-estar mínimo. Sob d uniforme, t=2 também maximiza o bem-estar esperado4 e tem arrependimento esperado1/12.

problem:
Can you check my bootstrap argument? I have observations from a uniform distribution with an unknown upper endpoint. I resampled the observations and used bootstrap percentiles of the sample maximum as a confidence interval for that endpoint. Why might increasing the number of bootstrap repetitions fail to fix this?

Let X1,...,Xn be independent Uniform[0,v], with unknown v>0 and integer n>=1. Set M=max(X1,...,Xn). An ordinary nonparametric bootstrap draws n observations independently with replacement from the observed empirical distribution and computes M_star. Conditional on the original data, assume the observed maximum is unique; this holds almost surely. Let r=exp(-1), a declared constant.

Derive the exact distribution of M/v and its first two moments. Give an unbiased endpoint estimator and its variance. Derive the finite-sample CDF of T=n*(v-M)/v on[0,n] and its limiting distribution. For the bootstrap analogue T_star=n*(M-M_star)/M, calculate exactly the conditional probability T_star=0 and its limit. Use this to prove that the ordinary bootstrap does not reproduce the sampling law of this scaled endpoint error.

For the concrete observed sample(1,2,3), with n=3, compute the bootstrap probabilities of M_star=1,2,3, its conditional mean and variance, and the conditional bootstrap bias estimate for M. Explain why any percentile-only interval whose upper endpoint is a bootstrap quantile of M_star has zero coverage for v in this continuous model.

As a model-based alternative, generate n fresh Uniform[0,M] observations and their maximum M_param. Compare the exact conditional law of n*(M-M_param)/M to T. Derive a confidence interval for v with exact coverage7/8 when n=3, and evaluate it for the concrete sample. Distinguish an exact pivot under the uniform model from a distribution-free bootstrap claim. No simulation or listing of all resampled sequences.
thinking:
Before resampling, I should identify the relevant scale. For0<=z<=1, P(M/v<=z)=P(all Xi<=v*z)=z^n, giving density n*z^(n-1). Its k-th moment is n/(n+k), so E[M]=n*v/(n+1) and Var(M)=n*v^2/[(n+1)^2*(n+2)]. The estimator H=(n+1)*M/n is unbiased for v, with Var(H)=v^2/[n*(n+2)]. Endpoint error is of order1/n, so a root-n normal approximation would erase its actual limiting variation.

For the exact pivot, T=n*(1-M/v). On0<=t<=n, F_T(t)=P(M/v>=1-t/n)=1-(1-t/n)^n. At t=0 this is0; below0 it is0 and above n it is1. For fixed t>=0, (1-t/n)^n tends to exp(-t), so T tends to an exponential distribution of mean1. This calculation uses the support boundary directly instead of invoking a regular likelihood theorem whose assumptions fail here.

For the bootstrap atom, M_star equals M exactly when at least one resampled observation is the unique original maximum. Each draw misses it with probability1-1/n, so P(T_star=0|data)=1-(1-1/n)^n, tending to1-r. The true T has no mass at0 and its limiting CDF is continuous there with value0. The bootstrap conditional CDF at0 instead tends to1-r>0. That one probability disproves consistency of the scaled bootstrap law; additional repetitions only estimate the wrong conditional law more accurately.

For the concrete sample, the bootstrap empirical CDF is1/3 at1,2/3 at2 and1 at3. Since the resampled maximum has CDF F_emp(x)^3, its probabilities are1/27,7/27,19/27. I need only difference adjacent CDF values, not enumerate27 sequences. Its mean is[1+2*7+3*19]/27=8/3. The second moment is[1+4*7+9*19]/27=200/27; subtracting64/9 gives variance8/27. The bootstrap bias estimate E_star[M_star]-M is-1/3.

For the bias interpretation, the true bias is-v/(n+1), whereas the conditional resampling calculation measures bias under a discrete empirical distribution whose endpoint is M. A finite-sample bias number does not repair the nonvanishing atom in the scaled distribution. Nor should I identify a bootstrap conditional expectation with the unknown population parameter merely because many resamples estimate that expectation precisely.

For the percentile failure, every ordinary bootstrap maximum is at most M, so every one of its quantiles is at most M. But M<v almost surely in the continuous uniform model. Any interval with such an upper endpoint therefore excludes v almost surely, giving coverage0. This conclusion concerns the stated percentile-only construction for M; it does not rule out model-based pivots, transformed estimators or every conceivable bootstrap interval.

For a model-based repair, fresh Uniform[0,M] samples have M_param/M with CDF z^n exactly, conditional on the positive observed M. Hence n*(M-M_param)/M has the same finite-sample pivot law1-(1-t/n)^n as T. This holds because the correct continuous shape and support scaling are supplied by the uniform model. The ordinary empirical resampling distribution supplies an atom at its endpoint instead, so the two procedures cannot be treated as interchangeable.

For exact coverage7/8 at n=3, P(M/v>=1/2)=1-(1/2)^3=7/8. The event M/v>=1/2 is equivalent to v<=2*M, while v>=M already holds almost surely. Thus[M,2*M] has exact coverage7/8; the observed sample gives[3,6]. I can check the same interval with the pivot: v<=2*M means T<=3/2, and F_T(3/2)=1-(1-1/2)^3=7/8. This is a second route to the coverage calculation, not a Monte Carlo estimate.

General pattern: I inspect support, convergence scale and atoms before trusting resampling. A continuous endpoint problem can be nonregular even when its distribution is simple. An exact pivot uses the model's scale invariance; resampling the empirical distribution cannot create values beyond its observed endpoint, and more repetitions cannot correct that structural limitation.
reference_answer:
M/v has CDF z^n on[0,1]. Thus E[M]=n*v/(n+1), Var(M)=n*v^2/[(n+1)^2*(n+2)], and H=(n+1)*M/n is unbiased with variance v^2/[n*(n+2)].

The scaled error has CDF1-(1-t/n)^n and tends to an exponential law of mean1. The ordinary bootstrap instead puts mass1-(1-1/n)^n at zero, tending to1-r. This contradicts the continuous limiting law.

For sample(1,2,3), the maximum's bootstrap probabilities are(1,7,19)/27, mean8/3, variance8/27 and estimated bias-1/3. All its bootstrap quantiles are<=M<v almost surely, so the stated percentile-only interval has coverage0.

Uniform[0,M] parametric sampling reproduces the pivot law exactly under the assumed model. For n=3, P(M/v>=1/2)=7/8 yields the exact interval[M,2*M], or[3,6] here. This is model-based coverage, not a distribution-free empirical-bootstrap guarantee.

problem:
I've checked every pair of machines and their failure indicators are independent. Can I multiply the three failure probabilities to estimate a simultaneous shutdown, or am I missing a pattern?

Three indicators X1,X2,X3 take values0 or1, where1 means failure. Each has probability1/2 of failing. Every pair is independent, so P(Xi=1,Xj=1)=1/4 for i!=j. There is no assumption of mutual independence. Put N=X1+X2+X3 and t=P(X1=X2=X3=1).

Derive all joint laws compatible with these conditions in terms of t, without assuming exchangeability in advance. Find the sharp range of t and give an explicit probabilistic construction attaining every point in that range. Explain when the three variables are mutually independent and what happens to P(X3=1|X1=X2=1).

Find the distribution, mean and variance of N. Use the probability generating function G(z)=E[z^N] to exhibit a perturbation of the independent-binomial law whose first two derivatives at z1 vanish. Explain what information first and second moments miss.

Give the sharp ranges of P(N>=2) and P(N>=1), and compare with the fully independent case. Check your result through a second route using the covariance matrix or a parity construction. Please do not search a grid of possible distributions.
thinking:
Before multiplying probabilities, I should isolate the unidentified joint term. Write t=P(111). Pairwise independence gives P(110)=P(101)=P(011)=1/4-t. The marginal condition for X1 then gives P(100)=1/2-(1/4-t)-(1/4-t)-t=t, and the same argument applies to the other singleton failures. Normalization gives P(000)=1/4-t. The constraints force this structure without assuming exchangeability: every state with an odd number of failures has mass t, and every state with an even number has mass1/4-t.

For feasible laws, I can use nonnegative masses instead of trying candidate distributions. All masses are nonnegative exactly when0<=t<=1/4. There are four states of each parity, so total mass is4*t+4*(1/4-t)=1. Summing over either missing indicator gives each pair's four outcomes probability1/4. Thus every t in the interval satisfies every stated constraint, proving the bounds are sharp rather than just necessary.

For a constructive check, I should use two independent fair bits U,V. Set X1=U,X2=V. If X3=U XOR V, all outcomes have even parity and t0. If X3=1-(U XOR V), they have odd parity and t1/4. Choose the odd construction with independent probability4*t and the even construction otherwise. Each parity state's mass becomes t or1/4-t, exactly as derived. The construction reveals how a third-order relation can survive even though every pair looks independent.

For mutual independence, each of the eight states must have probability(1/2)^3=1/8. This happens exactly at t1/8. In contrast, conditioning on two failures gives P(X3=1|X1=X2=1)=t/(1/4)=4*t, ranging from0 to1. Conditioning on only one failure leaves the probability1/2 by pairwise independence. One additional piece of conditioning can therefore expose dependence invisible to every pairwise check.

For the count distribution, the parity pattern gives P(N=0)=1/4-t, P(N=1)=3*t, P(N=2)=3/4-3*t, P(N=3)=t. Its mean is3*t+2*(3/4-3*t)+3*t=3/2. Its second moment is3*t+4*(3/4-3*t)+9*t=3, hence Var(N)=3-(3/2)^2=3/4. Both are identical to Binomial(3,1/2) for every feasible t. This does not make the count binomial.

For a cheaper explanation of the missing information, I can factor the generating-function difference. G(z)=(1/4-t)+3*t*z+(3/4-3*t)*z^2+t*z^3 equals[(1+z)/2]^3+(t-1/8)*(z-1)^3. The perturbation and its first two derivatives vanish at z1. Therefore normalization, E[N]=G'(1) and E[N*(N-1)]=G''(1) all remain unchanged. Its third derivative is6*t, so E[N*(N-1)*(N-2)]=6*t detects precisely the unidentified triple-failure probability.

For an independent variance route, pairwise independence implies Cov(Xi,Xj)=0 and Var(Xi)=1/4. The covariance matrix is(1/4)*I, and Var(N)=3/4 by summing its entries. This confirms the generating-function moments but cannot determine t. Expanding E[(X1-1/2)*(X2-1/2)*(X3-1/2)] gives t-1/8, a third-order centered interaction that the covariance matrix omits. The matrix is nonsingular even at the extreme parity laws, so a well-behaved covariance matrix is not a certificate of mutual independence.

For shutdown events, I should sum the count probabilities rather than substitute a binomial formula. P(N>=2)=3/4-2*t ranges sharply from1/4 to3/4. P(N>=1)=3/4+t ranges sharply from3/4 to1. At mutual independence t1/8, these probabilities are1/2 and7/8, with triple failure1/8. At the even-parity endpoint, triple failure is impossible but at least two failures occurs with probability3/4. At the odd-parity endpoint, triple failure has probability1/4 and at least one failure is certain. Different tail events can move in different directions.

For the interpretation, I should preserve the distinction between assumptions and deductions. Pairwise independence is actually given and is stronger than merely knowing the mean and variance of N. Yet it still leaves t free. Multiplying all three marginal probabilities would add mutual independence, selecting only one of the feasible laws. The count generating function supplies a compact certificate of which information is fixed and which remains unresolved.

General pattern: I can eliminate joint probabilities using marginal constraints, then enforce nonnegative masses to obtain sharp identification bounds. A parity construction proves attainability without distribution search. Factoring a generating-function perturbation as(z-1)^3 explains why low-order moments stay fixed while a third-order event changes. Pairwise independence controls covariance, but multiplying three probabilities requires a stronger joint assumption.
reference_answer:
All compatible joint laws give mass t to each odd-parity state and1/4-t to each even-parity state. Nonnegative masses require0<=t<=1/4, and mixing even and odd XOR constructions attains every value. Mutual independence occurs only at t1/8. The conditional probability of the third failure after two failures is4*t.

The count probabilities are(1/4-t,3*t,3/4-3*t,t), with mean3/2 and variance3/4. The identity G(z)=[(1+z)/2]^3+(t-1/8)*(z-1)^3 shows why the first two factorial moments cannot identify t; the third factorial moment is6*t.

Sharp ranges are P(N>=2) in[1/4,3/4] and P(N>=1) in[3/4,1]. Full independence gives1/2 and7/8, respectively. Pairwise independence alone does not justify the triple probability1/8; the parity construction and covariance calculation independently verify the distinction.

problem:
Two governments want to stop competing for investment. If coordinated taxes collect more revenue, does that mean coordination improves real welfare? Work through this hypothetical model with an elastic total capital supply.

Jurisdiction i has production Fi(ki)=6*ki-ki^2/2, ki>=0. The two governments simultaneously choose unit capital taxes ti in[0,4], maximizing receipts Ri=ti*ki. Competitive firms take the net rental price r>=0 as given. Capital providers supply total K=k1+k2 with real opportunity cost C(K)=K^2/4, so market clearing gives r=C'(K)=K/2. At an active jurisdiction Fi'(ki)-ti=r; at a zero-capital corner use the corresponding inequality. Governments commit taxes before this competitive allocation.

Derive the allocation for every allowed tax pair and prove it is feasible, including corners. Find the unique tax Nash equilibrium and the unique taxes maximizing combined receipts, using global best responses and a structural change of coordinates instead of searching tax pairs.

All firms, capital providers and tax receipts belong to the same combined population. Receipts are rebated as lump-sum transfers. No public-spending benefit, collection cost or tax-financed external effect is present. Real welfare is F1+F2-C(K). Compute welfare, total capital and revenue under Nash competition and revenue coordination, plus the efficient allocation. Decompose welfare into capital-provider surplus, firms' residual profits and receipts, and derive an exact volume-versus-allocation loss identity. Explain the sign of the coordination welfare change.
thinking:
Before treating capital as fixed, I should solve its supply condition. Active firms satisfy ki=6-ti-r and providers require r=K/2. Summing gives K=12-t1-t2-K, so K=6-(t1+t2)/2 and r=3-(t1+t2)/4. Then k1=3-3*t1/4+t2/4 and k2=3-3*t2/4+t1/4. With ti in[0,4], both are nonnegative and K>=2. A zero quantity occurs only at a corner such as(t1,t2)=(4,0); its net marginal product at zero equals r, so the boundary condition holds. The interior linear formulas therefore extend continuously to every allowed pair without producing negative capital.

For global best responses, Ri=ti*(3-3*ti/4+tj/4). Its curvature is-3/2 and its unrestricted vertex is ti=2+tj/6, which lies in[2,8/3] for all allowed tj. This vertex is feasible and uniquely maximizes receipts over the full tax interval, including the zero-base corner. Solving the two responses gives t1=t2=12/5, k1=k2=9/5, K=18/5 and r=9/5. Each government receives108/25, so total revenue is216/25.

A cheaper coordination route uses the mean tax u=(t1+t2)/2 and half-difference d=(t1-t2)/2. Total capital is6-u, while k1-k2=-2*d. Combined receipts become R=6*u-u^2-2*d^2=9-(u-3)^2-2*d^2. This square certifies the global maximum over every feasible tax pair, and its vertex u3,d0 is feasible. Thus the unique coordinated taxes are both3, with k1=k2=3/2,K3,r3/2 and total receipts9. Coordination raises receipts by9/25 while reducing capital by3/5.

For welfare, tax payments are internal transfers but capital's opportunity cost is real. Write z=k1-k2. Since k1^2+k2^2=(K^2+z^2)/2, total production is6*K-(K^2+z^2)/4. Subtracting C(K)=K^2/4 gives W=6*K-K^2/2-z^2/4=18-(K-6)^2/2-z^2/4. The efficient allocation is K6,z0, hence k1=k2=3,W18. Both a smaller total stock and unequal allocation lower welfare. Maximizing receipts is a different objective from maximizing this resource expression.

For the outcome comparison, Nash has K18/5 and z0, so W=18-(12/5)^2/2=378/25. Revenue coordination has K3,z0 and W=18-3^2/2=27/2. Thus coordination changes welfare by27/2-378/25=-81/50. The output-allocation component is zero in both symmetric outcomes; the entire decline comes from additional suppression of capital supply. Neither the larger receipt nor the lower rental price by itself measures that lost surplus.

For the accounting check, capital-provider surplus is r*K-C(K)=K^2/4. Each firm's residual profit is Fi(ki)-(r+ti)*ki=ki^2/2, using its active marginal-product condition. Adding provider surplus, residual profits and receipts cancels all rental and tax payments, leaving F1+F2-C(K). At Nash these components are81/25,81/25 and216/25, summing to378/25. Under coordination they are9/4,9/4 and9, summing to27/2. Real capital income must subtract providers' opportunity cost rather than count all rental receipts as net surplus.

For an independent production check, symmetric allocation gives total production6*K-K^2/4. Nash production is459/25 and real capital cost81/25, giving378/25. Coordination production is63/4 and real cost9/4, giving54/4=27/2. The welfare loss relative to efficiency is72/25 at Nash and9/2 under coordination; their increase is81/50, matching the direct difference. This checks both the transfer ledger and the completed welfare square.

For the policy interpretation, a tax cut by one government attracts capital from its rival and also increases the total stock supplied. Revenue coordination removes the incentive to undercut but its receipt objective disregards the real surplus from additional investment. In this declared model there is no public benefit to offset the added distortion. A fixed-total-capital calculation would omit the volume term and could produce a different welfare comparison; the supply primitive must be established before drawing the conclusion.

General pattern: I should solve tax allocation jointly with the capital-supply condition, then verify nonnegative bases on the entire policy domain. Mean and difference coordinates turn revenue coordination and welfare into global squares. Rental income and tax receipts cancel as transfers, while opportunity cost remains real. Separating the total-volume loss from the allocation loss prevents a revenue improvement from being mistaken for a welfare gain.
reference_answer:
For every allowed pair, ki=3-3*ti/4+tj/4 and K=6-(t1+t2)/2 are feasible. Global best responses ti=2+tj/6 give the unique Nash taxes12/5, capital9/5 per jurisdiction and total receipts216/25.

Combined revenue is9-(u-3)^2-2*d^2, so coordination uniquely chooses taxes3 each, capital3/2 each and revenue9. Its revenue gain is9/25, but real welfare falls from378/25 to27/2, a decline81/50.

Efficient capital is3 per jurisdiction with welfare18. The exact loss is(K-6)^2/2+(k1-k2)^2/4. Both tax outcomes allocate capital symmetrically; coordination increases only the volume distortion. Provider surplus, firm profits and receipts sum respectively to378/25 and27/2, independently confirming the real-cost calculation.

problem: Die Matrix A=[[3,0],[0,−2]] wirkt auf R². Bestimme ihre Operatornorm zur euklidischen Norm und erkläre, welcher Richtungsmodus sie erreicht.
thinking:
Vor dem Maximieren über alle Vektoren nutze ich die orthogonale Diagonalform. Für Einheitsvektor x=(u,v) gilt ||Ax||²=9u²+4v²≤9(u²+v²)=9. Also ist die Operatornorm höchstens3.

Der Einheitsvektor(1,0) erreicht Gleichheit, daher ist die Norm genau3. Die stärkste Streckung liegt in der ersten Koordinatenrichtung; die negative Skalierung−2 auf der zweiten Achse reflektiert und streckt nur um2.

Die Spektralnorm ist die Quadratwurzel des größten Eigenwerts von AᵀA=diag(9,4), también3. Das kontrolliert die Maximierung unabhängig über die quadratische Form.

General pattern: Bei diagonalen Matrizen ist die euklidische Operatornorm der größte Betrag eines Eigenwerts. AᵀA macht Längenstreckung sichtbar und entfernt Richtungszeichen.
reference_answer: Die Operatornorm ist 3, erreicht in Richtung (1,0).

problem: Explain why the harmonic series diverges without adding its terms one by one. Use grouping and keep the proof compact.
thinking: Group terms in dyadic blocks; each block contributes a fixed positive lower bound.
reference_answer: Group terms as 1, then 1/2, then 1/3+1/4, then 1/5 through 1/8, and so on. Each later block has 2^k terms at least 1/2^(k+1), hence contributes at least 1/2; infinitely many such blocks force divergence.

problem: Explain opportunity cost using a student choosing between a shift and studying; finish with a formula-like phrase, no symbols.
thinking: Opportunity cost is the value of the best forgone alternative, not the sum of every alternative.
reference_answer: If the student takes a paid shift, the opportunity cost is the value of the best study benefit they give up. Opportunity cost equals the value of the best forgone option.

problem:
My simulated action frequencies are uniform and neither player benefits from switching permanently to one action. Is that enough to call the recommendations a correlated equilibrium? Please help me check the conditional incentives exactly.

Two players choose R,P,S. Player1's payoff matrix, with its actions as rows and player2's actions as columns in that order, is A=[[0,-1,1],[1,0,-1],[-1,1,0]]. Player2 gets the negative of A. A mediator draws an ordered action pair and privately recommends each player's own action. Consider the law assigning probability1/6 to each unequal-action pair and zero to equal-action pairs. Each player observes only their own recommendation.

A coarse correlated equilibrium permits deviations selected before seeing the recommendation: a fixed action or independently randomized action instead of obedience. A correlated equilibrium also permits a player to condition the deviation on their own observed recommendation. Use these definitions as given.

Compute the recommended payoffs, marginals and best fixed-deviation payoff. For each possible recommendation, find the best conditional deviation and its conditional gain; give a single recommendation-dependent rule and its overall gain. Decide whether the proposed law is coarse correlated, correlated or an independently mixed Nash profile.

Go beyond this one example: characterize every coarse correlated law by its marginals and expected payoff, and prove that the unique correlated law for this particular game is the independent uniform law. Prove the unique mixed Nash profile too. Your proof should use zero-sum security and nonnegative incentive gaps, not try probability tables one at a time. Explain why aggregate no-fixed-deviation checks miss the flaw.
thinking:
Before testing incentives, I should separate joint law from marginals. The six off-diagonal pairs each have probability1/6, so both players recommend R,P,S with probabilities1/3. Three pairs give player1 payoff1 and three give-1, hence both recommended expected payoffs are0. Against the opponent's uniform marginal, any fixed action gives0. Independent randomization over fixed actions also gives0 by linearity. Thus the law satisfies every coarse deviation check.

For the recommendation R, the opponent is P or S with conditional probability1/2 each. Obedient R averages(-1+1)/2=0. Switching to S averages(1+0)/2=1/2, whereas switching to P averages(0-1)/2=-1/2. Under recommendation P the best switch is R; under S it is P, each giving1/2 instead of0. The same calculations hold for player2 with their own action as the first argument of the symmetric win rule. Conditioning reveals information that was absent in the marginal action frequencies.

For a single profitable policy, I use g(R)=S,g(P)=R,g(S)=P. Each recommendation occurs with probability1/3 and has gain1/2, so the total unilateral gain is1/2. This is a valid private recommendation-dependent deviation, not a deviation requiring observation of the opponent. The law is therefore coarse correlated but not correlated. It is also not an independently mixed Nash profile: independent uniform actions would put1/9 on each of the nine pairs, including the diagonal.

For the full coarse characterization, write u for player1's expected recommended payoff, p for its marginal and q for player2's. A deviation to independent uniform play secures0 regardless of the opponent. The two coarse constraints therefore imply u>=0 and-u>=0, so u=0. Every player1 fixed deviation against q must then give at most0. The three action values are q_S-q_P,q_R-q_S,q_P-q_R, whose sum is0. All are at most0 only if all are0, hence q is uniform. Applying the same argument to player2 forces p uniform.

For the converse, any joint probability matrix with both marginals uniform and expected payoff u=0 satisfies the coarse conditions, because every fixed or independently randomized deviation gives0. Thus these conditions are necessary and sufficient. In matrix terms each row and column sum is1/3, and total mass on the three player1-winning cells equals total mass on the losing cells. Independence is not part of this characterization. Both the proposed off-diagonal law and the law concentrated equally on the three diagonal cells satisfy it.

For correlated uniqueness, any correlated law is also coarse, so it has uniform marginals and u=0. Fix a possible replacement action k for player1. For each recommendation i, the weighted obedience gap sum_j pi_ij*(A_ij-A_kj) is nonnegative by the correlated inequalities. Summing over i gives u minus the fixed-k payoff against the uniform q, which is0. A sum of nonnegative gaps can vanish only if every gap vanishes. Repeating for all k shows that at each recommendation every alternative action has the same conditional value as obedience.

For the conditional distribution implication, let q_given_i be the opponent's probabilities conditional on recommendation i. The three conditional action values must all coincide; their sum is0, so all are0. The same cyclic-difference equations force q_given_i=(1/3,1/3,1/3). Each recommendation i itself has marginal probability1/3, hence pi_ij=(1/3)*(1/3)=1/9 for every pair. Conversely this independent uniform law gives zero conditional incentive gaps for both players. It is therefore the unique correlated equilibrium, proved by equality certificates rather than searching joint distributions.

For mixed Nash uniqueness, independent uniform play gives security0 to each player. At any Nash equilibrium the two security inequalities force value0. The fixed-deviation inequalities then force each opponent marginal uniform by the same cyclic-difference argument. Independent private randomization therefore gives the unique Nash joint law with all entries1/9. There is no pure equilibrium because no pure action distribution is uniform. The zero-sum argument links the Nash, coarse and correlated questions while respecting their different information and deviation sets.

General pattern: I test incentives with the information available when a deviation is chosen. Uniform marginals and zero fixed-action regret can conceal profitable conditional rules. In a zero-sum game, security forces the value; nonnegative conditional gaps whose aggregate is zero can then pin down the entire recommendation law.
reference_answer:
The proposed law has uniform marginals and payoff0 to both players. Every fixed deviation also gives0, so it is coarse correlated. After observing a recommendation, each player can use R->S,P->R,S->P and gain1/2 conditionally and overall. It is not correlated and not an independent Nash law.

Every coarse correlated law is characterized by uniform marginals and expected payoff0; these conditions are also sufficient. In contrast, correlated inequalities force every conditional obedience gap to be zero, then force the opponent's conditional distribution to be uniform. The unique correlated law is therefore the all-1/9 matrix. The unique mixed Nash profile is independent uniform play, with payoff0. Aggregate fixed-action checks omit the information revealed by recommendations.

problem: A restricted regression has residual sum of squares120. An unrestricted model adds2 regressors and has residual sum of squares90, using n=50 observations and5 unrestricted parameters. Compute the partial F-statistic for the joint null that both added coefficients are zero, and state the degrees of freedom.
thinking:
The restricted model loses30 units of residual sum of squares when two regressors are added. The partial F-statistic divides the average reduction per restriction by the unrestricted residual variance estimate: F=[(120−90)/2]/[90/(50−5)]=15/2=7.5.

The numerator degrees of freedom are2 restrictions; the denominator degrees of freedom are50−5=45 residual degrees. Under the classical homoskedastic Gaussian linear model and the joint null, this statistic follows an F distribution with(2,45) degrees of freedom.

The test asks whether the two added variables jointly improve fit beyond sampling noise; it does not test each coefficient separately. Their individual t-tests may differ because the estimates can be correlated, while the joint restriction is invariant to a reparameterization of the two coefficients.

As a check, the numerator uses the restricted-unrestricted RSS gap30 divided by2, and the denominator uses90 spread over45 residual degrees, equal2. Their ratio is7.5. The unrestricted model must be nested and estimated on the same observations for this comparison to be valid.

General pattern: A partial F-test compares the RSS improvement per restriction with the unrestricted residual variance per residual degree of freedom. Nesting, common samples, and the correct restriction count determine the reference distribution.
reference_answer: Partial F-statistic=7.5 with degrees of freedom(2,45).
