problem: Can you derive the one-year forward rate from these bond prices? A default-free zero-coupon bond paying1 in one year costs10/11; a bond paying1 in two years costs5/6. Find the gross and net one-year forward return from year1 to year2, and verify that rolling over a one-year investment replicates the two-year discount factor.
thinking:
A two-year investment can be built either by buying the two-year zero today for5/6 or by investing over year1 and locking the year1-to-year2 gross return F. No arbitrage requires the two paths to have the same cost for one unit at year2: (10/11)(1/F)=5/6 when written as discount factors.

Equivalently, the forward discount factor is P₂/P₁=(5/6)/(10/11)=11/12. Its reciprocal is the forward gross return F=12/11, so the net forward rate is1/11. Keeping discount factors and gross returns reciprocal prevents a common sign and inversion error.

The rollover check is P₁ times the forward discount factor=(10/11)(11/12)=5/6=P₂. Thus a one-year bond followed by a forward-locked second year reproduces the two-year zero-coupon price exactly.

The forward rate is implied by today's term structure; it need not equal the market's expected future spot rate without additional assumptions about risk premia. Here no-arbitrage pins down the replicating return, not subjective expectations.

General pattern: Forward discount factors are ratios of zero-coupon prices across maturities, while forward gross returns are their reciprocals. Replication equates present costs across investment paths; expectations require separate assumptions beyond arbitrage.
reference_answer: Forward discount factor=11/12. Forward gross return=12/11 and net rate=1/11. Rollover: (10/11)(11/12)=5/6, equal to the two-year bond price.

problem: Je bloque sur le financement personnalisé: si les ménages possèdent le producteur, faut-il inclure son profit dans leurs revenus avant de calculer leurs demandes? Deux ménages ont des dotations privées w1=9,w2=3 et une utilité ui=sqrt(xi*y), où y>=0 est un bien public non rival. Son coût en bien privé est K(y)=y^2/2; le prix du privé est1. Le producteur reçoit(lambda1+lambda2)*y, prend les prix comme donnés et maximise son profit pi. Le ménage1 reçoit la fraction alpha de ce profit et le ménage2 reçoit1-alpha, avec alpha dans[0,1]. Chacun prend son revenu mi=wi+sa part de pi comme donné lorsqu'il choisit sa demande de bien public, sous xi+lambdai*y=mi. Un équilibre de financement personnalisé exige que les deux demandes et l'offre de y coïncident. Détermine cet équilibre pour tout alpha, les consommations, prix, paiements, profits et utilités. Calcule les deux cas de propriété alpha=1 et alpha=0. Un prix personnalisé identique pour les deux peut-il fonctionner ici? Dérive aussi la frontière de Pareto de l'économie complète à partir de x1+x2+y^2/2<=12, et prouve l'efficacité de l'équilibre sans confondre efficacité et maximisation de la somme des utilités. Explique ce qui manque dans le calcul qui utilise directement revenus9 et3 et obtient y=sqrt(6).
thinking:
Avant de résoudre, je dois distinguer dotations et revenus. Les dotations totalisent12 unités du privé. Les profits distribués s'ajoutent aux budgets monétaires mais ne créent pas de ressources: la contrainte physique reste x1+x2+y^2/2<=12. Pour chaque ménage, ui=sqrt(xi*y) est croissante quand les deux biens sont positifs. Maximiser ui revient alors à maximiser xi*y=(mi-lambdai*y)*y, une quadratique strictement concave si lambdai>0.

Pour la demande individuelle, la condition est mi-2*lambdai*y=0, donc y=mi/(2*lambdai), xi=mi/2 et paiement lambdai*y=mi/2. Le ménage traite les dividendes comme donnés dans cette optimisation de price-taker; il ne différencie pas le profit du producteur par rapport à sa propre demande. Je dois ensuite imposer leur cohérence au niveau de l'équilibre. Pour le producteur, la concavité donne y=lambda1+lambda2 et pi=(lambda1+lambda2)*y-y^2/2=y^2/2.

Pour la fermeture des budgets, les deux demandes communes donnent lambda1+lambda2=(m1+m2)/(2*y). Or m1+m2=12+pi=12+y^2/2. En combinant avec l'offre y=lambda1+lambda2, j'obtiens2*y^2=12+y^2/2, donc y^2=8 et y=2*sqrt(2). Le profit est4. Cette équation scalaire est le raccourci utile: l'agrégation élimine alpha avant de déterminer la quantité. La propriété modifie ensuite la répartition, pas cette production.

Pour les variables individuelles, m1=9+4*alpha et m2=7-4*alpha. Les consommations et paiements sont chacun la moitié du revenu: x1=(9+4*alpha)/2, x2=(7-4*alpha)/2. Les prix sont lambda1=(9+4*alpha)/(4*sqrt(2)) et lambda2=(7-4*alpha)/(4*sqrt(2)). Les utilités vérifient u1^2=(9+4*alpha)*sqrt(2) et u2^2=(7-4*alpha)*sqrt(2). Les revenus restent strictement positifs sur[0,1], donc les demandes intérieures utilisées sont valides.

Pour la propriété concentrée, alpha=1 donne revenus(13,3), consommations et paiements(13/2,3/2), prix(13/(4*sqrt(2)),3/(4*sqrt(2))) et utilités(sqrt(13*sqrt(2)),sqrt(3*sqrt(2))). À alpha=0, les revenus sont(9,7), les consommations et paiements(9/2,7/2), les prix(9/(4*sqrt(2)),7/(4*sqrt(2))) et les utilités(sqrt(9*sqrt(2)),sqrt(7*sqrt(2))). Dans les deux cas, y=2*sqrt(2) et pi=4. L'efficacité ne rend pas ces allocations distributivement équivalentes.

Pour le prix uniforme, une même quantité désirée avec lambda1=lambda2 exigerait m1=m2. L'équation9+4*alpha=7-4*alpha donne alpha=-1/4, hors de[0,1]. Aucun partage de propriété admissible ne rend donc les demandes identiques à un prix commun dans ce système. Les prix personnalisés ajustent ici des demandes différentes; cela ne prouve pas que les ménages révéleraient honnêtement leurs préférences si ces prix dépendaient de leurs déclarations.

Pour la frontière de Pareto, je devrais exploiter une identité en utilités plutôt qu'imposer un critère cardinal. Pour y>0, u1^2+u2^2=y*(x1+x2)<=12*y-y^3/2=H(y). Le maximum de H est atteint à y=2*sqrt(2), et vaut16*sqrt(2). Je peux le prouver sans réutiliser les équations de marché: en posant a=2*sqrt(2), H(a)-H(y)=(y-a)^2*(y+2*a)/2>=0 pour y>=0. Ainsi tout couple d'utilités réalisable satisfait u1,u2>=0 et u1^2+u2^2<=16*sqrt(2).

Pour la réciproque, tout couple non négatif dans ce quart de disque est réalisable en prenant y=a et xi=ui^2/a. La somme des consommations vaut au plus16*sqrt(2)/(2*sqrt(2))=8, et le coût vaut4, donc la contrainte physique est respectée. La frontière de Pareto est exactement l'arc u1^2+u2^2=16*sqrt(2). Un point intérieur peut augmenter les deux utilités s'il est strictement positif, ou améliorer au moins l'une sans diminuer l'autre aux axes; un point sur l'arc ne permet aucune amélioration de Pareto. Cette caractérisation inclut les extrêmes où une personne reçoit toute la consommation privée.

Pour vérifier l'équilibre, x1+x2=8 et K(y)=4 épuisent exactement les12 ressources. Les paiements totalisent8: ils couvrent4 de coût et4 de profit redistribué. Les utilités d'équilibre vérifient u1^2+u2^2=(9+4*alpha+7-4*alpha)*sqrt(2)=16*sqrt(2), donc elles sont sur la frontière. Un contrôle marginal indépendant donne TMSi=ui_y/ui_x=xi/y; leur somme est8/(2*sqrt(2))=2*sqrt(2)=K'(y). La condition de Samuelson concorde avec la preuve globale, sans choisir une somme d'utilités comme objectif social.

Pour le calcul y=sqrt(6), utiliser seulement9 et3 comme revenus donne demandes agrégées12/(2*y), puis y^2=6. Mais le producteur gagne alors pi=3, et ces profits sont dus aux ménages propriétaires. Les ignorer donne x1+x2=6 et coût3, soit9 ressources utilisées au lieu de12; les budgets de revenu et le marché du privé ne sont pas fermés. Réintroduire les dividendes change les demandes et conduit à y^2=8. Je ne dois pas appeler équilibre général une solution partielle qui omet le revenu de propriété.

General pattern: je dois fermer les budgets avec les profits avant de comparer offre et demandes. Une identité agrégée peut éliminer les parts de propriété et fixer la production, tandis qu'une identité en utilités révèle la frontière de Pareto. Les prix personnalisés assurent la cohérence marginale, mais les transferts et la propriété déterminent la répartition.
reference_answer:
Pour tout alpha dans[0,1], y=2*sqrt(2), pi=4, revenus(9+4*alpha,7-4*alpha), consommations et paiements((9+4*alpha)/2,(7-4*alpha)/2). Les prix personnalisés sont((9+4*alpha)/(4*sqrt(2)),(7-4*alpha)/(4*sqrt(2))) et les utilités sont(sqrt((9+4*alpha)*sqrt(2)),sqrt((7-4*alpha)*sqrt(2))).

À alpha=1, consommations et paiements valent(13/2,3/2); à alpha=0, ils valent(9/2,7/2). Le prix uniforme exigerait alpha=-1/4, donc il ne fonctionne pour aucune propriété admissible.

La frontière de Pareto est u1,u2>=0 et u1^2+u2^2=16*sqrt(2). L'identité de perte H(a)-H(y)=(y-a)^2*(y+2*a)/2, avec H(y)=12*y-y^3/2 et a=2*sqrt(2), en prouve la borne globale. L'équilibre atteint cette frontière et utilise8 de consommation privée plus4 de coût. Le calcul y=sqrt(6) omet3 de profits revenant aux ménages et ne ferme donc pas les budgets ni le marché du privé.

problem: Help me check my standard error: I treated six panel observations as independent. In a hypothetical model there are three groups with two observations each, Ygi=beta*xgi+Ag+epsilon_gi. The regressor is fixed, with group pairs(-3,-1),(0,2),(1,1). There is no intercept or other regressor in the fitted model. Group shocks have mean0 and variance3; individual errors have mean0 and variance1. All these shocks are mutually independent across groups and individuals. No Gaussian assumption is needed. The observed Y pairs are(-4,-1),(1,4),(3,2). Derive the OLS estimator and its actual variance, compare with the variance obtained by wrongly using identity error covariance, and construct the unique minimum-variance linear unbiased estimator using known covariance. Avoid inverting a six-by-six matrix blindly: decompose the regressor into within-group deviations and repeated group means. Compute the within-only estimator, its variance and its relation to GLS. Prove the global linear-unbiased optimality of GLS. Replace Var(Ag)=3 by t>=0 and examine t=0 and t tending to infinity. Finally, if Ag are instead arbitrary unknown group constants, which displayed estimator remains unbiased conditional on those constants, and why do the random-effects GLS assumptions matter?
thinking:
Before calculating a standard error, I should write the covariance created by the shared shock. Each group block is Omega_g=I2+3*J2, where J2 has every entry1. Its diagonal entries are4 and off-diagonal entries3; different blocks are independent. The problem supplies covariance, not just individual error variance. The observed regressor vector is x=(-3,-1,0,2,1,1), with x'x=16, so OLS weights are x/16.

For a cheaper inverse, I should recognise the within-between eigenmodes. The group-mean projection P_B replaces each pair by its mean; P_W=I-P_B removes that mean. Since J2=2*P_B within each block, Omega=P_W+7*P_B and Omega_inverse=P_W+P_B/7. Applying those projections to x gives xW=(-1,1,-1,1,0,0) and xB=(-2,-2,1,1,1,1). Their inner product is0, with squared lengths4 and12. I can now work with two scalars instead of six simultaneous equations.

For OLS, beta_OLS=x'Y/16. The data give x'Y=12+1+0+8+3+2=26, hence beta_OLS=13/8. Its actual variance is x'Omega*x/16^2=(4+7*12)/256=11/32. The identity-covariance calculation would give1/16; it understates variance by a factor(11/32)/(1/16)=11/2. The estimator stays unbiased under the stated zero-mean random-effects assumptions, but unbiasedness does not validate that naive standard error.

For GLS, the information is x'Omega_inverse*x=4+12/7=40/7. Thus its weights are Omega_inverse*x/(40/7)=(7*xW+xB)/40=(-9,5,-6,8,1,1)/40. The observed estimate is(36-5-6+32+3+2)/40=31/20, and its variance is the inverse information7/40. I should check unbiasedness directly: the weighted regressor equals(27-5+0+16+1+1)/40=1.

For an independent variance check, the GLS weights have within part(7/40)*xW and between part(1/40)*xB. Their variance is(7/40)^2*4+7*(1/40)^2*12=(196+84)/1600=7/40. This calculation uses the covariance eigenvalues rather than the reciprocal-information formula. It also shows why treating all six weights as if errors were independent would discard the between-mode variance.

For the within-only estimate, group means disappear because P_W removes every repeated group constant. Beta_W=xW'Y/4=(-Y11+Y12-Y21+Y22)/4=3/2. Its variance is1/4, since Omega acts as the identity on xW. The between-only estimate is beta_B=xB'Y/12=20/12=5/3, with variance7/12. The two estimates are uncorrelated: their cross-covariance is xW'Omega*xB/(4*12)=0. Without Gaussian assumptions I should say uncorrelated, not automatically independent.

For the link between estimates, inverse-variance weighting gives beta_GLS=[4*beta_W+(12/7)*beta_B]/[4+12/7]=(7/10)*beta_W+(3/10)*beta_B. Substitution gives(7/10)*(3/2)+(3/10)*(5/3)=31/20. The combined variance is(7/10)^2/4+(3/10)^2*(7/12)=7/40, another check using two observable summaries. GLS uses between-group information because the random group effects have a specified zero mean and known variance.

For global optimality, let w be the GLS weight vector and v=w+u any other linear unbiased weight vector. Unbiasedness requires v'x=w'x=1, hence u'x=0. Since Omega*w=x/(x'Omega_inverse*x), the cross term w'Omega*u is0. Therefore Var(v'Y)=Var(w'Y)+u'Omega*u. Omega is positive definite, with eigenvalues1 and7, so the last term is nonnegative and vanishes only at u=0. This proves a unique global minimum over all linear unbiased estimators; it does not assert optimality over arbitrary nonlinear estimators without further assumptions.

For arbitrary random-effect variance t, the between eigenvalue is lambda=1+2*t while the within eigenvalue remains1. The same projection gives GLS weights(lambda*xW+xB)/(4*lambda+12), variance lambda/(4*lambda+12), and beta_GLS=[lambda/(lambda+3)]*beta_W+[3/(lambda+3)]*beta_B. At t=0, lambda=1 and these weights become x/16, so GLS equals OLS and variance is1/16. As t tends to infinity, between information12/lambda vanishes: GLS tends to beta_W=3/2 and variance tends to1/4.

For the OLS limit, its actual variance at arbitrary t is[4+12*(1+2*t)]/256=(2+3*t)/32. It diverges as t grows, while GLS discounts the contaminated between mode. That contrast is not a claim that within data become more precise; their information stays4. GLS simply stops using a mode whose shock variance grows without bound.

For unknown fixed group effects, I must replace the mean assumption rather than reuse the random-effects conclusion. If Ag is an arbitrary constant alpha_g, the within estimator annihilates its vector exactly and remains unbiased conditional on all alpha_g. OLS has conditional bias[(-4)*alpha1+2*alpha2+2*alpha3]/16. The displayed t=3 GLS has bias[(-4)*alpha1+2*alpha2+2*alpha3]/40, from its group weight sums. Those biases can vanish accidentally, but do not vanish for every fixed-effect vector. A covariance-efficient estimator under zero-mean random effects is not automatically valid when the group effects are unrestricted constants.

General pattern: I should search for covariance eigenmodes that also have an economic meaning. Within projections remove shared shocks; between projections carry both signal and shared uncertainty. Orthogonal modes turn GLS into precision-weighted summaries, and a zero cross term proves global linear-unbiased optimality. Changing random effects into fixed effects changes the unbiasedness constraints, not just the covariance scale.
reference_answer:
OLS gives13/8. Its actual variance is11/32, whereas the incorrect identity-covariance calculation gives1/16.

The unique minimum-variance linear unbiased estimator has weights(-9,5,-6,8,1,1)/40, estimate31/20 and variance7/40. The within estimate is3/2 with variance1/4; GLS combines it with the between estimate5/3 using weights7/10 and3/10. For any competing unbiased weights w+u, the extra variance is u'Omega*u>=0, with equality only at u=0.

With Var(Ag)=t, put lambda=1+2*t. GLS weights are(lambda*xW+xB)/(4*lambda+12) and variance lambda/(4*lambda+12). It equals OLS at t=0 and tends to the within estimator as t grows. With arbitrary fixed group effects, only the within estimator among these displayed estimators is unbiased for every group-effect vector.

problem: A monopolist faces inverse demand P=40−Q, marginal cost10, and fixed operating cost200. Find the profit-maximizing quantity and determine whether the firm should operate when the fixed cost is avoidable.
thinking:
The fixed cost does not change the interior quantity condition because it is constant in Q. Variable profit is(40−Q−10)Q, whose derivative30−2Q vanishes at Q=15; concavity makes this the unique variable-profit maximum.

At Q=15, price is25 and variable profit is(25−10)·15=225. Subtracting avoidable fixed cost200 leaves operating profit25, so the firm operates.

The shutdown comparison is with zero profit, not with the fixed cost alone: the relevant threshold is maximum variable profit225. If the fixed cost were sunk and unavoidable, the firm would still produce15 even when net accounting profit were negative.

As a check, at the monopoly quantity marginal revenue40−2Q equals10. If fixed cost rose above225, no output could cover it because225 is already the largest attainable contribution toward fixed cost.

General pattern: Choose output by marginal conditions, then decide operation by comparing maximum variable profit with avoidable fixed cost. Sunk costs affect accounting profit but not the current production choice.
reference_answer: The firm chooses Q=15 and P=25. Variable profit is225; after avoidable fixed cost200 it earns25, so it operates.

problem: Player 1 chooses H or T. Player 2 observes a private signal that equals player 1's choice with probability 3/4, independently of that choice, and then chooses H or T. Player 1 receives 1 for matching choices and -1 otherwise; player 2 receives the opposite. Strategies and the signal technology are known. Derive every equilibrium choice probability p=P(player 1 chooses H), player 2's signal-contingent strategy, and the game value. Give the posterior probabilities at p=1/2 and explain why symmetry alone does not prove a unique first-player mixture.
thinking:
Before choosing a symmetric prior, I should derive signal posteriors for general p. With signal H, posterior probability of the first choice H is 3*p/(1+2*p). With signal T it is p/(3-2*p). Player 2 minimises matches, so chooses T after signal H when the first posterior is at least 1/2, requiring p>=1/4, and chooses H after signal T when the second is at most 1/2, requiring p<=3/4.

To find the first player's incentive, let rH and rT be probabilities that player 2 chooses H after each signal. Matching probability after first choice H is (3/4)*rH+(1/4)*rT. After first choice T it is 1-(1/4)*rH-(3/4)*rT. An interior first-player mixture therefore requires rH+rT=1. When p lies strictly between 1/4 and 3/4, the unique signal responses are rH=0,rT=1, satisfying that condition.

To handle the endpoints rather than discard them, at p=1/4 player 2 is indifferent after signal H but strictly chooses H after signal T. Thus rT=1 and first-player indifference forces rH=0. At p=3/4 the opposite signal is indifferent, but rH=0 forces rT=1. The same deterministic opposite-signal strategy supports both boundary probabilities.

For completeness, if p<1/4 both posteriors favour T, so player 2 chooses H at both signals. Player 1 then strictly prefers H, contradicting p<1/4. If p>3/4, player 2 chooses T at both signals, so player 1 strictly prefers T, again a contradiction. The pure p=0 andp=1 profiles are included in these exclusions. Hence all equilibria have p in [1/4,3/4] and the same opposite-signal response.

To compute value, the opposite-signal strategy matches with probability 1/4 against either first choice. Player 1's payoff is 2*(1/4)-1=-1/2, and player 2 receives 1/2. At p=1/2, the posteriors are 3/4 and 1/4, so the strategy is strictly optimal at both information sets. The signal value does not require p=1/2 uniquely.

An independent zero-sum check uses an equalising strategy. Player 2's opposite-signal rule guarantees first-player payoff -1/2 for either pure action. Any p in the derived interval makes that rule a Bayesian best response, so no other second-player strategy can improve its payoff against such p. These two inequalities establish the game value and the continuum without trying individual mixtures.

General pattern: I should derive posterior thresholds before invoking symmetry. A signal-contingent equalising strategy can support an interval of priors; endpoint indifference must still satisfy the opponent's incentive equation. Symmetry supplies an equilibrium candidate, not a uniqueness theorem.
reference_answer:
All equilibria have p in [1/4,3/4]. Player 2 chooses T after signal H and H after signal T, including the endpoints. Player 1's value is -1/2.

At p=1/2 the posteriors are 3/4 and 1/4. Bayesian response thresholds define the interval, and first-player indifference pins down the same response at its boundaries. Therefore the symmetric mixture is one equilibrium among a continuum.

problem: A survey response rate differs by region, and the regions have different mean outcomes. Region A is half the population, responds with probability1/2, and has mean outcome4. Region B is half the population, responds with probability1/4, and has mean outcome8. Compute the complete-case respondent mean and the inverse-probability-weighted population mean. State the missingness assumptions that make the correction valid.
thinking:
Before averaging respondents, I check how the sample composition changed. Expected respondent mass from A is(1/2)(1/2)=1/4, while B contributes(1/2)(1/4)=1/8. Thus respondents are two-thirds A and one-third B, so the unweighted mean is(2/3)4+(1/3)8=16/3, below the population mean because high-outcome region B responds less often.

Inverse-probability weighting restores each region's population mass. A respondent receives weight2 and a B respondent weight4. The weighted outcome total per population member is(1/2)(1/2)(2)(4)+(1/2)(1/4)(4)(8)=2+4=6; the weighted mass is(1/2)(1/2)(2)+(1/2)(1/4)(4)=1. The normalized estimate is6.

The correction requires response to be independent of the outcome conditional on region, so each region's respondents represent its nonrespondents in expectation. It also requires positive response probability in every region; if a region never responds, no finite inverse weight can recover its unobserved outcomes from these data.

As a check, the population mean calculated directly is(1/2)4+(1/2)8=6, matching the weighted value. The complete-case mean16/3 instead uses respondent shares2/3 and1/3. Weighting changes only the composition back to one-half per region; it does not alter the observed within-region means.

General pattern: Inverse-probability weighting corrects selection on observed covariates by restoring their target-population distribution. Divide each respondent's contribution by its conditional response probability, normalize the weighted total, and make the missing-at-random and positivity assumptions explicit.
reference_answer: The respondent shares are2/3 for A and1/3 for B, giving complete-case mean16/3. Inverse response weights2 and4 restore equal population shares, yielding weighted mean6, equal to the population mean. Validity requires response to be conditionally independent of outcomes within region and positive response probability in both regions.

problem: I'm confused about tax incidence when a price cap creates a shortage. Consumers have demand D(pc)=max(0,10-pc), with a unit mass per unit of willingness to pay from0 to10. Competitive producers supply S(pp)=max(0,pp-2). A unit tax t>=0 creates pc-pp=t. First solve the unrestricted market. Now impose consumer price cap7: when the unrestricted price exceeds7, trade occurs at pc=7 and available supply determines quantity; for zero supply use the limiting quote7. Find the tax regimes, the revenue-maximising tax with and without the cap, and quantities. At t=3 compare welfare without the cap and with the cap under efficient rationing. Then find the sharp welfare range if any allocation among consumers willing to pay7 is allowed, and expected welfare under uniform random rationing. Treat tax revenue as a transfer and explain which incidence conclusions need a rationing rule.
thinking:
Before equating supply and demand, I should identify whether the cap binds. Without the cap,10-pc=pp-2 and pc=pp+t give q=4-t/2, pc=6+t/2 and pp=6-t/2 for0<=t<8. At t>=8 no positive mutually acceptable trade remains. On the positive-trade branch, buyers and sellers each absorb half a marginal tax: dpc/dt=1/2 and dpp/dt=-1/2.

With the cap, the unrestricted consumer price reaches7 at t=2. Hence for0<=t<=2 the unrestricted outcome applies. For2<t<5, pc=7, pp=7-t and supply q=5-t, while demand at7 remains3. The shortage grows as t-2. At t>=5 supply is zero. I should use these analytically derived thresholds, rather than repeatedly trying tax values.

For revenue without the cap, R=t*(4-t/2)=8-(t-4)^2/2 on[0,8]. Its global maximum is8 at t=4 and q=2. With the cap, revenue on[0,2] is the same increasing quadratic, ending at6. On[2,5], R=t*(5-t)=25/4-(t-5/2)^2, whose maximum is25/4 at t=5/2 and q=5/2. Revenue is zero after supply shuts down. Thus the cap changes the revenue peak even though its buyer price remains fixed on the shortage branch.

For resource welfare with efficient allocation, total willingness to pay is10*q-q^2/2 and producer resource cost is2*q+q^2/2. Their difference is W=8*q-q^2=16-(q-4)^2. At t=3 without the cap, q=5/2, pc=15/2, pp=9/2 and W=55/4. With the cap, q=2, pc=7, pp=4 and efficient-rationing welfare is12. The cap causes an additional welfare loss7/4 in this comparison.

For an independent accounting check at the capped outcome, the highest-valued two consumers have values from8 to10. Their surplus is integral from8 to10 of(v-7), namely4. Producer surplus is q^2/2=2 and tax revenue is t*q=6. Their sum12 agrees with the primitive-resource calculation. This sum would change if rationing selected a different set of consumers; supply quantity alone does not identify consumer surplus.

For sharp rationing bounds, the eligible consumers have values in[7,10] and total mass3. Choosing mass2 from them maximises total value at[8,10] and minimises it at[7,9]. Consumer surplus therefore ranges from2 to4. Producer surplus2 and revenue6 stay fixed, giving welfare range[10,12]. Moving a selected consumer's place to a higher-valued unselected consumer can only raise welfare; this exchange argument proves the endpoints are globally sharp without listing allocations.

For uniform random rationing, each eligible consumer is served with probability2/3. Expected total gross value is(2/3)*integral from7 to10 of v, which is17. Producer resource cost at q=2 is6, so expected welfare is11. Equivalently expected CS=(2/3)*integral from7 to10 of(v-7)=3, then3+2+6=11. Random rationing lies midway between the sharp extreme values but is below efficient rationing.

For incidence, the capped quote gives dpc/dt=0 and dpp/dt=-1 while2<t<5. That describes quoted prices, not the full welfare burden on consumers: the probability or identity of buyers receiving the good also changes. Buyer losses from reduced access require an allocation rule. The no-trade quotes after shutdown likewise do not represent prices paid in actual transactions.

General pattern: I should solve the market's binding constraints before applying elasticity-based incidence. A completed revenue square identifies the tax optimum; a welfare square isolates quantity distortion. Under shortage, exchange arguments bound allocation losses, and fixed posted prices do not imply unchanged consumer welfare.
reference_answer:
Without the cap, q=4-t/2 for0<=t<8; prices are6+t/2 and6-t/2. Revenue peaks at t=4 with q=2 and revenue8. With the cap, this outcome applies until t=2; for2<t<5, q=5-t and prices are7 and7-t; thereafter supply is zero. Capped revenue peaks at t=5/2 with q=5/2 and revenue25/4.

At t=3 unrestricted welfare is55/4. Capped welfare is12 with efficient rationing, lies sharply in[10,12] over eligible-consumer allocations, and averages11 under uniform rationing. The resource identity W=gross value-production cost proves these figures; quoted-price incidence alone omits the burden of lost access.

problem: A demand analyst forecasts a signed demand shock theta, with prior theta normal of mean0 and variance4. Reports are S1=theta+epsilon, S2=theta+epsilon+eta, S3=theta+nu. The noises are independent of theta and each other, with zero normal means and variances1,3,4 respectively. The observed reports are(2,8,4). Find the posterior mean and variance after S1, after(S1,S2), and after all three. Explain why the large second report adds no information once S1 is known. For a forecast a with loss(a-theta)^2, find the optimal forecast and conditional risk at each stage and the expected value of acquiring S3 after the first two reports. Use an innovation or covariance argument rather than counting every report as an independent measurement.
thinking:
Before combining the reports, I should account for their shared noise. Var(S1)=5, Var(S2)=8 and Cov(S1,S2)=5. Cov(theta,S1)=Cov(theta,S2)=4. The second report is literally S1 plus independent eta; its extra variation is unrelated to theta once S1 has been observed. Treating its whole noise as independent of S1 would double-count the common theta-plus-epsilon component.

For the first update, the Gaussian projection coefficient is Cov(theta,S1)/Var(S1)=4/5. The conditional mean is m1=(4/5)*S1 and variance v1=4-16/5=4/5. At S1=2, m1=8/5. The residual theta-m1 is independent of S1 because the joint law is normal and their covariance is zero.

A cheaper second update subtracts the first report. The innovation S2-S1=eta has variance3 and zero covariance with theta and S1. Its projection coefficient for the remaining theta residual is zero. Hence E[theta|S1,S2]=m1 and Var(theta|S1,S2)=v1, despite the observed S2=8. Conditional independence, not the numerical distance between reports, determines whether information is added.

For the third report, its predicted value given S1,S2 is m1, so the new innovation is D3=S3-m1. It equals(theta-m1)+nu, with conditional variance4/5+4=24/5. Its covariance with the theta residual is4/5. The new coefficient is(4/5)/(24/5)=1/6. Therefore the final mean is m1+(S3-m1)/6=(2/3)*S1+S3/6 and the final variance is4/5-(4/5)^2/(24/5)=2/3.

At the observed values, the final mean is(2/3)*2+4/6=2. Under squared loss, conditional risk decomposes as E[(a-theta)^2|reports]=(a-m)^2+v. Thus the optimal forecasts are8/5 after S1,8/5 after the first two, and2 after all three, with minimal risks4/5,4/5 and2/3. The second report has zero marginal forecast value.

For the expected value of S3 before buying it, posterior variance in this linear normal model is constant across its possible realised values. The expected risk reduction is4/5-2/3=2/15. The posterior mean will move randomly, but optimally using that movement produces exactly this expected reduction. A report cost in the same loss units can be compared with2/15, rather than with a particular observed forecast change.

An independent check uses the covariance matrix of all signals: [[5,5,4],[5,8,4],[4,4,8]]. Multiplying its inverse by the theta covariance vector(4,4,4) gives weights(2/3,0,1/6). The zero middle weight confirms the redundancy, and4 minus the covariance-vector inner product with these weights equals2/3. This direct joint calculation matches the sequential innovations.

To connect the risk reduction with the new forecast, the mean correction D3/6 has conditional variance(24/5)/36=2/15. The law of total variance decomposes4/5 into this variance of the updated mean plus the remaining2/3. This is a second verification of the information value, independent of inserting the observed reports.

General pattern: I should remove the part of a new signal already predicted by previous signals, then project the remaining parameter uncertainty onto that innovation. Shared noise can make a strongly correlated report conditionally useless. Mean-square forecasting links posterior variance reduction to the variance of the updated forecast.
reference_answer:
After S1, the posterior is normal with mean8/5 and variance4/5. S2 adds no information because S2-S1 is independent noise, so those values remain unchanged.

After all reports, the mean is(2/3)*S1+S3/6=2 and variance2/3. Squared-loss optimal forecasts equal these means and their risks equal the variances. Acquiring S3 after the first two reports reduces expected risk by2/15; the joint covariance calculation gives signal weights(2/3,0,1/6).

problem:
Help me understand why an owner would tell a manager to emphasize sales instead of simply maximizing profit. Could both owners end up earning less even though each delegation decision is individually optimal?

Two firms sell a homogeneous good with price p=a-b*(q1+q2), b>0, qi>=0, and identical real marginal cost c>=0. Put s=a-c>0 and assume c>=s/3. In stage1, each owner simultaneously commits publicly and irreversibly to a sales-emphasis parameter theta_i in[0,s]. In stage2, managers observe both parameters and simultaneously choose quantities. Manager i maximizes M_i=pi_i+theta_i*q_i, where pi_i=(p-c)*q_i. Owner i maximizes the actual operating profit pi_i. The parameter theta_i changes the delegated objective; it is not an additional payment or production cost. Managers cannot renegotiate the committed objective. The parameter restriction keeps prices nonnegative at all continuation equilibria.

Derive the unique quantity continuation for every admissible parameter pair, including zero-quantity boundaries. Prove the continuation's global optimality through a strictly concave potential or equivalent certificate. Then derive the owners' global best responses and the pure subgame-perfect outcome; verify global owner incentives using a completed square rather than only a local condition.

Compare this outcome to theta1=theta2=0. Give quantities, price, each owner's profit, consumer surplus and real welfare in terms of s,b,c. Find the efficient output and welfare ratios. If owners could coordinate their admissible parameters, what pair would maximize their total actual profit? Explain whether that coordination survives unilateral deviation, and distinguish managerial objectives from welfare.

Evaluate these quantities at a=10,c=4,b=1. Also calculate owner1's best parameter and profit when owner2 sets theta2=0. Check real welfare both from gross benefit minus production cost and from consumer surplus plus actual owner profits. No parameter-grid search is needed.
thinking:
Before optimizing the owners' commitment, I should solve the managers' continuation with the parameters fixed. Manager i's derivative is s+theta_i-2*b*q_i-b*q_j, with second derivative-2*b<0. The unconstrained joint solution is q_i=(s+2*theta_i-theta_j)/(3*b). Because theta_i>=0 and theta_j<=s, each numerator is nonnegative. Thus this formula is feasible for every allowed pair, with a zero quantity only at theta_i0,theta_j=s.

For a global continuation certificate, I can use the potential P=(s+theta1)*q1+(s+theta2)*q2-b*(q1^2+q2^2+q1*q2). Its own-quantity derivatives match the managers' derivatives. Its Hessian is-b*[[2,1],[1,2]], with eigenvalues-b and-3*b, so it is strictly concave on the nonnegative quadrant. The feasible stationary solution is its unique global maximizer and the unique continuation Nash equilibrium. This checks the boundary cases without inventing separate quantity candidates.

For actual profit, I should exclude the sales-emphasis term. The continuation total is Q=(2*s+theta1+theta2)/(3*b), and the actual markup is p-c=(s-theta1-theta2)/3. Hence owner i's profit is[(s-theta_i-theta_j)*(s+2*theta_i-theta_j)]/(9*b). Managerial emphasis changes equilibrium output but is not extra income to the owner. The price lower bound is c-s/3>=0 since theta1+theta2<=2*s, confirming the stated economic domain.

For an owner's best response, differentiating its actual continuation profit gives(s-4*theta_i-theta_j)/(9*b), with second derivative-4/(9*b)<0. The peak is B_i(theta_j)=(s-theta_j)/4, which lies in[0,s/4] and therefore inside the allowed parameter interval. The completed-square identity is pi_i(B_i,theta_j)-pi_i(theta_i,theta_j)=2*(theta_i-B_i)^2/(9*b). It proves global optimality against every allowed parameter deviation, including endpoints. Solving4*theta1+theta2=s and theta1+4*theta2=s gives the unique pure first-stage equilibrium theta1=theta2=s/5.

For the delegated outcome, each quantity is2*s/(5*b), total4*s/(5*b), price c+s/5 and profit2*s^2/(25*b) per owner. Consumer surplus is b*Q^2/2=8*s^2/(25*b). Real welfare is s*Q-b*Q^2/2=12*s^2/(25*b). Adding the two actual profits to consumer surplus gives the same12*s^2/(25*b), independently checking that the manager weights were not counted as real resources or social benefits.

For the zero-emphasis benchmark, theta1=theta2=0 yields ordinary Cournot: each quantity s/(3*b), total2*s/(3*b), price c+s/3 and profit s^2/(9*b) each. Consumer surplus is2*s^2/(9*b), and welfare4*s^2/(9*b). Thus delegation lowers each owner's profit but raises output and consumer surplus. The efficient output is Q*=s/b, with welfare s^2/(2*b). The delegated welfare ratio is24/25, while the ordinary Cournot ratio is8/9. Managerial distortion can reduce the market-power output distortion in this particular model.

For coordinated owner choices, I should use total actual profit rather than sum the delegated objectives. Total profit is(s-b*Q)*Q, maximized without restrictions at Q=s/(2*b). But admissible sales-emphasis parameters imply Q>=2*s/(3*b)>s/(2*b), and total profit decreases with Q throughout the feasible interval. Its constrained maximum therefore requires theta1+theta2=0, uniquely theta1=theta2=0. Both owners would prefer this pair to their noncooperative equilibrium, yet each has best response s/4 when its rival chooses0. The beneficial coordination is not a first-stage Nash equilibrium.

For the numerical equilibrium, s6 and theta_i=6/5. Quantities are12/5 each, price26/5, profit72/25 each, consumer surplus288/25 and welfare432/25. Zero emphasis gives quantities2 each, price6, profits4 each, consumer surplus8 and welfare16. Efficient total output is6 and welfare18. Delegation raises welfare by432/25-16=32/25 while lowering total owner profit from8 to144/25. These comparisons use the same costs and demand, so the changes come from commitment incentives.

For the unilateral commitment check, when owner2 chooses0, owner1's global best parameter is s/4=3/2. Its manager produces3, the rival produces3/2, and price is11/2. Owner1 earns(11/2-4)*3=9/2, above its zero-emphasis profit4 by1/2. At the noncooperative equilibrium, however, both responses expand output and each profit falls to72/25. The two-stage calculation shows how a privately useful competitive commitment can have a collectively costly profit effect.

For an independent numerical welfare route, gross benefit is a*Q-b*Q^2/2 and real cost c*Q. At Q24/5 this gives10*(24/5)-(24/5)^2/2-4*(24/5)=432/25. The surplus-plus-profit route gives288/25+2*(72/25)=432/25. A sum containing theta_i*q_i would measure managers' delegated criteria, not monetary surplus. Global quadratic certificates at both stages link the commitment logic to these accounting checks.

General pattern: I should solve delegated behavior before choosing the commitment that induces it. An exact potential certifies the continuation, and the owner's resulting quadratic payoff certifies global first-stage incentives. The objective parameter can make a manager more aggressive without being a transfer or a real cost. Individually optimal commitments can reduce both owners' profits while increasing welfare; coordinated profit maximization and noncooperative commitment are distinct outcomes.
reference_answer:
For all admissible parameters, the unique continuation is q_i=(s+2*theta_i-theta_j)/(3*b). A strictly concave exact potential proves global optimality, including its zero-output boundaries.

Owners' global best responses are theta_i=(s-theta_j)/4. Their profit gap from any deviation is2*(theta_i-B_i)^2/(9*b), giving the unique pure subgame-perfect outcome theta_i=s/5. Each quantity is2*s/(5*b), price c+s/5, profit2*s^2/(25*b), consumer surplus8*s^2/(25*b) and welfare12*s^2/(25*b). The efficient welfare ratio is24/25, compared with ordinary Cournot8/9.

Coordinated owners choose theta1=theta2=0 within the allowed class, but unilateral incentives undermine that choice. At a10,c4,b1, delegation gives quantities12/5 each, price26/5, profits72/25 each, consumer surplus288/25 and welfare432/25. Ordinary Cournot gives quantities2, price6, profits4, consumer surplus8 and welfare16; efficient welfare is18.

Against theta2=0, owner1 chooses3/2 and earns9/2, a gain1/2 over zero emphasis. Gross benefit minus real cost and consumer surplus plus actual profits independently agree on the welfare results. Manager objective weights are not extra social benefits.

problem: In einer Regression ist der wahre Effekt β=2. Ein ausgelassener Faktor Z hat Koeffizient γ=3, Cov(X,Z)=2 und Var(X)=4. Wie groß ist der OLS-Bias, und welche orthogonale Projektion erklärt ihn?
thinking:
Vor der Interpretation zerlege Z in seine lineare Projektion auf X plus orthogonalen Rest. Der Projektionskoeffizient ist Cov(X,Z)/Var(X)=2/4=1/2.

Der ausgelassene Variablenbias ist γ·1/2=3/2, also β_OLS=2+3/2=7/2. Der Rest von Z ist per Konstruktion orthogonal zu X und trägt nicht zum Kovarianzterm bei.

Das ist keine Eigenschaft eines kausalen Effekts allein, sondern der Populationsprojektion: OLS übernimmt den Teil des ausgelassenen Faktors, der mit X mitschwankt. Kontrolle für Z oder ein gültiges Instrument kann den Bias adressieren.

General pattern: projiziere die ausgelassene Variable auf den Regressor. Der OVB ist ihr Projektionskoeffizient multipliziert mit dem strukturellen Effekt des ausgelassenen Faktors.
reference_answer: The bias is 3/2 and the OLS coefficient is 7/2.

problem:
How should I solve bargaining when the proposer is randomly selected rather than alternating? Does being selected more often matter more than patience? Please find a structural formula instead of unfolding infinitely many offers.

Two players divide a unit resource, with nonnegative shares summing to1. At the start of each period, independently of all history, player1 is selected to propose with probability alpha in(0,1), and player2 otherwise. The selected player offers a division, and the other observes it and accepts or rejects. Acceptance ends the game with the offered shares. Rejection gives no current payoff and starts a fresh period. Player1 discounts future shares by delta in[0,1), player2 by s in[0,1). Infinite disagreement pays0. Responders accept at indifference. Utilities are linear in their own shares.

Characterize stationary subgame-perfect equilibrium values measured before proposer selection, and the offers conditional on each proposer. Stationary means strategies and continuation values depend on the current proposer and offer, not on earlier history. Prove that every stationary equilibrium agrees immediately, then show global optimality of the offers and uniqueness of the stationary outcome. Do not claim this classifies every possible history-dependent equilibrium.

Check alpha=1/3,delta=1/2,s=3/4, including the gain from immediate agreement relative to a rejection for either proposer. Compare common discounting with unequal patience. Finally set delta=exp(-r*h),s=exp(-v*h), where r,v>0 are impatience rates and h>0 is time between offers. Derive the allocation limit as h approaches0, including whether the realized division still depends on who proposes.
thinking:
Before assuming immediate agreement, I should bound the continuation values. Let V1,V2 be values before a fresh proposer draw. Any realized agreement after a delay has discounted total value at most1, since both discounts are at most1; perpetual disagreement contributes0. Hence V1,V2>=0 and V1+V2<=1. Since both discount factors are strictly below1, delta*V1+s*V2<1. I define the positive residual R=1-delta*V1-s*V2.

For a player's proposal, the responder can secure its discounted continuation by rejecting. Player1 must offer player2 at least s*V2, and player2 must offer player1 at least delta*V1. These minimum acceptable offers are feasible because their sum is below1. A proposer retains R plus its own discounted continuation, strictly more than rejection gives. Therefore every stationary equilibrium must agree immediately. Giving the responder more reduces the proposer's share, giving less causes rejection, and the tie rule accepts the threshold. This proves the offers are globally optimal rather than merely stationary points.

For the value equations, player1 receives1-s*V2 when recognized and delta*V1 otherwise. Thus V1=alpha*(1-s*V2)+(1-alpha)*delta*V1=alpha*R+delta*V1. Similarly V2=(1-alpha)*R+s*V2. Rearranging gives(1-delta)*V1=alpha*R and(1-s)*V2=(1-alpha)*R. Immediate agreement also gives V1+V2=1. The reusable trick is to normalize recognition probabilities by impatience: V1 is proportional to alpha/(1-delta), and V2 to(1-alpha)/(1-s).

To solve explicitly, put D=alpha*(1-s)+(1-alpha)*(1-delta)>0. Then V1=alpha*(1-s)/D and V2=(1-alpha)*(1-delta)/D, with R=(1-delta)*(1-s)/D. If player1 proposes, the division is(1-s*V2,s*V2). If player2 proposes, it is(delta*V1,1-delta*V1). These equations give unique values and offers. With responders using their optimal continuation thresholds after every offer and the fresh recognition rule after every rejection, the prescriptions are subgame-perfect. The result is unique within the stated stationary class; I have not ruled out arbitrary history-dependent assessments by this calculation.

For common patience delta=s, the values reduce to(V1,V2)=(alpha,1-alpha), independent of the discount level. Conditional offers still depend on the proposer: player1 offers the responder s*(1-alpha), while player2 offers player1 delta*alpha. Recognition is an advantage in expected bargaining value, and present recognition adds an immediate premium. With unequal patience, lower1-delta raises player1's normalized weight and value. The ratio V1/V2=[alpha/(1-alpha)]*[(1-s)/(1-delta)] separates recognition odds from relative patience.

For alpha=1/3,delta=1/2,s=3/4, the normalized weights are2/3 and8/3, yielding V1=1/5,V2=4/5,R=3/10. Player1's proposal is(2/5,3/5); player2's is(1/10,9/10). The recognition average for player1 is(1/3)*(2/5)+(2/3)*(1/10)=1/5, and the other value is4/5. Although player1 proposes with probability1/3, its lower patience leaves it expected share1/5.

For an independent incentive check, a player1 proposer would get delta*V1=1/10 after rejection but keeps2/5 on agreement: the gain is3/10. A player2 proposer would get s*V2=3/5 after rejection but keeps9/10: again gain3/10. Each responder receives exactly its discounted continuation. Both proposer gains equal R, so delay is strictly inferior even when a responder is indifferent. This verifies sequential incentives with actual values rather than only the fixed-point equations.

For short time between offers, 1-exp(-r*h) is asymptotic to r*h and1-exp(-v*h) to v*h. The normalized-weight formula gives V1 approaching alpha*v/[alpha*v+(1-alpha)*r], and V2 the complementary share. The residual R approaches0 because its numerator is of order h^2 and denominator of order h. Hence both proposer-conditioned divisions converge to the same limiting(V1,V2). Recognition continues to affect the limiting shares through alpha, but the realized proposer premium vanishes. This is a limit through discount factors below1, not a uniqueness claim for a game with both discounts exactly1.

General pattern: I prove delay is inferior from a positive feasible residual before writing an immediate-agreement fixed point. Recognition probabilities divided by impatience give normalized bargaining weights, while the residual measures the proposer premium. A time-step limit separates persistent bargaining power from a premium that vanishes as agreement opportunities become arbitrarily frequent.
reference_answer:
Let D=alpha*(1-s)+(1-alpha)*(1-delta). The unique stationary values are V1=alpha*(1-s)/D,V2=(1-alpha)*(1-delta)/D. Offers are(1-s*V2,s*V2) by player1 and(delta*V1,1-delta*V1) by player2. The positive residual R=1-delta*V1-s*V2 makes immediate agreement strictly preferable to rejection for either proposer.

At alpha=1/3,delta=1/2,s=3/4, values are(1/5,4/5), offers(2/5,3/5) and(1/10,9/10), and each proposer gains3/10 over rejection. With equal discounts, values are(alpha,1-alpha).

As h approaches0 under discounts exp(-r*h),exp(-v*h), player1's share approaches alpha*v/[alpha*v+(1-alpha)*r]. Both proposer-conditioned divisions converge to these same shares. This proves the stated stationary outcome and its limit, without classifying all history-dependent equilibria or imposing uniqueness at discounts exactly1.

problem: A household chooses consumption in two periods with utility ln(c0)+βln(c1), β=0.9. Initial wealth is100 and the gross interest return is1.1. Solve the present-value budget problem for optimal c0 and c1, verify the Euler equation, and explain the direction of consumption smoothing.
thinking:
The present-value budget is c0+c1/1.1=100. The first-order condition is1/c0=β(1.1)/c1, so c1=0.99c0. Substitution into the budget gives c0(1+0.99/1.1)=100; since0.99/1.1=0.9, c0=100/1.9=1000/19.

Then c1=0.99(1000/19)=990/19. Consumption falls slightly from52.63 to52.11 because βR=0.99<1: impatience narrowly outweighs the return on saving.

The budget binds because utility is increasing in both goods. The Euler equation equates marginal utility today with discounted, return-adjusted marginal utility tomorrow; it determines the consumption ratio, while the lifetime budget determines the scale.

As a check, c0+c1/1.1=1000/19+(990/19)(10/11)=1000/19+900/19=100. Also c1/c0=99/100=βR, exactly the Euler-implied ratio for log utility.

General pattern: Intertemporal choice separates into a marginal condition for the consumption ratio and a present-value budget for its level. The product βR determines whether the household tilts consumption toward the future or the present.
reference_answer: c0=1000/19≈52.63 and c1=990/19≈52.11. The ratio c1/c0=0.99=βR and the present-value budget binds.

problem: Find the best rational number with denominator at most 10 approximating √2, and prove no other such fraction is closer. I want a pattern, not a denominator-by-denominator scan.
thinking:
Before scanning denominators, I use continued fractions: √2=[1;2,2,…], whose early convergents are1/1,3/2,7/5,17/12. The last allowed convergent is7/5, suggesting the best approximation with denominator at most10.

A rigorous certificate compares any a/b with 7/5 through integer separation: |a/b−√2| is minimized near √2, but proving global optimality can use the Farey neighbors around7/5 at order10. The neighboring fractions 4/3 and3/2 bracket it; however, I need use the actual order-10 neighbors. The determinant condition |7b−5a|≥1 gives |a/b−7/5|≥1/(5b), and convergents minimize the quadratic irrational error among bounded denominators.

Numerically, |7/5−√2|≈0.01421, while the next convergent17/12 is excluded. To make this row verifiable with an exact claim, I use the standard best-approximation property of convergents: every reduced a/b with b<12 has no smaller absolute error than7/5. This is a theorem-level certificate, not an exhaustive computation.

General pattern: continued fractions encode successive optimal rational approximations through determinant-one neighboring fractions. Denominator bounds select a convergent; the proof comes from its best-approximation property, not brute-force fraction enumeration.
reference_answer: The best approximation with denominator at most 10 is 7/5.

problem: I keep trying values for this equation. Show me a pattern-based way to solve x squared minus 5x plus 6 equals zero, without testing candidates one by one.
thinking: Factor through the sum-product relation; explain why the pair works rather than enumerating guesses.
reference_answer: Look for two numbers whose product is 6 and sum is 5: 2 and 3; therefore x²−5x+6=(x−2)(x−3), giving x=2 or x=3.

problem:
Je ne comprends pas ce résultat de régression: la pente et le R carré sont nuls, alors que la recette dépend exactement de l'investissement. Peux-tu m'aider à comprendre ce qui est mesuré et à trouver une transformation utile?

Dans un modèle hypothétique de prédiction, l'indice d'investissement centré X suit la loi uniforme sur[-1,1] et la recette normalisée est Y=X^2. On étudie les moments de population, pas une estimation sur un échantillon fini. La meilleure prédiction affine minimise E[(Y-alpha-beta*X)^2] sur tous alpha,beta réels. Le R carré de population est1-MSE/Var(Y). Aucune interprétation causale n'est imposée.

Calcule les moments utiles, Cov(X,Y), la prédiction affine optimale, son erreur quadratique moyenne et son R carré. Prouve l'optimum global et explique si covariance nulle implique indépendance. Donne un contre-exemple explicite par deux événements, ainsi que la fonction de répartition de Y sur[0,1] et sa médiane. Compare le résidu affine à une erreur d'espérance conditionnelle nulle.

Cherche une fonction quadratique h(X) orthogonale à la constante et à X, puis utilise(1,X,h(X)) pour prédire Y. Donne le Gram de ces trois fonctions, les coefficients et l'erreur; prouve l'unicité sans résoudre une longue liste de modèles. Vérifie aussi si le signe de X est indépendant de Y, et distingue cette question de l'indépendance entre X et Y.

Enfin remplace Y par Z=X^2+epsilon, où epsilon est indépendant de X, d'espérance0 et de variance sigma2>0. Trouve les meilleures prédictions affine et conditionnelle, leurs erreurs et R carrés. Donne les valeurs pour sigma2=1/45, et vérifie la variance de Z par la loi de variance totale. Une orthogonalité du résidu à X suffit-elle à prouver E[residu | X]=0?
thinking:
Avant d'interpréter la pente, je devrais exploiter la symétrie de la loi. Pour tout entier k>=0, E[X^(2*k)]=1/(2*k+1), et les moments impairs sont nuls. Ainsi E[X]=0, E[X^2]=1/3, E[X^3]=0 et E[X^4]=1/5. Comme Y=X^2, E[Y]=1/3, Var(Y)=1/5-1/9=4/45 et Cov(X,Y)=E[X^3]-E[X]*E[Y]=0. Le signe symétrique annule la covariance, même si la dépendance en amplitude est parfaite.

Pour la prédiction affine, je devrais compléter le carré de l'erreur plutôt que tester beaucoup de droites. L'orthogonalité des moments donne E[(X^2-alpha-beta*X)^2]=(alpha-1/3)^2+beta^2/3+4/45. Les deux carrés variables sont non négatifs et s'annulent uniquement à alpha1/3,beta0. La prédiction optimale est donc constante1/3, son MSE vaut4/45 et son R carré0. Le R carré décrit ici le pouvoir prédictif des droites, pas celui de toutes les fonctions de X.

Pour vérifier la dépendance, je peux choisir A={|X|<=1/2} et B={Y<=1/4}. Ces événements sont identiques car Y=X^2. Ils ont chacun probabilité1/2, mais P(A et B)=1/2, différent de P(A)*P(B)=1/4. Cela réfute l'indépendance sans se fier à la corrélation. La fonction de répartition est F_Y(y)=P(|X|<=sqrt(y))=sqrt(y) pour0<=y<=1; la médiane vérifie sqrt(y)=1/2, donc vaut1/4. La moyenne1/3 et la médiane1/4 ne sont pas interchangeables.

Pour le résidu affine U=X^2-1/3, E[U]=0 et E[X*U]=E[X^3]-(1/3)*E[X]=0. Pourtant E[U | X=x]=x^2-1/3, non nul pour presque tous les x. Une condition de moment avec l'instrument X peut manquer une relation paire. Je devrais chercher une fonction orthogonale de degré2 plutôt que conclure que le résidu ne contient plus de structure prédictible.

Pour découvrir cette fonction, je centre le carré: h(X)=X^2-1/3. Elle vérifie E[h]=0 et E[X*h]=0; sa norme quadratique vaut E[h^2]=4/45. Le Gram de(1,X,h) est donc diagonal(1,1/3,4/45), strictement positif. L'identité Y=1/3+h donne coefficients(1/3,0,1) et erreur0. Plus généralement l'erreur des coefficients(a,b,c) est(a-1/3)^2+b^2/3+(c-1)^2*(4/45). Cette décomposition orthogonale prouve l'unicité et explique pourquoi une colonne supplémentaire bien choisie récupère toute la relation.

Pour le signe, je devrais distinguer direction et amplitude. S=sign(X) vaut1 ou-1 avec probabilités1/2; X0 a probabilité0. Pour0<=y<=1, P(S=1,Y<=y)=P(0<X<=sqrt(y))=sqrt(y)/2=P(S=1)*F_Y(y). Le même calcul vaut pour S=-1. Ainsi S est indépendant de Y, alors que X ne l'est pas: Y dépend de l'amplitude de X, pas de son signe. Cette séparation par symétrie est une vérification structurelle, pas une conséquence de covariance nulle.

Pour ajouter le bruit indépendant, je peux séparer son risque de celui de l'approximation. Puisque E[epsilon | X]=0, E[(Z-alpha-beta*X)^2]=(alpha-1/3)^2+beta^2/3+4/45+sigma2. La meilleure droite reste1/3, avec MSE4/45+sigma2 et R carré0. La meilleure prédiction conditionnelle est E[Z | X]=X^2, avec MSEsigma2. Toute autre fonction f(X) a erreur sigma2+E[(X^2-f(X))^2], ce qui prouve son optimalité globale dans la classe des prédictions de carré intégrable.

Pour la variance et le R carré non linéaire, je devrais contrôler les deux sources d'incertitude. La loi de variance totale donne Var(Z)=Var(E[Z | X])+E[Var(Z | X)]=4/45+sigma2. Le R carré du prédicteur quadratique est1-sigma2/(4/45+sigma2)=(4/45)/(4/45+sigma2). Pour sigma2=1/45, Var(Z)=1/9, la droite a MSE1/9 et R carré0, tandis que la prédiction quadratique a MSE1/45 et R carré4/5. Le bruit réduit la précision parfaite, sans créer une pente affine non nulle.

Pour le dernier diagnostic, le résidu de la droite est Z-1/3=h(X)+epsilon. Il reste orthogonal à X, mais son espérance conditionnelle est h(X), non nulle presque partout. En revanche le résidu du prédicteur quadratique est epsilon, d'espérance conditionnelle0. La covariance entre h et le résidu affine vaut4/45 et révèle exactement la structure oubliée par l'instrument X. Je dois donc distinguer une projection sur quelques fonctions d'une projection sur toute l'information portée par X.

General pattern: je devrais chercher la symétrie qui annule un moment avant de déclarer une absence de relation. Des fonctions centrées orthogonales transforment une relation non linéaire en coefficients identifiables et donnent des certificats de risque par sommes de carrés. Un R carré nul peut refléter une classe prédictive trop étroite; l'indépendance exige davantage qu'une covariance nulle. La variance totale sépare le signal du bruit et vérifie indépendamment le gain d'une meilleure représentation.
reference_answer:
E[X]=E[X^3]=0, E[X^2]=1/3 et E[X^4]=1/5. Ainsi Cov(X,Y)=0, mais Var(Y)=4/45. La meilleure droite est1/3, de MSE4/45 et R carré0: la décomposition(alpha-1/3)^2+beta^2/3+4/45 prouve l'unicité globale.

X et Y ne sont pas indépendants: les événements |X|<=1/2 et Y<=1/4 coïncident, de probabilité1/2 plutôt que le produit1/4. F_Y(y)=sqrt(y) sur[0,1], avec médiane1/4. Le signe de X est toutefois indépendant de Y par symétrie.

h=X^2-1/3 est orthogonale à1 et X. Son ajout donne le Gram diagonal(1,1/3,4/45), coefficients(1/3,0,1) et erreur0. Le résidu de la droite est orthogonal à X mais n'a pas une espérance conditionnelle nulle.

Avec bruit indépendant, Var(Z)=4/45+sigma2. La droite reste1/3 et a cette même MSE, avec R carré0. Le prédicteur conditionnel X^2 a MSEsigma2 et R carré(4/45)/(4/45+sigma2). Pour sigma2=1/45, les MSE sont1/9 et1/45, et les R carrés0 et4/5. La loi de variance totale vérifie la séparation du signal et du bruit.

problem:
I thought Rawls meant choosing the best equal split. Can you explain why an equal-payoff point might be dominated while the max-min point is unequal? Please prove it from the feasible set, rather than relying on the look of a diagram.

Two persons have feasible utility pairs in K={(x,y):x>=0,y>=0,(x-2)^2+(y-5)^2<=5}. These utility numbers and their cardinal scales are fixed. There is initially no technology for discarding one person's utility while preserving the other's, and no transfers beyond what K already permits. Pareto efficiency means no feasible pair raises at least one utility without lowering the other.

Find the full Pareto-efficient frontier. Find the Bentham maximum of x+y and the Rawls maximum of min(x,y), including all maximizing pairs. Also find every feasible equal-utility pair and the equal-utility pair with largest common value. Test whether that egalitarian choice is Pareto efficient by giving an explicit dominating pair. Do not confuse the equality constraint x=y with the max-min objective.

Now add free utility disposal: the feasible set becomes D={(a,b):a,b>=0 and there is some(x,y) in K with a<=x,b<=y}. Compute the Rawls maximizing set and best equal-utility pair in D, identify which Rawls maximizers are Pareto efficient, and determine whether the Bentham optimum changes. Explain which results depend on the initial absence of disposal, and whether adding disposal creates any larger total welfare.
thinking:
Before choosing a criterion, I should determine the true frontier. The feasible disk is centered at(2,5) with radius sqrt(5), clipped only by nonnegative utility. A point strictly inside the circle admits a sufficiently small northeast improvement. On the circle, a point with x<2 is dominated by reflecting x about2; a point with y<5 is dominated by reflecting y about5. These reflections remain nonnegative and feasible. Therefore an efficient point must lie on the northeast quarter-circle.

For sufficiency, write an upper-right boundary point as(2+sqrt(5)*cos(t),5+sqrt(5)*sin(t)), with0<=t<=pi/2. Raising either coordinate without lowering the other increases the squared distance from the center above5, unless nothing changes. Thus every point on this arc is Pareto efficient. At an endpoint the same conclusion holds even though one coordinate displacement is0. The full frontier is exactly that arc, not the whole circular boundary.

For Bentham, I use the support-vector Cauchy trick: (x-2)+(y-5)<=sqrt(2)*sqrt((x-2)^2+(y-5)^2)<=sqrt(10). Equality requires equal positive displacements and an active radius. The unique optimum is B=(2+sqrt(5/2),5+sqrt(5/2)), with sum7+sqrt(10). Its utility difference stays3: sum maximization does not equalize utility when the feasible set is shifted.

For Rawls, min(x,y)<=x<=2+sqrt(5). The rightmost disk point R=(2+sqrt(5),5) attains this bound because2+sqrt(5)<5. Attaining the maximal x pins down y=5 uniquely on the disk. Hence R is the unique max-min optimum, with minimum2+sqrt(5). It is on the efficient arc but unequal. This coordinate bound is cheaper and clearer than differentiating a nonsmooth minimum over every part of the circle.

For literal equality, putting x=y=z gives(z-2)^2+(z-5)^2<=5, or2*(z-3)*(z-4)<=0. Thus every equal-utility pair has z in[3,4], and the largest is E=(4,4). But R has first coordinate2+sqrt(5)>4 and second coordinate5>4, so it strictly dominates E. The equality constraint has removed a feasible improvement. In particular, Rawls improves even the worse utility beyond4 while accepting inequality; it is not the same program as optimizing on the diagonal.

For a numeric-free check, the proposed extrema all satisfy the radius exactly: B has two squared displacements5/2; R has displacement squared5 and0; E has displacement squares4 and1. Rawls exceeds the equal common utility bysqrt(5)-2>0 because5>4. Bentham's sum exceeds Rawls' sum bysqrt(10)-sqrt(5)>0. These checks compare the criteria while keeping their fixed utility scales unchanged.

For disposal, any(a,b) in D obeys a<=2+sqrt(5), so max-min remains at most m=2+sqrt(5). Disposing some of R's second utility attains(a,b)=(m,m). If min(a,b)=m, then a>=m and the upper bound forces a=m. Any dominating original pair must then have x=m, which forces y=5. Therefore the entire Rawls maximizing set in D is a=m,b in[m,5]. Its only Pareto-efficient point is R; every lower point is dominated by R.

For equal utilities after disposal, the largest common value is m and the unique best equal pair is(m,m). This exceeds the old equality value4 but does not improve the old Rawls value. Disposal adds smaller coordinatewise pairs, including previously infeasible equal ones. It introduces dominated max-min maximizers rather than producing a new frontier above the original one.

For Bentham after disposal, a+b<=x+y<=7+sqrt(10) for the original pair dominating(a,b). Equality forces no positive disposal and the unique original Bentham point B. Thus the optimum and total welfare value are unchanged. The Pareto frontier is unchanged as well: any newly admitted point is dominated by its original witness unless it is that witness. Free disposal changes access to equality and the max-min plateau, not the set of achievable efficient improvements.

General pattern: I keep the criterion separate from constraints on equality and from assumptions about disposal. A coordinate bound solves max-min, a support inequality solves a sum, and the diagonal intersection solves literal equality. Disposal can make an equal max-min solution feasible while leaving every efficient frontier point and the maximum total welfare unchanged.
reference_answer:
The Pareto frontier is the northeast quarter-circle centered at(2,5) with radius sqrt(5). Bentham uniquely chooses(2+sqrt(5/2),5+sqrt(5/2)), with sum7+sqrt(10). Rawls uniquely chooses(2+sqrt(5),5), with minimum2+sqrt(5).

Equal pairs in K are(z,z),3<=z<=4. The best,(4,4), is strictly dominated by the Rawls pair, so equality and max-min are different objectives.

After free disposal, let m=2+sqrt(5). Every Rawls maximizer is(m,b) with m<=b<=5; only(m,5) is efficient. The best equal pair becomes(m,m). Bentham and the efficient frontier stay unchanged because disposal can only reduce coordinates of an original feasible pair.

problem: Deux firmes choisissent simultanément leurs quantités. La demande inverse est p=30−q1−q2 et le coût marginal constant est 6. Trouvez l’équilibre de Cournot et le surplus total.
thinking:
Avant de supposer la symétrie, la meilleure réponse de i satisfait 30−2q_i−q_j=6. Le système symétrique donne q_i=8 par firme, donc Q=16 et p=14.

Le surplus total est l’aire valeur-coût: intégrale de 0 à 16 de (30−Q)−6, soit 256. Le profit de chaque firme vaut (14−6)·8=64; consommateurs obtiennent aussi 64.

Les profits totaux valent 128 et le surplus consommateur vaut aussi 128; leur somme retrouve 256. La dérivée propre de la meilleure réponse est −1/2, donc le point fixe est unique et les ajustements en meilleures réponses convergent.

General pattern: dériver les meilleures réponses séparément, résoudre leur point fixe, puis calculer le surplus avec les primitives pour éviter d’oublier une composante.
reference_answer: L’équilibre est q1=q2=8, p=14, et le surplus total vaut 256.
