problem: Per interpolare i punti (0,1), (1,3), (2,7) con un polinomio di grado al più 2, qual è il polinomio? Voglio anche un controllo che non dipenda dal sostituire i tre punti uno per uno.
thinking:
Prima di risolvere tre coefficienti, riconosco le differenze seconde: i valori 1,3,7 hanno prime differenze2,4 e seconda differenza2, quindi il coefficiente quadratico è1. Scrivo p(x)=x²+bx+c.

Da p(0)=1 segue c=1; da p(1)=3 segue b=1. Quindi p(x)=x²+x+1. Il trucco delle differenze finite è una versione discreta della derivata seconda costante.

Per un controllo strutturale, tre valori distinti determinano al più un quadratico: la differenza di due candidati avrebbe tre zeri e grado al più2, dunque sarebbe il polinomio nullo. Il candidato trovato è quindi unico, e le sostituzioni confermano l'esistenza.

General pattern: usa le differenze finite per leggere il grado e i coefficienti, poi usa il limite sul numero di zeri per provare unicità dell'interpolante.
reference_answer: Il polinomio è p(x)=x²+x+1, unico tra i polinomi di grado al più 2 che interpolano i tre punti.

problem:
How can I choose a membership fee and usage price without losing customers I meant to serve? I was told a two-part tariff should set the usage price at marginal cost, but that seems to ignore different customer demands.

A unit mass of consumers has two types. A fraction alpha in(0,1) has gross utility U_L(q)=2*q-q^2/2; the remaining fraction1-alpha has U_H(q)=4*q-q^2/2. Each consumes q>=0. Outside utility is0, and there is no income constraint. A monopolist has zero marginal and fixed costs. It offers one deterministic common tariff: membership fee F>=0 and usage price p>=0. Only members can consume, and a member's net utility is U_i(q)-p*q-F. At indifference a consumer joins. The seller cannot price-discriminate by type or offer a second tariff.

Solve the consumer usage and participation decisions, then the seller's global problem for every alpha. Compare a tariff serving both types with one serving only high-demand consumers; show why these exhaust positive-revenue possibilities. Derive the exact threshold and treat equality. Prove optimality rather than compare a grid of fees and prices.

Give profit, buyer rent and real welfare for the optimal full-coverage and high-only tariffs. Compare with efficient consumption. Can a positive usage markup be optimal despite zero marginal cost?

Then ban membership fees, keeping every other assumption. Derive the best linear price globally. At alpha=3/5, compare its profit and welfare to the unrestricted optimal tariff. Does permitting a membership fee necessarily improve welfare? Check welfare both from gross utilities and from seller profit plus consumer rent. State which changes come from usage distortion and which come from exclusion.
thinking:
Before choosing the fee, I should solve usage conditional on membership. A type with intercept a chooses q=max(a-p,0), and its surplus before the fee is CS_a=(max(a-p,0))^2/2. It joins when F<=CS_a. High-type surplus is never below low-type surplus, so positive consumption by low types cannot coexist with exclusion of high types. The only positive-revenue coverage patterns are both types consuming or high types alone. A price at least4 produces no positive consumption and cannot support a positive fee.

For both types to consume, I must have0<=p<2 and F<=CS_L=(2-p)^2/2. For fixed p, profit increases with F until that bound, with low-type participation preserved by the tie rule. Substituting the binding fee gives R_all=p*[alpha*(2-p)+(1-alpha)*(4-p)]+(2-p)^2/2=2+2*(1-alpha)*p-p^2/2. Completing the square proves the unique price peak p_all=2*(1-alpha), strictly inside(0,2), and the fee F_all=2*alpha^2.

For the full-coverage allocation, quantities are qL=2*alpha,qH=2+2*alpha. Profit is R_all*=2+2*(1-alpha)^2. Low net rent is0. High net rent equals CS_H-CS_L=6-2*p_all=2+4*alpha, so expected rent is(1-alpha)*(2+4*alpha). Resource welfare is profit plus rent=6-2*alpha-2*alpha^2. The positive usage price is not a production-cost claim; it reduces the high type's rent advantage while the common fee is limited by low participation.

For high-only coverage, I can again raise the fee to that participant's surplus. With0<=p<4, F=CS_H=(4-p)^2/2 gives high profit per customer p*(4-p)+(4-p)^2/2=8-p^2/2. Its maximum is p_high=0,F_high=8. Low consumers then reject because their gross surplus2 is below the fee8. High consumers buy4 and have net rent0. Aggregate profit and welfare both equal8*(1-alpha). This bounds every high-only tariff, including those with a positive usage price.

For global selection, I should compare the two certified peaks. R_all*-R_high*=2*(alpha^2+2*alpha-2). The feasible crossing is alpha0=sqrt(3)-1. Below it, serve only high types at p=0,F=8. Above it, serve both types at p=2*(1-alpha),F=2*alpha^2. At equality both tariffs maximize profit. The other quadratic root is negative, outside the population-share domain. Fee0 with p>=2 is already covered by the high-only bound, so no participation boundary has been omitted.

For efficient consumption, zero real cost implies qL*=2,qH*=4 and welfare W*=8-6*alpha. With full coverage, the quantity of each type is reduced by p_all, giving loss p_all^2/2=2*(1-alpha)^2. With the high-only tariff, high usage is efficient but low consumers are excluded, giving loss2*alpha. At the profit-indifference threshold, full coverage has strictly greater welfare because it leaves positive buyer rent while high-only coverage extracts all its surviving surplus. Profit ties need not be welfare ties.

For the fee ban, I should re-solve the restricted problem rather than keep the old usage price. For p in[0,2], revenue is p*(4-2*alpha-p), uniquely peaked at p_linear=2-alpha. Its profit is(2-alpha)^2. For p in[2,4], only high consumers buy, and revenue(1-alpha)*p*(4-p) peaks at the boundary p=2 with value4*(1-alpha). The first peak exceeds that value by alpha^2>0. Thus p_linear is globally optimal, with qL=alpha,qH=2+alpha, and all consumers have positive usage.

For the linear-price welfare, I can use the same loss square. Relative to efficient consumption, each type is short by p_linear, so W_linear=8-6*alpha-(2-alpha)^2/2=6-4*alpha-alpha^2/2. The tariff can earn more profit when a fee is allowed, but its chosen coverage may change. It is therefore invalid to infer a welfare improvement from the seller's expanded choice set alone.

For the numerical counterexample, alpha=3/5 is below sqrt(3)-1. The unrestricted optimum is p=0,F=8, serving only the high fraction2/5. Profit and welfare are16/5, with buyer rent0. Under the fee ban, the best price is7/5 and quantities are3/5,13/5. Profit is49/25 and welfare171/50. Allowing the fee raises profit by16/5-49/25=31/25, but lowers welfare by171/50-16/5=11/50. The seller's gains do not imply an increase in total surplus.

For an independent resource check at that linear price, gross utilities are51/50 for the low type and351/50 for the high type. Their weighted sum is(3/5)*(51/50)+(2/5)*(351/50)=171/50. Consumer surplus averages73/50, and profit49/25=98/50, again totaling171/50. At the unrestricted high-only tariff, gross high utility8 times fraction2/5 gives16/5, identical to profit plus zero rent. Price payments and fees are transfers because all real costs are zero.

For the source of the reversal, I should compare the losses to the efficient welfare22/5. The linear tariff loses49/50 through reduced usage by both types. The unrestricted tariff loses6/5 through low-type exclusion, while high usage remains efficient. Since6/5>49/50, exclusion is more costly here than the previous usage distortion. A feasible full-coverage two-part tariff at this alpha would have profit58/25 and welfare102/25, but the seller prefers the higher profit16/5 from high-only coverage.

General pattern: I should solve usage before participation, then optimize the fee at the binding participant surplus. Heterogeneous willingness to join can make an above-cost usage price optimal under a common fee. Global profit comparisons select coverage, and centered utility squares separate usage loss from exclusion loss. A larger pricing choice set guarantees weakly higher seller profit, while welfare requires its own resource and rent accounting.
reference_answer:
For full coverage, the optimal tariff is p=2*(1-alpha),F=2*alpha^2, with quantities(2*alpha,2+2*alpha). Profit is2+2*(1-alpha)^2, expected buyer rent(1-alpha)*(2+4*alpha), and welfare6-2*alpha-2*alpha^2.

For high-only coverage, p=0,F=8 yields high quantity4, profit and welfare8*(1-alpha), and zero buyer rent. The seller chooses high-only below alpha=sqrt(3)-1 and full coverage above; both maximize profit at equality. Consumer surplus caps and concave revenue peaks establish global optimality.

With fees banned, the global optimum is p=2-alpha, profit(2-alpha)^2 and welfare6-4*alpha-alpha^2/2. At alpha=3/5, unrestricted profit/welfare are16/5,16/5, compared with49/25,171/50 under the ban. Profit rises31/25 but welfare falls11/50. Gross-utility and profit-plus-rent calculations agree. Here the new low-type exclusion costs more than the usage distortion it replaces.

problem: An entrant chooses Enter or Stay Out. Staying out gives payoffs (0,2). After entry, the incumbent chooses Fight, giving (−1,0), or Accommodate, giving (2,1). Find the subgame-perfect outcome and explain why the announced fight threat does not deter entry.
thinking:
I solve the proper continuation first. After entry, the incumbent compares its own payoffs0 from Fight and1 from Accommodate, so sequential rationality selects Accommodate.

Anticipating that response, the entrant compares2 from Enter with0 from Stay Out and enters. The subgame-perfect outcome is Enter followed by Accommodate, with payoffs (2,1).

The threat to fight is not credible because once entry has occurred it sacrifices the incumbent's payoff. A Nash outcome based on that threat would fail the stronger requirement that every continuation prescribe optimal behavior in its subgame.

As a check, replace the continuation by its backward-induction value: Enter is worth2 to the entrant, strictly above0. The incumbent's accommodation payoff1 is also strictly above its fight payoff0, so neither decision is tied.

General pattern: In a finite sequential game, solve terminal decisions first and propagate their values backward. A threat deters only when carrying it out is optimal at the history where it would be used.
reference_answer: The subgame-perfect outcome is Enter, then Accommodate; payoffs are (2,1). Fight is a noncredible threat.

problem: Je dois produire au moins8 unités avec la technologie q=sqrt(x*y). Le prix de x est1 et celui de y est4. Trouve les quantités d'intrants qui minimisent le coût et le coût minimal. Je voudrais une preuve globale par une inégalité, puis une vérification par les conditions du premier ordre, plutôt qu'une recherche numérique.
thinking:
Avant d'utiliser un solveur, je cherche une borne valable pour tout panier faisable. Par l'inégalité arithmético-géométrique, x+4y>=2sqrt(4xy)=4sqrt(xy). Pour produire q>=8, tout panier coûte donc au moins4q>=32. Cette borne inférieure est un certificat global, pas seulement une condition locale.

L'égalité dans AM-GM exige x=4y; la contrainte de production lie au minimum, donc xy=64. Il vient y=4 et x=16. Le coût est16+4*4=32, qui atteint exactement la borne. Les ressources sont affectées dans le rapport x/y=4 parce que y est quatre fois plus cher par unité, alors que la technologie traite les intrants symétriquement.

Les conditions de Lagrange confirment ce panier: avec contrainte xy>=64, les dérivées donnent1=lambda*y et4=lambda*x, donc x=4y. En combinant avec xy=64, on retrouve(16,4), avec lambda=1/4. La fonction de coût est linéaire en q, C(q)=4q, comme le certificat AM-GM le prédit.

Comme contrôle indépendant, au panier obtenu la production est sqrt(16*4)=8 et le coût est32. L'écart entre les deux côtés de l'inégalité s'annule: x+4y-4sqrt(xy)=16+16-32=0. Tout autre panier faisable a un coût au moins aussi élevé, puisque la borne s'applique avant toute optimisation.

General pattern: En minimisation convexe, une inégalité adaptée peut fournir un certificat dual global. Je repère sa condition d'égalité, puis j'impose la contrainte de production; les conditions du premier ordre servent de seconde route et révèlent les prix relatifs des facteurs.
reference_answer:
Le panier de coût minimal est(x,y)=(16,4). Il produit sqrt(16*4)=8 et coûte16+4*4=32.

Pour tout panier faisable, x+4y>=4sqrt(xy)>=32. L'égalité est atteinte lorsque x=4y et xy=64, soit x=16 et y=4; cette inégalité prouve le minimum global.

problem: A manufacturer with marginal cost20 sells through a retailer to demand p=100−Q. The manufacturer sets wholesale price w first; the retailer then chooses Q. Find the decentralized equilibrium prices, quantity and profits. Compare with vertical integration and a two-part tariff that restores the efficient channel outcome.
thinking:
Given w, the retailer maximizes(100−Q−w)Q, so its best response isQ=(100−w)/2. Anticipating this, the manufacturer chooses w to maximize(w−20)(100−w)/2. The first-order condition givesw=60, soQ=20 and retail price80.

Manufacturer profit is(60−20)20=800; retailer profit is(80−60)20=400. Total channel profit is1200. The retailer's markup over wholesale cost compounds the manufacturer's markup, reducing output below the integrated optimum.

An integrated channel maximizes(100−Q−20)Q, givingQ=40 and price60. Profit is(60−20)40=1600. A two-part tariff can set wholesale pricew=20, inducing the efficient retail quantity40, then charge a fixed fee up to the retailer's variable profit1600; the channel captures the integrated profit without double marginalization.

As a check, at the two-part tariff's marginal-cost wholesale price, the retailer's FOC is100−2Q−20=0, henceQ=40. The fixed fee transfers surplus between firms but does not change the quantity condition; decentralized linear wholesale pricing alone yields only20.

General pattern: Successive monopolists each add a margin, creating double marginalization. Vertical integration or a two-part tariff sets the per-unit transfer at marginal cost and uses a fixed payment to divide the channel surplus without distorting output.
reference_answer: Wholesale price60, retail price80, quantity20; manufacturer profit800 and retailer profit400. Integrated outcome: price60, quantity40, profit1600. A two-part tariff with w=20 and fixed fee1600 restores Q=40.

problem: J'ai deux estimateurs indépendants et sans biais du même paramètre θ. Le premier a une variance1 et le second une variance4. Comment les combiner linéairement pour obtenir la plus petite variance possible? Compare la combinaison optimale à la moyenne simple et explique le rôle du poids de précision.
thinking:
Je préserve l'absence de biais en imposant des poids qui somment à1. Si w pondère le premier estimateur, la variance de wT1+(1−w)T2 est w²+4(1−w)², car les estimateurs sont indépendants. L'optimisation se réduit à une parabole strictement convexe.

La dérivée vaut2w−8(1−w)=10w−8, donc w*=4/5. Le second poids vaut1/5: l'estimateur plus précis reçoit quatre fois le poids, proportionnellement à l'inverse de sa variance. La variance résultante est(4/5)²+4(1/5)²=4/5.

La complétion du carré donne V(w)=5(w−4/5)²+4/5. Elle prouve directement la borne minimale pour tout poids réel, sans comparer une collection de combinaisons candidates. La moyenne simple, w=1/2, a variance1/4+4/4=5/4; l'optimalité réduit cette variance de9/20.

Comme contrôle indépendant, les précisions sont1 et1/4; les poids normalisés sont donc (1)/(1+1/4)=4/5 et(1/4)/(1+1/4)=1/5. Si les deux variances deviennent égales, les poids redeviennent1/2; si la variance du premier tend vers zéro, son poids tend vers1. Ces limites suivent la logique de précision.

General pattern: Parmi les combinaisons linéaires sans biais d'estimateurs indépendants, l'inverse-variance weighting minimise la variance. La contrainte de somme des poids impose l'absence de biais; la courbure positive de la variance certifie le minimum global.
reference_answer: La combinaison optimale est(4/5)T1+(1/5)T2 et sa variance vaut4/5. La moyenne simple a une variance5/4. Les poids optimaux sont proportionnels aux précisions1 et1/4, et la complétion du carré donne V(w)=5(w−4/5)²+4/5.

problem: A prisoner's dilemma is played for three publicly known periods with common discount factor 1/4. Stage payoffs are (3,3) for (C,C), (5,0) for (D,C), (0,5) for (C,D), and (1,1) for (D,D). First find the subgame-perfect outcome without extra payments. Then suppose a committed external contract pays each player bonus B>=0 at the end of period 3 exactly if both players chose C in every period. Find the smallest B supporting the strategy: cooperate while all past actions were C, and defect forever after any D. Check deviations at every cooperative history and punishment histories. Does the existence of that strategy make it the unique equilibrium?
thinking:
Before proposing cooperation, I should examine the terminal stage. Without the contract, D strictly dominates C in period 3 after every history. Given that fixed continuation, D strictly dominates in period 2 and then period 1. The unique subgame-perfect outcome is D,D throughout, with each player's discounted payoff 1+1/4+1/16=21/16.

For the bonus contract, I should compare a one-period defection with its full continuation value. If m periods remain at an unbroken cooperative history, cooperation under the proposed strategy gives 3*sum(delta^j,j=0..m-1)+delta^(m-1)*B. Defecting now gives 5+sum(delta^j,j=1..m-1), since punishment begins next period and the bonus is lost. The cooperation-minus-deviation difference is -2+2*sum(delta^j,j=1..m-1)+delta^(m-1)*B.

To find all constraints symbolically, set delta=1/4. At the last period m=1 the requirement is B>=2. With m=2, it is -2+1/2+B/4>=0, giving B>=6. With m=3, it is -2+2*(1/4+1/16)+B/16>=0, giving B>=22. Hence the smallest common bonus is 22. The first-period constraint binds, not the final-period constraint, because the promised reward is heavily discounted.

For completeness, after any past defection the bonus can never be earned. Both prescribed actions are D and the stage dominance makes D sequentially optimal at every remaining punishment history. At cooperative histories with B=22, the first-period deviation is indifferent, while later deviations are strictly worse. The one-deviation principle for this finite perfect-monitoring game therefore establishes subgame perfection of the prescribed strategy.

An independent payoff check starts at period 1. Cooperation with B=22 gives 3*(1+1/4+1/16)+22/16=85/16. Immediate defection gives 5+1/4+1/16=85/16, confirming the binding constraint. In period 2 cooperation gives 3+(3+22)/4=37/4, exceeding the deviation value 5+1/4=21/4. In period 3 cooperation gives 25 rather than deviation payoff 5.

To assess uniqueness, always choosing D is still a subgame-perfect strategy profile with the contract. Against an opponent who always defects, changing one's own action to C cannot earn the joint bonus and lowers the current payoff from 1 to 0. Thus the bonus creates a cooperative equilibrium without removing the defecting equilibrium. The contract changes incentives, but existence and selection remain different questions.

General pattern: I should compare complete discounted continuation values, not just the final-stage temptation. A terminal reward can make an earlier constraint bind more tightly when discounting is strong. Verify punishment credibility and distinguish a supported equilibrium from a unique one.
reference_answer:
Without a bonus, the unique subgame-perfect outcome is defection in all periods, worth 21/16 per player.

The smallest bonus supporting the stated cooperative strategy is B=22. The three constraints are B>=2, B>=6 and B>=22; the first-period constraint is strongest. At B=22 cooperation and immediate defection both yield 85/16 at the start, and punishment histories remain sequentially rational.

The cooperative equilibrium is not unique: always defecting remains subgame-perfect because unilateral cooperation cannot obtain the joint bonus.

problem: Una actividad genera un beneficio fijo, igual con o sin precaución. Sin precaución, la probabilidad de accidente es 1/5; tomar precaución cuesta 4 y reduce la probabilidad a 1/20. Cada accidente causa un daño real de 40. Las indemnizaciones también son 40 y constituyen transferencias entre responsable y víctima. No hay errores sobre la causalidad. Bajo responsabilidad estricta se indemniza cada accidente. Bajo la regla de negligencia, no tomar precaución es negligente: se absuelve erróneamente con probabilidad 1/2; tomando precaución, se declara negligencia por error con probabilidad 1/4, condicionalmente a un accidente. Compare la precaución socialmente óptima y la decisión privada bajo ambas reglas. Derive la condición general de incentivos de la regla de negligencia.
thinking:
Antes de comparar reglas, debo separar el daño real de su transferencia indemnizatoria. El coste social sin precaución es (1/5)*40=8. Con precaución es 4+(1/20)*40=6. El beneficio fijo se cancela, por lo que tomar precaución mejora el excedente en 2. Sumar otra vez las indemnizaciones al daño duplicaría una transferencia.

Para derivar la condición general, sean p0 y pI las probabilidades de accidente, I el coste de precaución, F la indemnización, beta1 el falso positivo con precaución y beta2 la absolución errónea sin ella. El coste privado negligente sin precaución es p0*(1-beta2)*F. Con precaución es I+pI*beta1*F. La precaución es óptima privadamente si I<=[p0*(1-beta2)-pI*beta1]*F. Esta comparación utiliza probabilidades de error condicionadas a que haya accidente.

Al sustituir los datos, sin precaución el coste privado es (1/5)*(1/2)*40=4; con precaución es 4+(1/20)*(1/4)*40=9/2. El umbral de coste compatible con los incentivos es 4-1/2=7/2, inferior al coste 4. Por ello la regla de negligencia induce ausencia de precaución, aunque socialmente convenga tomarla.

Una comprobación independiente usa responsabilidad estricta. El coste privado es 8 sin precaución y 6 con ella, igual a los costes sociales porque F coincide con el daño y se paga por cada accidente. Así la responsabilidad estricta induce precaución y recupera 2 de excedente frente a la regla de negligencia descrita.

Para generalizar, el umbral social es (p0-pI)*H. Sin errores, el umbral de la regla de negligencia es p0*F, porque quien cumple no indemniza. Los errores lo reducen en F*(p0*beta2+pI*beta1). Con F=H, la diferencia entre el umbral social y el negligente es F*(p0*beta2-pI*(1-beta1)); su signo depende de los parámetros. Aquí es 5/2>0, por lo que el umbral privado queda por debajo del social. No debo confundir la negligencia sin errores con responsabilidad estricta.

General pattern: debo calcular costes esperados por conducta y por regla, multiplicando correctamente las probabilidades condicionadas. Comparar el umbral privado con el social revela la distorsión, mientras la contabilidad de transferencias evita contar dos veces el daño.
reference_answer:
La precaución es socialmente óptima: el coste esperado baja de 8 a 6. La responsabilidad estricta reproduce esa comparación e induce precaución. La regla de negligencia produce costes privados de 4 sin precaución y 9/2 con ella, por lo que no induce precaución y pierde 2 de excedente.

En general, la regla de negligencia induce precaución cuando I<=[p0*(1-beta2)-pI*beta1]*F. Con indemnización igual al daño, con estos datos, el umbral privado queda por debajo del social. Las indemnizaciones son transferencias; el coste social incluye precaución y daño, no una segunda copia de la compensación.

problem: Ein Hemd kostet 50 Euro. Es gibt 10 Prozent Rabatt. Wie viel kostet es danach?
thinking: Zehn Prozent von 50 sind 5; ich ziehe den Rabatt vom ursprünglichen Preis ab.
reference_answer: Das Hemd kostet danach 45 Euro.

problem: Help me interpret a job-training experiment without assuming everybody benefits. Binary potential employment outcomes are Y1 with training and Y0 without it. Random assignment is independent of both potential outcomes, and population employment probabilities are known exactly: P(Y1=1)=3/5 and P(Y0=1)=2/5. Only one potential outcome can be observed per person. Find the average treatment effect and sharp bounds on the fractions helped and harmed, and on the variance of individual treatment effects. Construct observationally indistinguishable populations attaining the bounds. A universal programme would impose utility cost1/10 on each person, and employment has utility value1: does its positive average net gain establish majority support? Finally impose the additional assumption Y1>=Y0 for every person and explain what becomes identified and what randomisation alone did not establish.
thinking:
Before translating an average into individual gains, I should distinguish observed marginals from counterfactual pairs. Randomisation identifies E[Y1]-E[Y0]=3/5-2/5=1/5. It does not reveal both potential outcomes for any person. Let t=P(Y1=1,Y0=1). The helped fraction is3/5-t, the harmed fraction2/5-t, and the neither-employed fraction is t; the always-employed fraction is t. Nonnegative masses require0<=t<=2/5.

For sharp individual-effect bounds, helped lies in[1/5,3/5] and harmed in[0,2/5]. Their difference is always1/5, agreeing with the average effect. Every admissible t gives a valid joint distribution with the same treatment and control marginals. No treatment-assignment randomness can recover this missing dependence from a single observed outcome per person without another restriction or additional data structure.

For the variance, tau=Y1-Y0 is1 for helped people, -1 for harmed people and0 for the other types. Thus E[tau^2]=1-2*t and Var(tau)=1-2*t-(1/5)^2=24/25-2*t. Its sharp range is[4/25,24/25]. The difference in average employment rates identifies the mean effect but not the heterogeneity around it.

For endpoint constructions, at t=0 the population consists of3/5 helped and2/5 harmed, with no other types. At t=2/5 it consists of2/5 always employed,1/5 helped and2/5 never employed, with nobody harmed. Both populations yield treatment employment3/5 and control employment2/5. Independent random assignment therefore produces the same observed treatment-outcome distribution in each population, despite very different individual consequences.

For the universal programme, an individual's net utility change is tau-1/10. Its population mean is1/5-1/10=1/10>0. Only people with tau=1 gain; people with tau=0 or -1 lose. Thus the supporting fraction is exactly3/5-t, ranging from1/5 to3/5. A strict majority supports the programme precisely when t<1/10. The first endpoint population has a supporting majority, while the second has only1/5 supporters, though their average net gains are identical.

For the monotonicity restriction Y1>=Y0, the harmed fraction must vanish. Then2/5-t=0 gives t=2/5, identifying the always-employed fraction2/5, helped fraction1/5 and never-employed fraction2/5. Individual-effect variance becomes4/25, and only1/5 strictly support the cost-imposing universal policy. The nonnegative average effect is necessary for this assumption to be compatible with the marginals, but does not prove that it holds person by person.

For an independent variance check, monotonicity makes tau Bernoulli with success probability1/5, so Var(tau)=(1/5)*(4/5)=4/25. At the opposite endpoint tau is1 with probability3/5 and -1 with probability2/5, giving second moment1 and variance24/25. These direct type calculations confirm the moment formula without treating the potential outcomes as independent Bernoulli variables.

General pattern: I should separate randomisation's marginal causal identification from the unidentified joint distribution of counterfactual outcomes. Nonnegative type masses give sharp effect-heterogeneity bounds and explicit observational-equivalence witnesses. Average surplus, majority support and a no-harm assumption are different statements requiring different evidence.
reference_answer:
The average treatment effect is1/5. Helped and harmed fractions lie sharply in[1/5,3/5] and[0,2/5]; individual-effect variance lies in[4/25,24/25]. The free joint mass t=P(Y1=1,Y0=1) ranges from0 to2/5 and constructs every feasible population.

The universal policy's mean net gain is1/10, but its supporting fraction is3/5-t, so majority support is not identified. Under the extra no-harm assumption, t=2/5, helped1/5, harmed0 and variance4/25. Randomisation identifies the marginals, not that assumption or each person's counterfactual pair.

problem: Une activité génère un bénéfice marginal privé de 30−Q et un dommage marginal externe égal à Q. Quel est le niveau de marché sans taxe, le niveau efficace et la taxe pigouvienne?
thinking:
Avant de comparer les niveaux, le marché ignore le dommage: 30−Q=0 donne Qm=30. Le planificateur ajoute le dommage au coût marginal social et résout 30−Q=Q.

La quantité efficace est 15 et la taxe unitaire égale le dommage marginal en ce point, soit 15. Sous cette taxe, l'agent choisit 30−Q=15, ce qui reproduit l'optimum.

La taxe n'est pas le dommage à la quantité non régulée, qui serait 30. Une charge de 30 réduirait l'activité à zéro; le bon prélèvement évalue les dégâts à la marge sociale efficace.

General pattern: obtenir l'équilibre privé et la quantité sociale à partir de leurs conditions marginales, puis évaluer le dommage marginal au point social.
reference_answer: Le marché choisit 30, l’optimum est 15 et la taxe pigouvienne vaut 15.

problem: A firm with inverse demand p=50−2Q faces constant marginal cost 10 and a per-unit tax t=4. Find output, consumer price, producer net price, and tax revenue.
thinking:
Before treating the tax as a fixed cost, insert it into marginal cost. Total surplus-maximizing/private competitive supply equates willingness to pay to 10+4, so 50−2Q=14 and Q=18.

Consumers pay 14 while producers receive 10; the wedge is exactly 4. Tax revenue is tQ=72.

The untaxed equilibrium would solve 50−2Q=10, yielding Q=20. The two-unit reduction agrees with the slope rule ΔQ=−t/2, a comparative-static check.

General pattern: a per-unit tax creates a price wedge; demand slope converts that wedge into a quantity response, while revenue multiplies the wedge by traded quantity.
reference_answer: Quantity is 18; consumer price is 14; producer net price is 10; revenue is 72.

problem: Wie schätze ich eine konstante Ausfallrate, wenn nicht bei allen Personen das Ereignis beobachtet wird? Vier unabhängige Laufzeiten sind1,2,3,4; die ersten beiden und die vierte enden mit einem Ereignis, die dritte wird nach3 Einheiten rechtszensiert. Unter einer Exponentialverteilung mit nichtinformativer Zensierung leite die Maximum-Likelihood-Schätzung der Rate her. Berechne Ereigniszahl und Gesamtexpositionszeit und beweise, dass der Schätzer das eindeutige Maximum ist.
thinking:
Bevor ich zensierte Zeiten als Ereignisse behandle, schreibe ich ihre Likelihood-Beiträge. Ein beobachtetes Ereignis bei Zeit t trägt lambda*exp(-lambda*t) bei; eine Rechtszensierung bei t trägt nur die Überlebenswahrscheinlichkeit exp(-lambda*t) bei. Zusammen ergibt sich L(lambda)=lambda^D*exp(-lambda*T), wobei D die beobachtete Ereigniszahl und T die gesamte Expositionszeit ist.

Hier ist D=3 und T=1+2+3+4=10. Die Log-Likelihood ist3 ln(lambda)-10lambda; ihre Ableitung3/lambda-10 verschwindet bei lambda=3/10. Die zweite Ableitung -3/lambda² ist für lambda>0 negativ. Außerdem fällt die Log-Likelihood an beiden Rändern gegen minus unendlich, also ist dies das eindeutige globale Maximum.

Die Beobachtung bei Zeit3 trägt Expositionszeit bei, aber keine Ereignis-Potenz von lambda. Würde ich sie fälschlich als Ereignis zählen, erhielte ich4/10 statt3/10. Würde ich ihre Zeit verwerfen, verlöre ich drei Einheiten Information über das Überleben. Die kompakte Statistik(D,T) erhält genau die Information, die diese Exponential-Likelihood über lambda enthält.

Als unabhängige Kontrolle zerfällt der Score in Ereignisbeiträge1/lambda und den konstanten Abzug der gesamten Risikozeit T. Gleichsetzen bedeutet Ereigniszahl=geschätzte Rate mal Expositionszeit, also3=(3/10)*10. Das bestätigt sowohl die Schätzung als auch die Rolle der zensierten Beobachtung.

General pattern: Bei unabhängiger nichtinformativer Rechtszensierung zerlege ich jeden Beitrag in Ereignisindikator und beobachtete Risikozeit. Die Exponential-Likelihood reduziert sich auf Ereigniszahl und Exposition; Randverhalten und negative zweite Ableitung sichern das globale Maximum.
reference_answer:
Die Exponential-Likelihood ist proportional zu lambda³ exp(-10lambda). Es gibt3 Ereignisse und10 Einheiten Expositionszeit. Die eindeutige Maximum-Likelihood-Schätzung ist lambda_hat=3/10.

Die rechtszensierte Beobachtung bei3 erhöht die Expositionszeit, aber nicht die Ereigniszahl. Die Log-Likelihood hat zweite Ableitung -3/lambda²<0 und maximiert sich eindeutig bei3/lambda=10.

problem: A monopolist faces inverse demand p=100−Q and constant marginal cost20. Find the profit-maximizing output and deadweight-loss triangle, and show how the elasticity condition checks the markup.
thinking:
Before differentiating revenue, write profit=(100−Q−20)Q. The first-order condition is80−2Q=0, so Qm=40 and pm=60. At the efficient quantity price equals marginal cost, giving Q*=80.

The lost trades span quantities40 to80, and the demand-cost wedge falls linearly from40 to0. Deadweight loss is the triangle area one half·40·40=800.

At the monopoly point the absolute demand elasticity is p/(Q·slope)=60/40=3/2. Lerner's index is(p−MC)/p=40/60=2/3=1/|ε|, an independent markup check.

General pattern: linear monopoly output is half the efficient output under zero intercept shift in marginal cost. The demand-cost wedge integrates to a triangle, while the Lerner relation links optimal markup to elasticity.
reference_answer: Qm=40, pm=60, Q*=80, deadweight loss=800, and |ε|=3/2.

problem: A fair coin is tossed twice. Let X be the first toss coded 1 for heads, and let Z be the total number of heads. Compute E[X|Z=1] and explain the symmetry that makes it immediate.
thinking:
Before conditioning by cases, I use exchangeability. Given exactly one head, the two equally likely sequences are HT and TH. The first toss is heads in exactly one of them, so the conditional expectation is1/2.

The symmetry swapping toss positions preserves the event Z=1 and exchanges the indicator X with the second-toss indicator. Their conditional expectations must match; their sum is Z=1, so each conditional mean is1/2. This argument generalizes beyond listing the two outcomes.

Unconditionally, E[X]=1/2 as well, but that coincidence is not automatic for every conditioning event. Here the conditional symmetry and fixed total force it. A finite conditional-probability calculation confirms the value.

General pattern: under an exchangeable condition with a fixed total, symmetry equalizes component expectations; summing them recovers the total. This replaces outcome enumeration with a conservation argument.

problem: 请用一句话解释什么是“机会成本”。
thinking: 用户要求一句话，我用最优替代方案的价值来给出简洁定义。
reference_answer: 机会成本是作出一个选择时，放弃的最佳替代方案的价值。

problem: Je veux voir la décomposition de Slutsky en nombres. L'utilité est u(x,y)=√(xy), le revenu100 et les prix initiaux(1,1). Le prix de x passe à2, y restant à1. Calculez les paniers marshalliens initial et nouveau, puis les effets de substitution et de revenu sur x avec compensation hicksienne à l'utilité initiale.
thinking:
Avec des parts budgétaires égales, le panier initial est(50,50) et l'utilité vaut50. Après la hausse de prix, la demande marshallienne est x=100/(2·2)=25 et y=100/(2·1)=50. L'effet total sur x est donc−25.

Pour isoler la substitution, je garde l'utilité50 et minimise2x+y. La demande hicksienne Cobb-Douglas est x_h=u√(p_y/p_x)=25√2 et y_h=u√(p_x/p_y)=50√2. L'effet de substitution sur x vaut25√2−50, environ−14,645.

L'effet revenu est la différence entre la demande marshallienne nouvelle et la demande hicksienne:25−25√2, environ−10,355. Les deux effets s'additionnent: (25√2−50)+(25−25√2)=−25, exactement l'effet total. Ici les deux sont négatifs parce que x est normal et son prix augmente.

Comme contrôle, le panier hicksien maintient l'utilité: (25√2)(50√2)=2500, donc√(xy)=50. Il coûte2(25√2)+50√2=100√2, le revenu compensatoire requis aux nouveaux prix.

General pattern: La décomposition de Slutsky compare la nouvelle demande marshallienne à une demande hicksienne qui maintient l'utilité initiale. L'effet de substitution vient du prix relatif; l'effet revenu vient du pouvoir d'achat, et leur somme égale la variation totale.
reference_answer: Panier initial(50,50), utilité50. Nouveau panier marshallien(25,50). Panier hicksien(25√2,50√2). Effet substitution sur x=25√2−50; effet revenu=25−25√2; effet total=−25.

problem: Um projeto custa 500 hoje e paga 300 no fim de cada um dos próximos dois anos. Com taxa de desconto10%, calcule o valor presente líquido e decida se deve ser aceito.
thinking:
Antes de comparar valores em datas diferentes, desconto cada pagamento: VPL=−500+300/1,1+300/1,1². Com1,1=11/10, isso é−500+3000/11+30000/121=2500/121.

O VPL é ligeiramente positivo, cerca de20,661, então o projeto deve ser aceito sob a regra de maximizar valor presente. A proximidade de zero torna o cálculo exato especialmente útil.

A forma geométrica confirma: o valor dos recebimentos é300[(1−(10/11)²)/(1/10)]=55000/121, maior que500=60500/121 por2500/121.

General pattern: trazer todos os fluxos à mesma data com o fator de desconto apropriado. Um VPL negativo significa que o retorno não compensa o custo de oportunidade ao desconto escolhido.
reference_answer: The NPV is 2500/121, approximately 20.661, so accept the project.

problem: Two independent samples have n1=25, mean1=12, s1=5 and n2=36, mean2=10, s2=6. Compute the Welch standard error and t statistic for testing equal population means without assuming equal variances.
thinking:
Welch's variance estimate for the mean difference is s1²/n1+s2²/n2=25/25+36/36=2, so the standard error is√2. The observed difference is2, giving t=2/√2=√2.

The statistic measures the mean gap in estimated standard-error units. Unequal sample variances are retained separately; pooling them would impose a common-variance assumption not given in the problem.

A p-value additionally needs Welch–Satterthwaite degrees of freedom and the alternative's tail. The statistic alone establishes the standardized gap, not a significance conclusion.

As a check, each sample contributes exactly1 to the estimated variance of the difference. Their sum2 gives standard error√2, whose square multiplied by t²=2 recovers the squared mean gap4.

General pattern: Welch inference builds uncertainty from each group's own variance divided by its sample size. It avoids pooling and adjusts reference degrees of freedom for unequal precision.
reference_answer: Welch standard error=√2 and t statistic=√2 for the mean difference2.

problem: My five completed datasets give estimates [2,3,4,3,3], and each completed-data variance estimate is1. Pool them with Rubin's rules: compute the combined point estimate, within-imputation variance, between-imputation variance, total variance, and the large-sample degrees of freedom. Explain why treating the completed-data variance alone as final understates uncertainty.
thinking:
I average the five estimates first: Qbar=3. Their within-imputation variances are all1, so Ubar=1. The deviations from3 are−1,0,1,0,0; their squared sum is2, hence the between-imputation variance is B=2/(5−1)=1/2.

Rubin's total variance adds within-imputation uncertainty to the inflation for missing-data uncertainty: T=Ubar+(1+1/m)B=1+(6/5)(1/2)=8/5. The pooled standard error is therefore the square root of8/5, larger than the complete-data standard error1. Imputation does not erase uncertainty about values that were missing; variation among completed datasets records part of it.

For the requested large-sample degrees of freedom, the relative increase in variance is r=(1+1/m)B/Ubar=3/5. Rubin's approximation isν=(m−1)(1+1/r)²=4(8/3)²=256/9. The estimate stays3, but its reference distribution reflects both sampling uncertainty within datasets and instability across imputations.

As a check, if every imputation estimate were identical, B would be zero, T would reduce to Ubar, and the degrees of freedom would diverge in this approximation. Here B is positive, so T=8/5>1 andν=256/9 is finite. This limiting case confirms that the extra variance is driven by disagreement between imputations.

General pattern: Rubin pooling separates average within-imputation variance from between-imputation variation. Combine them as Ubar+(1+1/m)B; then use the relative variance increase to adjust degrees of freedom. Never report the complete-data standard error as if the missing values were known.
reference_answer: The pooled estimate is3. The within variance is1 and between variance is1/2, so total variance is8/5 and standard error√(8/5). The relative variance increase is3/5, giving large-sample degrees of freedom256/9. Ignoring between-imputation variation would leave variance1 and understate uncertainty.

problem: Pour un revenu y>=100, l'impôt est T(y)=y/5+2*sqrt(y)-20 et une prestation vaut B(y)=max(0,30-y/5). Le revenu disponible est R(y)=y-T(y)+B(y). Déterminez où le taux moyen T(y)/y augmente et où le taux marginal T'(y) diminue. Donnez les taux à y=100 et y=225. Calculez le taux marginal effectif 1-R'(y), y compris ses limites au seuil de prestation. Peut-on déduire la progressivité moyenne ou l'incitation marginale en regardant uniquement la courbure de T?
thinking:
Avant de classer l'impôt, je dois différencier le taux moyen lui-même. T'(y)=1/5+1/sqrt(y) et T''(y)=-1/(2*y^(3/2))<0: le taux marginal diminue sur tout le domaine. Le taux moyen est A(y)=1/5+2/sqrt(y)-20/y, donc A'(y)=(20-sqrt(y))/y^2. Il augmente pour 100<=y<400, stationne à 400 et diminue au-delà.

Pour retrouver le critère sans recalculer un quotient, je me rappelle A'=(T'-A)/y. Ici T'-A=(20-sqrt(y))/y. Le taux moyen augmente lorsque le marginal lui est supérieur, même si ce dernier diminue. La concavité de T ne suffit donc pas à conclure que le taux moyen diminue: le terme constant -20 change le rapport taxe-revenu.

Pour vérifier numériquement, à y=100, T=20, A=1/5 et T'=3/10. À y=225, T=55, A=11/45 et T'=4/15. Le taux moyen monte de 1/5 à 11/45 alors que le marginal descend de 3/10 à 4/15. À y=400 les deux taux coïncident à 1/4, ce qui confirme le seuil trouvé par la dérivée.

Pour mesurer l'incitation réelle, la prestation s'éteint à y=150. En dessous, B'=-1/5 et 1-R'=T'-B'=2/5+1/sqrt(y). Au-dessus, B'=0 et le taux effectif est 1/5+1/sqrt(y). R est continu à 150 mais non différentiable: les limites gauche et droite du taux effectif sont 2/5+1/sqrt(150) et 1/5+1/sqrt(150). La baisse est exactement 1/5.

Un contrôle indépendant utilise une petite hausse du revenu. À y=100, un euro supplémentaire augmente l'impôt d'environ 3/10 et réduit la prestation d'environ 1/5; le revenu disponible augmente donc d'environ 1/2. Cela confirme le taux effectif 1/2, différent du marginal fiscal 3/10. À y=225 la prestation est déjà nulle, donc le taux effectif coïncide avec 4/15.

Pour interpréter proprement, la progressivité moyenne concerne A'(y), l'incitation locale concerne le revenu disponible et les prestations, et la courbure T'' concerne seulement l'évolution du taux marginal fiscal. Le modèle montre des directions différentes sans contradiction. Je dois indiquer les taux unilatéraux au seuil au lieu d'y attribuer une dérivée inexistante.

General pattern: je dois comparer taux marginal et taux moyen par l'identité du quotient, puis ajouter les retraits de prestations au calcul marginal effectif. Un terme fixe et un seuil peuvent modifier la redistribution et l'incitation de façons qu'une simple courbure fiscale ne révèle pas.
reference_answer:
Le taux marginal diminue partout pour y>=100. Le taux moyen augmente jusqu'à 400, puis diminue; à 400 les deux valent 1/4.

À y=100, les taux moyen, marginal et effectif valent respectivement 1/5, 3/10 et 1/2. À y=225, ils valent 11/45, 4/15 et 4/15.

La prestation s'éteint à 150: le taux effectif baisse de 1/5 à ce seuil. La progressivité moyenne dépend de T'-T/y, tandis que l'incitation dépend aussi du retrait des prestations.

problem: Two independent competitive markets have constant producer price and marginal cost 1. With nonnegative unit taxes t1,t2, their quantities are q1=10-t1 and q2=10-2*t2, with t1<=10 and t2<=5. The government must collect exactly 12: R=t1*q1+t2*q2=12. Transfers do not directly change welfare. Find the taxes that globally minimise deadweight loss, give exact radical expressions, and prove that the other revenue-solving branch is inferior. Derive rather than assume a small-tax Ramsey approximation.
thinking:
Before applying a Ramsey rule, I should keep the exact tax bases. Relative to zero taxes, demand reductions are d1=t1 and d2=2*t2. The welfare triangles give L=(d1^2+d2^2/2)/2. Revenue is R=10*(d1+d2/2)-(d1^2+d2^2/2). Taxes shrink their own bases, so replacing R by 10*t1+10*t2 would solve a different problem.

A cheaper route to a global proof is weighted Cauchy rather than solving arbitrary candidates. Put S=d1+d2/2 and D=d1^2+d2^2/2=2*L. Then S^2<= (1+1/2)*D=3*L, with equality exactly when d1=d2. Consequently R<=10*sqrt(3*L)-2*L. Any feasible loss must satisfy 12<=10*sqrt(3*L)-2*L.

To solve the lower bound, let u=sqrt(3*L)>=0. The inequality is 12<=10*u-(2/3)*u^2, or u^2-15*u+18<=0. Its lower root is (15-3*sqrt(17))/2. Therefore L>=(3/4)*(5-sqrt(17))^2. Equality can be attained by d1=d2=z, because then u=3*z/2, R=15*z-(3/2)*z^2 and L=3*z^2/4.

To construct the minimiser, the equation R=12 gives z=5-sqrt(17) or z=5+sqrt(17). Both lie between 0 and 10 and are feasible common demand reductions. Since L increases strictly with z>=0, the smaller branch uniquely minimises loss. Thus t1=5-sqrt(17), t2=(5-sqrt(17))/2 and q1=q2=5+sqrt(17). The minimum loss is 63/2-(15/2)*sqrt(17). The larger-root policy collects the same amount by taxing much more heavily on depleted tax bases.

An independent local check uses the exact multiplier equations. In tax coordinates, the gradients of L are t1 and 2*t2, while those of R are 10-2*t1 and 10-4*t2. Setting their ratios equal gives t1/(10-2*t1)=2*t2/(10-4*t2), hence t1=2*t2. This matches equal demand reductions and the Cauchy equality condition. The bound also covers boundaries, so the local calculation is a check rather than the global proof.

To connect the result to Ramsey intuition, the less responsive first market has half the slope magnitude and receives twice the unit tax. Here the statement is exact because the two untaxed quantities are equal and the independent linear demands make the weighted bound sharp. It is not a general rule for arbitrary uncompensated demands, cross-price effects or redistribution objectives.

General pattern: retain the exact revenue constraint, express welfare losses as a positive quadratic form, and seek a sharp inequality linking revenue to loss. Equality identifies the tax proportions; the lower feasible root selects the efficient branch without a grid search.
reference_answer:
The unique loss-minimising taxes are t1=5-sqrt(17) and t2=(5-sqrt(17))/2. Both taxed quantities equal 5+sqrt(17); revenue is exactly 12. Minimum deadweight loss is 63/2-(15/2)*sqrt(17).

Weighted Cauchy gives R<=10*sqrt(3*L)-2*L. The proposed taxes attain its lower feasible loss bound because their demand reductions are equal. The second revenue root, 5+sqrt(17), gives strictly greater loss and is therefore inferior.

problem: What is the mean of 4, 6, 8, and 10?
thinking: The mean is the sum divided by the number of observations.
reference_answer: The mean is 7.

problem: Uma experiência económica observa cinco decisões independentes de cooperação Xi, cada uma Bernoulli(p), com 0<p<1. O estimador inicial de p é T=X1. Use S=sum(Xi) para construir um estimador não enviesado com menor variância, sem enumerar os 32 resultados possíveis. Prove a suficiência e a completude de S e conclua sobre a variância mínima entre estimadores não enviesados. Verifique o limite de Cramér-Rao e calcule as variâncias e a redução quando p=2/5.
thinking:
Antes de calcular, devo explorar a permutabilidade. Condicionalmente a S=k, as cinco posições têm a mesma probabilidade de conter um sucesso, e a soma das expectativas condicionais é k. Logo E[X1|S=k]=k/5. O estimador melhorado é S/5, obtido por condicionamento, não por procura nos vetores de observações.

Para comparar precisão, E[T]=p e Var(T)=p*(1-p). Como S é binomial com parâmetros 5 e p, E[S/5]=p e Var(S/5)=p*(1-p)/5. A decomposição da variância dá Var(T)=Var(E[T|S])+E[Var(T|S)], portanto a redução é 4*p*(1-p)/5>0. A vantagem resulta de remover a variação que não altera a contagem suficiente.

Para provar suficiência, a probabilidade de qualquer vetor observado é p^S*(1-p)^(5-S); a dependência do parâmetro passa apenas por S. Para completude, suponho E[g(S)]=0 para todo p em (0,1). Dividindo por (1-p)^5 e definindo t=p/(1-p)>0, obtenho sum(g(k)*binomial(5,k)*t^k,k=0..5)=0 para todo t>0. Um polinómio que se anula num intervalo tem todos os coeficientes nulos, logo g(k)=0 para todos os k. Esta é uma prova de identidade polinomial, não uma amostragem de valores de p.

Para estabelecer a conclusão global, qualquer estimador não enviesado pode ser condicionado em S sem aumentar a variância. O resultado condicionado continua não enviesado e é função de S. A completude obriga essa função a coincidir com S/5. Assim S/5 tem variância uniformemente mínima entre todos os estimadores não enviesados, não apenas os lineares.

Uma verificação independente usa a informação de Fisher. A pontuação é S/p-(5-S)/(1-p)=(S-5*p)/(p*(1-p)); a sua média é zero. A informação é Var(S)/(p^2*(1-p)^2)=5/(p*(1-p)). O limite para a variância não enviesada é o inverso p*(1-p)/5, atingido por S/5. A restrição 0<p<1 evita as singularidades da pontuação nas fronteiras.

Ao substituir p=2/5, Var(T)=6/25, Var(S/5)=6/125 e a redução é 24/125. A soma 6/125+24/125=6/25 verifica a decomposição. O estimador eficiente usa todas as decisões; usar apenas a primeira é não enviesado, mas desperdiça informação.

General pattern: devo condicionar numa estatística que preserva a informação sobre o parâmetro e usar simetria para calcular a esperança condicional. Suficiência e completude transformam a melhoria de variância numa conclusão global; a informação de Fisher fornece uma verificação independente da eficiência.
reference_answer:
O estimador melhorado é S/5, com variância p*(1-p)/5, contra p*(1-p) para X1. A redução é 4*p*(1-p)/5.

S é suficiente pela fatorização da verosimilhança e completo pela identidade polinomial em p/(1-p). O condicionamento reduz a variância, e a completude garante que S/5 é o estimador não enviesado de variância uniformemente mínima. A informação de Fisher é 5/(p*(1-p)), cujo limite inverso é atingido.

Para p=2/5, as variâncias são 6/25 e 6/125, com redução 24/125. A prova usa simetria e momentos binomiais em vez de enumerar os resultados individuais.

problem: For vectors u,v, prove ||u+v||≤||u||+||v|| by squaring both sides, and identify the equality geometry.
thinking:
Before squaring, note both sides are nonnegative. Expanding gives ||u+v||²=||u||²+||v||²+2u·v. Cauchy bounds u·v≤||u||||v||, so this is at most (||u||+||v||)².

Taking square roots proves the triangle inequality. Equality requires u·v=||u||||v||, so the vectors point in the same direction, including the zero-vector case.

The reverse triangle inequality follows by applying the result to u=(u+v)−v: ||u||−||v||≤||u+v||, and swapping u,v gives the absolute-value form.

General pattern: square a norm inequality only after confirming nonnegativity, then reduce the cross term to Cauchy-Schwarz. Equality conditions compose to identify alignment.
reference_answer: ||u+v||≤||u||+||v||, with equality when u and v are positively collinear (or one is zero).

thinking: 流量恒定时，总量等于每分钟流量乘以分钟数。

problem: A study reports an association but no randomized design. Give a two-sentence caveat without dismissing the result.
thinking: Acknowledge descriptive evidence, then distinguish association from causal identification.
reference_answer: The association is useful evidence about how the variables move together in this sample. Without a design that addresses confounding, it does not by itself establish causation.

problem: Two households face independent losses, each equal to100 with probability0.1 and zero otherwise. Compute the expected loss and variance per household before pooling, then after they share total losses equally. Explain the insurance gain.
thinking:
Each household's expected loss is0.1·100=10 and variance is0.1·0.9·100²=900. Their expected pooled loss per household remains10 by linearity.

With independent risks, the variance of the average loss is(900+900)/4=450, half the variance borne alone. Pooling leaves expected loss unchanged but reduces dispersion through imperfectly correlated outcomes.

The variance reduction would be smaller with positive correlation and vanish under perfect comovement. Independence is therefore doing substantive work; sharing does not diversify a common shock.

As a check, the individual loss indicators have zero covariance, so Var((L1+L2)/2)=[Var(L1)+Var(L2)]/4=450. The mean is still(10+10)/2=10.

General pattern: Risk pooling averages independent losses, preserving their mean while dividing variance by the number of pooled risks. Correlation determines how much of that diversification survives.
reference_answer: Before pooling, each household has mean loss10 and variance900. After equal pooling, mean loss remains10 and variance falls to450.

problem: A regulator chooses either a fixed emissions cap or a tax before learning the marginal-benefit intercept. Marginal benefit is a−3e, marginal damage is e, and a is8 or12 with equal probability. Find the optimal pre-announced cap and tax, then compare expected welfare losses to the state-contingent first best.
thinking:
In state a, efficient emissions solve a−3e=e, so e*(a)=a/4. A fixed cap chosen before learning maximizes expected surplus: E[a]−4e=0, hence e_cap=10/4=5/2. The expected marginal-benefit intercept is10.

Under a tax t, firms choose e=(a−t)/3. The regulator chooses t to maximize expected surplus before observing a, so expected social marginal surplus must be zero: E[a−4e]=0. Substituting gives10−4(10−t)/3=0, hence t=5/2. The induced emissions are11/6 when a=8 and19/6 when a=12, averaging5/2.

For a quadratic surplus, the loss from emissions e versus the state optimum is one half times curvature4 times(e−e*)². The cap's deviation is±1/2 in the two states, so its expected loss is1/2. The tax deviations are±1/6, so its expected loss is1/18. The tax is better because marginal benefit is relatively steep compared with damage curvature: errors in emissions are smaller.

As a check, state-contingent optimal emissions are2 and3. Under the cap5/2, each state's error has magnitude1/2; under the tax, errors are−1/6 and+1/6. Both instruments induce the same expected emissions, but uncertainty makes their state-by-state variability different.

General pattern: Under uncertainty, choose a price or quantity by maximizing expected surplus before the state is known. Compare instrument losses using the curvature of net surplus and the induced emissions error; the better instrument depends on relative slope uncertainty and damage curvature.
reference_answer: Optimal cap=5/2 and optimal tax=5/2. State-optimal emissions are2 or3. Expected welfare loss is1/2 under the cap and1/18 under the tax, so the tax performs better.

problem: Peux-tu m'aider à voir exactement d'où vient la perte de monopole? La demande inverse est p=20-Q et le coût total est C(Q)=4Q+Q²/2, avec Q>=0. Trouve le prix et la quantité de monopole, le surplus total sous monopole, l'allocation socialement efficace et la perte sèche. Je veux aussi comprendre pourquoi poser prix égal au coût marginal ne donne pas le choix privé, et vérifier la perte par une aire géométrique indépendante.
thinking:
Avant d'optimiser, je distingue prix et recette marginale. La recette est20Q-Q², donc sa dérivée vaut20-2Q; le coût marginal est4+Q. Le monopole égalise ces deux grandeurs, d'où20-2Q=4+Q et Qm=16/3. Le prix demandé est44/3. Confondre recette marginale et prix conduirait directement à l'allocation efficace, pas à la décision du monopole.

La condition de maximum est suffisante: le profit est concave, avec dérivée seconde -3. Au choix privé, recette marginale et coût marginal valent tous deux28/3, tandis que le prix dépasse le coût marginal de16/3. Le monopole internalise la baisse de prix sur les unités inframarginales, ce qui crée ce markup.

Pour le bien-être, le surplus brut des consommateurs est l'aire sous la demande,20Q-Q²/2; le coût réel est4Q+Q²/2. Leur différence à Qm vaut16Q-Q²=512/9. Je n'ajoute pas le prix aux ressources: les paiements sont des transferts entre acheteurs et vendeur.

L'optimum social égalise la valeur marginale20-Q au coût marginal4+Q, donc Q*=8. Son surplus est64. La perte sèche est donc64-512/9=64/9. Comme contrôle géométrique, entre Qm et8 l'écart demande moins coût marginal décroît linéairement de16/3 à0 sur une base8/3; le triangle vaut (1/2)(8/3)(16/3)=64/9.

General pattern: Le monopole choisit recette marginale égale au coût marginal, alors que l'efficacité compare directement valeur marginale et coût marginal. Pour calculer la perte sèche, j'intègre cet écart marginal entre les quantités ou j'utilise l'aire sous la courbe d'écart; les deux routes doivent coïncider.
reference_answer:
Le monopole produit Qm=16/3 et fixe p=44/3. Son surplus total est512/9. L'optimum social est Q*=8 avec surplus64; la perte sèche vaut64/9.

Le monopole égalise recette marginale20-2Q et coût marginal4+Q. L'optimum social égalise demande20-Q et coût marginal. La perte sèche est aussi le triangle de base8/3 et de hauteur16/3.

problem: Je veux construire le portefeuille risqué de Sharpe maximal. Deux actifs ont des rendements espérés8% et12%, une matrice de covariance [[0,04,0,01],[0,01,0,09]], et le taux sans risque vaut2%. Trouvez les poids du portefeuille tangent sans vente à découvert, son rendement et sa variance. Expliquez le rôle de l'inverse de covariance.
thinking:
Je forme les rendements excédentaires μ−r_f=(0,06,0,10). Pour un portefeuille de poids w, le carré du ratio de Sharpe est[wᵀ(μ−r_f)]²/(wᵀΣw). Le vecteur tangent est proportionnel àΣ⁻¹(μ−r_f): l'inverse de covariance réduit le poids des expositions risquées redondantes.

L'inverse deΣ appliqué aux rendements excédentaires donne des poids bruts(44/35,34/35). Leur somme vaut78/35; la normalisation budgétaire donne w=(22/39,17/39). Les deux poids sont positifs, donc la contrainte d'absence de vente à découvert est satisfaite sans projection sur une frontière.

Le rendement espéré est(22/39)0,08+(17/39)0,12=19/195≈9,744%. La variance wᵀΣw vaut1057/30420≈0,03475. Le rendement excédentaire est151/1950 et son carré divisé par la variance vaut151/875, le carré du Sharpe maximal.

Comme vérification indépendante, Σw=(35/78)(μ−r_f), ce qui confirme la condition du portefeuille tangent après normalisation. La covariance positive entre actifs réduit le bénéfice de les traiter comme deux paris indépendants.

General pattern: Le portefeuille tangent pondère les rendements excédentaires par l'inverse de leur matrice de covariance, puis normalise les poids. Cette transformation tient compte simultanément des rendements, des risques propres et des covariances entre actifs.
reference_answer: Poids tangents=(22/39,17/39). Rendement espéré=19/195≈9,744%. Variance=1057/30420≈0,03475. Les deux poids sont positifs.

problem: Une population contient10 dossiers, dont4 comportent une erreur. On en tire3 sans remise. Calculez la probabilité d'obtenir exactement2 dossiers erronés et comparez-la à l'approximation binomiale avec remise.
thinking:
Sans remise, la probabilité hypergéométrique est C(4,2)C(6,1)/C(10,3)=6·6/120=3/10.

Avec remise, l'approximation binomiale de paramètre0,4 donne C(3,2)(0,4)^2(0,6)=0,288=36/125. L'écart est3/10−36/125=3/250, soit0,012.

L'échantillonnage sans remise crée une dépendance négative entre indicatrices d'erreur: après avoir tiré une erreur, il en reste moins dans la population. La loi binomiale ignore cet ajustement fini et n'est qu'une approximation.

Comme contrôle, les combinaisons favorables comptent36 tirages non ordonnés sur120. L'approximation0,288 est proche mais inférieure à0,3; l'écart calculé est exactement12 millièmes.

General pattern: Sans remise, utiliser la loi hypergéométrique qui suit le nombre fixe de succès dans la population. L'approximation binomiale devient meilleure quand la fraction échantillonnée est faible.
reference_answer: Probabilité exacte=3/10. Approximation binomiale=36/125=0,288; différence=3/250=0,012.

problem: Calcule pgcd(252,198) et trouve des coefficients de Bézout. Peux-tu réutiliser les restes au lieu de chercher les coefficients séparément?
thinking:
Avant de remonter les coefficients, l'algorithme d'Euclide donne252=1·198+54, 198=3·54+36, 54=1·36+18, 36=2·18. Donc le pgcd est18.

La remontée conserve les mêmes restes: 18=54−36=54−(198−3·54)=4·54−198=4(252−198)−198=4·252−5·198. Les coefficients de Bézout sont donc4 et−5.

Je vérifie à la fois la divisibilité et la combinaison:18 divise252 et198, et4·252−5·198=18. L'algorithme certifie aussi que tout diviseur commun divise chaque reste, donc aucun diviseur commun plus grand n'existe.

General pattern: l'algorithme d'Euclide calcule le pgcd; la remontée des restes produit automatiquement une identité de Bézout. Chaque division euclidienne conserve l'ensemble des diviseurs communs.

problem: A monopolist sells in two separated markets with inverse demands p1=20−q1 and p2=12−q2, at constant marginal cost4. Find third-degree discriminatory prices and quantities, then compare total output with a single uniform price.
thinking:
Before imposing one price, optimize each market separately. The monopoly condition equates marginal revenue to4: in market1,20−2q1=4 gives q1=8,p1=12; in market2,12−2q2=4 gives q2=4,p2=8.

With discrimination total output is12. Under a uniform price p, total demand is(20−p)+(12−p)=32−2p while both markets are active; revenue maximization gives p=10 and Q=12. Here total quantity happens to match, although its allocation across markets differs.

At p=10, q1=10 and q2=2, yielding the same aggregate12. The price discrimination profit is(12−4)8+(8−4)4=80; uniform-price profit is(10−4)12=72. Segmentation raises profit by8 without changing aggregate output in this parameterization.

General pattern: under third-degree discrimination, set marginal revenue equal across markets and to marginal cost. Compare with uniform pricing using aggregate demand; quantities can coincide while surplus distribution and profit differ.
reference_answer: Discrimination gives (p1,q1)=(12,8),(p2,q2)=(8,4), profit80. Uniform p=10 gives total Q=12, profit72.

problem:
Mon modèle prédit le risque de défaut et on me dit qu'il est bien calibré. Est-ce que cela prouve qu'il prédit mieux ? J'aimerais une démonstration courte, pas seulement une intuition.

Une entreprise tirée au hasard appartient à l'un des quatre groupes équiprobables. La probabilité réelle de défaut dans ces groupes est p=(1/5,2/5,3/5,4/5). Le défaut Y vaut0 ou1 ; conditionnellement au groupe, Y suit une Bernoulli de paramètre p. Un premier modèle annonce F=(1/10,3/10,7/10,9/10). Ce sont des probabilités de population connues dans cet exercice, et non des fréquences estimées.

Le score de Brier est E[(Y-F)^2], à minimiser. Pour une prévision quelconque F, pose q(F)=E[Y|F] et mu=E[Y]. Démontre la décomposition score=mu*(1-mu)-Var(q(F))+E[(q(F)-F)^2]. Explique le sens de la résolution et du défaut de calibration, et pourquoi annoncer partout mu peut être parfaitement calibré sans être optimal.

Calcule le score et les trois termes de la décomposition pour le premier modèle. Compare avec un modèle qui annonce3/10 aux deux premiers groupes et7/10 aux deux derniers, avec le modèle qui annonce exactement p, et avec la constante1/2. Une meilleure calibration garantit-elle ici un score strictement meilleur ? Compare aussi la précision de classification des trois modèles non constants avec une décision positive si la probabilité dépasse1/2.

Enfin prouve, pour une probabilité réelle p, que la prévision déterministe p minimise uniquement le score conditionnel. Si la prévision Q est randomisée indépendamment de Y conditionnellement au groupe, de moyenne a et variance v, décompose son risque et explique si cette randomisation peut améliorer le score. Ne confonds pas incertitude de l'événement et bruit ajouté par le prévisionniste.
thinking:
Avant de juger la calibration, je dois préciser la perte. Conditionnellement à F, je peux écrire Y-F=(Y-q)+(q-F), où q=E[Y|F]. Le terme croisé a une espérance nulle puisque E[Y-q|F]=0. Ainsi E[(Y-F)^2]=E[Var(Y|F)]+E[(q-F)^2]. C'est la projection conditionnelle : l'écart de prévision se sépare en incertitude restante et erreur de moyenne conditionnelle.

Pour relier ce résultat au taux global, j'utilise la variance totale. Y étant binaire, Var(Y)=mu*(1-mu). La décomposition Var(Y)=E[Var(Y|F)]+Var(q) donne score=mu*(1-mu)-Var(q)+E[(q-F)^2]. La résolution est Var(q), la variation des risques réels distingués par la prévision. Le défaut de calibration est E[(q-F)^2]. Une prévision constante mu a q=mu, donc défaut0 et résolution0 : elle est calibrée mais ne distingue aucun risque.

Pour le premier modèle, les quatre valeurs de F sont distinctes, donc connaître F identifie le groupe et q=p. Le taux global vaut1/2, l'incertitude1/4. La résolution est[(1/5-1/2)^2+(2/5-1/2)^2+(3/5-1/2)^2+(4/5-1/2)^2]/4=1/20. Chaque erreur de calibration a une valeur absolue1/10, donc le défaut vaut1/100. Le score est1/4-1/20+1/100=21/100.

Pour une vérification indépendante, je peux conditionner sur le groupe plutôt que sur F. Si le risque réel est p et la prévision f, la perte attendue est p*(1-f)^2+(1-p)*f^2=p*(1-p)+(f-p)^2. La moyenne des variances Bernoulli vaut1/5, et la moyenne des erreurs au carré1/100. Leur somme21/100 retrouve le score précédent. La formule distingue l'aléa du défaut individuel et une prévision qui éloigne inutilement la moyenne annoncée du risque réel.

Pour le modèle regroupé, une annonce3/10 rassemble les risques1/5 et2/5, dont la moyenne est3/10. Une annonce7/10 rassemble3/5 et4/5, de moyenne7/10. Le modèle est donc calibré : q=F. Sa résolution est(3/10-1/2)^2=1/25, et son score1/4-1/25=21/100. Par rapport au premier modèle, il élimine1/100 de défaut de calibration, mais perd exactement1/100 de résolution. Une meilleure calibration n'assure donc pas ici une amélioration stricte du score.

Pour utiliser toute l'information disponible, je devrais recalibrer sans fusionner les groupes. Le modèle F=p a défaut0, résolution1/20 et score1/5. Le premier modèle peut atteindre ce résultat en remplaçant chaque annonce par sa fréquence conditionnelle q(F), car ses valeurs distinctes conservent l'identité du groupe. La constante1/2 a défaut0 mais score1/4. Ainsi deux prévisions calibrées peuvent avoir des performances différentes ; calibration, regroupement et utilisation de l'information ne sont pas synonymes.

Pour contrôler la classification, le seuil1/2 donne la même décision avec les trois modèles non constants : aucun défaut prédit dans les deux premiers groupes, défaut prédit dans les deux derniers. La probabilité de décision correcte est[(1-1/5)+(1-2/5)+3/5+4/5]/4=7/10. Cette égalité ne contredit pas les scores probabilistes différents. La précision binaire ne distingue pas deux probabilités différentes qui restent du même côté du seuil.

Pour prouver la propriété de score, je peux compléter le carré sans chercher plusieurs annonces. Avec le groupe connu, E[(Y-f)^2|groupe]=p*(1-p)+(f-p)^2, strictement minimisé à f=p. La valeur minimale est la variance Bernoulli p*(1-p), pas0 sauf pour un événement certain. Le carré supplémentaire est un certificat global sur tout f dans[0,1]. La prévision optimale reste honnête sur un événement incertain au lieu d'annoncer une certitude artificielle.

Pour une annonce randomisée Q indépendante de Y conditionnellement au groupe, sa moyenne a et sa variance v donnent E[(Y-Q)^2|groupe]=p*(1-p)+(a-p)^2+v. Je retrouve cette identité en annulant la covariance conditionnelle entre Y et Q et en décomposant E[(Q-p)^2]. Remplacer Q par sa moyenne a réduit le score de v ; choisir ensuite a=p élimine le carré de biais. La randomisation ne peut améliorer cette perte quadratique sous l'indépendance précisée.

General pattern: je dois choisir la perte avant de comparer des prévisions. La projection conditionnelle sépare calibration et résolution ; le carré complété prouve que le risque réel est l'annonce optimale. Regrouper peut améliorer la calibration tout en détruisant de l'information, et une précision binaire identique peut masquer des scores probabilistes différents. Une vérification par variances Bernoulli protège le raisonnement contre ces confusions.
reference_answer:
La décomposition est E[(Y-F)^2]=mu*(1-mu)-Var(E[Y|F])+E[(E[Y|F]-F)^2]. Elle découle de la projection conditionnelle puis de la variance totale.

Le premier modèle a incertitude1/4, résolution1/20, défaut de calibration1/100 et score21/100. Le modèle regroupé est calibré, mais sa résolution tombe à1/25 : son score reste21/100. Le modèle F=p est calibré avec score1/5 ; la constante1/2 est calibrée avec score1/4. La calibration seule ne garantit donc pas la meilleure prévision. Les trois modèles non constants ont pourtant la même précision binaire7/10 au seuil1/2.

Pour un groupe de risque p, le score d'une annonce f est p*(1-p)+(f-p)^2, uniquement minimisé par f=p. Avec une annonce randomisée indépendante de l'événement, de moyenne a et variance v, il devient p*(1-p)+(a-p)^2+v. Le bruit ajouté n'améliore pas le score ; la variance de l'événement demeure même avec une prévision optimale.
