problem: Drei Projektüberschüsse besitzen Erwartungswerte (1,2,3) und Kovarianzmatrix Sigma=[[1,0,1],[0,1,1],[1,1,2]]. Gewichte w erfüllen w1+w2+w3=1. Zunächst sind negative Gewichte zulässig. Bestimme das Portfolio minimaler Varianz bei Zielerwartungswert m, trotz der singulären Kovarianzmatrix; gib auch ein risikoloses Portfolio an. Danach sind alle Gewichte nichtnegativ. Bestimme den gesamten effizienten Varianzverlauf für1<=m<=3 mit den aktiven Grenzen, ohne numerische Designs durchzuprobieren. Berechne beide Optima bei m=2 und m=3. Unterscheide ein Nullrisiko-Portfolio von einer Lösung für einen beliebigen positiven Zielerwartungswert.
thinking:
Bevor ich Sigma invertiere, sollte ich ihre Struktur prüfen. Die dritte Zufallskomponente ist in Kovarianz und Mittelwert die Summe der ersten beiden. Die Varianz eines Portfolios ist (w1+w3)^2+(w2+w3)^2. Mit den Expositionen x=w1+w3 und y=w2+w3 wird der Erwartungswert x+2*y. Die Budgetbedingung gibt w3=x+y-1,w1=1-y,w2=1-x. Die Singularität verschwindet aus dem Optimierungsproblem, sobald ich diese zwei unabhängigen Risikofaktoren verwende.

Für ein beliebiges Ziel m gilt x+2*y=m. Cauchy-Schwarz liefert m^2<=(1^2+2^2)*(x^2+y^2)=5*V. Gleichheit verlangt (x,y)=(m/5,2*m/5). Daher ist die globale Mindestvarianz m^2/5 mit Gewichten (1-2*m/5,1-m/5,3*m/5-1). Diese Lösung benötigt keine inverse Kovarianzmatrix und beweist die optimale Varianz unmittelbar.

Für das Nullrisiko, x=y=0 bedeutet Gewichte (1,1,-1). Sie summieren sich zu1 und haben Erwartungswert1+2-3=0. Die Kovarianzmatrix besitzt den Nullvektor (1,1,-1), aber daraus folgt kein risikofreier positiver Erwartungswert. Bei m>0 zwingt die globale Schranke V>=m^2/5 eine strikt positive Varianz. Singularität allein ist kein Zertifikat für ein beliebiges Ziel bei Nullrisiko.

Für die Nichtnegativität parametrisiere ich durch z=w3. Dann w2=m-1-2*z und w1=2-m+z. Zulässigkeit verlangt max(0,m-2)<=z<=(m-1)/2. Die Varianz ist (2-m+2*z)^2+(m-1-z)^2, ein strikt konvexes Quadratpolynom mit zweiter Ableitung10. Sein freier Minimierer ist z=3*m/5-1. Ich muss diesen Wert auf das zulässige Intervall projizieren.

Im Bereich1<=m<=5/3 liegt der freie Minimierer unter null, also z=0. Gewichte sind (2-m,m-1,0), Varianz (2-m)^2+(m-1)^2. Für5/3<=m<=5/2 sind alle freien Gewichte nichtnegativ, sodass Varianz m^2/5 und die Cauchy-Gleichheitsgewichte gelten. Für5/2<=m<=3 unterschreitet der freie Wert die untere Grenze m-2; deshalb w1=0,w2=3-m,w3=m-2 und Varianz1+(m-2)^2. Die obere Grenze erzeugt im Inneren keinen zusätzlichen Bereich.

Bei m=2 ergeben beide Varianten Gewichte (1/5,3/5,1/5) und Varianz4/5. Bei m=3 ist die freie Lösung (-1/5,2/5,4/5), Varianz9/5; ohne negative Gewichte bleibt nur (0,0,1), Varianz2. Die zusätzliche Restriktion kostet dort Varianz1/5. Für Ziel1 ist ohne Restriktion die freie Varianz1/5 möglich, während ohne negative Gewichte nur das erste Projekt mit Varianz1 zulässig ist.

Eine unabhängige Prüfung kontrolliert Übergänge und Ableitungen. Bei m=5/3 trifft z=0 die freie Lösung und beide Varianzformeln ergeben5/9. Bei m=5/2 trifft w1=0 die freie Lösung und beide Formeln geben5/4. Da die freie Lösung das jeweilige Randgewicht genau null macht und das Varianzpolynom strikt konvex ist, liefern diese aktiven Grenzen globale Optima auf dem gesamten Intervall.

General pattern: ich sollte eine singuläre Kovarianz über unabhängige Risikofaktoren zerlegen. Cauchy-Schwarz gibt die freie effiziente Grenze, und Nichtnegativität wird zur Projektion auf ein skalares Intervall. Nullrisiko hängt gleichzeitig von Kovarianz, Budget und Zielmittelwert ab.
reference_answer:
Mit negativen Gewichten ist die Mindestvarianz m^2/5 bei (1-2*m/5,1-m/5,3*m/5-1). Das Nullrisiko-Portfolio (1,1,-1) hat Mittelwert0.

Ohne negative Gewichte ist die Mindestvarianz (2-m)^2+(m-1)^2 für1<=m<=5/3, m^2/5 für5/3<=m<=5/2, und1+(m-2)^2 für5/2<=m<=3. Bei m=2 gilt in beiden Fällen Varianz4/5. Bei m=3 sind die Optima9/5 ohne und2 mit Nichtnegativität; die Randprojektion beweist die globalen Lösungen.

problem: Ich verstehe nicht, wie ein einziger Ausreißer den Mittelwert ruiniert, aber den Median fast gar nicht bewegt. Betrachte die Stichprobe1,2,3,4,5. Ersetze zunächst den Wert5 durch M und berechne Mittelwert und Median. Bestimme dann für beide Schätzer den kleinsten Anteil von Beobachtungen, die durch beliebig große Werte ersetzt werden müssen, damit der Schätzer unbeschränkt werden kann. Begründe die Mediangrenze allein über die Rangposition, statt mögliche Datensätze aufzuzählen. Erkläre, was der Breakdown-Punkt aussagt und was nicht.
thinking:
Bevor ich rechne, unterscheide ich lokale Ausreißerwirkung von Breakdown. Für die Originaldaten sind Mittelwert und Median beide3. Ersetze5 durch M>5: Der Mittelwert ist(10+M)/5 und wächst ohne Grenze, während die sortierte Stichprobe1,2,3,4,M den Median3 behält.

Für den Breakdown-Punkt zählt die Rangposition. Bei fünf Beobachtungen ist der Median der dritte geordnete Wert. Mit höchstens zwei Ersetzungen bleiben mindestens drei ursprüngliche endliche Werte; ein Gegner kann den dritten Rang nicht beliebig weit verschieben, denn zwei Kontaminationen besetzen höchstens zwei Plätze am oberen Rand. Mit drei Ersetzungen kann er die drei größten Werte auf M setzen und dadurch den dritten Rang beliebig weit treiben. Der kleinste Anteil ist also3/5.

Beim Mittelwert genügt eine einzige Ersetzung: ihr Koeffizient ist1/5, also bleibt der neue Mittelwert linear unbeschränkt in M. Sein endlicher Stichproben-Breakdown-Punkt ist1/5. Die beiden Maße reagieren damit strukturell verschieden: der Mittelwert addiert Größen, der Median nutzt nur die Ordnung.

Als Kontrolle setze ich M=5005. Dann ist der Mittelwert1004 und der Median3. Bei zwei ersetzten größten Beobachtungen bleibt der Median5; bei drei wird er M. Das erreicht die Rangargumentation genau am behaupteten kritischen Anteil.

Ein hoher Breakdown-Punkt garantiert keine kleine Varianz bei sauberen normalverteilten Daten und macht den Median nicht für jedes Ziel überlegen. Er sagt nur, welcher minimale Anteil adversarial veränderter Beobachtungen die Schätzung beliebig weit treiben kann.

General pattern: Für robuste Kennzahlen untersuche ich, welche Ordnungstatistik definiert wird und wie viele ursprüngliche Rangplätze Kontamination verdrängen kann. Ein Breakdown-Beweis braucht eine untere Schranke für alle kleineren Kontaminationsmengen und eine Konstruktion, die die Grenze erreicht.
reference_answer:
Beim Ersetzen von5 durch M>5 ist der Mittelwert(10+M)/5 unbeschränkt, aber der Median bleibt3. Der Mittelwert hat Breakdown-Punkt1/5. Der Median hat Breakdown-Punkt3/5: zwei Ersetzungen können den dritten Rang nicht unbeschränkt verschieben, drei können es.

Für M=5005 sind Mittelwert1004 und Median3. Der Breakdown-Punkt misst Widerstand gegen beliebig große Kontamination, nicht Varianz oder Effizienz unter einem bestimmten Verteilungsmodell.

problem:
Wie löse ich den Preiswettbewerb, wenn beide Firmen Kapazitätsgrenzen haben und der Preis0 nicht stabil ist? Bitte leite eine echte gemischte Strategie her und überprüfe alle Preisabweichungen, statt nur zu sagen, dass es kein reines Gleichgewicht gibt.

Zwei Firmen setzen gleichzeitig nichtnegative Preise für dasselbe Gut. Grenzkosten sind0, jede Kapazität ist1/2. Nachfrage D(p)=max(0,1-p). Bei verschiedenen Preisen bedient die billigere Firma zuerst die Konsumenten mit der höchsten Zahlungsbereitschaft und verkauft min(1/2,D(ihres Preises)). Die teurere verkauft min(1/2,max(0,1-ihres Preises-1/2)). Bei gleichen Preisen verkauft jede min(1/2,D(p)/2). Kapazitätskosten sind versunken. Zahlungsbereitschaften sind gleichmäßig auf[0,1] mit Masse1 verteilt.

Finde ein symmetrisches Nash-Gleichgewicht mit unabhängigen Preisziehungen aus einer stetigen Verteilung mit Intervallträger. Leite unteren und oberen Preis, Verteilungsfunktion und Dichte aus der Indifferenz ab. Prüfe auch Abweichungen außerhalb des Trägers und gegen den Preis0 des Konkurrenten.

Berechne mittleren Firmenpreis, mittleren höchsten Preis und dessen zweites Moment. Nutze delta=log(2) für exakte Ausdrücke. Daraus bestimme erwartete Gesamtmenge, gesamten realen Überschuss, Konsumentenrente und Gewinnsumme sowie Verlust gegenüber effizienter Produktion zu Grenzkosten0. Kontrolliere den Überschuss durch das direkte Ressourcenintegral und durch die Verteilung der Zahlungen. Nicht alle Käufer zahlen denselben Preis; berücksichtige die Rationierungsregel. Suche keine Preispaare auf einem Raster.
thinking:
Vor der Verteilungssuche prüfe ich einen sicheren Abweichungsgewinn. Zum Preis1/4 verkauft eine Firma mindestens1/4: ist der Konkurrent billiger, bleibt diese Restnachfrage; ist er teurer, verkauft sie ihre Kapazität1/2. Sie garantiert damit Gewinn1/16. Im stetigen symmetrischen Gleichgewicht muss der gemeinsame Gewinn mindestens diesen Wert erreichen.

Am oberen Trägerende u hat der Konkurrent fast sicher einen niedrigeren Preis. Der Grenzgewinn ist dann u*max(1/2-u,0). Ein Ende u>=1/2 gäbe Gewinn0 und widerspräche der Garantie. Für u<1/2 ist diese Restgewinnparabel höchstens1/16, mit eindeutiger Spitze bei u=1/4. Indifferenz am oberen Ende erzwingt daher u=1/4 und gemeinsamen Gewinn pi=1/16. Am unteren Ende l ist die Firma fast sicher billiger und verkauft1/2, also l/2=pi und l=1/8.

Innerhalb des Trägers nutze ich die Gewinnindifferenz, um die unbekannte Verteilung zu entdecken. Mit Wahrscheinlichkeit1-F(p) bin ich billiger und verkaufe1/2; mit F(p) bin ich teurer und verkaufe1/2-p. Der erwartete Gewinn ist p*(1/2-p*F(p)). Gleichsetzen mit1/16 ergibt F(p)=1/(2*p)-1/(16*p^2), für1/8<=p<=1/4. Außerhalb gilt F=0 beziehungsweise1. Die Dichte f(p)=(1-4*p)/(8*p^3) ist auf dem Träger nichtnegativ; F(1/8)=0 und F(1/4)=1 beweisen die Normalisierung ohne Atome.

Für die globale Prüfung betrachte ich Preisbereiche analytisch. Unter1/8 ist die Firma stets billiger und verdient p/2<1/16. Über1/4 bis1/2 ist sie stets teurer und verdient p*(1/2-p)<=1/16; darüber ist ihre Restnachfrage0. Im Träger ergibt die abgeleitete F stets1/16. Gleichpreise haben Wahrscheinlichkeit0 unter der stetigen Verteilung. Somit ist jede Preisabweichung abgeprüft und die Konstruktion ein Nash-Gleichgewicht. Gegen einen Konkurrentenpreis0 liefert1/4 ebenfalls1/16, während0 nur0 liefert.

Für die Momente verwende ich Ordnungsstatistik. Ein einzelner Preis hat E[p]=integral from1/8 to1/4 of p*f(p)dp=(1-delta)/2. Der höchste Preis H=max(p1,p2) hat Verteilungsfunktion F(h)^2 und Dichte2*F(h)*f(h). Die entsprechenden Integrale ergeben E[H]=1/6 und E[H^2]=3/8-delta/2. Als Plausibilitätskontrolle ist der mittlere niedrigere Preis L daher2*E[p]-E[H]=5/6-delta; alle diese Preise liegen zwischen den Trägergrenzen.

Für Mengen und Ressourcen berücksichtige ich die Reihenfolge der Käufer. Die billigere Firma liefert1/2 an Zahlungsbereitschaften zwischen1/2 und1. Die teurere liefert1/2-H an Zahlungsbereitschaften zwischen H und1/2. Insgesamt Q=1-H, also E[Q]=5/6. Der reale Überschuss ist integral from H to1 of v dv=(1-H^2)/2. Daraus folgen E[W]=5/16+delta/4 und Verlust zur effizienten Menge1 von3/16-delta/4.

Für die unabhängige Zahlungskontrolle berechne ich die Konsumentenrente bei realisierten Preisen L,H. Sie ist integral from1/2 to1 of(v-L)dv+integral from H to1/2 of(v-H)dv=1/2-(L+H)/2+H^2/2. Die Gewinnsumme ist L/2+H*(1/2-H)=(L+H)/2-H^2. Addition gibt wieder(1-H^2)/2. Im Mittel ist die Gewinnsumme(1-delta)/2-(3/8-delta/2)=1/8, genau zweimal der Gleichgewichtsgewinn1/16; Konsumentenrente ist3/16+delta/4.

Zum Abschluss prüfe ich die ökonomische Grenze der Nullpreisintuition. Die gemeinsame Kapazität1 reicht zwar für Nachfrage bei0, aber jede einzelne Firma kann nur die Hälfte bedienen. Der Rivale zum Preis0 lässt somit profitable Restnachfrage für einen positiven Preis. Der zufällige höchste Preis bestimmt den letzten bedienten Käufer und daher den realen Verlust; der einfache mittlere Firmenpreis genügt dafür nicht.

General pattern: Ich pinne den oberen Preis mit einem garantierten Restgewinn und den unteren mit Kapazitätserlös fest. Gewinnindifferenz erzeugt die Verteilung, globale Abweichungsgrenzen beweisen das Gleichgewicht. Für Wohlfahrt verbinde ich Ordnungsstatistik mit der tatsächlichen Rationierung und lasse Zahlungen im Ressourcencheck wegfallen.
reference_answer:
Der stetige symmetrische Preis-Mix hat Träger[1/8,1/4], F(p)=1/(2*p)-1/(16*p^2) und f(p)=(1-4*p)/(8*p^3) im Inneren. Jede Firma erzielt1/16. Preise außerhalb bringen höchstens diesen Gewinn; gegen den Konkurrentenpreis0 ist1/4 profitabel.

E[p]=(1-delta)/2, E[H]=1/6 und E[H^2]=3/8-delta/2. Gesamtmenge ist1-H, also im Mittel5/6. Erwarteter realer Überschuss ist5/16+delta/4, Konsumentenrente3/16+delta/4 und Gewinnsumme1/8. Der Effizienzverlust ist3/16-delta/4.

Bei realisierten Preisen L,H ist die Konsumentenrente1/2-(L+H)/2+H^2/2 und die Gewinnsumme(L+H)/2-H^2. Ihre Summe entspricht dem direkten Ressourcenintegral(1-H^2)/2. Gesamtkapazität allein erzwingt somit keinen Nullpreis, und die Momente des höchsten Preises bestimmen die Wohlfahrt.

problem: How should I spend a sampling budget when observations within a workplace share the same shock? Outcomes are Yij=mu+Ai+epsilonij. Workplace shocks Ai have mean0 and variance1; individual errors have mean0 and variance8. All workplace shocks and individual errors are mutually independent, except that people in the same workplace share its Ai. Sample N workplaces and m people per workplace, and estimate mu by the grand mean. Both N,m are positive integers. Visiting each workplace costs8 and observing each person costs1; total cost cannot exceed240. Prove the globally variance-minimising design without trying all integer pairs. Calculate its estimator variance, the variance from incorrectly treating sampled people as independent, the design effect and equivalent independent sample size. Compare with the feasible design N=24,m=2, then derive the interior continuous-allocation formula for general positive shock variance, individual variance and costs.
thinking:
Before counting sample size, I should write the shared-noise decomposition. The grand mean is mu+(1/N)*sum Ai+(1/(N*m))*sum epsilonij. Its variance is1/N+8/(N*m). Averaging more people within a workplace reduces individual noise but not that workplace's common shock. Each individual outcome has variance9, and two different people in one workplace have covariance1; outcomes from different workplaces have covariance0.

For a global design certificate, the budget N*(8+m)<=240 gives1/N>=(8+m)/240. Therefore Var(mean)>=(1+8/m)*(8+m)/240=(16+m+64/m)/240. The arithmetic-geometric bound m+64/m>=16 has equality only at m=8. Thus every positive-integer design has variance at least32/240=2/15. This lower bound did not require enumeration of divisors, workplace counts or person counts.

For attainment, m=8 permits N=240/(8+8)=15, an integer. The design spends the whole budget and reaches variance1/15+8/120=2/15. Both inequalities require m=8 and full budget utilisation; then N=15. Hence this is the unique globally optimal integer pair, not a rounded continuous candidate whose feasibility has been assumed.

For the naive independence calculation, there are120 people and marginal variance9. Treating them as independent would give variance9/120=3/40, below the correct2/15. Their ratio is(2/15)/(3/40)=16/9. The true standard error is therefore4/3 times the independence standard error. The equivalent count of independent observations with marginal variance9 is9/(2/15)=135/2, or67.5; this is an information comparison, not a literal number of sampled people.

For an independent covariance check, the120 diagonal terms contribute120*9. There are N*m*(m-1)=15*8*7=840 ordered off-diagonal within-workplace pairs, each contributing covariance1. Dividing1080+840 by120^2 gives1920/14400=2/15. Equivalently the intraclass correlation is1/9 and the design effect1+(m-1)/9=1+7/9=16/9. This direct count confirms the shared-noise decomposition.

For the alternative design N=24,m=2, cost is24*(8+2)=240, but variance is1/24+8/48=5/24, larger than2/15. It pays for more independent workplaces while making too little use of each visit to reduce individual error. Conversely, spending almost everything within a single workplace leaves the common shock largely undiluted.

For general positive workplace variance vA, individual variance vE, setup cost c0, person cost c1 and budget B, the continuous full-budget variance is(vA+vE/m)*(c0+c1*m)/B. Its variable terms are[vA*c1*m+vE*c0/m]/B, with stationary replication mStar=sqrt(vE*c0/(vA*c1)). The remaining terms vA*c0+vE*c1 are constant. This formula is an interior relaxation: integer counts, minimum replication1 and at least one affordable workplace still need feasibility checks. In the given case equality is attainable exactly, which is why the bound already proves the integer solution.

General pattern: I should decompose common and individual noise before translating budget into sample size. A budget inequality plus arithmetic-geometric equality proves an integer design globally when its equality case is feasible. Covariance counts independently check the variance, and effective sample size must use the same marginal-variance benchmark.
reference_answer:
The unique optimal design is N=15 workplaces with m=8 people each, costing240. Its variance is2/15. The budget and m+64/m>=16 prove that no integer design can do better.

Ignoring clustering gives variance3/40; the design effect is16/9 and equivalent independent count135/2. The alternative N=24,m=2 has variance5/24. Generally the interior relaxed replication is sqrt(vE*c0/(vA*c1)), followed by actual budget and integer-feasibility checks.

problem: How can waiting be more valuable than investing when the project has positive NPV? At date 0 an irreversible project costs 8. Its date-1 payoff X is 4 or 16 with equal probability. The discount factor per period is 0.9. If the firm waits, it observes X at date 1 and may then pay 8 to receive X at date 2; it can abandon otherwise. Compare immediate investment with waiting and state the optimal date-1 decision.
thinking:
I compare values at date 0 and keep the timing explicit. Investing now gives −8+0.9 E[X]=−8+0.9(10)=1. The positive NPV means immediate investment is feasible and worthwhile, but irreversibility makes waiting a separate option rather than a costless delay of the same decision.

At date 1, after observing X, the investment payoff is −8+0.9X. For X=4 this is −4.4, so abandon; for X=16 it is6.4, so invest. The option value at date 0 is0.9 E[max(−8+0.9X,0)]=0.9(0+6.4)/2=2.88.

Waiting dominates immediate investment by1.88. The gain comes from truncating the downside after information arrives: the low state is discarded while the high state is retained. Comparing only expected payoffs would miss this convexity because max is applied state by state before taking the expectation.

As an independent check, the expected date-1 net payoff conditional on forced investment is−8+0.9(10)=1, so the date-0 value of forced delayed investment would be0.9. Flexibility raises it to2.88 by replacing the negative low-state payoff with zero. This decomposition isolates the value of the abandonment option.

General pattern: With irreversible investment, waiting has value when information arrives before commitment and the firm can abandon. Evaluate the option as the expectation of the positive part of state-contingent NPV; convexity makes that at least as large as acting on the average payoff.
reference_answer: Immediate investment NPV=1. Waiting value=2.88. At date 1 invest if X=16 and abandon if X=4; waiting is better by1.88.

problem: I estimated an outcome on one regressor and got a slope that seems too large. The centered variables satisfy Var(x)=4, Var(z)=9 and Cov(x,z)=3, while the true relation is y=2x+3z. Derive the slope from regressing y on x alone, identify the omitted-variable bias, and show that including both regressors recovers the structural coefficients.
thinking:
I view a one-regressor slope as a projection: b_x=Cov(x,y)/Var(x). Since y=2x+3z, Cov(x,y)=2Var(x)+3Cov(x,z)=8+9=17, so b_x=17/4. The bias relative to the structural coefficient2 is9/4.

The bias factorizes as the omitted effect3 times the projection of z onto x, Cov(x,z)/Var(x)=3/4. Thus 17/4=2+3×3/4. The sign is positive because z raises y and is positively correlated with x; this predicts the direction before arithmetic.

With both regressors, the normal equations use covariance matrix [[4,3],[3,9]] and outcome covariances (17,33). Its determinant is36−9=27, so it is invertible. Solving gives coefficients2 and3. The nonzero determinant certifies that the two effects are separately identified by these second moments.

As an independent check, substituting the recovered pair into the covariance equations gives 2×4+3×3=17 and 2×3+3×9=33. If Cov(x,z)=0, the omitted-variable bias formula collapses to zero; if either the omitted effect or correlation changes sign, the bias changes accordingly. These limiting cases expose exactly which link causes the distortion.

General pattern: Omitted-variable bias is a product of the omitted variable's causal coefficient and its linear projection onto the included regressor. Projection geometry turns a vague confounding warning into a signed, computable bias; the full regression removes it when the covariance matrix has full rank.
reference_answer: The short-regression slope is17/4 and its bias is9/4. The decomposition is2+3×(3/4), where3 is the effect of z and3/4 is the slope from projecting z on x. Including both regressors yields coefficients2 and3; the regressor covariance determinant is27, so the system has full rank.

problem: Two equally sized groups have means10 and14, with within-group variances4 and9. Compute the overall mean and variance using the law of total variance. Explain how much variation comes from differences between group means.
thinking:
Equal group sizes give overall mean μ=12. The within-group component is the average conditional variance: (4+9)/2=13/2.

The between-group component is the variance of conditional means around12: ((10−12)^2+(14−12)^2)/2=4. Total variance is therefore13/2+4=21/2.

This decomposition separates residual dispersion within groups from systematic differences between group means. Ignoring the second term would understate total variance by4, even though each group's variance was measured correctly.

As a check, the second moment is the average of variance plus squared mean: ((4+100)+(9+196))/2=309/2. Subtracting μ²=144 gives21/2, matching the decomposition.

General pattern: Total variance equals expected conditional variance plus variance of conditional expectations. Grouping explains variation only through the between-means term; within-group noise remains.
reference_answer: Overall mean=12. Within-group variance component=13/2; between-group component=4; total variance=21/2.

problem: Country A can produce4 units of cloth or2 units of wine per worker-hour. Country B can produce1 unit of cloth or1 unit of wine. Identify comparative advantage and a range of mutually beneficial terms of trade, then show gains from one feasible exchange.
thinking:
Opportunity cost of one cloth unit is1/2 wine in A and1 wine in B. A has comparative advantage in cloth; B's opportunity cost of wine is1 cloth versus2 cloth in A, so B has comparative advantage in wine.

A mutually beneficial world price must lie between their opportunity costs: one cloth trades for more than1/2 but less than1 wine. Choose3/4 wine per cloth, strictly inside the interval.

Let A devote one hour to4 cloth and exchange it for3 wine. A could have produced2 wine in that hour, so it gains1 wine. B pays3 wine, which takes3 hours and could have produced3 cloth; importing4 cloth instead leaves B one cloth ahead.

The gains are positive because the trade price3/4 wine per cloth lies strictly between A's cost1/2 and B's cost1. Each side specializes according to comparative advantage, and both gain relative to using the same resources domestically.

General pattern: Comparative advantage depends on opportunity cost, not absolute productivity. Any terms of trade strictly between the two costs can create gains for both sides through specialization and exchange.
reference_answer: A has comparative advantage in cloth; B in wine. Mutually beneficial terms satisfy1/2< wine per cloth <1; for example3/4.

problem: Tre elettori hanno preferenze A>B>C, B>C>A e C>A>B. Si usa un'agenda binaria: due alternative vengono votate per prime e la vincente affronta la terza. Calcola le maggioranze a coppie. Confronta gli esiti se ogni voto è sincero sulla coppia corrente con gli esiti del voto sofisticato: nel primo turno ciascun elettore vota per il ramo che porta al suo esito finale preferito, anticipando voti sinceri nell'ultimo turno. Considera le tre possibili coppie iniziali. Quale coppia iniziale deve scegliere un presidente che vuole A nei due regimi? Non presentare questi esiti come gli unici equilibri di tutti i possibili giochi di voto.
thinking:
Prima di analizzare l'agenda, devo ridurre le preferenze al ciclo di maggioranza. A batte B con gli elettori primo e terzo; B batte C con primo e secondo; C batte A con secondo e terzo. Ogni confronto è 2 contro 1. Non esiste un vincitore di Condorcet, quindi non posso cercare una graduatoria sociale transitiva da applicare a tutte le agende.

Per i voti sinceri, devo comporre due confronti di maggioranza. Se la prima coppia è A,B, vince A e poi C batte A, dando C. Se è B,C, vince B e poi A batte B, dando A. Se è C,A, vince C e poi B batte C, dando B. Il presidente che vuole A sceglie quindi la coppia iniziale B,C.

Per trovare il voto sofisticato, devo sostituire ogni ramo con il suo esito finale. Con prima coppia A,B, la vittoria iniziale di A porta a C, mentre quella di B porta a B. Gli elettori confrontano dunque C con B e la maggioranza preferisce B. Selezionano il ramo B, che batte poi C: l'esito finale è B, sebbene A battesse B nel confronto immediato sincero.

Per generalizzare il calcolo alle altre coppie, con prima coppia B,C i rami finali sono A e C; la maggioranza preferisce C, quindi sceglie il ramo C e l'esito finale è C. Con prima coppia C,A i rami finali sono B e A; la maggioranza preferisce A, quindi sceglie il ramo A e l'esito finale è A. Sotto la regola sofisticata il presidente che vuole A deve scegliere C,A, non l'agenda sincera B,C.

Un controllo indipendente osserva il ciclo: per ogni coppia iniziale, il vincitore sincero perde contro l'alternativa rimasta. Il perdente sincero invece batte l'alternativa rimasta. La scelta anticipata tra gli esiti finali favorisce quindi il perdente del primo confronto immediato. Questo spiega i tre risultati tramite un solo schema, senza provare tutte le sequenze di voti individuali.

Per delimitare la conclusione, l'enunciato specifica una regola comportamentale di voto sofisticato basata sugli esiti finali. In un gioco con schede simultanee, voti non decisivi e indifferenze strategiche, altri profili possono essere equilibri deboli. I risultati qui seguono dalla regola dichiarata e non dimostrano unicità generale di tutti gli equilibri del voto.

General pattern: devo trasformare i rami intermedi nei loro esiti finali prima di confrontare le preferenze strategiche. Un ciclo di maggioranza rende l'agenda rilevante, e l'anticipazione può invertire l'agenda che implementa lo stesso obiettivo del presidente.
reference_answer:
Le maggioranze formano il ciclo A>B>C>A, ciascuna per 2 a 1. Per coppie iniziali (A,B), (B,C), (C,A), gli esiti sinceri sono rispettivamente C,A,B.

Secondo la regola sofisticata indicata, gli esiti sono B,C,A: gli elettori confrontano gli esiti finali dei rami. Per ottenere A, il presidente sceglie B,C nel regime sincero e C,A nel regime sofisticato. Questi sono esiti delle regole specificate, senza una pretesa di unicità generale degli equilibri di voto.

problem: A city is considering a congestion toll. The inverse demand for peak trips is p=30−Q and marginal external congestion cost is Q. Find efficient trips and the Pigouvian toll, then compare with the untolled equilibrium when private marginal cost is zero.
thinking:
Before setting the toll, equate marginal willingness to pay with marginal social cost:30−Q=Q, yielding Q*=15. The marginal external cost at that quantity is15, so the Pigouvian toll is15.

Without a toll, private users take trips until30−Q=0, so Qm=30. The toll shifts private generalized cost to15 and reduces demand to15.

The toll equals marginal external damage at the efficient quantity, not at the untolled quantity. Evaluating damage at30 would overcorrect because the toll itself changes the number of trips.

General pattern: set a Pigouvian toll equal to marginal external cost evaluated at the social optimum. Solve the social condition first; then verify the private response reproduces that quantity.
reference_answer: Efficient trips are 15, the toll is 15, and untolled trips are 30.

problem:
Two risk-neutral bidders take part in a first-price sealed-bid auction for one indivisible object. Each bidder's value is drawn independently from the uniform distribution on [0, 1], the values are private information, and the seller values the object at zero. A reserve price r with 0 <= r <= 1 is announced in advance: bids strictly below r are not accepted, the highest accepted bid wins, the winner pays his own bid, and if no bid reaches r the seller keeps the object and no money changes hands. Ties occur with probability zero.

Find the symmetric strictly increasing equilibrium bid function on the values that participate, prove that no bidder of any value can gain by bidding anything else, and identify the lowest participating value.

Compute the expected revenue as a function of r in two ways: from the joint distribution of the highest and second-highest values, and from the winner's own bid and win probability. Find the revenue-maximising reserve price, its revenue, and compare it with the revenue at r = 0.

Compute the expected surplus of each bidder and the value destroyed at the revenue-maximising reserve, and verify the accounting identity that links revenue, bidder surplus, and the value created.

Explain the connection between the optimal reserve and the posted price a monopolist facing one such buyer would charge, and state why the second-price auction with the same reserve raises the same expected revenue.
thinking:
Before computing, I restrict imitation to x in [r,1]. Against an increasing rival bid b(x), bidding b(x) wins with probability x and gives U(v,x)=(v-b(x))*x. Participation below r cannot be profitable because every accepted bid costs at least r > v.

To discover the differential identity, the interior imitation condition at x=v is v*b'(v)+b(v)=v, or (v*b(v))'=v. For 0<r<1 the threshold type has zero surplus and bids b(r)=r. Integration gives b(v)=v/2+r^2/(2*v) for v>=r. Its derivative is (1-r^2/v^2)/2 > 0 for v>r, and b(v)<=v. For r=0 the continuous extension is b(v)=v/2 and b(0)=0; the equation r*(r-b(r))=0 alone would not determine the zero boundary.

To prove global incentives, substitution gives U(v,x)=v*x-x^2/2-r^2/2. Its curvature is -1, so for v in [r,1] the maximiser is x=v, with payoff (v^2-r^2)/2. For v<r, U=-(x-v)^2/2-(r^2-v^2)/2<0. Bids below r lose and give zero. Bids above b(1) already win surely and cost more than b(1), so none improves on the boundary imitation x=1. Thus the argument covers arbitrary bids, not just those inside the equilibrium image. Threshold types are indifferent; r=1 produces no sale almost surely.

To compute revenue from the actual first-price rule, the highest value H has density 2*h. Therefore R(r)=integral(2*h*b(h), h=r..1)=integral(h^2+r^2,h=r..1)=1/3+r^2-4*r^3/3. Realised revenue is b(H), not the second-highest value. Differentiation yields R'=2*r*(1-2*r), positive up to 1/2 and negative thereafter; R(0)=1/3, R(1)=0, R(1/2)=5/12.

An independent mechanism check uses the second-price auction explicitly. When both values exceed r, its expected payment contribution is integral(2*z*(1-z),z=r..1); when exactly one qualifies, the contribution is r*2*r*(1-r). Their sum is 1/3+r^2-4*r^3/3. Alternatively the joint order-statistic density is 2 on 0<=z<=h<=1, so the same second-price expectation is 2*integral(integral(max(r,z),z=0..h),h=r..1). Equal expected revenues do not mean the mechanisms have equal realised payments.

To account for surplus, each bidder's ex ante payoff is integral((v^2-r^2)/2,v=r..1)=1/6-r^2/2+r^3/3. Created value is integral(2*h^2,h=r..1)=2/3-2*r^3/3. Revenue plus twice bidder payoff equals created value identically. At r=1/2, each bidder gets 1/12, both get 1/6, created value is 7/12, and excluded value is 2/3-7/12=1/12. The no-sale probability r^2=1/4 is a probability, not the value loss itself.

To link the reserve to pricing, a uniform buyer's virtual value is v-(1-v)/1=2*v-1. Its zero is 1/2, matching the maximiser of the single-buyer posted-price revenue r*(1-r). Here the auction earns 5/12 while that posted price earns 1/4. The equality of optimal reserve and posted price relies on this uniform, risk-neutral, independent-values model with seller value zero.

General pattern: transform an incentive condition into an integrable derivative and fix its constant through a valid participation boundary. Check the entire bid domain, including bids outside the strategy image. Compute payments using the actual mechanism and use accounting or a separately derived mechanism comparison to verify expectations.
reference_answer:
For r>0 and v>=r, equilibrium bids are b(v)=v/2+r^2/(2*v); lower values stay out. At r=0 use b(v)=v/2 including b(0)=0. Imitation payoff is a concave quadratic maximised at the true value; rejected bids and bids above the strategy image cannot improve it.

Expected first-price revenue is 1/3+r^2-4*r^3/3, maximised at r=1/2 with revenue 5/12 rather than 1/3 without reserve. At that reserve each bidder's expected surplus is 1/12, total bidder surplus is 1/6, created value is 7/12, and excluded value is 1/12.

The second-price auction has the same expected revenue, as a separate integration of its payment rule shows. Its realised payment is generally different. The optimal reserve also equals the uniform single-buyer monopoly price; this is a model-specific result.

problem:
Help me make sense of this: I asked several analysts to estimate a project's cost, and only the lowest estimate was kept. Does that selection change what I should believe about the true cost?

Use this hypothetical model, not a real procurement contract. True cost theta is uniform on[0,2]. Analyst i reports Yi=theta+Ui, where Ui are independent uniform[-1,1], independent of theta. There are n>=2 analysts and I observe only M=min(Yi)=0; n is known. The reports are noisy estimates, not binding prices. Derive the posterior density and mean of theta for general n. For n=2, find the posterior variance and compare with observing Y1=0 from one analyst chosen before seeing any reports. Explain why conditioning on an exact continuous observation is valid through densities and why treating the selected report as an ordinary single observation fails.

The project gives a known benefit b=3/5 and costs theta if undertaken. I am risk neutral and can decline for payoff0. Decide whether to undertake it given only M=0 for n=2 and for n=3. For n=2, suppose I can instead recover the other report H=max(Y1,Y2) at no cost. Derive its conditional density given M=0, the posterior mean given the full pair(0,H), and the resulting decision rule. Compute the conditional expected payoff with and without that extra information and its exact value. Include an independent probability or expectation check. Do not sample possible costs or enumerate report pairs.
thinking:
Before computing, I should condition on the selection mechanism, not only the recorded number. The event M=0 has probability zero, so I use a regular conditional density at this interior observation. Given theta in[0,1], F_Y(0|theta)=(1-theta)/2 and f_Y(0|theta)=1/2. Outside this interval the observation is impossible. The minimum-density identity gives f_M(0|theta)=n*f_Y(0|theta)*(1-F_Y(0|theta))^(n-1)=n*(1+theta)^(n-1)/2^n. The other n-1 reports must all exceed0; that is the information discarded by a single-observation likelihood.

A cheaper route is to normalize the translated power. The constant prior density cancels, and integral_0^1(1+theta)^(n-1)dtheta=(2^n-1)/n. Thus f(theta|M=0)=n*(1+theta)^(n-1)/(2^n-1) on[0,1]. With z=1+theta, E[theta|M=0]=n*(2^(n+1)-1)/[(n+1)*(2^n-1)]-1. Increasing n tilts this density toward larger theta: the next likelihood ratio is proportional to1+theta, an increasing function. This is a monotone-likelihood-ratio trick, not a list of candidate costs. As n grows, the posterior concentrates at theta=1, the largest true cost compatible with a report0.

For two analysts, the posterior is2*(1+theta)/3. Its mean is(2/3)*(1/2+1/3)=5/9 and its second moment is(2/3)*(1/3+1/4)=7/18, so Var(theta|M=0)=7/18-(5/9)^2=13/162. For one analyst selected in advance, the likelihood of Y1=0 is constant on[0,1], giving mean1/2 and variance1/12. The selected report is optimistic: the posterior mean exceeds the naive single-report mean by1/18. Individual unbiased reporting, E[Yi|theta]=theta, does not imply unbiased selection, E[min(Yi)|theta]=theta-1+2/(n+1).

For the decision, I need expected net benefit rather than the most likely cost. At n=2, b-E[theta|M=0]=3/5-5/9=2/45>0, so I undertake the project. At n=3, the mean is17/28, giving3/5-17/28=-1/140<0, so I decline. More analysts with the same retained minimum0 can reverse the decision: a low minimum is easier to obtain from noise when more reports were screened. I should keep the known sample size in the likelihood.

To recover the missing report, I should use the joint ordered density. For n=2, f_(M,H)(0,h|theta)=2*(1/2)^2=1/2 wherever theta lies in[max(0,h-1),1], with0<=h<=2. The factor2 accounts for which analyst produced the minimum; it is constant in theta. Integrating the uniform prior gives joint density length/4. The marginal f_M(0) is integral_0^1(1+theta)/4 dtheta=3/8. Hence f_H(h|M=0)=2/3 for0<=h<=1 and2*(2-h)/3 for1<h<=2. The second branch shrinks because a large second report excludes small true costs.

For the full pair, the surviving interval gives the entire posterior without more algebra: theta|(M=0,H=h) is uniform[max(0,h-1),1]. Its mean mu(h) is1/2 for h<=1 and h/2 for h>1. The former retains the single-report mean because the second report adds no new support restriction; the latter raises it. The project is attractive exactly when mu(h)<3/5, equivalently h<6/5. At h=6/5 either action has payoff0. I use the support-intersection trick to discover the threshold, not numerical searches over h.

For the information value, conditional on M=0 the best expected payoff with H is E[max(0,3/5-mu(H))]. It equals integral_0^1(1/10)*(2/3)dh + integral_1^(6/5)(3/5-h/2)*2*(2-h)/3 dh =1/15+7/1125=82/1125. Without H it is max(0,3/5-5/9)=2/45=50/1125. Thus the extra report is worth32/1125. Recovering H does not reduce expected true cost; it permits declining precisely the unfavorable realizations that were averaged into the original decision.

For an independent check, the H density integrates to2/3+1/3=1. The tower identity gives E[mu(H)|M=0]=(1/2)*(2/3)+integral_1^2(h/2)*2*(2-h)/3 dh=1/3+2/9=5/9, matching the direct posterior. I can also price the flexibility from the rejected region alone: integral_(6/5)^2(h/2-3/5)*2*(2-h)/3 dh=32/1125. This must equal the information gain because the no-information policy always builds, while the informed policy changes only on that region. Convexity of max(0,b-mu) also requires a nonnegative gain.

General pattern: I should reconstruct how an observation was selected before applying Bayes. Order-statistic likelihoods expose the missing comparisons; translated powers and support intersections replace enumeration. For a risk-neutral binary decision, the posterior mean sets the threshold, while the value of an extra signal comes from adapting the action. The tower identity checks the posterior, and the rejected-region integral independently checks the value of that flexibility.
reference_answer:
The selected minimum gives f(theta|M=0)=n*(1+theta)^(n-1)/(2^n-1) on[0,1], with mean n*(2^(n+1)-1)/[(n+1)*(2^n-1)]-1. This likelihood includes the other reports exceeding0. For n=2, mean5/9 and variance13/162 replace the single prespecified report's mean1/2 and variance1/12.

At benefit3/5, undertake the project for n=2: expected payoff2/45. For n=3, decline: its expected net payoff if undertaken would be-1/140.

For n=2, H|M=0 has density2/3 on[0,1] and2*(2-h)/3 on(1,2]. The full-pair posterior is uniform[max(0,h-1),1]; its mean is1/2 for h<=1 and h/2 otherwise. Undertake for h<6/5, decline for h>6/5, and choose either at equality. Conditional expected payoff with H is82/1125, so its value is32/1125. The posterior tower identity and the avoided-loss integral both confirm the result.

problem: Three bidders have independent uniform[0,1] values in a second-price auction. Under truthful bidding, what is the seller's expected revenue? Use the middle order statistic, not simulations.
thinking:
Before integrating revenue, identify the payment: the winner pays the second-highest value. With three bidders, this is the middle order statistic.

Its density is6x(1−x), since one value lies below x, one above, and one at x in the order-statistic density. Thus expected revenue is∫₀¹6x²(1−x)dx=6(1/3−1/4)=1/2.

The general mean of the k-th order statistic among n uniform draws is k/(n+1); here k=2,n=3 also gives1/2. Truthful bidding is weakly dominant in a second-price auction, so this payment distribution is induced by truthful values.

General pattern: map an auction payment to an order-statistic rank, then use its density or known mean. Incentive compatibility connects bids to values; order statistics determine revenue.
reference_answer: Expected seller revenue is 1/2.

problem: My economic simulation estimates μ=E[X], but each run also returns a correlated control Y with known mean2. Suppose Var(X)=9, Var(Y)=4, and Cov(X,Y)=3. For the adjusted draw X−b(Y−2), choose b to minimize variance and calculate the variance of the mean over100 independent runs. Compare it with the unadjusted Monte Carlo estimator and explain why the adjustment stays unbiased.
thinking:
I center the control at its known expectation so it changes variance without changing the target mean. For one simulation draw, Var[X−b(Y−2)]=9−6b+4b². This convex quadratic is minimized where its derivative−6+8b vanishes, giving b*=3/4.

Substitution yields variance27/4 per draw. For100 independent runs, the adjusted sample mean has variance27/400; the ordinary sample mean has variance9/100. The reduction is1−(27/400)/(9/100)=1/4, or25 percent. Averaging independent replications divides each per-draw variance by100.

Unbiasedness follows from E[Y−2]=0, so E[X−b(Y−2)]=E[X]=μ for any fixed b. The control helps only because it is correlated with X: the positive covariance lets the subtraction remove some simulation noise. If covariance were zero, the optimal b would be zero and adjustment would provide no gain.

As an independent check, completing the square gives9−6b+4b²=27/4+4(b−3/4)², which proves the global minimum and nonnegative variance for every coefficient. At b=3/4 the residual simulation noise is orthogonal to the control: Cov(X−b(Y−2),Y)=3−(3/4)4=0.

General pattern: A control variate subtracts a centered, known-mean quantity to reduce Monte Carlo variance without shifting the estimand. Choose the coefficient as Cov(X,Y)/Var(Y); completing the square proves optimality, and the residual becomes uncorrelated with the control.
reference_answer: The optimal coefficient isb*=3/4. Adjusted variance is27/4 per run and27/400 for the mean of100 runs, versus9/100 without adjustment, a25% reduction. Centering Y at its known mean2 preserves unbiasedness.

problem: Project u=(3,1) onto the line spanned by v=(1,2). Give the projection, the squared distance, and an orthogonality certificate.
thinking:
Before minimizing a quadratic in a scalar, I use the geometry of projection. The coefficient is (u·v)/(v·v)=5/5=1, so the projection is v=(1,2). The residual is u−v=(2,−1).

The residual is perpendicular to the line because (2,−1)·(1,2)=0. Its squared length is4+1=5, which is the squared distance. Orthogonality is the certificate of optimality: every other point on the line adds a perpendicular squared component.

For an independent optimization check, ||u−tv||²=(3−t)²+(1−2t)² has derivative10t−10, so its unique minimizer is t=1 and the minimum is5. The scalar calculation agrees with the projection theorem.

General pattern: decompose a vector into parallel and orthogonal parts. The orthogonality residual certifies nearest-point optimality, and Pythagoras gives the distance immediately.
reference_answer: The projection is (1,2), the squared distance is 5, and the residual (2,−1) is orthogonal to (1,2).

problem: A risky asset pays100 in a good state and50 in a bad state, each with probability1/2. The stochastic discount factor is0.8 in the good state and1.2 in the bad state. Compute the asset price and explain why it is below the expected payoff.
thinking:
The price is the expected discounted payoff: E[mX]=0.5·0.8·100+0.5·1.2·50=70. The expected payoff itself is75, so the asset price is lower.

The discount factor averages to1, but covaries negatively with payoff: high payoff occurs when marginal value m is low. Algebraically price=E[m]E[X]+Cov(m,X)=75−5=70.

This is the risk-adjustment channel: states in which the asset pays more are relatively less valuable to investors, so its price is lower than the discounted mean under a constant discount factor.

As a check, the good-state contribution to price is40 and the bad-state contribution30. Their sum70 matches expected payoff75 plus covariance−5.

General pattern: Asset prices equal expected stochastic discount factor times payoff, not simply expected payoff. Covariance with the discount factor captures state-dependent valuation and risk premia.
reference_answer: The asset price is70. Expected payoff is75 and covariance with the discount factor is−5.

problem: A study conducts10 hypothesis tests and wants family-wise error at most0.05. One unadjusted p-value is0.008. Apply the Bonferroni rule and compute its adjusted p-value; state the decision.
thinking:
Bonferroni divides the family-wise level by the number of tests: the per-test threshold is0.05/10=0.005. Since0.008 exceeds0.005, this result is not significant under the family-wise rule.

Equivalently, the adjusted p-value is min(10·0.008,1)=0.08, which exceeds0.05. The two calculations must agree because multiplying each p-value by the test count is the dual form of dividing the threshold.

The guarantee uses the union bound and does not require independent tests, though it can be conservative when tests are strongly dependent. It controls the probability of at least one false rejection across the family.

As a check, ten events each with probability at most0.005 have union probability at most10·0.005=0.05. The observed0.008 fails that sufficient per-test bound.

General pattern: Bonferroni controls family-wise error by allocating the total error budget across tests. Compare p with alpha divided by m, or compare min(m·p,1) with alpha.
reference_answer: Bonferroni threshold=0.005; adjusted p-value=0.08. Do not reject at family-wise level0.05.

problem: There are n>=1 identical quantity-setting firms with qi>=0, common marginal cost c>0 and inverse demand p=1/sqrt(Q) for positive total output Q. A firm produces at cost c*qi. When Q=0 all profits are defined to be zero. Find and prove uniqueness of Cournot equilibrium for every n. Derive consumer gross benefit, equilibrium welfare and efficient welfare, including exact efficiency ratio. Evaluate quantities, price, profits and welfare for n=2,c=1. Explain how to handle the infinite demand value at zero without discarding the model or treating zero output as an equilibrium.
thinking:
Before differentiating at the singular boundary, I should compare zero output with a positive deviation. If every firm produces zero, one firm can choose q>0 and earn sqrt(q)-c*q, which is positive for0<q<1/c^2. Thus zero aggregate output cannot be equilibrium. Infinite willingness to pay at zero is integrable; it does not mean infinite total consumer value.

For positive total output, firm i's profit derivative is Q^(-1/2)-qi/(2*Q^(3/2))-c. The second derivative is -Q^(-3/2)+(3/4)*qi*Q^(-5/2)=-(qi/4+Q-qi)/Q^(5/2)<0. Holding rivals fixed, profit is strictly concave wherever Q>0, and as own output grows the negative linear cost dominates the square-root revenue. Hence an interior stationary quantity is the global best response.

To prove all firms active, any active firm satisfies p*(1-si/2)=c, where si=qi/Q>0. Consequently p>c. An inactive firm would have initial marginal profit p-c>0 and would enter. For n>1 this excludes a zero quantity in equilibrium. For n=1 the earlier positive deviation already excludes shutdown.

To discover symmetry rather than assume it, the interior conditions have common p and c, so1-si/2=c/p is identical for every firm. All output shares are equal, si=1/n. Therefore p=c/(1-1/(2*n)), Q=(1-1/(2*n))^2/c^2 and qi=Q/n. The forced common shares and positive concave best responses prove existence and uniqueness for every n, including monopoly.

For welfare, consumer gross benefit is the improper integral from0 toQ of z^(-1/2), equal to2*sqrt(Q). Its lower limit is finite. Net resource welfare is2*sqrt(Q)-c*Q=1/c-c*(sqrt(Q)-1/c)^2. The unique efficient total output is1/c^2, with welfare1/c. This square works in sqrt(Q), the natural curvature variable, and avoids a lengthy quotient calculation.

At Cournot output, sqrt(Q)=(1-1/(2*n))/c. The efficiency ratio is therefore1-1/(4*n^2). The loss is1/(4*n^2*c), shrinking quadratically in the number of firms. Each firm's markup is p-c=p/(2*n), consistent with its own output share and the inverse-demand elasticity.

For n=2,c=1, Q=9/16, each quantity9/32 and price4/3. Each profit is(1/3)*(9/32)=3/32. Gross benefit3/2 minus cost9/16 gives welfare15/16; efficient welfare is1. Consumer surplus is3/2-(4/3)*(9/16)=3/4, and adding total profit3/16 gives15/16 independently. At n=1, the ratio becomes3/4, matching the square-root monopoly result.

General pattern: I should test a singular boundary by feasible deviations and integrate demand before judging its welfare. Interior conditions can force symmetry through equal output shares. A completed square in the transformed aggregate quantity gives the exact welfare loss and its competitive limit.
reference_answer:
The unique equilibrium has Q=(1-1/(2*n))^2/c^2, qi=Q/n and p=c/(1-1/(2*n)). Efficient output is1/c^2 and welfare1/c; Cournot achieves the fraction1-1/(4*n^2).

At n=2,c=1, quantities are9/32 each, price4/3, profits3/32 each and welfare15/16. Zero output is not equilibrium because a small unilateral quantity earns positive profit, while the demand singularity has finite integrated benefit.

problem: In the public-goods exercise, I get the same investment choices whether people move together or one after the other. Can you check what I missed? I also used the proposed investment advantage Gi-150-75*p when the other invests with probability p; please check that formula. Two people choose I(invest) or N(abstain). If both invest, each pays75; a lone investor pays150; with neither investing there is no project. Whenever someone invests, both receive their respective monetary benefits GA,GB. Utilities are benefit minus own payment, or0 without the project. Analyse the source cases(GA,GB)=(100,100),(200,200),(200,100). Find all simultaneous Nash equilibria, including mixed equilibria, and all subgame-perfect equilibria when A moves first and B observes A. State the provision probabilities and expected real social surplus. Explain whether reversing the order changes the asymmetric case. Then analyse the additional boundary GA=GB=150: characterise all simultaneous mixed equilibria and all behavioural subgame-perfect equilibria, allowing arbitrary mixing when indifferent. Give the sequential off-path actions too. Use payoff differences and backward induction rather than a strategy-profile search.
thinking:
Before comparing timing, I should check the proposed payoff difference. If the other invests with probability p, investing gives(1-p)*(Gi-150)+p*(Gi-75), while abstaining gives p*Gi. Their difference is Di(p)=Gi-150+(75-Gi)*p. The proposed Gi-150-75*p incorrectly removes the benefit Gi against probability1 rather than against p. An endpoint check exposes it: at p=1, investing pays Gi-75 and abstaining pays Gi, so the difference must be-75 regardless of Gi. My derived expression has that property. I can classify best responses from this affine expression, without searching profiles.

For benefits100,100, Di(p)=-50-25*p<0 throughout[0,1]. Both strictly abstain. The simultaneous equilibrium is uniquely(N,N), provision probability0 and surplus0. Sequentially, B abstains after either action of A; A then prefers0 from N to-50 from I. The unique subgame-perfect strategy is A:N, B:N after I and N after N. A positive aggregate project surplus100+100-150=50 does not make solo financing privately attractive.

For benefits200,200, Di(p)=50-125*p. The interior indifference probability is p=2/5. The simultaneous pure equilibria are(I,N) and(N,I). In either, the investor receives50 and the free rider200, with provision probability1 and real surplus250. If one player mixes strictly, the other's probability must be2/5; that player's own indifference forces the first probability to2/5 as well. Thus the only additional equilibrium is independent mixing with probabilities(2/5,2/5). No asymmetric partial mixture survives these best-response conditions.

For mixed welfare, I should count construction cost once and use the budget identity as an independent check. Failure requires both to abstain, probability(3/5)^2=9/25. Provision probability is16/25, giving expected real surplus(200+200-150)*(16/25)=160. Each player's expected private payoff equals the abstention payoff200*(2/5)=80 by indifference, so the private sum80+80=160 agrees. The incorrect proposed difference would predict probabilities2/3, resource surplus2000/9 and private sum800/3; their disagreement supplies a second way to reject it.

For sequential benefits200,200, B chooses N after A:I because200>125, and I after A:N because50>0. Anticipating these responses, A obtains50 by investing and200 by waiting. The unique subgame-perfect strategy is A:N, B:N after I and I after N. The project is provided with probability1 and surplus250. Moving first makes A the free rider; it selects one of the simultaneous pure equilibria and eliminates mixed coordination failure. This conclusion depends on observed actions, not on an unobserved recommendation.

For asymmetric benefits200,100, B's difference is-50-25*pA<0, so B strictly abstains. A's best response to pB=0 is I because200-150=50>0. Thus the simultaneous equilibrium is uniquely(I,N). Sequentially with A first, B chooses N in both subgames and A invests. If B moves first, A abstains after B:I because200>125, and invests after B:N because50>0; B then prefers free-rider gain100 to solo-investor loss-50. The realised outcome stays A:I,B:N, provision probability1 and surplus150. Benefits determine the payer here, while timing matters in the symmetric high-benefit case.

For the boundary benefits150,150, the difference is Di(p)=-75*p. Investing is strictly inferior if the other invests with positive probability, and is indifferent when the other certainly abstains. Therefore all simultaneous behavioural Nash equilibria are exactly pA,pB in[0,1] with pA*pB=0. This includes both abstaining, either pure lone investor, and any mixture by one player while the other abstains surely. Provision probability is pA+pB on these axes; expected surplus is150*(pA+pB). There is no equilibrium with both probabilities positive.

For boundary backward induction, B must abstain after A:I, since free-rider payoff150 exceeds75. After A:N, B may invest with any probability r in[0,1], because solo investment and abstention both give0. If A invests it obtains0; if it abstains it obtains150*r. Let p be A's investment probability. For r>0, optimality requires p=0; for r=0, any p is optimal. Thus every behavioural subgame-perfect equilibrium is given by B:N after I, investment probability r after N, and p*r=0 with p,r in[0,1]. Provision probability is p+(1-p)*r=p+r on this set, and expected real surplus is150*(p+r). Specifying only a realised allocation would miss the required off-path abstention after I.

General pattern: I should check a binary provision payoff difference at its endpoints, then solve each observed subgame. An independent private-payoff versus resource-surplus identity can expose a mistaken cancellation before it contaminates the equilibrium. Strict incentives pin down backward induction; a zero solo gain creates whole axes of equilibria, so I must preserve indifference rather than impose an arbitrary tie-break.
reference_answer:
For(100,100), the simultaneous and sequential equilibrium is no investment; B abstains after either first action, and provision and surplus are0.

For(200,200), simultaneous Nash equilibria are(I,N),(N,I), and mixing with each investment probability2/5. The pure outcomes give provision1 and surplus250; the mixed outcome gives provision16/25 and expected surplus160. Sequentially A waits; B abstains after I and invests after N. This unique subgame-perfect equilibrium provides the project with surplus250.

For(200,100), the unique simultaneous outcome is A:I,B:N, with provision1 and surplus150. Both move orders give this outcome. With A first, B abstains in both subgames; with B first, A abstains after I and invests after N.

At benefits150, all simultaneous equilibria satisfy pA*pB=0. Sequential equilibria have B abstain after I, arbitrary investment probability r after N, and A's probability p satisfying p*r=0. Provision is pA+pB or p+r respectively, and surplus is150 times that probability. These sets follow from Di(p)=Gi-150+(75-Gi)*p and complete subgame best responses.

problem:
ساعدني في تنفيذ استراتيجية عشوائية: هل آخذ احتمال كل قرار من الخطة الأصلية ثم أرمي قطعة مستقلة عند كل عقدة؟ أشك أن هذا ينسى العلاقة بين القرارات التي اختارتها الخطة نفسها.

يختار اللاعب1 أولا A أو B. يرى اللاعب2 هذا الاختيار، ثم يختار التوقف أو الاستمرار. عند التوقف تنتهي اللعبة بمنفعة0 للاعب1. عند الاستمرار يتحرك اللاعب1 ثانية، ويتذكر اختياره الأول ويختار0 أو1. منافع اللاعب1 عند(A,0),(A,1),(B,0),(B,1) هي(-1,5,-4,2). يمكن أن تكون منافع اللاعب2 أي قيم معلومة؛ لا نحتاج حل توازن هنا، بل مقارنة تنفيذ الخطة المعطاة ضد أي سلوك له.

الخطة النقية للاعب1 هي(a,bA,bB)، حيث bA وbB قراراه المحتملان عند الاستمرار بعد كل فرع. يسحب سرا الخطة(A,1,0) باحتمال1/2، والخطة(A,0,1) باحتمال1/4، والخطة(B,0,1) باحتمال1/4. اللاعب2 لا يرى السحب، ويستمر باحتمال x بعد A وباحتمال y بعد B، مع x,y in[0,1]، وعشوائيته مستقلة عن السحب الخاص.

جد احتمالات سلوكية عند العقد التي تعطي قانون النهايات نفسه ضد جميع x,y. قارنها بوصفة تأخذ احتمال A والهامشين غير المشروطين لقرار1 في كل فرع، وتستخدم رميات مستقلة. احسب منفعة اللاعب1 بالطريقتين، وبخاصة عند x=y=1. هل يمكن استعادة توزيع السحب على كل الخطط من قانون النهايات وحده؟

احسب حجم مصفوفة الشكل الاستراتيجي دون كتابة جميع الخطط، واشرح هل وجود ألعاب فرعية صحيحة يمنع وجود هذه المصفوفة. أخيرا ادمج عقدتي القرار الثاني في مجموعة معلومات واحدة ينسى فيها اللاعب1 اختياره الأول. عند استمرار اللاعب2 دائما، هل احتمال سلوكي واحد للقرار1 يستطيع استنساخ قانون النهايات الأصلي؟ أثبت الجواب بشهادة جبرية قصيرة. لا تعدّد كل الاستراتيجيات أو حلول محتملة.
thinking:
قبل تنفيذ الرميات أحدد ما تكشفه الحركة الأولى عن الخطة الخاصة. احتمال A هو3/4 واحتمال B هو1/4. بين الخطط التي اختارت A، تقع الخطة ذات bA=1 بكتلة1/2، لذلك P(bA=1|A)=(1/2)/(3/4)=2/3. بعد B لا تبقى إلا الخطة ذات bB=1، فيكون احتمال1 هناك1. أستخدم حيلة التكييف على التاريخ الذي وقع، لا هامش القرار في خطط لم تصل إلى ذلك الفرع.

للتحقق ضد اللاعب الآخر أكتب الكتل المحققة. بعد A والاستمرار تكون كتلة0 هي x/4 وكتلة1 هي x/2، والتوقف بعد A كتلته3*(1-x)/4. بعد B تكون كتلة1 هي y/4، وكتلة0 هي0، والتوقف كتلته(1-y)/4. الرميات السلوكية باحتمالات(3/4,2/3,1) تعطي هذه الكتل نفسها. الاستمرار لا يكشف معلومات إضافية عن السحب الخاص داخل الفرع، لأن اللاعب2 يعتمد على الفرع المرصود فقط وعشوائيته مستقلة عنه.

لفحص الوصفة الهامشية أجد P(bA=1)=1/2 وP(bB=1)=1/2 في السحب الأصلي. استخدامهما دون شرط يعطي كتل الاستمرار(A,0),(A,1),(B,0),(B,1) مساوية(3*x/8,3*x/8,y/8,y/8). هذا يولّد النهاية(B,0) التي كانت مستحيلة في السحب الأصلي. الاحتمال الهامشي لخيار خارج المسار ليس احتماله بين الخطط التي وصلت إلى ذلك المسار.

للمنفعة أضرب الكتل في العوائد. التنفيذ الصحيح يعطي -x/4+5*x/2+2*y/4=9*x/4+y/2. التنفيذ الهامشي يعطي -3*x/8+15*x/8-4*y/8+2*y/8=3*x/2-y/4. الفرق3*(x+y)/4. عند x=y=1 تكون المنفعتان11/4 و5/4. هذا فحص مستقل للقانون المحقق: ليس اختلافا في كتابة الاحتمالات فقط، بل اختلاف في التوقعات الفعلية.

لاستعادة السحب الأصلي ألاحظ أن بعض تعليمات الخطة لا تنفذ أبدا. إذا اختارت الخطة A فلن يؤثر bB على أي نهاية، وإذا اختارت B فلن يؤثر bA. يمكنني مثلا تغيير bB في كل الخطط التي تبدأ A دون تغيير قانون النهايات ضد أي x,y. لذلك القانون المحقق لا يحدد التوزيع الكامل على الخطط. التكافؤ السلوكي يحدد التوقعات على المسارات الممكنة، وليس التعليمات غير المستعملة.

لحساب الشكل الاستراتيجي أستخدم حاصل ضرب الخيارات في مجموعات المعلومات. اللاعب1 له اختيار أول ذو بديلين وتعليمتان لاحقتان لكل منهما بديلان، فيملك2^3=8 خطط نقية. اللاعب2 له قرار مستقل عند كل فرع، فيملك2^2=4. إذن مصفوفة8 في4 موجودة، رغم أن الشجرة الأصلية تضم ألعابا فرعية صحيحة بعد الحركة الأولى. وجود لعبة فرعية لا يمنع تمثيل لعبة منتهية بالشكل الاستراتيجي؛ الذي يتغير هو أن مصفوفة ناش وحدها لا تختبر تلقائيا عقلانية السلوك داخل كل لعبة فرعية.

بعد دمج الذاكرة أبحث عن شهادة رتبة. عند الاستمرار دائما، مصفوفة قانون النهايات، بصفين A,B وعمودين0,1، هي [[1/4,1/2],[0,1/4]]. محددها1/16. لكن سياسة سلوكية بفرصة A تساوي p وفرصة القرار الثاني1 تساوي q تعطي [[p*(1-q),p*q],[(1-p)*(1-q),(1-p)*q]]، ومحددها0. فلا يمكنها مطابقة القانون المطلوب. وبصيغة شرطية، يحتاج الفرع A إلى q=2/3 والفرع B إلى q=1، بينما المجموعة المدمجة تسمح بقيمة واحدة فقط.

General pattern: أستخرج رمية العقدة بالتكييف على تاريخ قرارات اللاعب نفسه، وأفحص قانون المسارات قبل حساب العوائد. التعليمات غير المحققة لا تحدد من البيانات، وفقدان تذكر الفرع قد يفرض استقلالا سلوكيا لا يحترمه السحب السابق للخطط. شهادة المحدد تكشف هذا القيد دون تعداد الخطط.
reference_answer:
التنفيذ السلوكي المكافئ يختار A باحتمال3/4، ثم1 بعد A باحتمال2/3 وبعد B باحتمال1. كتل الاستمرار هي(x/4,x/2,0,y/4)، والمنفعة9*x/4+y/2.

الهامشان غير المشروطين كلاهما1/2. رميات مستقلة بهما تعطي(3*x/8,3*x/8,y/8,y/8) ومنفعة3*x/2-y/4. عند الاستمرار دائما، المنفعة الصحيحة11/4 والمخطئة5/4. قانون النهايات لا يستعيد تعليمات الخطط في الفروع غير المستعملة.

الشكل الاستراتيجي8 في4، ووجود ألعاب فرعية لا يمنع المصفوفة. عند نسيان الفرع، يحتاج القانون المطلوب إلى مصفوفة محددها1/16، بينما كل سياسة سلوكية ذات احتمال ثان واحد تعطي محددا0. إذن لا يمكن استنساخه بعد دمج مجموعتي المعلومات بهذه الطريقة.

problem: Je veux comprendre concrètement le mécanisme pivot de Clarke. Deux citoyens valorisent un projet public à10 et4; son coût réel est8, et le choix est construire ou ne pas construire. Applique la règle efficiente et calcule le paiement pivot de chacun. Vérifie la vérité des rapports par l'identité de bien-être qui fonde l'incitation, puis indique si les paiements couvrent le coût du projet et qui finance le déficit.
thinking:
Avant de calculer les transferts, je choisis l'issue qui maximise le surplus déclaré: construire donne10+4-8=6, contre0 sans projet. Le projet est donc construit. Les paiements pivot mesurent l'externalité que chaque citoyen impose à l'autre, en comparant le meilleur surplus des autres quand l'agent est absent au surplus des autres dans l'issue retenue.

Sans le citoyen1, le surplus maximal du citoyen2 et du projet est max(0,4-8)=0; dans l'issue construite, ce surplus vaut4-8=-4. Le paiement de1 est donc4. Sans le citoyen2, l'autre citoyen et le projet obtiennent max(0,10-8)=2; dans l'issue retenue ils obtiennent aussi10-8=2. Le paiement de2 est0.

Le mécanisme est incitatif parce que, pour un rapport fixé des autres, le transfert de l'agent i soustrait un terme indépendant de son propre rapport. Son utilité sous issue q devient sa vraie valeur v_i*q plus la valeur déclarée des autres moins le coût, moins ce terme fixe. Rapporter v_i choisit donc l'issue maximisant le surplus total avec sa vraie préférence; toute fausse déclaration ne peut l'améliorer.

Les paiements totalisent4, alors que le projet coûte8. Le mécanisme efficient a donc un déficit budgétaire4, couvert par une subvention externe; il n'est pas ex post budgétairement équilibré. C'est une tension structurelle dans ce petit bien public: l'agent1 est pivotal pour la construction, tandis que l'agent2 ne l'est pas, donc les externalités pivot ne révèlent pas à elles seules assez de recettes pour payer le coût.

Comme contrôle, la somme des vraies valeurs moins le coût est6, et les utilités privées après paiements sont6 pour le citoyen1 et4 pour le citoyen2. Avec le déficit externe4, la somme des ressources nettes est6, conforme au surplus social. Les transferts redistribuent les gains mais ne changent pas la règle d'efficacité.

General pattern: La règle pivot internalise l'effet d'un rapport sur le bien-être des autres et rend le rapport vrai dominant sous utilités quasi linéaires. L'efficacité et l'incitation n'impliquent pas l'équilibre du budget: les paiements mesurent des externalités, pas une formule générale de recouvrement du coût.
reference_answer:
Le projet est construit, car10+4-8=6>0. Le paiement pivot du citoyen1 est4; celui du citoyen2 est0. Le total4 ne couvre pas le coût8: il faut une subvention externe de4.

La vérité du rapport maximise le surplus total, car le transfert de pivot ne dépend pas du rapport propre de l'agent. Les utilités nettes des citoyens sont6 et4. La subvention4 est financée par les contribuables; citoyens et contribuables ont donc un surplus agrégé10-4=6, égal aux valeurs brutes14 moins le coût8.

problem: Find the number of onto maps from a 3-element set to a 2-element set and explain why it is 2^3−2 rather than 2^3.
thinking:
Before listing maps, count all2^3=8 functions. Exactly two are constant, each missing one target value; remove them to leave6 surjections.

Equivalently, an onto map assigns a nonempty proper subset of the domain to the first target. There are2^3−2 such subsets, again6.

The complement pairs the preimage of the first target with that of the second. It must be neither empty nor full, which explains precisely the two excluded functions.

General pattern: for maps onto two labeled targets, surjectivity is equivalent to choosing a nonempty proper preimage. Complementation gives a direct count and identifies the excluded constant maps.
reference_answer: There are 6 onto maps.

problem: Two goods have gross utility U=q1+q2-(q1^2+2*alpha*q1*q2+q2^2)/2, with -1<alpha<1 and constant marginal cost c=1/4. Initially separate firms compete in nonnegative quantities. They then merge and jointly choose both quantities, without changing technology. At alpha=-1/2 compute quantities, prices, total profit and welfare before and after merger and at the social optimum. Derive the sign of the merger's welfare change as a function of alpha and explain why the complementarity case differs from substitutes.
thinking:
Before predicting the merger effect, I should identify what alpha means. The cross derivative of marginal willingness to pay is -alpha. Negative alpha means complementary goods: raising one quantity increases the other's willingness to pay. The quadratic matrix A has eigenvalues 1+alpha and 1-alpha, both positive on the domain, so welfare and the joint-profit problem have strictly concave objectives.

For separate firms, own FOCs are 1-c-2*qi-alpha*qj=0. Their unique symmetric equilibrium is qC=(1-c)/(2+alpha). For joint ownership, total profit is (1-c)*(q1+q2)-q'*A*q. Differentiation gives 1-c-2*qi-2*alpha*qj=0, so qM=(1-c)/(2*(1+alpha)). The planner's quantities are q*=(1-c)/(1+alpha). The merger internalises the cross-good revenue effect that each separate firm ignores.

At alpha=-1/2, the quantities per good are qC=1/2, qM=3/4 and q*=3/2. Prices are pC=3/4, pM=5/8 and efficient price c=1/4. Separate firms' total profit is 2*qC^2=1/2; merged profit is 2*(pM-c)*qM=9/16, a private gain of 1/16. Output rises and price falls because jointly producing complementary goods strengthens their joint demand.

For welfare, put s=1-c=3/4. At a symmetric allocation W=2*s*q-(1+alpha)*q^2. The separate, merged and efficient values at alpha=-1/2 are respectively 5/8, 27/32 and 9/8. The merger raises welfare by 7/32, while still leaving its quantities at half the efficient level. Internalising a complementarity can benefit consumers without eliminating monopoly distortion.

To find the general sign, all relevant surplus expressions scale with s^2. The efficient surplus is W*=s^2/(1+alpha), the merged ratio W_M/W*=3/4 and the separate ratio is W_C/W*=(3+alpha)*(1+alpha)/(2+alpha)^2. Subtracting gives (W_M-W_C)/W*=-alpha*(alpha+4)/(4*(alpha+2)^2). On -1<alpha<1, every factor other than -alpha is positive, so the merger raises welfare for complements, leaves it unchanged at independence and lowers it for substitutes.

An independent check uses consumer surplus. For symmetry CS=(1+alpha)*q^2. At the complementary merged allocation this is 9/32; adding merged profit 9/16 gives 27/32. Before merger CS=1/8 plus profit 1/2 gives 5/8. Both match resource welfare and confirm that the private profit gain and the welfare gain are different quantities.

General pattern: I should inspect the sign of cross-demand effects before applying a merger intuition. Joint ownership doubles the cross term in each quantity condition. Scaling cancels level parameters from welfare ratios, and a factored ratio difference proves the welfare ranking across complements and substitutes.
reference_answer:
At alpha=-1/2, per-good quantities rise from 1/2 to 3/4 after merger, prices fall from 3/4 to 5/8, and total profit rises from 1/2 to 9/16. Welfare rises from 5/8 to 27/32, a gain of 7/32; efficient welfare is 9/8.

The general normalised welfare change is -alpha*(alpha+4)/(4*(alpha+2)^2). Thus coordination benefits welfare for complementary goods, leaves it unchanged for independent goods and harms it for substitutes. The sign follows from the internalised cross-demand effect.

problem: Country A has120 labor hours and needs2 hours per unit of X or4 per unit of Y. Country B also has120 hours and needs6 hours per X or3 per Y. Show comparative advantage, autarky production if each country splits labor equally, and a mutually beneficial trade at one unit of X for one unit of Y.
thinking:
Opportunity cost of one X is0.5Y in A and2Y in B. A has comparative advantage in X; B has comparative advantage in Y. This follows from relative costs, not absolute productivity: A is more productive in both goods, but its advantage is larger in X.

With half of each country's labor in each sector, autarky output is A:(30X,15Y) and B:(10X,20Y), for totals(40X,35Y). Full specialization gives A60X and B40Y. At the terms of trade1X=1Y, exchange16X for16Y: A consumes(44X,16Y) and B consumes(16X,24Y).

Each country's consumption exceeds its autarky bundle in both goods: A gains14X and1Y; B gains6X and4Y. The trade price lies strictly between A's opportunity cost0.5Y per X and B's2Y per X, so both can gain from exchange.

As a check, world resources after trade remain60X and40Y, equal to specialized production; only allocation changes. Relative to autarky, aggregate output rises by20X and5Y because labor moves toward each country's lower-opportunity-cost sector.

General pattern: Comparative advantage is determined by opportunity cost. Mutually beneficial terms of trade lie between the countries' relative costs, allowing specialization and exchange to produce consumption bundles outside each country's autarky production point.
reference_answer: A's opportunity cost of X is1/2Y; B's is2Y, so A specializes in X and B in Y. Autarky totals=(40X,35Y). After specialization and 16-for-16 trade, A consumes(44,16) and B(16,24), both better off.

problem: Four consecutive integers add up to 54. What are they?
thinking: Represent them as n through n+3. Their sum is 4n+6, so n=12; no search is needed.
reference_answer: The integers are 12, 13, 14, and 15.

problem: A randomized encouragement changes treatment take-up from1/4 to3/4, and mean outcomes change from6 in the unencouraged group to7 in the encouraged group. Under random assignment, exclusion, and monotonicity, calculate the first stage, reduced form, complier share, and local average treatment effect. Explain why the Wald ratio is not automatically the population average treatment effect.
thinking:
I separate the effect of assignment from the effect of treatment received. The first stage is3/4−1/4=1/2; the reduced form is7−6=1. Under monotonicity, assignment changes treatment status only for compliers, so the first stage equals their population share, one half.

Random assignment balances potential outcomes across encouragement groups, and exclusion removes any direct path from encouragement to outcome. Thus the reduced-form outcome difference is the complier share multiplied by the average treatment effect for compliers. Dividing1 by1/2 gives a local average treatment effect of2.

The identifying ratio targets compliers because they are the people whose treatment receipt responds to the instrument. Always-takers and never-takers do not contribute to the first stage; without additional assumptions, their treatment effects are not identified by this Wald comparison. A population-wide ATE would require stronger information or homogeneity.

As a check, multiplying the estimated complier effect2 by the complier share1/2 reconstructs the observed reduced form1. If the first stage were zero, the ratio would be undefined and the instrument would reveal no complier effect; with a small first stage, sampling noise in the ratio would be amplified.

General pattern: The Wald estimand is reduced-form effect divided by first-stage effect. Random assignment, exclusion, and monotonicity turn that ratio into a complier-average causal effect; the treatment-uptake shift identifies whose effect is being averaged.
reference_answer: The first stage is1/2, the reduced form is1, and the complier share is1/2. The Wald ratio is1/(1/2)=2, the local average treatment effect for compliers. It is not automatically the population ATE because noncompliers' treatment effects are not identified by this instrument alone.

problem: A lender only knows that a borrower's random operating profit X has mean3 and variance4; no distributional shape is specified. Insolvency is defined here as X+k<=0 after a deterministic cash buffer k>=0. Find the sharp worst-case insolvency probability at k=0 and the least buffer guaranteeing probability at most1/20 for every distribution with those moments. Prove sharpness with an extremal distribution rather than assuming normality. What changes if insolvency instead means strictly negative profit, X<0, at zero buffer?
thinking:
Before choosing a distribution, I should formulate a moment bound that holds for all of them. Let Y=3-X, so E[Y]=0 and E[Y^2]=4. Insolvency at buffer k is the event Y>=a with a=3+k>0. For any b>=0, this event implies(Y+b)^2>=(a+b)^2. Markov's inequality therefore gives probability at most(4+b^2)/(a+b)^2.

A cheaper route is completing a square in the bound rather than trying many shifts b. The identity(4+b^2)/(a+b)^2-4/(4+a^2)=(a*b-4)^2/((a+b)^2*(a^2+4)) proves the minimum is4/(4+a^2), attained at b=4/a. This is the one-sided Cantelli bound. Two-sided Chebyshev would discard the directional information and be weaker.

To prove sharpness, I should also make Markov's inequality an equality. Choose Y=a with probability4/(4+a^2) and Y=-4/a otherwise. The shifted square(Y+4/a)^2 is zero off the event and constant on it. The random variable Y has mean0 and variance4, so the construction meets the specified moments and attains the bound. In X coordinates, the two values are -k and3+4/(3+k).

At zero buffer, a=3. The worst probability is4/13, attained by X=0 with probability4/13 and X=13/3 with probability9/13. Their weighted mean is3, and the centred second moment is(4/13)*9+(9/13)*(4/3)^2=4. The point mass at exactly zero matters because insolvency includes equality.

For the target1/20, sharpness makes the inequality both necessary and sufficient: 4/(4+(3+k)^2)<=1/20. This reduces to(3+k)^2>=76. Since3+k is positive, the least buffer is k=2*sqrt(19)-3. At that buffer, the extremal distribution places probability1/20 at X=-k and19/20 at X=3+4/(3+k), so a smaller buffer cannot provide the required uniform guarantee.

To examine the strict event X<0 at k=0, the same upper bound4/13 remains valid but is not attained. At its equality construction, the bad value is0 and therefore excluded. Put the bad value at -epsilon with epsilon>0 instead, and set the other at3+4/(3+epsilon). Its bad-state probability4/(4+(3+epsilon)^2) approaches4/13 as epsilon decreases to zero. Thus4/13 is the supremum, with no maximising distribution for the strict event.

For nonattainment, equality in the sharp bound would force equality in both the optimised square bound and Markov's inequality. On the strict bad event Y>3, the shifted square is strictly larger than the event threshold. Positive event probability therefore makes the Markov inequality strict. This explains the missing maximum directly, not just by looking at one proposed distribution.

An independent check of the extremal family uses its separation a+4/a and the variance formula p*(1-p)*(a+4/a)^2. With p=4/(a^2+4), the variance is exactly4. Its mean cancellation is equally exact. A normal tail calculation would answer a different problem because the given moments alone permit this discrete worst case.

General pattern: I should optimise an inequality's auxiliary parameter, then inspect its equality conditions to discover an extremal distribution. A sharp moment bound gives necessary and sufficient robust constraints. Strict versus weak event thresholds can preserve a supremum while changing whether it is attained.
reference_answer:
The sharp worst-case probability is4/(4+(3+k)^2), so it is4/13 at zero buffer. Equality is attained by a two-point distribution, with mass at -k and3+4/(3+k).

The least buffer for a1/20 guarantee is2*sqrt(19)-3. If zero-buffer insolvency is strictly X<0, its supremum remains4/13 but is unattained; two-point laws with a negative value approaching zero attain probabilities approaching that supremum.

problem: Je veux résumer l'inégalité de ces revenus sans me fier seulement à la moyenne. Les revenus observés, déjà ordonnés, sont1,2,3,6. Calcule la courbe de Lorenz aux parts cumulées de population, le coefficient de Gini par l'aire sous la courbe, puis vérifie-le avec la formule des écarts absolus entre paires. Interprète aussi la part du revenu détenue par la moitié la plus pauvre.
thinking:
Je normalise d'abord par la population4 et le revenu total12. Les parts cumulées de population sont0,1/4,1/2,3/4,1; les parts cumulées de revenu sont0,1/12,1/4,1/2,1. La moitié la plus pauvre détient donc(1+2)/12=1/4 du revenu, tandis que le dernier quart en détient1/2.
