La courbe de Lorenz est linéaire entre ces points pour le calcul empirique. L'aire trapézoïdale vaut (1/4)[(0+1/12)/2+(1/12+1/4)/2+(1/4+1/2)/2+(1/2+1)/2]=1/3. Le Gini, deux fois l'aire entre la diagonale d'égalité et la courbe, vaut1−2(1/3)=1/3.

Je contrôle par l'identité pairwise: les six écarts absolus non redondants sont1,2,5,1,4,3, dont la somme est16. La formule G= somme des écarts pour i<j divisée par n² fois la moyenne donne16/(16×3)=1/3. Les deux constructions concordent: l'une compare la distribution à la diagonale, l'autre agrège les distances entre ménages.

La moyenne3 ne révèle pas seule cette concentration: le revenu6 du quart supérieur représente la moitié du total, alors que les deux revenus les plus faibles n'en représentent qu'un quart. Si les quatre revenus étaient égaux, l'aire de Lorenz serait1/2 et chaque écart pairwise nul, donnant G=0; cette borne contrôle le sens de l'indicateur.

General pattern: Le Gini mesure une même inégalité soit par l'écart entre la courbe de Lorenz et la diagonale, soit par les différences absolues entre paires. Le calcul par Lorenz rend les parts cumulées lisibles; la formule pairwise fournit un contrôle indépendant et clarifie la sensibilité aux écarts de revenus.
reference_answer: Les parts cumulées de revenu sont0,1/12,1/4,1/2,1. La moitié la plus pauvre reçoit1/4 du revenu. L'aire sous la courbe de Lorenz vaut1/3, donc le Gini vaut1/3. La somme des six écarts absolus est16 et donne aussi16/(16×3)=1/3.

problem: Comment prévoir la volatilité après un choc important? Mon modèle GARCH(1,1) est h(t+1)=ω+αe(t)^2+βh(t), avec ω=1/10, α=1/5, β=7/10. Aujourd'hui h(t)=2 et le dernier résidu vaut e(t)=3. Calcule les prévisions de variance pour les trois prochaines périodes, la variance de long terme, et explique la condition de convergence.
thinking:
Je sépare la prévision immédiate des horizons futurs. Le choc observé entre directement dans le premier pas: h(t+1)=1/10+(1/5)9+(7/10)2=33/10. Le grand résidu relève fortement la variance prévue au prochain pas.

À partir du pas suivant, le résidu futur n'est pas observé; sa variance conditionnelle espérée est la variance que je prévois. La récurrence devient donc h(t+k)=ω+(α+β)h(t+k−1). Elle donne h(t+2)=307/100 puis h(t+3)=2863/1000.

Le niveau fixe satisfait hbar=ω/(1−α−β)=1, car α+β=9/10<1. Les prévisions suivent alors h(t+k)=1+(9/10)^(k−1)(33/10−1): l'écart initial2.3 décroît géométriquement vers zéro. La condition α+β<1 garantit une variance inconditionnelle finie et la convergence des prévisions vers elle.

Comme contrôle indépendant, les écarts au niveau fixe sont23/10 au premier horizon,207/100 au deuxième, et1863/1000 au troisième; chacun est neuf dixièmes du précédent. Le modèle conserve ainsi la mémoire du choc tout en faisant revenir la volatilité vers son niveau de long terme.

General pattern: Dans un GARCH, le dernier choc observé détermine le premier forecast; aux horizons suivants, on remplace les innovations futures inconnues par leur variance conditionnelle prévue. La persistance α+β contrôle alors la vitesse de retour vers ω/(1−α−β).
reference_answer: Les prévisions sont h(t+1)=33/10, h(t+2)=307/100 et h(t+3)=2863/1000. La variance de long terme est1 puisque α+β=9/10. Les écarts au niveau fixe sont multipliés par9/10 à chaque horizon, donc les prévisions convergent géométriquement.

problem:
Can you check my spreadsheet? I randomly selected two firms and multiplied their average revenue by the number of firms. My colleague says random selection does not make this unbiased when firms have different chances of being included. How can I correct it, and how should I calculate uncertainty?

A fixed population has three firms with revenues y=(10,20,30). These revenues are fixed, not random draws from a model. The sampling design chooses exactly two distinct firms. Its probabilities of choosing the unordered pairs{1,2},{1,3},{2,3} are1/2,1/3,1/6 respectively. Let I_i indicate inclusion, pi_i=E[I_i], and pi_ij=E[I_i*I_j]. Randomness and expectations refer only to repeated sampling under this design. The actual observed sample is{1,3}.

Find the inclusion probabilities and the inverse-inclusion-probability estimator T_HT=sum_i I_i*y_i/pi_i of population total T. Prove its design unbiasedness and give its observed estimate. Compare it to T_N=(3/2)*sum_i I_i*y_i: calculate the naive estimator's expectation, bias, variance and mean squared error. Calculate the exact variance of T_HT, including all dependence terms; also give the incorrect variance obtained by pretending the indicators are independent.

Use the identity sum_i I_i=2 to derive a squared-difference formula for Var(T_HT). Turn it into an unbiased variance estimator based only on the observed firms and known sampling probabilities. Evaluate it for sample{1,3}, and check its expectation equals the true variance. Explain whether this one sample's naive estimate equalling T proves the naive procedure unbiased. Do not search over estimators or assume independent inclusion.
thinking:
Before correcting the spreadsheet, I should fix the probability space: revenues are constants and only inclusion varies. The inclusion probabilities follow from adding the pair probabilities containing each firm: pi1=1/2+1/3=5/6, pi2=1/2+1/6=2/3, pi3=1/3+1/6=1/2. Their sum is2, as required by the fixed sample size. The joint inclusion probabilities are the specified pair probabilities, not products of the marginals.

A cheaper route to unbiasedness is inverse-probability cancellation. Let a_i=y_i/pi_i, giving a=(12,30,60). Then E[T_HT]=sum_i E[I_i]*a_i=sum_i y_i=60 for any fixed revenue vector. In the observed sample{1,3}, T_HT=12+60=72. An unbiased procedure need not give the true total in a particular sample; unbiasedness is an expectation identity over the sampling design.

For the spreadsheet estimator, E[T_N]=(3/2)*sum_i pi_i*y_i=(3/2)*(25/3+40/3+15)=55. Its bias is55-60=-5. In the actual sample, T_N=(3/2)*(10+30)=60, exactly the true total. That coincidence does not contradict its negative design bias. Randomness alone is insufficient; equal inclusion probabilities would have been needed for this unweighted expansion to be unbiased for every revenue vector.

For uncertainty, I should use the covariance matrix of the inclusion indicators. Its diagonal entries are pi_i*(1-pi_i), and its off-diagonal entries are pi_ij-pi_i*pi_j. Thus C=[[5/36,-1/18,-1/12],[-1/18,2/9,-1/6],[-1/12,-1/6,1/4]]. Each row sums to0, because Cov(I_i,sum_j I_j)=Cov(I_i,2)=0. This row-sum check catches a false independent-inclusion calculation immediately.

With the quadratic-form shortcut, Var(T_HT)=a^T*C*a. The diagonal contribution is20+200+900=1120. The doubled off-diagonal contribution is2*(-20-60-300)=-760, so the actual variance is360. Pretending inclusion is independent gives1120 and discards the negative dependence created by selecting exactly two firms. For T_N the coefficient vector is b=(15,30,45), so its variance is b^T*C*b=125. Its mean squared error for the fixed total is125+(-5)^2=150. At this population it has smaller squared-error risk than HT despite being biased; unbiasedness and risk minimization are different claims.

To find a reusable variance identity, I should exploit C*1=0 instead of expanding every term again. Expanding sum_{i<j} C_ij*(a_i-a_j)^2 gives diagonal coefficients sum_{j!=i} C_ij=-C_ii and cross terms-2*C_ij*a_i*a_j. Hence a^T*C*a=-sum_{i<j} C_ij*(a_i-a_j)^2. Here this becomes(1/18)*18^2+(1/12)*48^2+(1/6)*30^2=18+192+150=360. The squared-difference route independently checks the matrix computation and explains why a constant a_i would produce zero variance with a fixed sample size.

For an observable variance estimate, I should apply inverse-probability cancellation to pairs as well as individual firms. Since E[I_i*I_j/pi_ij]=1 and every pi_ij is positive, V_hat=-sum_{i<j} I_i*I_j*(C_ij/pi_ij)*(a_i-a_j)^2 has expectation Var(T_HT). It uses only sampled revenues. In sample{1,3}, C13=-1/12 and pi13=1/3, so V_hat=(1/4)*(12-60)^2=576. A variance estimate from one sample can differ from the true repeated-sampling variance360; its unbiasedness is again an expectation statement.

For the final check, substituting E[I_i*I_j]=pi_ij into E[V_hat] cancels every joint probability and gives the same18+192+150=360. No simulation or search over possible answers is needed. The two cancellations operate at different levels: pi_i corrects estimated totals, while pi_ij corrects estimated variance. Using marginal probabilities in place of joint inclusion would destroy this second identity.

General pattern: I should match weights to the actual randomization unit. Unequal individual inclusion calls for inverse-probability weights; dependent pair inclusion determines uncertainty. Fixed sample size creates a covariance null direction, which converts the variance into weighted squared differences and supplies an independent check. A correct estimate in one realized sample does not establish unbiasedness, and an unbiased estimator need not have the smallest mean squared error at every population.
reference_answer:
The inclusion probabilities are(5/6,2/3,1/2). HT weights revenues into(12,30,60), so its expectation is T=60 and its observed estimate is72. The naive estimator has expectation55, bias-5, variance125 and mean squared error150; its observed value60 is only a sample-specific coincidence.

The inclusion covariance matrix is[[5/36,-1/18,-1/12],[-1/18,2/9,-1/6],[-1/12,-1/6,1/4]]. HT variance is360, whereas the false independent-inclusion calculation gives1120. Fixed sample size implies C*1=0, yielding Var(T_HT)=-sum_{i<j} C_ij*(a_i-a_j)^2=18+192+150=360, with a_i=y_i/pi_i.

An unbiased observable variance estimator is -sum_{i<j} I_i*I_j*(C_ij/pi_ij)*(a_i-a_j)^2. It equals576 for sample{1,3}. Taking expectations cancels pi_ij and recovers360, proving its design unbiasedness without an independence assumption.

problem: Help me see why two consumer-price indices give different inflation. In the base period prices are(2,4) and quantities are(5,2); in the current period prices are(3,3) and quantities are(4,3). Compute the Laspeyres and Paasche indices, compare them exactly, and explain how the change in the consumption basket drives their difference.
thinking:
I keep prices and quantities from different periods paired consistently. The Laspeyres index prices the base basket twice: its cost rises from2×5+4×2=18 to3×5+3×2=21, so PL=21/18=7/6. It holds quantities fixed to isolate the price change faced by the original basket.

The Paasche index instead prices the current basket at both price vectors. Current-period cost is3×4+3×3=21, while that same basket at base prices costs2×4+4×3=20, giving PP=21/20. The exact gap is7/6−21/20=7/60; Laspeyres reports16 2/3 percent inflation and Paasche5 percent.

The direction follows the quantity shift. Good1's price rises from2 to3, while good2's falls from4 to3; consumption shifts away from good1 and toward good2. The base basket gives more weight to the sharply rising price, so its index is larger than the current-basket index. This is a weighting effect, not an arithmetic contradiction.

As a check, all four basket costs are18,21,20,21 in the roles just stated: old basket at old prices, old basket at new prices, new basket at old prices, and new basket at new prices. Each index is a ratio of the appropriate matched pair. If quantities had not changed, the two indices would coincide; the observed difference comes from rebasing the weights.

General pattern: Laspeyres fixes base quantities and Paasche fixes current quantities. When consumers shift away from goods with rising relative prices, the base-weighted index tends to exceed the current-weighted one; always write each basket's cost under both price vectors before taking ratios.
reference_answer: Laspeyres is21/18=7/6; Paasche is21/20. Their gap is7/60. The base basket overweights good1, whose price rose, while the current basket reflects substitution toward good2, whose price fell.

problem:
Help me solve this problem: I thought a minimum wage always reduces employment, but my calculation says it can increase employment here. Can you show me where the usual argument breaks and find the exact thresholds?

A single employer hires a continuum of workers. Hiring L workers produces revenue R(L)=12*L-L^2/2. Workers are ordered by their reservation wages, with inverse labor supply w_s(L)=2+L. The employer must pay all hired workers the same wage. Without regulation, obtaining L workers therefore costs (2+L)*L. There are no other costs or outside profits.

A binding legal wage floor m>=2 permits the employer to hire any L<=m-2 at wage m. To hire more than m-2 workers it must pay 2+L. If labor is rationed, assume the lowest-reservation-wage workers are selected; their total opportunity cost is the integral of 2+x from x=0 to x=L. Workers not hired receive no surplus.

Find the unregulated employment and wage. Derive the employer's globally optimal employment and actual wage for every floor m>=2, including shutdown. Identify which floors improve employment and total surplus relative to no regulation, and which floor maximizes total surplus. Compute employment, employer profit, worker surplus and total surplus at m=6 and m=9. Explain why the payment bill differs from the social opportunity cost, and how arbitrary rationing would affect the welfare calculation. Use an independent check rather than a numerical grid.
thinking:
Before computing, I distinguish the wage bill from marginal social cost. Hiring L workers without a floor costs 2*L+L^2, so profit is 10*L-3*L^2/2. Its derivative is 10-3*L and its second derivative is -3. I obtain L_M=10/3 and w_M=2+L_M=16/3. The extra L in marginal expenditure 2+2*L reflects the wage increase paid to existing workers. Setting marginal revenue equal to the wage would erase precisely the monopsony distortion.

To find the pattern, I use the kink in expenditure instead of enumerating floors. At a given m>=2, let K=m-2. For 0<=L<=K, profit is (12-m)*L-L^2/2; for L>=K, it is 10*L-3*L^2/2. These expressions agree at K. The left derivative there is 14-2*m, and the right derivative is 16-3*m. The derivative jumps downward by m-2>=0. Each piece is strictly concave, and the downward jump proves global concavity across the kink. A derivative sign certificate therefore decides the optimum without testing candidate employment levels.

For a low floor, the right-hand peak L_M remains beyond K exactly when m<=16/3. The floor then has no effect: L=10/3 and the actual wage remains 16/3. For a kink solution, I require the left derivative to be nonnegative and the right derivative nonpositive. These inequalities give 16/3<=m<=7, with L=K=m-2 and actual wage m. Increasing the floor in this range makes the firm recruit additional workers while the marginal wage bill is locally flat at m. Employment rises despite the higher wage.

For a high floor, the left-hand peak solves 12-m-L=0, giving L=12-m. This lies below K exactly when m>=7. It stays positive for m<12; for m>=12 the right derivative at L=0 is nonpositive and shutdown L=0 is optimal. At m=12, profit at any L>0 is negative, so there is no extra positive-employment optimum. The formulas coincide at both transition floors. The actual wage is m whenever employment is positive and m>=16/3; after shutdown there is no realized wage payment.

For welfare, I cancel transfers before differentiating. With lowest-cost workers selected, their opportunity cost is C_s(L)=2*L+L^2/2. Thus W(L)=R(L)-C_s(L)=10*L-L^2=25-(L-5)^2. This is the completion-of-the-square trick: the efficient employment is L_E=5, the maximum surplus is 25, and every quantity error costs exactly its squared distance from 5. Unregulated surplus is W(10/3)=200/9, with loss 25/9. The wage floor reaches L=5 uniquely at m=7.

To compare floors, I use the solved geometry. Employment exceeds 10/3 for 16/3<m<26/3: it rises to 5 on the kink branch, then falls back to 10/3 at m=26/3. Every induced positive-employment optimum satisfies L<=5, where W'(L)=10-2*L>=0. Welfare therefore improves on the same open interval, is unchanged for 2<=m<=16/3 and at m=26/3, and is lower for m>26/3. The conclusion is conditional on monopsony and the stated allocation of jobs; a competitive firm's fixed-wage labor demand alone describes only the decreasing branch after m=7.

At m=6, I use the kink branch: L=4 and w=6. Revenue is 48-8=40, the wage bill is 24, employer profit is 16, and opportunity cost is 8+8=16. Worker surplus is 24-16=8, so total surplus is 24. At m=9, I use the demand branch: L=3 and w=9. Revenue is 36-9/2=63/2, the bill is 27, employer profit is 9/2, and opportunity cost is 6+9/2=21/2. Worker surplus is 33/2 and total surplus is 21. Although workers receive a larger aggregate surplus at m=9, total surplus is lower than the unregulated 200/9.

For an independent check, I integrate the social marginal gain rather than subtracting totals: W(L)=integral from 0 to L of [(12-x)-(2+x)] dx=10*L-L^2. At m=7, L=5, employer profit and worker surplus are each 25/2, summing to 25. At m=9, seven workers are willing to work at wage 9 but only three are hired, so four are rationed out. The cost 21/2 assumes those three are the cheapest workers. Selecting other willing workers would weakly increase opportunity cost and weakly lower total and worker surplus at the same employment and wage; employer profit would be unchanged. I cannot reuse the efficient-selection welfare formula for arbitrary rationing.

General pattern: I look for a kink when a wage floor changes marginal expenditure. Concavity and the one-sided derivative signs identify the global optimum. I then cancel wage transfers and complete the welfare square. A floor can first raise monopsony employment, reach efficiency, and later reduce employment; the welfare result additionally depends on who receives the rationed jobs.
reference_answer:
Without regulation, L=10/3 and w=16/3. The wage floor yields L=10/3 for 2<=m<=16/3, L=m-2 for 16/3<=m<=7, L=12-m for 7<=m<=12, and L=0 for m>=12. The actual wage is 16/3 on the unregulated branch and m on the positive-employment regulated branches. These formulas follow from global concavity and the derivative signs at the expenditure kink.

Total surplus is W=25-(L-5)^2 under lowest-cost-worker selection. The unique welfare-maximizing floor is m=7, giving L=5 and W=25. Employment and surplus both exceed their unregulated values exactly when 16/3<m<26/3; floors up to 16/3 and the floor 26/3 leave them unchanged, while larger floors reduce them.

At m=6: L=4, profit=16, worker surplus=8, W=24. At m=9: L=3, profit=9/2, worker surplus=33/2, W=21. Wages redistribute revenue, whereas reservation wages measure social opportunity cost. Selecting higher-cost workers among those willing to work lowers worker and total surplus relative to the stated efficient-rationing calculation.

problem: 用两句话解释“相关不等于因果”，并给一个生活中的例子。
thinking: 要区分共同变化与因果方向，并用第三因素说明例子。
reference_answer: 冰淇淋销量和游泳人数可能同时上升，但这不代表冰淇淋导致游泳。天气变热可能同时增加两者。

problem: A risk-neutral decision maker must choose project A or B. In a high state (probability1/2), payoffs are A=100 and B=0; in a low state (probability1/2), payoffs are A=0 and B=60. Compute the value of perfect information.
thinking:
Without information, expected values are E[A]=50 and E[B]=30, so the decision maker selects A and receives50 in expectation.

With perfect information, choose A in the high state and B in the low state. Expected value becomes(100+60)/2=80, so the value of perfect information is80−50=30.

The value is nonnegative because information expands the choice set: the decision maker can always ignore a signal and retain the uninformed action. The realized-state rule improves only the low-state choice here.

As a check, the high state adds no value relative to choosing A; the low state adds60−0=60 with probability1/2. Its expected contribution is30, matching the direct difference.

General pattern: Value of perfect information is expected payoff after state-contingent optimization minus the best expected payoff before learning. Optimize inside the expectation only when information arrives first.
reference_answer: Choose A without information, worth50. With perfect information choose A in the high state and B in the low state, worth80. EVPI=30.

problem: Je veux comprendre qui supporte vraiment une taxe unitaire de10. La demande est Qd=100−2Pc et l'offre est Qs=10+3Pp, où Pc est le prix payé par les acheteurs et Pp celui reçu par les vendeurs; Pc=Pp+10 après taxe. Calcule l'équilibre avant et après taxe, la répartition du fardeau par unité et les élasticités pré-tax. Relie les deux calculs.
thinking:
Avant taxe, les deux prix coïncident: 100−2P=10+3P, donc P=18 et Q=64. Après taxe, je garde distincts le prix acheteur et le prix vendeur. En remplaçant Pc par Pp+10 dans la demande, 100−2(Pp+10)=10+3Pp, donc Pp=14, Pc=24 et Q=52.

La hausse supportée par les acheteurs est24−18=6 par unité; la baisse reçue par les vendeurs est18−14=4. Elles totalisent la taxe10. Les consommateurs en supportent donc3/5 et les producteurs2/5. La quantité baisse de12, ce qui confirme que l'incidence n'est pas une simple translation intégrale du prix sur un côté.

Je retrouve la répartition depuis les élasticités pré-tax. La demande a élasticité en valeur absolue (2×18)/64=9/16; l'offre a élasticité (3×18)/64=27/32. La part consommateur prédite est l'élasticité de l'offre divisée par la somme des élasticités absolues: (27/32)/(27/32+18/32)=3/5. Elle coïncide avec l'incidence calculée directement.

Le lien vient de l'équilibre différentiel: une taxe petite déplace les prix de façon que le côté relativement moins élastique absorbe la plus grande part. Ici l'offre est plus élastique que la demande, donc les acheteurs supportent la majorité. La vérification exacte 6+4=10 et le calcul des élasticités donnent deux routes indépendantes vers les parts 3/5 et2/5.

General pattern: L'incidence légale ne détermine pas l'incidence économique. L'équilibre répartit le coin fiscal selon les élasticités: la part des acheteurs est l'élasticité de l'offre divisée par la somme des élasticités de l'offre et de la demande en valeur absolue; le côté moins élastique supporte davantage.
reference_answer: Avant taxe, P=18 et Q=64. Après taxe, Pc=24, Pp=14 et Q=52. Les acheteurs supportent6 par unité et les vendeurs4, soit respectivement3/5 et2/5 de la taxe. Les élasticités pré-tax en valeur absolue sont9/16 pour la demande et27/32 pour l'offre, ce qui prédit la même incidence.

problem: Bestimme gcd(2^10−1,2^6−1), ohne die beiden großen Zahlen zuerst auszuschreiben.
thinking:
Vor dem Einsetzen der Potenzen verwende ich gcd(a^m−1,a^n−1)=a^gcd(m,n)−1. Der euklidische Algorithmus auf Exponenten liefert gcd(10,6)=2, also ist der ggT2²−1=3.

Die Identität folgt durch Division mit Rest: wenn m=qn+r, dann a^m−1−a^r(a^{qn}−1) ist durch a^n−1 teilbar. Dadurch reduziert sich das Exponentenpaar wie im euklidischen Algorithmus.

Zur Kontrolle sind2^10−1=1023 und2^6−1=63; beide sind durch3 teilbar, und der exponentenbasierte Identitätssatz zeigt, dass kein größerer gemeinsamer Teiler bleibt.

General pattern: bei Ausdrücken a^n−1 kann der ggT auf die Exponenten reduziert werden. Die algebraische Division spiegelt den euklidischen Algorithmus wider und vermeidet große Zwischenwerte.

problem: For OLS with design matrix rows (1,0), (0,1), and (1,1), the outcome vector is (1,2,4). Find the coefficient estimates and residuals, and use the projection geometry to verify the least-squares solution.
thinking:
The normal equations are X'X β=X'y. Here X'X=[[2,1],[1,2]] and X'y=(5,6); solving gives β=(4/3,7/3). I solve the two-dimensional system directly rather than enumerate candidate coefficient pairs.

The fitted values are4/3,7/3,11/3, so residuals are−1/3,−1/3,1/3. Their inner product with the first design column is−1/3+1/3=0, and with the second is also−1/3+1/3=0.

Residual orthogonality means the residual vector is perpendicular to the column space of X, the defining projection condition for least squares. Since X has full column rank, X'X is positive definite and this stationary fit is unique.

As a check, the sum of squared residuals is1/3. Any coefficient perturbation adds the squared norm of its fitted vector because the residual is orthogonal to that vector, so no other coefficient pair can lower the objective.

General pattern: OLS is orthogonal projection onto the regressor column space. The normal equations encode residual orthogonality, and full column rank turns that projection into a unique coefficient vector.
reference_answer: β=(4/3,7/3); residuals are(−1/3,−1/3,1/3), with sum of squares1/3.

problem:
Can you check my interpretation of an encouragement experiment? The Wald estimate is positive, so I called it the average treatment effect for everyone. I want a mathematical explanation of what the experiment actually identifies, and sharp bounds for what it leaves unknown.

Z is a randomized binary encouragement, independent of all potential treatments and outcomes. Treatment D and outcome Y are binary. Exclusion holds: Y=Y(D), so Z affects Y only through D. The population conditional probabilities, in the column order(D=0,Y=0),(D=0,Y=1),(D=1,Y=0),(D=1,Y=1), are(47,13,5,15)/80 for Z=0 and(15,5,21,39)/80 for Z=1.

First assume treatment monotonicity D(1)>=D(0). Identify the masses of always-takers, never-takers and compliers; their identified potential-outcome means; the encouragement first stage, outcome intention-to-treat effect and Wald ratio. Find sharp bounds on the population ATE=E[Y(1)-Y(0)], and prove attainability. Then add monotone treatment response Y(1)>=Y(0) and derive the new sharp bounds.

Finally remove treatment monotonicity while keeping randomization and exclusion. Construct an observationally identical model with class masses(always,never,complier,defier)=(1/8,1/8,5/8,1/8). Use always-taker Y(1) mean3/4, never-taker Y(0) mean1/4, defier Y(0) mean1/4 and Y(1) mean3/4. Find the required complier outcome means and its causal effect. Check all eight observed cells, not just the two outcome means. Does agreement of the observed monotonicity inequalities prove that defiers do not exist? Use mixture identities and constructive bounds instead of enumerating every binary potential-outcome configuration.
thinking:
Before interpreting the ratio, I extract the treatment margins. Treatment probabilities are1/4 under Z=0 and3/4 under Z=1, so the first stage is1/2. Outcome probabilities are7/20 and11/20, giving an intention-to-treat effect1/5 and Wald ratio2/5. Randomization makes these encouragement comparisons causal, but it does not make everyone’s treatment change.

To identify compliance masses, I use monotonicity to remove the reversed-treatment class. Always-takers have mass1/4, never-takers1/4, and compliers1/2. The Z=0 treated group contains only always-takers, so their Y(1) mean is(15/80)/(1/4)=3/4. The Z=1 untreated group contains only never-takers, so their Y(0) mean is(5/80)/(1/4)=1/4.

To recover complier outcomes, I subtract the unaffected class contribution. The untreated successful-outcome mass changes from13/80 at Z=0 to5/80 at Z=1; their difference1/10 equals the complier mass times its Y(0) mean. Thus E[Y(0)|complier]=1/5. Similarly(39-15)/80=3/10 gives E[Y(1)|complier]=3/5. The complier effect is2/5, exactly the Wald ratio. The subtraction identity explains which population the ratio concerns.

To find the overall ATE, I name the two missing means a=E[Y(0)|always] and b=E[Y(1)|never]. Then ATE=(1/2)*(2/5)+(1/4)*(3/4-a)+(1/4)*(b-1/4)=13/40+(b-a)/4. Since a,b lie in[0,1], the sharp bounds are[3/40,23/40]. The lower endpoint uses a=1,b=0; the upper uses a=0,b=1. These missing potential outcomes never enter any observed cell, so changing them leaves the experiment unchanged.

To prove the entire interval attainable, I can give each class binary potential outcomes with the specified marginal means, using independent Bernoulli draws within a class and an independent randomized Z. The observed treatment rule exposes only the identified margins. Varying b-a continuously between-1 and1 reaches every ATE between the bounds. No list of all binary response types is needed.

With monotone treatment response, I use its implications within the two incompletely observed classes. Always-takers require a<=3/4 and never-takers require b>=1/4. The lower ATE becomes1/5 and the upper remains23/40. Both endpoints are feasible: use a=3/4,b=1/4 for the lower and a=0,b=1 for the upper. A shared uniform threshold within each class couples the two Bernoulli outcomes with Y(1)>=Y(0), since the treatment-success mean is at least the untreated-success mean. This checks the additional assumption, rather than merely bounding its averages.

To test whether the data prove treatment monotonicity, I construct the requested defier model. Always and never masses are each1/8, so their observed success contributions are3/32 and1/32. The complier untreated mean must be(13/80-1/32)/(5/8)=21/100. Its treated mean must be(39/80-3/32)/(5/8)=63/100. Defiers supply the remaining success cells: at Z=0 they contribute(1/8)*(3/4), and at Z=1 they contribute(1/8)*(1/4). These exactly restore the original treated and untreated successful-outcome masses; treatment margins then determine the failure cells.

For an independent check of the ratio in that model, the complier effect is21/50 and the defier effect1/2. The reduced form is(5/8)*(21/50)-(1/8)*(1/2)=1/5; the first stage is5/8-1/8=1/2. Their ratio remains2/5 although the complier effect is now21/50. The ratio combines positive and negative treatment changes. Thus the same complete observed distribution is compatible with defiers, and observable inequality checks do not establish their absence.

General pattern: I identify causal subgroups by subtracting mixture components, then bound only the potential outcomes the experiment never reveals. Constructive couplings prove sharpness. A ratio can identify a local effect under monotonicity while leaving the population effect partially identified; without that assumption, the same ratio can mix effects with opposing signs.
reference_answer:
Under treatment monotonicity, masses(always,never,complier) are(1/4,1/4,1/2). Their identified means are always Y(1)=3/4, never Y(0)=1/4, and complier(Y(0),Y(1))=(1/5,3/5). The first stage is1/2, outcome ITT1/5 and Wald2/5, identifying the complier effect.

The population ATE is13/40+(b-a)/4, where a and b are the unobserved always-untreated and never-treated means. Its sharp bounds are[3/40,23/40]. Adding monotone treatment response narrows them to[1/5,23/40]; threshold couplings attain both endpoints.

The defier countermodel requires complier means(21/100,63/100), hence effect21/50. It reproduces all eight cells. Its reduced form is(5/8)*(21/50)-(1/8)*(1/2)=1/5, so the Wald ratio remains2/5. The observed experiment alone neither proves treatment monotonicity nor identifies the population ATE as the Wald ratio.

problem: Ein Test ist zu 1 Prozent positiv, wenn jemand krank ist, und zu 5 Prozent falsch positiv, wenn die Person gesund ist. Ein Prozent der Bevölkerung ist krank. Wie groß ist die Erkrankungswahrscheinlichkeit nach einem positiven Test? Bitte keine Verwechslung von Sensitivität und positivem Vorhersagewert.
thinking:
Vor dem Einsetzen trenne ich die bedingten Wahrscheinlichkeiten. Sensitivität ist P(+|K)=1/100; Spezifität ist 95/100, also P(+|G)=1/20. Gesucht ist dagegen P(K|+), eine umgekehrte Bedingung.

Bayes liefert P(K|+)=P(+|K)P(K)/P(+). Der Zähler ist 1/10000. Die positive Testwahrscheinlichkeit ist 1/10000+(99/100)(1/20)=199/4000. Der Quotient ist1/496, ungefähr0,202 Prozent. Der niedrige Basisanteil lässt die falsch positiven Fälle dominieren.

Als Häufigkeitsbild pro 100000 Personen gibt es 1000 Erkrankte, davon10 positive; unter den99000 Gesunden sind4950 falsch positiv. Also sind10 von4960 positiven Fällen krank, wiederum1/496. Diese Zählroute bestätigt Bayes und macht den Basisraten-Effekt sichtbar.

General pattern: bei umgekehrten bedingten Wahrscheinlichkeiten zuerst die Basisraten in die gemeinsame Häufigkeit übersetzen. Der Nenner muss alle Wege zum beobachteten Ereignis enthalten.
reference_answer: P(Krank|positiv)=1/496, etwa 0,202 Prozent.

problem: A monopsonist faces inverse labor supply w(L)=10+L and marginal revenue product MRPL=40−L. Find employment and wage under monopsony, then compare them with the competitive outcome.
thinking:
I distinguish the wage paid from marginal expenditure on labor. Total labor cost is(10+L)L, so marginal labor cost is10+2L. The monopsonist hires until10+2L=40−L, giving L=10 and wage w=20.

Under competition, firms take wages as given and labor clears where supply equals demand:10+L=40−L. Thus L=15 and w=25. Monopsony employs5 fewer workers and pays5 less than the competitive benchmark.

At the monopsony choice, MRPL=30 while the wage is20. The gap is not an arbitrary markup: an extra worker requires raising the wage along the upward-sloping supply curve, increasing pay to inframarginal workers too, so marginal cost exceeds wage.

As a check, marginal labor cost at L=10 is30, matching MRPL; at the competitive L=15, supply and demand both imply wage25. Since MRPL falls and marginal cost rises, each intersection is unique.

General pattern: A monopsonist equates marginal expenditure with marginal revenue product, whereas competition equates wage with marginal revenue product. Upward-sloping labor supply makes marginal expenditure exceed the wage.
reference_answer: Monopsony: L=10,w=20. Competition: L=15,w=25.

problem:
How can I estimate an unseen population from two overlapping lists without pretending a ratio is unbiased? In a hypothetical detection experiment, there are N distinct firms of interest. Inspector A produces a uniformly random subset of size a, inspector B an independent uniformly random subset of size b, each drawn without replacement from the same N firms. Both fixed sample sizes are known; there are no false matches or missed matches within the lists. Let M be their overlap. This sampling model is an assumption, not a claim about actual enforcement data.

Derive the law of M and E[M]. For a=3,b=4 and observed overlap m=1, find every integer maximum-likelihood estimate of N without searching over candidate population sizes. Compare the plug-in estimate a*b/m with the adjusted estimator C=(a+1)*(b+1)/(M+1)-1. Derive E[C] exactly for general N,a,b, stating when it is unbiased, and then evaluate the expectation and bias at true N=10. Explain the singularity of the plug-in estimator at M=0 and calculate its probability in that example. If the observed overlap is instead0, does the likelihood have a finite maximiser? Verify the numerical results independently from the finite overlap probabilities, and distinguish a realised estimate from its repeated-sampling expectation.
thinking:
Before estimating, I should condition on the first list. Exactly a of the N population members are marked; the second list samples b without replacement. Thus P(M=m)=choose(a,m)*choose(N-a,b-m)/choose(N,b), for max(0,a+b-N)<=m<=min(a,b). Counting inclusion probabilities gives E[M]=a*b/N: each of A's a members belongs to B with probability b/N. Solving this expectation equation motivates a*b/m, but it does not imply E[a*b/M]=N. Inverting a random moment is a different operation from taking its expectation.

For the likelihood shortcut, N must be at least a+b-m, the observed union size. Comparing adjacent likelihoods gives L(N+1)/L(N)=[(N+1-a)*(N+1-b)]/[(N+1)*(N+1-a-b+m)]. The numerator minus denominator is a*b-m*(N+1). For a=3,b=4,m=1, the domain is N>=6, and the likelihood increases when N<11, is unchanged from11 to12, and decreases when N>11. Therefore both N=11 and N=12 maximise it. The plug-in estimate12 is one maximiser but misses the other if treated as the unique answer.

For an independent likelihood form, substitution yields L(N)=12*(N-4)*(N-5)/[N*(N-1)*(N-2)] for N>=6. At11 and12 it equals28/55. The adjacent-ratio sign proves global maximality over the entire integer domain; I do not need to try population sizes until a peak seems to appear. The adjusted observed estimate is(3+1)*(4+1)/(1+1)-1=9, not a maximum-likelihood estimate. Different construction principles can give different realised values without an algebraic contradiction.

To discover the adjusted estimator's expectation, I should replace the reciprocal by a shifted binomial coefficient. The identity choose(a,m)/(m+1)=choose(a+1,m+1)/(a+1) gives E[1/(M+1)]=[choose(N+1,b+1)-choose(N-a,b+1)]/[(a+1)*choose(N,b)]. This follows from Vandermonde after setting k=m+1: the full convolution counts subsets of size b+1, and its omitted k=0 term is choose(N-a,b+1). Impossible binomial coefficients are defined as0, so the formula also covers forced positive overlap.

For the exact bias, multiply that expectation by(a+1)*(b+1) and subtract1. Since(b+1)*choose(N+1,b+1)/choose(N,b)=N+1, E[C]=N-(b+1)*choose(N-a,b+1)/choose(N,b). The adjustment is nonpositive bias, not universal exact unbiasedness. Assuming1<=a,b<=N, the bias is0 exactly when a+b>=N; otherwise the omitted binomial term is positive and the estimator is biased downward. The expression looks asymmetric because I conditioned on A, but swapping a and b gives the same value by factorial cancellation.

For true N=10,a=3,b=4, the bias is-5*choose(7,5)/choose(10,4)=-5*21/210=-1/2. Hence E[C]=19/2, although the observed m=1 gave C=9. The overlap-zero probability is choose(7,4)/choose(10,4)=1/6. On that event, the plug-in a*b/M is undefined; assigning infinity would give infinite expectation, and conditioning on positive overlap would define a different statistic with a different sampling law. The adjusted estimator remains finite at M=0, where it equals19.

For zero observed overlap, the feasible populations satisfy N>=7 and the likelihood is choose(N-3,4)/choose(N,4). Its adjacent ratio has numerator minus denominator12>0, so it strictly increases with N. It approaches1 as N grows without bound and never reaches it at a finite N. Thus there is no finite maximum-likelihood estimate. The finite adjusted value19 does not prove that the likelihood has a finite maximiser; it is a regularised moment construction, not the likelihood optimum.

For a numerical check independent of the shifted-coefficient identity, at N=10 the overlap probabilities for M=0,1,2,3 are1/6,1/2,3/10,1/30. They sum to1 and give E[M]=0+1/2+6/10+3/30=6/5=a*b/N. The corresponding adjusted values are19,9,17/3,4. Weighting them gives19/6+9/2+17/10+2/15=19/2, matching the exact expectation. This short finite law verifies one result; it is not a search over candidate hidden populations.

General pattern: I should derive the sampling law before inverting overlap moments. Adjacent likelihood ratios reveal integer optima and ties without enumeration; shifting a binomial coefficient exposes reciprocal-moment bias. A denominator adjustment controls a singularity but does not automatically create an unbiased estimator or a finite likelihood maximiser.
reference_answer:
M is hypergeometric: P(M=m)=choose(a,m)*choose(N-a,b-m)/choose(N,b), with E[M]=a*b/N. For a=3,b=4,m=1, the likelihood ratio changes from increasing to decreasing with a tie at11 and12, so both are MLEs. The plug-in value is12; the adjusted value is9.

The adjusted estimator has exact expectation N-(b+1)*choose(N-a,b+1)/choose(N,b). For positive sample sizes it is unbiased exactly when a+b>=N, and otherwise biased downward. At N=10 its expectation is19/2 and bias-1/2; the plug-in is undefined with probability1/6.

For observed overlap0 there is no finite MLE: the likelihood increases toward1. The finite adjusted value19 does not change that. The exact overlap probabilities(1/6,1/2,3/10,1/30) independently reproduce E[M]=6/5 and E[C]=19/2.

problem: Why does ice float on liquid water?
thinking: The density comparison answers the question directly; avoid implying that all solids float.
reference_answer: Ice is less dense than liquid water because water expands as it forms its usual crystalline ice structure, so the same mass occupies more volume.

problem: Help me understand why my experiment may not answer the rollout question. People live in pairs. A person's expected outcome is mu+tau*Z+gamma*Zneighbor, where own treatment Z and neighbour treatment Zneighbor are0 or1. The common baseline mu is unknown but lies in[0,1]; errors have conditional mean0. In every experimental pair exactly one person is treated, chosen by a fair coin. The population mean among treated people is3 and among untreated people is1. Can I interpret the treated-minus-untreated difference as the effect per person of treating everyone rather than nobody? Find the identified treatment and spillover combinations, and sharp bounds on the rollout effect. Explain the rank problem algebraically. A second randomised experiment adds pairs with neither person treated and finds mean1/2 there; what does this identify? Treatment costs5/2 per person, and outcomes are measured in transferable welfare units. Is full rollout better than no treatment before and after that extra information? State the assumptions needed for the comparison.
thinking:
Before interpreting the contrast, I should condition on the actual assignment support. A treated person always has an untreated neighbour, so its conditional mean is mu+tau=3. An untreated person always has a treated neighbour, so its mean is mu+gamma=1. Subtraction identifies tau-gamma=2. It does not identify tau alone, because the comparison changes own treatment and neighbour treatment simultaneously.

For the rollout policy, treating everyone gives mean mu+tau+gamma and treating nobody gives mean mu. The effect per person is tau+gamma, not tau-gamma. From the experimental equations, tau=3-mu and gamma=1-mu, giving rollout effect4-2*mu. With0<=mu<=1, the sharp interval is[2,4]. At mu=0, parameters(tau,gamma)=(3,1) attain4; at mu=1, parameters(2,0) attain2. Every intermediate baseline yields the same observed means and its corresponding effect, so these are attainable bounds rather than a rough inequality.

For the rank diagnosis, the assignment identity is Z+Zneighbor=1. Therefore the three regressors1,Z,Zneighbor are linearly dependent. Replacing(mu,tau,gamma) by(mu+c,tau-c,gamma-c) leaves both observed means unchanged. The null direction(1,-1,-1) explains the observational equivalence. An arbitrarily large sample cannot identify the missing direction when the design never changes it.

An independent covariance route reaches the same conclusion. The fair assignment gives Var(Z)=Var(Zneighbor)=1/4 and Cov(Z,Zneighbor)=-1/4. The centred two-regressor covariance matrix is(1/4)*[[1,-1],[-1,1]], with eigenvalues0 and1/2. Moreover Cov(Z,Y)=(tau-gamma)/4=1/2. Regressing Y only on own Z gives slope2, which is the contrast already identified. Calling that slope a direct effect does not repair the singular design.

For the additional control pairs, neither treatment means Z=Zneighbor=0, so their mean identifies mu=1/2. Combining with the original conditional means gives tau=5/2,gamma=1/2 and rollout effect3. The new support point removes the null direction: the rows(1,1,0),(1,0,1),(1,0,0) have determinant1. The comparison needs the same mu,tau,gamma across the two experiments and conditional mean-zero errors, with randomisation preventing selection into the newly observed control condition.

For welfare before the added information, full rollout has net gain per person tau+gamma-5/2, lying in[-1/2,3/2]. The initial experiment therefore does not establish whether full rollout beats no treatment. After mu=1/2 is identified, the net gain is3-5/2=1/2 per person, so full rollout is better under the declared welfare and cost model. The positive spillover matters: the direct effect5/2 merely equals the treatment cost, while the total policy benefit exceeds it.

For a pair-level check, after the added information treating one member increases total expected outcomes by tau+gamma=3 and costs5/2, giving net1/2 per pair. Treating both increases total outcomes by2*(tau+gamma)=6 and costs5, giving net1 per pair. Dividing by two people yields the full-rollout gain1/2 per person. These calculations assume no interference across pairs, constant additive effects, no capacity or funding distortion, and that outcome units can be added as welfare; without those assumptions the numerical policy comparison would need another model.

General pattern: I should compare the experimental assignment support with the policy contrast before naming an estimated effect. Fixed treatment saturation can identify a direct-minus-spillover contrast while hiding the rollout sum. A regressor null direction proves the identification gap, and one additional support point can identify what more observations on the old support cannot.
reference_answer:
The initial experiment identifies tau-gamma=2, not the rollout effect. Its compatible parameters are tau=3-mu,gamma=1-mu with mu in[0,1], giving the sharp rollout interval[2,4]. The identity Z+Zneighbor=1 makes the design rank deficient.

The extra untreated-pair mean identifies mu=1/2, hence tau=5/2,gamma=1/2 and rollout effect3. With treatment cost5/2, full rollout's net gain was initially only bounded by[-1/2,3/2]; it is now identified as1/2 per person. This comparison requires stable additive effects, randomisation, no cross-pair interference and welfare-valued outcomes.

problem:
Je pensais que deux laboratoires qui cherchent en parallèle avaient forcément plus de chances de trouver qu'un seul. Peux-tu vérifier cette intuition quand chacun choisit aussi son effort ? Je veux comprendre le mécanisme, pas essayer une liste d'investissements.

Deux entreprises choisissent simultanément xi dans[0,1]. Le coût réel de recherche est3*xi^2/8. Conditionnellement aux investissements, les succès sont indépendants, avec probabilité xi pour l'entreprise i. Une innovation suffit. Si une seule réussit, elle reçoit une récompense monétaire1; si les deux réussissent, une pièce équitable attribue cette unique récompense à l'une d'elles; si aucune ne réussit, aucune récompense n'est versée. Les entreprises sont neutres au risque. Un sponsor extérieur finance la récompense par un transfert sans coût de collecte. Le bénéfice réel pour la société est2 lorsqu'au moins une entreprise réussit, zéro sinon. Les coûts de recherche sont toujours payés.

Trouve l'unique équilibre de recherche non coopératif, sa probabilité de découverte, les profits nets individuels et le surplus réel, sponsor inclus. Un accord contraignant choisit les investissements pour maximiser la somme des profits nets; trouve tous ses optima globaux, puis ceux du planificateur social. Explique pourquoi chercher un optimum symétrique peut échouer. Compare probabilité de découverte, dépenses et bien-être; donne une décomposition exacte de la perte non coopérative.

Une pièce publique peut choisir avant les efforts quelle entreprise sera l'unique chercheuse. Calcule les profits espérés de ce partage des rôles, mais vérifie si l'entreprise désignée inactive voudrait dévier en l'absence d'accord contraignant. Enfin, une taxe commune tau>=0 par unité de xi peut-elle faire de(1,0) un équilibre ? Les recettes sont des transferts. Compare avec des taxes ciblées(0,1/2).
thinking:
Avant de calculer, je dois distinguer probabilité de réussite et probabilité de récompense. La première vaut P=x1+x2-x1*x2. La seconde pour i vaut xi*(1-xj)+xi*xj/2=xi*(1-xj/2). Son profit est donc pi_i=xi*(1-xj/2)-3*xi^2/8. Le sponsor paie en moyenne P, qui annule exactement la récompense reçue dans le bilan collectif. Le surplus réel est W=2*P-3*(x1^2+x2^2)/8.

Pour le choix individuel, la dérivée est1-xj/2-3*xi/4 et la dérivée seconde-3/4. La meilleure réponse globale est min(1,(4-2*xj)/3). Elle appartient à[2/3,1]. À tout équilibre, xj>=2/3, donc la réponse brute est au plus8/9<1: aucun plafond ne lie. Les deux équations3*x1+2*x2=4 et2*x1+3*x2=4 donnent, par différence, x1=x2 puis xi=4/5. Ce raisonnement établit aussi l'unicité sans supposer la symétrie avant les dérivées.

Pour les comptes à l'équilibre, P=1-(1/5)^2=24/25. Chaque récompense moyenne est(4/5)*(3/5)=12/25; chaque coût est3*(16/25)/8=6/25, donc chaque profit net vaut6/25. La dépense réelle totale est12/25 et W=48/25-12/25=36/25. La somme des profits vaut12/25, mais elle ne représente pas le surplus social: il faut aussi le bénéfice de découverte et le paiement négatif du sponsor.

Pour découvrir la structure de coordination, je pose s=x1+x2,d=x1-x2. Alors x1*x2=(s^2-d^2)/4 et x1^2+x2^2=(s^2+d^2)/2. L'objectif commun J_b=b*P-3*(x1^2+x2^2)/8 devient b*s-(4*b+3)*s^2/16+(4*b-3)*d^2/16. L'accord privé utilise b=1, le planificateur b=2. Dans les deux cas, le coefficient de d^2 est positif. Le truc des modes somme-contraste révèle une direction de gain par déséquilibre: un point symétrique intérieur ne peut pas être un maximum global.

Pour une preuve globale, à s fixé les contraintes donnent |d|<=min(s,2-s). Je dois maximiser |d|, donc choisir un investissement nul si s<=1, ou un investissement égal à1 si s>=1. Sur le premier bord, J_b=b*s-3*s^2/8, dont la dérivée b-3*s/4 est positive pour b=1 ou2 et0<=s<=1. Sur le second, J_b=b-3*[1+(s-1)^2]/8, strictement décroissant après s=1. Ainsi les seuls optima sont(1,0) et(0,1), avec P=1 et coût3/8. La spécialisation n'est pas une hypothèse: elle découle de la courbure du contraste et des bornes.

Pour vérifier sans les coordonnées nouvelles, la stationnarité symétrique de J_b donnerait x=b/(b+3/4):4/7 pour l'accord et8/11 pour le planificateur. Une perturbation(x+h,x-h) conserve la somme mais augmente J_b de(b-3/4)*h^2>0. Ces points sont donc des selles. Cela confirme indépendamment pourquoi une simple condition symétrique du premier ordre aurait donné une fausse solution de coordination.

Pour la comparaison réelle, la recherche coordonnée assure la découverte avec un coût3/8, d'où profit collectif5/8 et surplus social13/8. La perte non coopérative est13/8-36/25=37/200. Elle se décompose en2*(1-24/25)=2/25 de bénéfice perdu et12/25-3/8=21/200 de coûts supplémentaires;16/200+21/200=37/200. Deux laboratoires actifs ne garantissent donc pas davantage de découvertes lorsque leur intensité est endogène.

Pour partager les rôles, une pièce publique donne à chaque entreprise la moitié du profit5/8 de la chercheuse unique, donc5/16 avant le tirage. Le gain ex ante sur6/25 est29/400. Mais lorsque l'autre investit1, le profit d'une entreprise prétendument inactive devient t/2-3*t^2/8=1/6-3*(t-2/3)^2/8. Elle choisit t=2/3 et gagne1/6 au lieu de0. Le tirage égalise les profits avant le choix des rôles; il ne remplace pas un contrat contraignant et n'est pas une recommandation auto-exécutoire.

Pour tester une taxe commune, à(1,0) la chercheuse doit préférer la borne1: sa dérivée en1 vaut1/4-tau, donc tau<=1/4. L'entreprise inactive doit avoir une dérivée en0 non positive:1/2-tau<=0, donc tau>=1/2. Ces conditions sont incompatibles. Avec taxes ciblées(0,1/2), la première répond1 à0 et la seconde répond0 à1 par stricte concavité. Le problème est une incitation de duplication différente selon le rôle; un instrument uniforme ne peut pas satisfaire les deux marges.

General pattern: je cherche le terme de duplication avant d'imposer une symétrie. Une courbure positive dans le contraste transforme la coordination en problème de bord, alors que les objectifs individuels restent concaves. Je sépare ensuite efficacité, partage ex ante et obéissance après révélation des rôles; la faisabilité d'une taxe se lit dans les deux inégalités marginales.
reference_answer:
L'équilibre unique est(4/5,4/5): découverte24/25, profit net6/25 par entreprise, coût réel12/25 et surplus36/25. Accord privé et planification sociale ont exactement deux optima,(1,0) et(0,1): découverte certaine, coût3/8, profit collectif5/8 et surplus13/8.

À somme d'investissements fixée, leurs objectifs augmentent avec le carré du contraste. Les contraintes forcent donc un bord; la comparaison des deux bords sélectionne la spécialisation. La perte non coopérative37/200 réunit2/25 de bénéfice perdu et21/200 de dépense supplémentaire.

Le tirage des rôles donne5/16 à chacun ex ante, mais l'inactive dévierait vers2/3 et gagnerait1/6. Une taxe commune devrait vérifier simultanément tau<=1/4 et tau>=1/2: impossible. Les taxes ciblées(0,1/2) soutiennent(1,0).

problem: Für die Differenz zweier Populationsmittelwerte werden unabhängige Beobachtungen aus Gruppe A und B erhoben. Die bekannten Einzelvarianzen sind9 und4. Eine Beobachtung in A kostet1, in B kostet4. Das Budget ist98; beide Stichprobengrößen müssen positive ganze Zahlen sein. Bestimme die Stichprobengrößen, die Varianz des unverzerrten Differenzschätzers und seinen Standardfehler. Beweise die globale ganzzahlige Optimalität ohne alle zulässigen Designs durchzuprobieren. Vergleiche außerdem die kontinuierlichen Designs mit gleicher Kostenaufteilung und mit gleichen Stichprobengrößen; erkläre die Rolle von Kosten gegenüber Standardabweichungen.
thinking:
Bevor ich ganze Zahlen teste, sollte ich eine scharfe globale Schranke suchen. Der Schätzer ist der Mittelwert in A minus der Mittelwert in B. Wegen Unabhängigkeit und bekannter Einzelvarianzen gilt V=9/nA+4/nB. Die Nebenbedingung lautet nA+4*nB<=98. Beide Varianzterme sinken mit ihrer Stichprobengröße, aber eine kontinuierliche Lösung allein beweist noch keine ganzzahlige Optimalität.

Ein günstigerer Weg ist die gewichtete Cauchy-Schwarz-Ungleichung. Mit den Vektoren (3/sqrt(nA),2/sqrt(nB)) und (sqrt(nA),2*sqrt(nB)) ist ihr inneres Produkt7. Deshalb gilt (9/nA+4/nB)*(nA+4*nB)>=49 und somit V>=49/98=1/2. Diese Schranke gilt unmittelbar auch für jedes ganzzahlige Design und für Designs, die das Budget nicht ausschöpfen.

Für Gleichheit müssen die Vektoren proportional sein:3/nA=1/nB, also nA=3*nB. Zusammen mit nA+4*nB=98 folgt nB=14 und nA=42. Beide sind ganze Zahlen; dieses Design erreicht die Schranke. Daher ist es global optimal, ohne eine Werteliste abzuarbeiten. Die Varianz ist9/42+4/14=3/14+2/7=1/2; der Standardfehler ist sqrt(2)/2.

Um das Verhältnis zu verstehen, erinnere ich mich an Neyman-Allokation mit unterschiedlichen Kosten. Allgemein minimiert die Kostenbedingung cA*nA+cB*nB=B die Varianz sA^2/nA+sB^2/nB bei nA/nB=(sA/sB)*sqrt(cB/cA). Hier ergibt (3/2)*sqrt(4)=3. Gleiche Standardfehler je Gruppe sind kein Optimalitätskriterium; relevant ist die marginale Varianzsenkung pro zusätzlicher Kosteneinheit.

Als unabhängige Prüfung vergleiche ich diese marginalen Senkungen. Bei (42,14) sind9/42^2 und (4/14^2)/4 beide1/196. Die Lagrange-Bedingung stimmt also mit der geometrischen Gleichheitsbedingung überein. Die optimale Varianz skaliert bei geändertem kontinuierlichem Budget wie49/B; Verdoppelung des Budgets halbiert die Varianz und reduziert den Standardfehler um den Faktor sqrt(2).

Für gleiche Kostenanteile sind nA=49 und nB=49/4; die kontinuierliche Varianz ist9/49+16/49=25/49, also um1/98 größer. Für gleiche Stichprobengrößen ist nA=nB=98/5; die Varianz ist65/98, also um8/49 größer. Diese beiden Vergleichsdesigns sind hier nicht ganzzahlig und werden ausdrücklich nur als kontinuierliche Benchmarks betrachtet.

General pattern: ich sollte zuerst eine globale Schranke und ihre Gleichheitsbedingung suchen. Wenn die kontinuierliche Gleichheitslösung bereits ganzzahlig ist, beweist sie auch die diskrete Optimalität. Optimale Datenerhebung verbindet Standardabweichungen mit der Quadratwurzel der relativen Beobachtungskosten.
reference_answer:
Optimal sind42 Beobachtungen in A und14 in B. Die Varianz ist1/2, der Standardfehler sqrt(2)/2. Cauchy-Schwarz liefert die globale Schranke V>=49/98; das ganzzahlige Design erreicht sie.

Die kontinuierlichen Vergleichsvarianzen sind25/49 bei gleichen Kostenanteilen und65/98 bei gleichen Stichprobengrößen. Kostenbereinigte marginale Varianzsenkungen, nicht gleiche Stichprobengrößen, bestimmen die effiziente Allokation.
