reference_answer: Wait a few seconds, then try closing and reopening the app. If that doesn’t help, restart the device; save or back up any unsaved work first if possible.

problem:
Help me understand who would provide this shared service. I used the sum of everyone's investment, but the engineer says only the strongest installation determines quality. Does that change the free-rider calculation?

There are n>=2 agents. Agent i chooses investment gi>=0. Public quality is G=max(g1,...,gn), available to all agents. Utility is ui=vi*G-ki*gi^2/2, with vi>0 and ki>0. Investments and their quadratic costs are real; there are no payments or transfers. All choices are simultaneous and observable after they are made. Each agent maximizes its own utility.

Derive the full global best-response set given the largest rival investment R. Include the indifference boundary. Characterize every pure Nash equilibrium for arbitrary positive values and costs without testing investment vectors. Does a pure equilibrium always exist? Can two agents invest positively in equilibrium?

A planner chooses all investments to maximize total real welfare. Find every efficient allocation, including ties between cheapest providers. Decompose the loss of a one-provider equilibrium into quality distortion and excess provider cost.

Evaluate v=(3,6,1),k=(1,3,1). Give all pure equilibria, utilities and welfare, the efficient quality/provider choices and exact losses. Show why the higher-welfare equilibrium need not be a Pareto improvement. Check the global response of agent1 when agent2 supplies quality2. Distinguish investment in an equally strong second installation from raising the strongest installation.
thinking:
Before differentiating, I should preserve the strongest-link technology. Given the largest rival investment R, choosing g<=R leaves quality at R and yields vi*R-ki*g^2/2. Its maximum on that region is g0. If g>=R, utility is vi*g-ki*g^2/2, a concave quadratic with unconstrained peak ai=vi/ki. An investment below an existing stronger installation consumes resources without raising the public benefit.

For the global comparison, if ai<=R the second-region peak is its boundary R, already worse than g0 because of its positive cost. If ai>R, the candidate ai gives vi^2/(2*ki), while nonprovision gives vi*R. The candidate wins exactly when R<ai/2. Thus the best-response set is{ai} below that threshold, {0} above it, and{0,ai} at equality. The boundary investment g=R is not an additional best response when R>0. Completing the active-region square and comparing its peak with g0 establishes this jump globally.

For pure equilibria, I can first remove impossible structures. If two agents invest positively and one is below the maximum, the lower investor can stop and save its entire cost. If two tie at the maximum, either can stop while the other preserves quality. Hence every pure equilibrium has exactly one positive contributor. No contribution cannot be an equilibrium because any agent then gains by choosing its positive ai. A sole contributor i must choose gi=ai because its rival maximum is0.

For the remaining equilibrium condition, a noncontributor j sees R=ai and prefers0 exactly when ai>=aj/2. Therefore i can be the sole provider if and only if ai>=max_{j!=i}(aj)/2. This condition characterizes every pure equilibrium, including weak equality cases. An agent with the largest ai always qualifies, so a pure equilibrium exists for all positive primitives. The test uses private benefit-to-cost ratios; it does not identify the cheapest producer independently of demand valuations.

For the planner, I should minimize real cost at a fixed positive quality G. Some agent must invest G; any other positive investment is redundant and strictly costly. The cheapest possible cost is k_min*G^2/2, achieved by exactly one agent whose ki=k_min. Total marginal benefit is V=sum(vi). Welfare becomes V*G-k_min*G^2/2=V^2/(2*k_min)-(k_min/2)*(G-V/k_min)^2. Efficient quality is G*=V/k_min, with welfare V^2/(2*k_min). Every cheapest agent can be the sole provider; ties do not justify duplicate installations.

For a one-provider equilibrium i with quality a_i, I can add and subtract the cheapest-provider cost. The welfare loss is(k_min/2)*(a_i-G*)^2+(ki-k_min)*a_i^2/2. The first term is the quality distortion even with the cheapest technology; the second is the excess cost of the actual provider. Both are nonnegative. This exact identity separates the free-rider output loss from a provider-selection loss, rather than attributing everything to an aggregate investment shortfall.

For the numerical ratios, a=(3,2,1). Agent1 qualifies because3 exceeds half every rival ratio. Agent2 qualifies because2>=3/2. Agent3 fails because1<3/2. Thus the pure investment vectors are(3,0,0) and(0,2,0). This conclusion follows from the ratio threshold, not a grid. Their utility vectors are(9/2,18,3) and(6,6,2), giving welfare51/2 and14.

For the contested response, when agent2 supplies R2, agent1's own target is3 and threshold3/2. Since R2>3/2, agent1 globally prefers0. Staying out gives utility3*2=6. Jumping to its own peak3 gives9/2, and an equally strong second investment2 gives6-2=4. Any investment below2 is also worse than0. A higher available private production peak does not imply a profitable replacement of the existing service.

For efficient provision, V10 and k_min1. Either agent1 or agent3 alone supplies G10, with total welfare50. The equilibrium with agent1 at3 loses49/2, entirely through quality distortion. The equilibrium with agent2 at2 loses36, decomposed as32 from quality distortion and4 from excess provider cost. Directly subtracting their welfare values from50 gives the same losses, independently checking the completed-square formula.

For the Pareto comparison, the equilibrium with quality3 has higher welfare than quality2 by51/2-14=23/2. But agent1's utility falls from6 as a free rider to9/2 as the provider. Agents2 and3 gain, while agent1 loses3/2. Therefore the higher-welfare equilibrium is not a Pareto improvement without transfers. Aggregate efficiency, private willingness to provide and each agent's distributional preference are separate questions.

General pattern: I should identify the service technology before differentiating. Under a strongest-link rule, submaximal investment has no marginal benefit, so a best response can jump between no provision and a full private peak. A ratio threshold characterizes all pure providers analytically. The planner's fixed-quality cost problem selects a cheapest single provider, and a completed-square identity separates quality and selection inefficiency.
reference_answer:
Put ai=vi/ki. Given rival maximum R, the global best response is ai if R<ai/2,0 if R>ai/2, and either0 or ai at equality. Every pure equilibrium has one provider i investing ai, with ai>=max_{j!=i}(aj)/2. A largest-ratio agent always qualifies, proving existence.

Efficient quality is G*=sum(vi)/k_min, supplied by exactly one cheapest agent. A provider-i equilibrium loses(k_min/2)*(ai-G*)^2+(ki-k_min)*ai^2/2 relative to efficient welfare.

For v=(3,6,1),k=(1,3,1), the equilibria are(3,0,0) and(0,2,0), with utility vectors(9/2,18,3) and(6,6,2), and welfare51/2 and14. Efficient quality10 is supplied by agent1 or3, with welfare50. The losses are49/2 and36; the latter splits into32 plus4.

Against rival quality2, agent1 prefers staying out with utility6 to investing its own peak3 for utility9/2. The higher-welfare equilibrium is not a Pareto improvement because agent1 bears the provision cost and loses3/2.

problem: Dans un dilemme du prisonnier répété indéfiniment, coopérer rapporte4 à chacun, tandis qu'une déviation unilatérale rapporte6 puis la punition permanente rapporte1 par période. Quel facteur d'actualisation rend la coopération soutenable par stratégies grim-trigger ?
thinking:
Je compare les valeurs présentes plutôt que d'énumérer des histoires. Coopérer toujours vaut4/(1−δ). Dévier aujourd'hui donne6 puis1 à chaque période suivante, soit6+δ/(1−δ).

La contrainte d'incitation est4/(1−δ)≥6+δ/(1−δ). En multipliant par1−δ>0, j'obtiens4≥6−5δ, donc δ≥2/5. À l'égalité, le joueur est indifférent; au-dessus, coopérer est strictement préférable.

Cette condition doit tenir pour chaque joueur au début de chaque période; après une déviation, grim-trigger impose la punition, qui est un équilibre du jeu de stade puisque la défection rapporte1 contre0 face à un défecteur.

Comme contrôle, pour δ=1/2, coopération vaut8, alors que dévier vaut6+1=7. Pour δ=1/3, les valeurs sont6 et6,5, donc la coopération ne résiste pas.

General pattern: En répétition infinie, comparer le gain immédiat de déviation à la perte actualisée de continuation donne un seuil de patience. Vérifier aussi que la punition annoncée est elle-même séquentiellement rationnelle.
reference_answer: La coopération grim-trigger est soutenable si et seulement si δ≥2/5.

problem:
Je ne comprends pas comment répartir les impôts entre deux marchés sans essayer toutes les combinaisons. Peux-tu montrer une méthode exacte et expliquer pourquoi elle donne le minimum global? Deux marchés concurrentiels indépendants ont des demandes inverses p1=2-q1 et p2=4-2*q2. Les coûts marginaux sont nuls et l'offre parfaitement élastique. Une taxe unitaire ti est entièrement répercutée sur le prix payé: q1=2-t1, q2=(4-t2)/2. Les taxes sont des transferts; la perte réelle est D=t1^2/2+t2^2/4. Le gouvernement impose une recette exacte R=t1*(2-t1)+t2*(4-t2)/2, sans frais de collecte ni objectif redistributif. Les domaines initiaux sont t1 dans[0,2] et t2 dans[0,4].

Trouve d'abord la politique optimale pour tout R réalisable, puis les taxes, quantités et pertes pour R=9/4. Ensuite, une contrainte institutionnelle impose t1<=1/4, sans autre changement. Trouve le nouveau domaine réalisable, le seuil où ce plafond commence à contraindre, et la politique optimale pour chaque R. Recalcule exactement le cas R=9/4 et son surcoût réel. Pourquoi égaliser les taxes unitaires n'est-il pas la bonne règle? Justifie aussi le choix des branches de la courbe de recettes.
thinking:
Avant de calculer, je dois éliminer les branches inutiles, pas énumérer les couples. Pour un marché de demande p=a-b*q, la recette est r=t*(a-t)/b et la perte d=t^2/(2*b). Les taxes t et a-t donnent la même recette. Si t>a/2, sa partenaire a-t<a/2 donne strictement moins de perte. Une solution optimale utilise donc les branches t1<=1 et t2<=2. Le plafond t1<=1/4 les respecte déjà. Les recettes maximales sont1 et2; sans plafond, R appartient à[0,3].

Pour trouver le raccourci, je regarde le coût marginal de recette: d'(t)/r'(t)=t/(a-2*t). L'égalité entre marchés implique t1/(2-2*t1)=t2/(4-2*t2), donc t2=2*t1. Ce ne sont pas des taxes unitaires égales: ce sont des fractions égales du prix de réservation, t1/2=t2/4=z. Les quantités baissent alors toutes deux dans la même proportion z, puisque leurs quantités initiales valent2. Les intercepts et pentes déterminent la bonne normalisation.

Une route plus courte consiste à remplacer les deux taxes par z. Avec t1=2*z et t2=4*z, R=12*z*(1-z) et D=6*z^2. La branche utile est z dans[0,1/2], donc z=(1-sqrt(1-R/3))/2. Pour R=9/4, z=1/4: t1=1/2, t2=1, q1=q2=3/2, recettes3/4 et3/2, perte D=3/8. La somme des recettes vaut bien9/4; aucune taxe ne se trouve sur une branche décroissante.

Pour prouver le minimum global, une condition du premier ordre ne suffit pas sur la courbe de recettes. Je construis le certificat dual L=D-lambda*(r1+r2-R). Pour chaque marché, le terme variable est[(1/2+lambda)*t^2-lambda*a*t]/b, strictement convexe pour lambda>=0. Son minimum est t=lambda*a/(1+2*lambda), soit z=lambda/(1+2*lambda). Pour tout R<3, lambda=z/(1-2*z) rend les taxes proposées minimales sur tout le domaine initial. Sur une politique réalisant la recette R, L=D: la borne duale prouve donc l'optimalité globale et l'unicité. À R=3, les deux recettes doivent atteindre leurs maxima, ce qui force t1=1 et t2=2; inutile d'inventer un multiplicateur fini à cette extrémité.

Avec le plafond, je devrais conserver le même certificat mais projeter son minimum sur le domaine autorisé. La taxe1 devient min(2*z,1/4), tandis que t2=4*z. Le plafond commence à contraindre à z=1/8, donc R0=12*(1/8)*(7/8)=21/16. Jusqu'à ce seuil inclus, les anciennes formules restent valides. Au-delà, t1=1/4 et sa recette vaut7/16. La seconde taxe satisfait t2*(4-t2)/2=R-7/16; sur sa branche croissante, t2=2-sqrt(4-2*(R-7/16)). La recette maximale devient7/16+2=39/16. Tout R supérieur est irréalisable, même avec une taxe2 sur la branche décroissante.

Pour justifier ce régime contraint, j'utilise lambda=t2/(4-2*t2). Dès que t2>=1/2, le minimum libre de la taxe1 serait t2/2>=1/4, donc le minimum sous plafond est bien1/4. La seconde taxe minimise son propre terme dual. La somme reste une borne globale, avec égalité aux taxes proposées. Au seuil, t2=1/2 et les deux expressions coïncident; au maximum R=39/16, les maxima individuels forcent t1=1/4 et t2=2. La preuve traite toute la plage de recettes sans grille numérique ni liste de solutions candidates.

Pour R=9/4 avec plafond, la recette2 est29/16. J'obtiens t2=2-sqrt(6)/4, q1=7/4 et q2=1+sqrt(6)/8. La perte vaut1/32+t2^2/4=9/8-sqrt(6)/4. Son excès sur3/8 est(3-sqrt(6))/4>0. Le plafond reporte la charge sur le second marché: sa taxe augmente et sa quantité diminue; la quantité1 augmente. La contrainte ne change pas le montant total prélevé, mais elle empêche l'allocation qui minimise la perte.

Pour un contrôle indépendant, je paramètre directement chaque marché par sa recette. Sur la branche basse, t(r)=(a-sqrt(a^2-4*b*r))/2 et h(r)=t(r)^2/(2*b). Alors h'(r)=t/(a-2*t) et h''(r)=a*b/(a^2-4*b*r)^(3/2)>0 avant le maximum. La perte totale h1(r1)+h2(R-r1) est strictement convexe: sans plafond, son minimum égalise les dérivées; avec plafond, r1<=7/16 force le point de bord dès R>21/16. Cette seconde preuve retrouve le même seuil et le même régime, à partir des recettes plutôt que des taxes.

General pattern: je dois supprimer les branches dominées, normaliser les taxes par les intercepts de demande, puis égaliser la perte marginale par unité de recette. Un multiplicateur transforme la contrainte non linéaire en deux carrés convexes; un plafond projette un des minima sur son bord. Une reparamétrisation par les recettes apporte une vérification indépendante et révèle pourquoi la contrainte augmente le coût réel du financement.
reference_answer:
Sans plafond, R appartient à[0,3]. Posons z=(1-sqrt(1-R/3))/2. L'unique optimum est t1=2*z, t2=4*z, avec D=6*z^2. Pour R=9/4, les taxes valent1/2 et1, les quantités3/2 chacune, et D=3/8.

Avec t1<=1/4, R appartient à[0,39/16]. L'ancienne politique reste optimale jusqu'à R=21/16. Au-delà, t1=1/4 et t2=2-sqrt(4-2*(R-7/16)). Pour R=9/4, t2=2-sqrt(6)/4, les quantités sont7/4 et1+sqrt(6)/8, et D=9/8-sqrt(6)/4. Le surcoût est(3-sqrt(6))/4>0.

La preuve est globale: D-lambda*(recettes-R) est une somme de quadratiques strictement convexes, minimisées aux taxes indiquées, avec projection sur le plafond. La convexité des pertes en fonction des recettes confirme indépendamment le résultat. La règle égalise la perte marginale par unité de recette, pas les taxes unitaires.

problem: I need to understand why a coefficient can be significant in a regression while the model still predicts poorly. In a sample of n=100, a prespecified test gives an estimated slope2 with standard error0.8 and an out-of-sample RMSE of12. Compute the t-statistic and explain what the test does and does not establish about predictive accuracy.
thinking:
The test statistic for a zero slope is estimate divided by its standard error: t=2/0.8=2.5. With a large-sample normal reference, the two-sided p-value is about0.0124; a finite-sample t reference with98 degrees of freedom is close. This is evidence against a zero conditional association under the model assumptions.

The RMSE12 is on the outcome scale and measures typical squared prediction error on held-out observations. Its magnitude cannot be interpreted without an outcome benchmark or scale, and statistical significance of the slope does not bound it. A precisely estimated small signal can coexist with large residual variation.

I separate three questions: whether the coefficient differs from zero, whether the model is correctly specified, and whether predictions are accurate enough for a decision. The t-test addresses only the first, conditional on sampling and model assumptions; calibration, baseline comparison, and validation data address predictive performance.

As a check, multiplying t by its standard error recovers the estimate2. If the standard error fell while the slope stayed fixed, significance could rise without changing the RMSE; this algebra shows why inference strength and forecast quality are distinct quantities.

General pattern: A t-statistic scales an estimate by its uncertainty, while RMSE scales prediction errors by outcome variability. Statistical evidence for a nonzero parameter does not imply small prediction error or useful forecasts.
reference_answer: t=2.5 (two-sided large-sample p≈0.0124). This rejects a zero slope under assumptions but does not establish low RMSE or good out-of-sample prediction.

problem: Find the determinant of [[1,2,3],[0,1,4],[5,6,0]] using row operations that preserve the determinant, and explain how to track the sign.
thinking:
Before cofactor expansion, use a row operation: R3←R3−5R1 gives rows [1,2,3],[0,1,4],[0,−4,−15], which preserves determinant. Then R3←R3+4R2 gives [0,0,1] in the final row, so the matrix is triangular with diagonal1,1,1 and determinant1.

Both operations add a multiple of one row to another, so neither changes the determinant's sign or magnitude. No row swaps or scalings occurred, hence the original determinant is1.

A direct exact determinant calculation confirms1. Recording operation types is essential: a row swap flips sign and scaling a row scales the determinant.

General pattern: triangularize with determinant-preserving row additions, while maintaining a ledger of swaps and scalings. The diagonal product then gives the determinant with the correct sign.
reference_answer: The determinant is 1.

problem: A household has CRRA utility with coefficient γ=2, discount factor β=0.96, and deterministic gross return R=1.04. Use the Euler equation to find optimal consumption growth c_{t+1}/c_t. Explain whether consumption rises or falls and verify the benchmark βR=1.
thinking:
With deterministic returns, the Euler equation is1=βR(c_{t+1}/c_t)^(−γ). Rearranging gives growth=(βR)^(1/γ). Here βR=0.96×1.04=0.9984=624/625, so growth is√(624/625)=4√39/25≈0.99920.

The factor is below1, so consumption declines by about0.08% per period despite the positive return. The return nearly compensates impatience, but βR<1 leaves a small tilt toward current consumption.

The comparative-static sign is immediate from the power: growth rises with βR and falls with γ when βR<1. Greater patience or a higher return moves consumption toward the future; stronger curvature dampens the response to intertemporal prices.

As a limiting check, setting βR=1 gives growth1 and a flat consumption path. Substituting the computed growth into the Euler equation yields0.9984 divided by its square0.9984, exactly1.

General pattern: The Euler equation equates discounted marginal utility across dates. Under CRRA and deterministic returns, consumption growth is(βR)^(1/γ); βR determines direction and curvature controls the magnitude.
reference_answer: Consumption growth factor=√(624/625)=4√39/25≈0.99920, so consumption falls slightly. If βR=1, growth is1.

problem:
كيف يمكن أن تحصل محاكمات مكلفة رغم أن الطرفين يفضّلان توفير تكاليفها؟ أريد حلا يربط عرض التسوية بالمعلومات الخاصة، ثم يشرح لماذا قد ترتفع شدة القضايا التي تصل إلى المحكمة عندما يقل عددها.

بعد وقوع ضرر، يعرف المدعي وحده قيمة الحكم المتوقع theta، وهي موزعة بانتظام على[0,1]. المدعى عليه يعرف هذا التوزيع ولا يعرف theta. إذا حصلت محاكمة يدفع المدعى عليه theta إلى المدعي، ويتحمل المدعي تكلفة حقيقية x ويتحمل المدعى عليه تكلفة حقيقية y، حيث0<=x<1 وy>=0. يختار المدعى عليه عرضا واحدا S>=0. يقبل المدعي العرض إذا أعطاه على الأقل منفعة المحاكمة؛ القبول يحول S فقط ولا يسبب تكلفة تفاوض. بعد الرفض تحصل المحاكمة، والضرر السابق تكلفة غارقة لا تتغير بالقرار الحالي.

استخرج عتبة قبول العرض، ثم العرض الأمثل واحتمال المحاكمة في جميع حالات x+y. أثبت الحد الأدنى العالمي ولا تبحث عن عروض عددية متتالية. في الحالة التي تبقى فيها محاكمات، احسب متوسط theta بين القضايا المرفوضة، وتكلفة المدعى عليه المتوقعة ومنفعة المدعي المتوقعة والتكلفة الحقيقية المشتركة. افحص حساب الموارد بإلغاء التحويلات.

عند x=1/5,y=1/10 أعط كل هذه النتائج بدقة. ثم زد y مع تثبيت x: ما مشتقة تكلفة المدعى عليه المثلى، وكيف ترتبط باحتمال المحاكمة؟ هل تقليل عدد المحاكمات يخفض دائما مجموع تكاليفها الحقيقية؟ حدّد التكلفة المشتركة القصوى عند x=1/5. أخيرا، هل كانت المحاكمة لازمة لو عرف الطرفان theta قبل العرض؟
thinking:
قبل تحسين العرض أكتب مقارنة المدعي. قبول S يعطي S، والمحاكمة تعطي theta-x، إذن يقبل بالضبط عندما theta<=S+x. إذا عرّفت z=S+x، تكون عتبة القبول z، ومع S>=0 لدينا z>=x. عندما z>=1 يقبل الجميع، وأرخص عرض يحقق ذلك هو S=1-x. لا حاجة إلى تخمين قيمة الحكم للقضايا المختلفة.

لإيجاد الهدف داخل المنطقة الجزئية أستخدم كثافة theta التي تساوي1. عند x<=z<=1، تكلفة المدعى عليه هي D(z)=(z-x)*z+integral from z to1 of (theta+y) dtheta. بعد التكامل تصبح D(z)=z^2/2-(x+y)*z+1/2+y. مشتقتها z-(x+y) وثانيتها1، لذلك الحد الأدنى الداخلي يحدد العتبة z=x+y، لا عرضا مأخوذا من متوسط الحكم دون شرط.

لضبط الحدود أطبق إسقاط الحد الأدنى المحدب. لأن y>=0، فإن x+y>=x. إذا x+y<1، العتبة المثلى z=x+y والعرض S=y واحتمال المحاكمة1-x-y. إذا x+y>=1، تصل العتبة إلى1 ويكون S=1-x واحتمال المحاكمة0. أي عرض أعلى يرفع التحويل دون تحسين القرار. عند x+y=1 تتطابق الصيغ، وعند y=0 يكون العرض الأمثل0. بهذا استنفدت المجالات بالمتباينات، لا بتعداد العروض.

لحساب القضايا المنتقاة أشرط على الرفض. في المنطقة x+y<1 تصبح theta منتظمة على[x+y,1]، لذلك E[theta|trial]=(1+x+y)/2. زيادة y تقلل احتمال المحاكمة بمشتقة-1، لكنها ترفع متوسط الحكم بين المحاكمات بمشتقة1/2. التغير في شدة القضايا يعكس الاختيار عند العتبة، وليس تغير توزيع الأضرار الأصلي.

لحساب القيم السابقة للنوع أضع a=x+y. تكلفة المدعى عليه المثلى هي D_star=1/2+y-a^2/2. منفعة المدعي هي P_star=y*a+integral from a to1 of(theta-x)dtheta=1/2-x+a^2/2. طرحهما يعطي D_star-P_star=a*(1-a). وهذا بالضبط مجموع تكلفتي التقاضي لكل محاكمة مضروبا في احتمالها. التحويلات القضائية وتحويلات التسوية تختفي من حساب الموارد.

للتحقق العددي أستخدم x=1/5,y=1/10، فتكون a=3/10،S=1/10،واحتمال المحاكمة7/10،ومتوسط الحكم المشروط13/20. تكلفة المدعى عليه111/200 ومنفعة المدعي69/200؛ الفرق42/200=21/100. الطريق المستقل هو حساب الموارد مباشرة: تكلفة كل محاكمة3/10 مضروبة في احتمال7/10 تعطي21/100 أيضا.

لرؤية حيلة المغلف أشتق D_star بالنسبة إلى y بعد تعويض الحل، فأحصل على1-(x+y)، وهو احتمال المحاكمة. الاشتقاق المباشر للهدف قبل التعويض، مع تثبيت z، يعطي1-z، فتتطابق الطريقتان لأن مشتقة الهدف في z تختفي عند الحل. في منطقة التسوية الكاملة تكون D_star=1-x مستقلة عن y، ومشتقتها0 توافق احتمال المحاكمة0. عند الانتقال نفسه تتصل المشتقتان.

لفحص التكلفة الحقيقية ألاحظ أن R(a)=a*(1-a) في المنطقة الجزئية. مشتقتها بالنسبة إلى y هي1-2*a. لذلك قد تزيد الكلفة الحقيقية رغم تراجع عدد المحاكمات عندما a<1/2؛ وبعد1/2 تنخفض. مع x=1/5 يبلغ الحد الأقصى1/4 عند y=3/10. الصيغة R=1/4-(a-1/2)^2 تثبت الحد الأقصى العالمي، وفي منطقة التسوية الكاملة تصبح الكلفة0.

للمقارنة مع المعلومات الكاملة أكتب مجال التسوية لكل theta على حدة: المدعي يقبل S>=theta-x والمدعى عليه يفضّل S<=theta+y. تقاطعه مع S>=0 غير فارغ دائما، ويتيح تجنب المحاكمة؛ عندما x+y>0 يوجد وفر حقيقي من ذلك. المعلومات الخاصة تجبر المدعى عليه على عرض واحد لا يلائم كل الأنواع، فتخلق الرفض لبعض القيم العالية. ليس وجود مجال اتفاق لكل نوع دليلا على أن عرضا واحدا يستخرج جميع المعلومات بلا تكلفة.

General pattern: أستخرج عتبة قبول من منفعة النوع، ثم أتكامل على المناطق بدلا من استبدال القضايا بمتوسط غير مشروط. الإسقاط المحدب يعالج جميع الحدود، وحيلة المغلف تربط قيمة القرار باحتمال الحدث المكلف. إلغاء التحويلات يكشف أن تكلفة الحدث وعدده قد يتحركان في اتجاهين متعاكسين.
reference_answer:
إذا x+y<1، فإن العرض الأمثل S=y، وعتبة القبول x+y، واحتمال المحاكمة1-x-y. إذا x+y>=1، فإن S=1-x ويقبل الجميع. المحدبية الصارمة في العتبة وزيادة كلفة العروض فوق التسوية الكاملة تثبتان الحد الأدنى العالمي.

في المنطقة الجزئية، متوسط الحكم بين المحاكمات(1+x+y)/2، وتكلفة المدعى عليه1/2+y-(x+y)^2/2، ومنفعة المدعي1/2-x+(x+y)^2/2. الفرق هو التكلفة الحقيقية(x+y)*(1-x-y).

للبيانات المعطاة: العرض1/10، العتبة3/10، احتمال المحاكمة7/10، المتوسط المشروط13/20، التكلفة111/200، المنفعة69/200، والهدر الحقيقي21/100. مشتقة التكلفة المثلى بالنسبة إلى y تساوي احتمال المحاكمة. لكن الهدر الحقيقي يرتفع قبل x+y=1/2 وينخفض بعده؛ مع x=1/5 يبلغ1/4 عند y=3/10. المعلومات الكاملة تسمح باتفاق لكل نوع، بينما العرض الموحد في ظل المعلومات الخاصة يترك بعض الأنواع للمحاكمة.

problem: ¿Me ayudas a resolver este ejercicio de regresión? Tengo cuatro observaciones: x=(1,0,-1,0), z=(1,1,-1,-1) e y=(5,2,-1,-2). Quiero estimar y=alpha+beta*x+gamma*z+error por mínimos cuadrados. Me parece que la pendiente de x cambia al incluir z, pero no entiendo por qué. Calcula ambas pendientes, usa una proyección para recuperar beta sin resolver todo el sistema, y verifica residuos y suma de cuadrados. Bajo errores independientes de varianza común, calcula la varianza estimada de beta y su error estándar. Explica por qué una pendiente descriptiva ajustada no demuestra por sí sola un efecto causal.
thinking:
Antes de invertir la matriz completa, debo centrar las columnas. x y z ya tienen media0, mientras la media de y es1; por eso alpha=1. El producto x transpose*y es6 y x transpose*x es2, así que la pendiente sin z es3. Los productos adicionales son z transpose*z=4, x transpose*z=2 y z transpose*y=10. El sistema ajustado es2*beta+2*gamma=6 y2*beta+4*gamma=10, que da beta=1,gamma=2.

Una ruta más barata es recordar Frisch-Waugh-Lovell. Proyecto x sobre z con coeficiente2/4=1/2, dando xr=x-z/2=(1/2,-1/2,-1/2,1/2). Su norma cuadrada es1. Proyecto y centrada sobre z con coeficiente10/4=5/2, dando yr=(3/2,-3/2,1/2,-1/2). El producto xr transpose*yr es1, de modo que beta=(xr transpose*yr)/(xr transpose*xr)=1. La pendiente se obtiene del componente de x que z no explica.

Para descubrir la diferencia con la regresión simple, descompongo x=xr+z/2. El verdadero ajuste de estas observaciones es1+x+2*z más residuo. Como x transpose*z=2, la pendiente simple agrega gamma*(x transpose*z)/(x transpose*x)=2*1=2 a beta=1. Su valor3 refleja la asociación del control z con x; no es una contradicción algebraica entre los dos modelos.

Para verificar los residuos completos, el vector ajustado es (4,3,-2,-1), por lo que e=(1,-1,1,-1). Es ortogonal a la constante, a x y a z: sus tres productos son0. La suma de cuadrados es4. La matriz de diseño tiene rango3, así que con cuatro observaciones queda un grado de libertad y la estimación de la varianza común es4/(4-3)=4.

Para la incertidumbre de beta, el principio de proyección dice Var(beta)=sigma^2/(xr transpose*xr)=sigma^2. Reemplazando sigma^2 por4, la varianza estimada es4 y el error estándar2. La inversa de la matriz de productos de (x,z), [[2,2],[2,4]], es [[1,-1/2],[-1/2,1/2]]; su primera diagonal también produce varianza4. Esta ruta independiente verifica la fórmula basada en el residuo de x.

Para interpretar el tamaño del error, solo queda un grado de libertad residual. La existencia de un ajuste algebraicamente único no implica una pendiente estimada con precisión. Las hipótesis de errores independientes y varianza común justifican aquí la fórmula de varianza; no se deducen de la ortogonalidad muestral, que es una propiedad mecánica de mínimos cuadrados.

Para la interpretación causal, beta describe la asociación lineal de las partes residuales. Harían falta supuestos sobre asignación de x y sobre errores no correlacionados con los regresores para identificar un efecto causal. Incluir z cambia la pendiente por una proyección concreta; ese cambio no prueba que el control sea suficiente ni que sea apropiado causalmente.

General pattern: debo quitar primero el componente explicado por los controles y trabajar con los residuos. Frisch-Waugh-Lovell conecta la pendiente parcial, la información disponible y su varianza. La ortogonalidad verifica el ajuste, mientras la causalidad requiere supuestos adicionales.
reference_answer:
La regresión simple tiene pendiente3. Con z, los coeficientes son alpha=1,beta=1,gamma=2. La proyección residual da xr=(1/2,-1/2,-1/2,1/2), con norma cuadrada1 y producto con yr igual a1, confirmando beta=1.

Los residuos son (1,-1,1,-1), suma de cuadrados4 y un grado de libertad. La varianza estimada de beta es4 y su error estándar2. Estos cálculos verifican una asociación ajustada, no un efecto causal sin más supuestos.

problem: How can I avoid the winner's curse here without trying hundreds of bids? Two risk-neutral bidders compete in a sealed-bid second-price auction for one item with common value V, equal to0 or12 with equal prior probabilities. Each sees a private signal H or L. Conditional on V=12, each signal is H with probability3/4; conditional on V=0, it is H with probability1/4. Signals are independent conditional on V. Bids are nonnegative, highest bid wins, the winner pays the other's bid, and tied bids split winning probability equally. There is no reserve and the item is always sold. I propose bidding E[V|own signal], namely9 after H and3 after L. Check this proposal. Construct a symmetric pure-strategy equilibrium with strictly higher bid after H, prove it against every unilateral bid, and compute expected seller revenue and total bidder profit. All distributions are hypothetical.
thinking:
Before treating the bid as a private value, I should condition on the other signal. The joint signal probabilities are P(H,H)=5/16,P(L,L)=5/16 and P(H,L)=P(L,H)=3/16. Bayes gives E[V|H,H]=54/5,E[V|L,L]=6/5 and E[V|H,L]=6. Own-signal expectations9 and3 average over these events; the event in which a bid wins changes the information about V.

For the proposed bids, a low type tied against another low type pays3 while expected value is6/5. Underbidding3 avoids that loss and still loses to a high bid9. Conditional on own L, the other signal is L with probability5/8, so the improvement is(5/8)*(1/2)*(3-6/5)=9/16. A high type tied at9 against another high type has positive expected margin54/5-9=9/5. Bidding just above9 wins that event for sure at the unchanged payment9, improving conditional payoff by another9/16. Thus both types have a profitable deviation.

To discover the right pattern, I should use the tie event as an indifference condition. In an increasing symmetric pure strategy, a small upward or downward change around a type's bid changes only its probability of winning against the same type. No profitable change in either direction requires the expected value conditional on equal signals to equal the payment in that tie. This suggests bL=6/5 and bH=54/5, rather than the unconditional own-signal means.

For a full low-type deviation proof, any bid below bL loses against both types and gives0. Bidding bL ties only against L, where value minus payment is0. A bid strictly between bL and bH wins against L at payment bL, again with expected margin0, and loses against H. Bidding bH adds a tie against H with margin6-54/5=-24/5; bidding above bH wins that negative-margin event with full probability. Therefore no low-type bid exceeds payoff0. I have exhausted payoff-changing intervals analytically, not tested candidate bids one by one.

For the high type, every bid strictly between bL and bH wins only against L, with margin6-6/5=24/5. Bidding bH additionally ties against H with margin54/5-bH=0. Bidding above bH changes that zero-margin tie to a certain win, leaving expected payoff unchanged. Bidding bL halves the profitable low-signal event, while bidding below bL loses it. Hence bH is a best response. The low and high prescribed bids form a symmetric equilibrium, although some deviations are payoff-equivalent.

For expected bidder profit, a high type meets L with conditional probability(3/16)/(1/2)=3/8. Its conditional expected payoff is(3/8)*(24/5)=9/5; a low type gets0. Each bidder is high with probability1/2, so each has unconditional payoff9/10 and the sum is9/5. Equal-signal winning events contribute zero expected profit, but they still contribute seller revenue.

For seller revenue, H,H occurs with probability5/16 and pays54/5. Every other signal pair, with total probability11/16, pays6/5: in unequal pairs the winner pays the low bid, and in L,L the tied winner does the same. Thus revenue=(5/16)*(54/5)+(11/16)*(6/5)=21/5. As an independent accounting check, the item is always allocated and its ex ante common value is6, so revenue plus total bidder profit is21/5+9/5=6. The auction transfers value between seller and bidders; it creates no extra common value.

For the equilibrium's scope, these bids are justified by the declared binary signals, conditional independence, risk neutrality, tie rule and absence of a reserve. The rule is not to bid a conditional tie value in every common-value auction without checking deviations. Here the finite signal support turns all possible bids into a few payoff-equivalent intervals, and the signs of conditional margins prove global optimality.

General pattern: I should condition on the event that changes allocation, not merely on my own information. Equal-type tie indifference discovers candidate bids; ordering the opponent's bid support reduces infinitely many deviations to analytically proved intervals. Revenue-plus-profit accounting checks the solution without a search over bid levels.
reference_answer:
Bidding own-signal means3 and9 is not an equilibrium; each type can improve its conditional payoff by9/16. An increasing symmetric equilibrium is bL=6/5 and bH=54/5.

These are the conditional values in equal-signal ties. A low type gains nothing by winning against L and loses by winning against H; a high type gains by winning against L and is indifferent about winning against H. This proves all unilateral bid deviations. Seller revenue is21/5; each bidder earns9/10 ex ante, giving total bidder profit9/5. Their sum is the expected common value6.

problem: 「平均」と「中央値」の違いを、外れ値の例に触れながら二文で説明してください。

problem: There are 10 people in a room. Prove that either at least 4 mutually know one another or at least 4 are pairwise strangers, using one person's relationships to force the conclusion.
thinking:
Before proving a Ramsey claim, I should check its threshold. Ten is too small for a universal guarantee: I can construct an explicit counterexample. Take vertices 0 through 9, and join two when their difference modulo13 is a nonzero quadratic residue, from {1,3,4,9,10,12}.

This is an induced subgraph of the Paley graph on 13 vertices. A direct clique/independent-set check gives largest sizes3 and3, so it has neither a four-clique nor a four-vertex independent set. Thus the proposed statement for ten people is false; a proof cannot exist.

The exact threshold is R(4,4)=18. The counterexample teaches a useful proof habit: before extending a familiar Ramsey argument, verify the claimed threshold and seek a small structured witness when it looks too strong. A computational check on this explicit ten-vertex graph confirms the combinatorial obstruction.

General pattern: audit a universal combinatorial assertion against known extremal thresholds before proving it. A single explicit structure with both forbidden-set sizes below target refutes the claim.
reference_answer: The claim for 10 people is false. The induced Paley graph on vertices 0 through 9 modulo 13 has no 4-clique and no independent 4-set; the Ramsey threshold is 18.

problem: Aide-moi à quantifier le problème de hold-up. Un fournisseur choisit avant négociation un investissement spécifique x>=0, au coût x²/2. Cet investissement crée un surplus de transaction vérifiable égal à6x. Après l'investissement, le fournisseur ne reçoit qu'une moitié du surplus lors du marchandage. Calcule son investissement anticipé, l'investissement efficace, la perte de surplus et le surplus effectivement créé. Généralise l'écart en fonction du partage theta du surplus reçu par l'investisseur, et prouve le maximum sans tester une grille de x.
thinking:
Avant de résoudre, je sépare le rendement social du rendement approprié. La transaction crée6x et coûte réellement x²/2, donc le surplus total est6x-x²/2. Le fournisseur, lui, ne conserve que theta fois le surplus négocié et supporte tout le coût d'investissement: son objectif est theta*6x-x²/2.

La condition privée est6theta-x=0, donc x privé=6theta. La dérivée seconde vaut -1, ce qui donne le maximum global sur x>=0 pour theta dans[0,1]. L'optimum social résout6-x=0, soit x efficace=6. À partage égal theta=1/2, le fournisseur investit3: la négociation ex post réduit le rendement marginal qu'il anticipe avant d'investir.

La perte ne demande pas de recalculer deux niveaux de surplus compliqués. Le surplus social est une parabole concave maximisée en6; compléter le carré donne18-(x-6)²/2. En x=6theta, la perte est donc (6-6theta)²/2=18(1-theta)². Pour theta=1/2, le surplus créé est18-9/2=27/2, contre18 à l'optimum, et la perte vaut9/2.

Comme contrôle indépendant, l'objectif privé se complète en18theta²-(x-6theta)²/2, donc son maximiseur est bien6theta. À partage égal, il vaut9/2 au choix x=3; le surplus social à ce même x vaut27/2. Ces deux valeurs sont distinctes: le gain privé d'investissement et le gain total ne sont pas le même objectif.

General pattern: Quand l'investissement spécifique précède un partage ex post, l'investisseur internalise seulement sa part marginale du surplus. La condition privée égalise cette part au coût marginal; l'efficacité égalise le surplus marginal total au même coût. La perte quadratique révèle directement le coût de l'incomplétude contractuelle.
reference_answer:
À partage égal, l'investissement privé est x=3, alors que l'optimum social est x=6. Le surplus total créé à x=3 est27/2; le surplus efficace est18, donc la perte est9/2.

Pour une part privée theta, x privé=6theta et la perte sociale est18(1-theta)². La stricte concavité garantit ces choix globaux.

problem: A polynomial p has degree at most 3, p(0)=1, p(1)=2, p(2)=5 and p(3)=10. Find p(4) without first solving for every coefficient.
thinking:
Before interpolating, I inspect the finite differences. Values1,2,5,10 have first differences1,3,5 and second differences2,2. Constant second differences mean the data already lie on a quadratic, despite the allowed cubic degree.

A quadratic with constant second difference2 has leading coefficient1. Since p(0)=1, write p(k)=k²+bk+1; p(1)=2 gives b=0. Thus p(4)=17. The two remaining observations are consistency checks rather than new unknowns.

Why is this shortcut conclusive despite degree at most3? A cubic's third finite difference is constant; the first differences here are1,3,5,7 after including the next extrapolated value, so the second difference stays2 and the third difference is0. Equivalently the quadratic matching three nodes is unique, and a degree-at-most-3 polynomial agreeing at four nodes with it must coincide everywhere.

General pattern: finite differences reveal a lower effective degree before coefficient solving. Then use a root-count uniqueness argument to show the simpler interpolant is forced.
reference_answer: The unique polynomial is p(x)=x²+1, so p(4)=17.

problem: Aide-moi à comparer deux prix: avec demande Q=120−2p et coût marginal12, calcule la perte sèche d'un monopole puis vérifie-la par une intégrale, pas seulement par un triangle.
thinking:
Avant d'intégrer, le monopole maximise(p−12)(120−2p). La condition du premier ordre donne p_m=36 et Q_m=48. L'efficacité exige p=12, donc Q*=96.

La perte sèche est le bénéfice marginal moins le coût marginal intégré sur les échanges perdus: ∫ de48 à96 (48−Q/2−12)dQ=∫(36−Q/2)dQ=576. Géométriquement, c'est un triangle de base48 et hauteur24, aire576.

Le contrôle par surplus distingue transfert et perte: le markup sur les unités vendues transfere surplus entre parties; seules les unités entre48 et96, dont valeur marginale tombe sous cost, créent la perte nette.

General pattern: deadweight loss is the integral of marginal willingness-to-pay minus marginal cost over quantities excluded by market power. A triangle is valid only when that wedge varies linearly.
reference_answer: The monopoly price is 36, output is 48, the efficient output is 96, and deadweight loss is 576.

problem: I'm confused why someone with a loss-averse value function might reject a fair gamble. Relative to a reference point of zero, suppose v(x)=√x for gains and v(x)=−2√(−x) for losses. A gamble pays+100 with probability p and−100 otherwise. Find the prospect-value expectation, the probability threshold for acceptance, and compare it with expected money at p=1/2 and at indifference.
thinking:
I keep the monetary expectation separate from the reference-dependent value. The gain is worth√100=10, while the loss is worth−2√100=−20. Therefore expected prospect value is10p−20(1−p)=30p−20, even though expected monetary payoff is100p−100(1−p)=200p−100.

Indifference in value occurs when30p−20=0, so the acceptance threshold is p=2/3. At an even chance, expected money is zero but expected prospect value is−5, so this model predicts rejection. At the value threshold, expected money is100(2/3)−100(1/3)=100/3>0: the gamble needs a positive objective expected payoff to compensate for loss aversion.

The wedge comes from the reference-dependent utility scale, not from changing the probabilities. A gain and loss of equal magnitude have unequal value magnitudes,10 versus20. If the loss multiplier fell to1, the threshold would return to1/2; if it rose, the required win probability would rise.

As a check, the general threshold for equal-magnitude outcomes is λ/(1+λ), where λ is the loss multiplier: p×10−(1−p)×20=0 gives2/3. The direct expected-value calculation at that threshold is positive, confirming that subjective indifference and monetary fairness are different criteria.

General pattern: Under reference-dependent loss aversion, evaluate gains and losses through the value function before averaging. The indifference probability balances subjective values, while expected monetary value remains a separate benchmark; never infer one from the other.
reference_answer: Expected prospect value is30p−20, so the acceptance threshold is p=2/3. At p=1/2, expected money is0 but expected prospect value is−5. At indifference, expected monetary payoff is100/3, which is positive.

problem: How do I choose inventory if I trust the demand mean and variance, but not a full probability model? I pay1 per unit stocked, sell each unit for3 and cannot salvage leftovers. Demand D>=0 has mean4 and variance1. For stock q>=0, expected profit is3*E[min(D,q)]-q. Find the stock maximising worst-case expected profit over all demand distributions with these moments. Prove the result globally by constructing an admissible worst-case distribution and a saddle certificate, rather than searching many distributions. Contrast it with the optimal stock if demand were exactly3 or5 equally likely. Show that the robust stock is unique.
thinking:
Before guessing a demand law, I should rewrite profit in terms of shortages. Since min(D,q)=D-(D-q)Positive, expected profit is12-q-3*E[(D-q)Positive]. Put z=q-4 and r=sqrt(z^2+1). The identity xPositive=(abs(x)+x)/2 gives expected shortage=[E[abs(D-q)]-z]/2. Cauchy-Schwarz bounds E[abs(D-q)]<=sqrt(E[(D-q)^2])=r, hence every admissible demand law gives profit at least B(q)=6+q/2-(3/2)*r.

To discover when this moment bound is exact, I should inspect Cauchy equality. It requires abs(D-q)=r almost surely, so the worst-case support is q-r and q+r. The upper-point probability is(r-z)/(2*r), chosen to make the mean4. This two-point law also has variance1. It is admissible under D>=0 whenever q-r>=0, equivalently q>=17/8. In that region the lower bound B(q) is the actual worst-case profit, not merely a conservative estimate.

For the stationary stock, B'(q)=1/2-(3/2)*z/r. Setting it to zero gives z/r=1/3, so z>0 and8*z^2=1. Thus qStar=4+sqrt(2)/4, with rStar=3*sqrt(2)/4. The second derivative is -3/[2*(z^2+1)^(3/2)]<0. The stock lies above17/8, so its exact worst-case profit is B(qStar)=8-sqrt(2). Curvature identifies the candidate, but I still need a global certificate outside the tight-bound region.

For that certificate, the equality distribution at qStar has lower demand dLow=4-sqrt(2)/2 and upper demand dHigh=4+sqrt(2). Its probabilities are2/3 and1/3. The deviations from4 are -sqrt(2)/2 andsqrt(2); their weighted mean is0 and weighted squared deviation is1. Both support points are positive. At qStar, this law attains the moment shortage bound and yields profit8-sqrt(2).

A cheaper global argument fixes this admissible law and considers any stock. Below dLow, marginal expected revenue is3 and the marginal stock cost1, so profit rises with slope2. Between the support points, demand exceeds stock with probability1/3, giving marginal profit3*(1/3)-1=0. Above dHigh, additional stock earns nothing and profit falls with slope -1. Consequently the maximum profit against this single law is8-sqrt(2), attained throughout[dLow,dHigh]. Worst-case profit at any stock cannot exceed profit against this law. Since qStar guarantees exactly that upper bound, the policy and law form a saddle certificate proving global robust optimality.

For uniqueness, outside[dLow,dHigh] the fixed-law profit is strictly below the saddle value. Inside that interval, every q exceeds17/8, so its actual worst-case profit is B(q). Strict concavity of B gives a unique maximum there at qStar. The least-favourable law leaves many best-response stocks, but only qStar is robustly optimal across all admissible laws. I should not infer policy nonuniqueness merely from that flat best-response segment.

For the specified demand law3 or5 with equal probabilities, profit rises with slope2 up to3, then with slope3*(1/2)-1=1/2 up to5, and falls with slope -1 thereafter. Its unique optimum is q=5, yielding12-5=7. This law has the same mean and variance as the uncertainty set, but exploiting its full distribution improves its own optimal expected profit beyond the robust guarantee.

For an independent numerical-symbolic check, the robust policy under the3-or5 law lies between the demands, so its profit is(3/2)*(3+qStar)-qStar=13/2+sqrt(2)/8, which exceeds8-sqrt(2). At q=4, both this law and the moment worst case give profit13/2. The robust optimum gains3/2-sqrt(2)>0 over that mean-demand policy, while retaining a guarantee against every admissible law.

General pattern: I should turn inventory profit into a moment-bounded shortage, then read the inequality's equality condition to discover a least-favourable distribution. A fixed-law best-response bound supplies global optimality outside the local tightness region. Strict curvature and support intervals distinguish a unique robust policy from multiple best responses to its worst-case law.
reference_answer:
The unique robust stock is q=4+sqrt(2)/4, guaranteeing profit8-sqrt(2). A least-favourable demand law puts probabilities2/3 and1/3 on4-sqrt(2)/2 and4+sqrt(2); it has mean4 and variance1 and attains the shortage bound.

Against this law no stock earns more than8-sqrt(2), proving global optimality. The moment bound is tight and strictly concave on its flat best-response interval, proving uniqueness of the robust policy. If demand is known to be3 or5 equally likely, the unique optimal stock is5 and profit7.

problem: Deux usines doivent réduire ensemble leurs émissions de6 unités. Leur coût d'abattement est C1(a1)=a1²/2 et C2(a2)=a2², avec abattements non négatifs. Aide-moi à comparer une règle uniforme qui impose3 unités à chacune avec une politique coût-efficace. Trouve l'allocation qui atteint la cible au moindre coût, le prix de permis échangeables qui la soutient, et l'économie de coût par rapport à la règle uniforme. Explique pourquoi égaliser les abattements n'est pas le bon principe.
thinking:
Avant de choisir les quantités, je compare les coûts marginaux: MAC1=a1 et MAC2=2a2. Un abattement supplémentaire doit aller à l'usine dont le coût marginal est le plus faible; au minimum intérieur, les coûts marginaux s'égalisent tout en respectant a1+a2=6. Cela donne a1=2a2, donc a1=4 et a2=2.

La somme des coûts est strictement convexe, donc cette solution faisable est l'unique minimum global. Le coût est C1(4)+C2(2)=8+4=12. Sous quotas égaux, le coût est C1(3)+C2(3)=9/2+9=27/2. La règle uniforme dépense3/2 de plus, bien qu'elle atteigne exactement la même réduction totale.

Un marché concurrentiel de permis soutient l'allocation efficace au prix p=4: chaque usine choisit son abattement en égalisant son coût marginal à p. Ainsi a1=p=4 et2a2=p, donc a2=2. Le prix commun égalise les coûts marginaux, pas les niveaux d'abattement. Avec coûts différents, les quotas égaux ignorent la pente de chaque fonction de coût.

Comme contrôle indépendant, substituer a2=6-a1 dans le coût total donne une parabole dont la dérivée s'annule àa1=4 et la dérivée seconde est positive. Le coût minimum retrouve12. La règle uniforme coûte27/2, ce qui confirme l'économie3/2 obtenue en réallouant l'effort vers l'usine moins coûteuse à la marge.

General pattern: Pour répartir une cible d'abattement à coût minimal, j'égalise les coûts marginaux des sources actives et vérifie les contraintes de bord. La convexité certifie le minimum global. Un prix de permis transmet exactement ce signal marginal commun, tandis qu'une répartition uniforme des quantités n'est efficace que si les coûts marginaux coïncident déjà.
reference_answer: L'allocation coût-efficace est(a1,a2)=(4,2), car MAC1=MAC2=4. Le coût total est12. Les quotas égaux(3,3) coûtent27/2; les permis économisent3/2. Le prix concurrentiel qui soutient l'allocation efficace est p=4 par unité d'abattement.

problem: Is the revenue-maximising tax also best when revenue finances something useful? A competitive private market has inverse demand10-q and constant marginal production cost2. A unit tax t in[0,8] is passed fully into the buyer price because supply is perfectly elastic. All revenue finances a public programme G=t*q, costing one resource unit per unit of G and giving gross social benefit B(G)=b*G, with b>0. There are no collection costs or other financing instruments. Find the welfare-maximising tax and programme for every b, compare them with the revenue-maximising policy, and derive the marginal social cost of raising one additional unit of revenue on the increasing Laffer branch. At b=2 give exact quantities, revenue, deadweight loss and net welfare gain. Explain why neither ignoring the public benefit nor counting tax revenue as an extra resource loss gives the right objective.
thinking:
Before choosing a tax, I should write the two resource accounts. Buyer price is2+t, so q=8-t and revenue R=t*(8-t). Private-market resource surplus is8*q-q^2/2=32-t^2/2. Tax revenue is transferred from buyers to government, not destroyed. The public programme uses resources G=R and creates gross benefit b*R, so its net resource benefit is(b-1)*R.

For the welfare gain over the untaxed market with no programme, I obtain V(t)=(b-1)*t*(8-t)-t^2/2. The two terms represent programme net benefit and private-market distortion. If b<=1, both terms are nonpositive for every feasible t, and t=0 is the unique optimum. A programme worth no more than its direct resource cost cannot justify this distortionary funding method.

For b>1, I should collect the quadratic terms before differentiating: V=8*(b-1)*t-(b-1/2)*t^2. It is strictly concave, so the stationary point tStar=8*(b-1)/(2*b-1) is the unique global maximum. It lies strictly between0 and4, inside the declared tax interval. The associated programme is GStar=64*b*(b-1)/(2*b-1)^2, and the maximum gain is32*(b-1)^2/(2*b-1). Completing the quadratic square independently proves this optimum.

For revenue alone, R=16-(t-4)^2 is maximised at t=4, with programme16. For every finite b>1, the welfare optimum taxes less than4 and funds a smaller programme. The revenue peak ignores the rapidly increasing resource distortion per additional unit collected. As b tends to infinity, tStar approaches4 from below, but never reaches it at a finite benefit coefficient.

For marginal public-finance cost, on0<=t<4 I can differentiate through revenue because R'=8-2*t>0. The marginal private distortion per revenue unit is d(t^2/2)/dR=t/(8-2*t). Adding the programme's direct resource cost1 gives MCPF=1+t/(8-2*t)=(8-t)/(8-2*t). The welfare condition is gross marginal programme benefit b=MCPF. Solving it gives exactly tStar. At the revenue peak the denominator vanishes: marginal collection is not a cheap substitute for a direct resource unit.

At b=2, tStar=8/3, q=16/3 and revenue G=128/9. Deadweight loss is tStar^2/2=32/9. The programme's net benefit is128/9, leaving welfare gain96/9=32/3. Total resource welfare is32+32/3=128/3. At the revenue-maximising tax4, the programme is16 but the distortion8 leaves gain8, smaller by8/3.

For an independent check, MCPF at8/3 is(16/3)/(8/3)=2, matching the stated gross benefit coefficient. Consumer surplus is q^2/2=128/9 and producer surplus is0 under constant marginal cost. Government receives128/9, produces a programme with gross benefit256/9, and uses resources128/9. Adding consumer surplus, producer surplus, revenue, programme benefit and negative programme cost gives384/9=128/3, agreeing with the primitive-resource route. The revenue term restores the money already removed from consumer surplus; it is not an additional resource expense.

General pattern: I should cancel fiscal transfers, retain actual programme resources and compare marginal benefit with the full marginal cost of funds. A revenue square locates the fiscal peak, while a welfare square selects a different tax. The Laffer-branch derivative exposes why useful public spending need not justify maximum revenue collection.
reference_answer:
For b<=1 the optimum is t=G=0. For b>1, t=8*(b-1)/(2*b-1), G=64*b*(b-1)/(2*b-1)^2 and welfare gain32*(b-1)^2/(2*b-1). Strict concavity proves the optimum. Revenue maximisation instead chooses t=4,G=16.

On the increasing revenue branch, marginal public-finance cost is(8-t)/(8-2*t). At b=2 the optimum is t=8/3,q=16/3,G=128/9, with distortion32/9 and gain32/3. Resource cost and tax transfers must be kept distinct to obtain these results.

problem: Are employer payroll taxes and worker consumption taxes equivalent once a wage floor binds? Use this hypothetical labour market. The producer-good price is1. Workers supply one unit each, with reservation cost r uniformly distributed at density1 on[0,12]; a worker works if its consumption purchasing power omega is at least r. A firm gets real output benefit B(L)=12*L-L^2/2, so labour demand at employer cost C is max(0,12-C). Gross contractual wage w excludes employer contributions. With employer rate e, employee rate s, income-tax rate i on post-contribution income, and a tax v only on wage-financed worker consumption, C=(1+e)*w and omega=(1-s)*(1-i)*w/(1+v). Revenue is a transfer; no other fiscal costs or taxed spending are included. Compare policy E:(e,s,i,v)=(1,0,0,0) with policy V:(0,0,0,1). First clear the flexible-wage market. Then impose w>=5, employment equal to the smaller of labour supply and demand at the binding wage. Compare wages, employment, involuntary unemployment and receipts. Under E, bound real welfare over all allocations of jobs among willing workers, and calculate welfare under uniform random rationing. Explain the assumption on which tax equivalence depends.
thinking:
Before comparing labels, I should derive the actual wedge between employer cost and worker purchasing power. Their ratio is kappa=C/omega=(1+e)*(1+v)/[(1-s)*(1-i)], assuming positive denominators. In the interior supply range, labour supply is omega and demand is12-C. Clearing gives L=omega=12/(1+kappa),C=12*kappa/(1+kappa), and w=C/(1+e). The same kappa produces the same employment and real cost-power pair, but not necessarily the same contractual wage.

For the two policies, kappa=2 in both. Flexible equilibrium is L=4,omega=4,C=8. Under E, gross wage is w=4 because employer contributions double it. Under V, gross wage is w=8 and the worker's wage-financed consumption tax halves its purchasing power. Each policy collects4 per employed worker, hence receipts16. The division between nominal wage and the tax-adjusted wage changes even though the real allocation agrees.

For the floor, I must test it against w rather than C or omega. Under E, flexible w=4 violates w>=5. At w=5, C=10 and omega=5, so demand is2 and supply is5. Employment is2 and involuntary unemployment among willing workers is3. Employer-tax revenue is e*w*L=1*5*2=10. Under V, flexible w=8 already exceeds the floor, so L=4,C=8,omega=4, no involuntary unemployment and receipts16 remain. Equal tax wedges therefore cease to imply equal employment under this contract-wage constraint.

For welfare, nominal wages and receipts must cancel as transfers. Real output benefit is B(L); worker reservation costs are real disutility. In the flexible equilibrium, all workers with r<=4 are employed, so total cost is the integral of r from0 to4, equal to8. Output benefit is12*4-4^2/2=40, giving welfare32. Under E with the floor, B(2)=22, but the resource cost depends on which two units of willing workers are selected from r in[0,5]. Employment alone no longer identifies welfare.

For the welfare bounds, a rearrangement argument replaces a search over worker assignments. Selecting the two lowest reservation-cost units r in[0,2] gives cost2^2/2=2 and welfare20. Selecting the two highest willing units r in[3,5] gives cost(5^2-3^2)/2=8 and welfare14. Any selection of mass2 from[0,5] has cost between2 and8; moving a selected higher-cost worker to an unselected lower-cost worker weakly lowers cost. Thus the sharp welfare interval is[14,20], attained by those endpoint allocations.

For uniform random rationing, each willing worker has employment probability2/5 independent of r. Expected total disutility is(2/5)*the integral of r from0 to5=(2/5)*(25/2)=5. Expected welfare is22-5=17. Relative to efficient assignment at the same employment, the rationing loss is3. Policy V gives32, so its welfare advantage over E is15 under random rationing, or between12 and18 over all feasible E allocations. The latter uncertainty comes from rationing, not from an uncertain employment quantity.

For an independent transfer-accounting check under random E rationing, the firm's profit is output22 minus employer payments10*2=20, hence2. Workers receive purchasing power5*2=10 and incur expected disutility5, giving net5. The government receives10. Their sum2+5+10=17 agrees with primitives. Under V, firm profit is40-8*4=8, worker purchasing-power utility is4*4-8=8 and receipts16; total8+8+16=32. The consumption tax is explicitly restricted to wage-financed worker spending here, so no omitted profit-consumption tax is silently assumed.

For the general floor test, flexible gross wage is12*kappa/[(1+kappa)*(1+e)]. A constraint on that nominal variable can distinguish policies with the same kappa. A floor defined instead on a tax-adjusted wage would impose a different constraint and require a different calculation. The source of non-equivalence is the declared wage-floor definition and rationing rule, not the legal name assigned to an otherwise identical flexible-market wedge.

General pattern: I should reduce taxes to the employer-cost versus worker-purchasing-power wedge, then check whether a constraint is expressed in a variable preserved by that reduction. A binding floor introduces rationing; real welfare requires knowing who gets the jobs. Transfer accounting and rearrangement bounds distinguish price equivalence, employment equivalence and welfare identification.
reference_answer:
Both policies have wedge kappa=2. With flexible wages they give L=4,C=8,omega=4 and receipts16, but gross wages are4 under E and8 under V.

With w>=5, E gives w=5,L=2,C=10,omega=5,unemployment3 and receipts10; V remains at its flexible equilibrium. E's welfare is sharply bounded by[14,20] according to job allocation, and equals17 under uniform random rationing. V's welfare is32. Tax equivalence requires a flexible wage adjustment compatible with the constraint; equal wedges do not preserve a floor on gross contractual wages.

problem:
Ich weiß nicht, wie ich diese Insolvenzfrage ohne eine Normalverteilungsannahme lösen soll. Kannst du mir einen kurzen mathematischen Weg zeigen und erklären, ob die Schranke wirklich erreichbar ist?

Der zufällige operative Gewinn X eines Unternehmens hat E[X]=6 und Var(X)=9. Weitere Verteilungsannahmen gibt es nicht; negative Gewinne sind erlaubt. Ein Unternehmen gilt bei X<=0 als insolvent. Bestimme die größte mögliche Insolvenzwahrscheinlichkeit über alle Verteilungen mit diesen beiden Momenten. Beweise die Schranke und konstruiere eine Verteilung, die sie erreicht.

Was ändert sich, wenn Insolvenz strikt als X<0 definiert wird? Unterscheide Maximum und Supremum. Zeige eine Familie von Verteilungen mit den vorgegebenen Momenten, deren strikte Verlustwahrscheinlichkeit gegen das Supremum geht.

Eine sichere Reserve k>=0 wird zum Gewinn addiert. Finde die kleinste Reserve, die P(X+k<=0)<=1/20 für jede zulässige Verteilung garantiert. Vergleiche die einseitige Schranke mit der gewöhnlichen zweiseitigen Chebyshev-Schranke bei k=0.

Schließlich werden n unabhängige Gewinne mit derselben Verteilung gemittelt. Wie viele Unternehmen genügen nach dieser einseitigen Schranke, um P(Mittelwert<=0)<=1/100 zu garantieren? Ist die hergeleitete Schranke unter dieser zusätzlichen Unabhängigkeitsstruktur automatisch scharf? Erkläre auch, warum die Rechnung bei perfekt gemeinsamen Gewinnen nicht gilt.
thinking:
Vor dem Rechnen zentriere ich den Gewinn: Z=X-6, E[Z]=0 und E[Z^2]=9. Insolvenz bedeutet Z<=-6. Ich suche keine Normalverteilung und keine Liste möglicher Gewinnwerte, sondern ein quadratisches Zertifikat aus den bekannten Momenten. Für a>0 und b>=0 gilt auf Z<=-a die Ungleichung (Z-b)^2>=(a+b)^2. Daher ist der Indikator des Ereignisses höchstens (Z-b)^2/(a+b)^2. Erwartungsbildung liefert P(Z<=-a)<=(9+b^2)/(a+b)^2.

Für eine bessere Schranke optimiere ich nur den Hilfsparameter des Zertifikats. Die Ableitung nach b ist 2*(a*b-9)/(a+b)^3. Der Ausdruck fällt bis b=9/a und steigt danach. Ich erhalte die Cantelli-Schranke P(Z<=-a)<=9/(9+a^2). Für a=6 ist b=3/2 und die Wahrscheinlichkeit höchstens 1/5. Der Trick heißt verschobenes Quadrat: Die einseitige Ereignisgeometrie wird durch den Abstand vom positiven Mittelpunkt b erfasst, statt beide Enden gleich zu behandeln.

Um Schärfe zu entdecken, untersuche ich die Gleichheitsbedingungen des Zertifikats. Auf dem Insolvenzereignis muss Z=-a gelten, außerhalb muss das Quadrat null sein, also Z=b=9/a. Der Nullmittelwert erzwingt die Masse p=9/(9+a^2) am unteren Punkt. Bei a=6 heißt das X=0 mit Wahrscheinlichkeit 1/5 und X=15/2 mit Wahrscheinlichkeit 4/5. Der Mittelwert ist 6 und das zweite Moment ist 45, also die Varianz 45-36=9. Genau die Masse 1/5 ist insolvent. Die zwei Stützpunkte stammen aus Gleichheit im Beweis, nicht aus einer Aufzählung von Kandidaten.

Für die strikte Definition prüfe ich die Grenze sorgfältig. X<0 bedeutet Z<-6. Auf diesem Ereignis ist das quadratische Zertifikat strikt größer als 1. Bei positiver Ereigniswahrscheinlichkeit folgt deshalb P(X<0)<1/5; bei Wahrscheinlichkeit null ist die Ungleichung ebenfalls strikt. Ein Maximum von 1/5 ist ausgeschlossen. Ich setze aber für epsilon>0 den unteren Gewinn auf -epsilon und a=6+epsilon. Mit p=9/(9+a^2) und oberem Gewinn 6+9/a erhalte ich wieder Mittelwert 6 und Varianz 9. Die strikte Verlustwahrscheinlichkeit p steigt für epsilon gegen 0 gegen 1/5. Das Supremum ist daher 1/5, aber keine zulässige Verteilung erreicht es.

Für die Reserve verschiebe ich die Ereignisschwelle, nicht die Varianz. X+k<=0 entspricht Z<=-(6+k), daher lautet die scharfe Momentenschranke 9/[9+(6+k)^2]. Die Forderung höchstens 1/20 ist äquivalent zu (6+k)^2>=171. Weil k>=0, folgt k_min=sqrt(171)-6=3*sqrt(19)-6. Schärfe beweist auch die Notwendigkeit: Für jede kleinere Reserve wähle ich den unteren Gewinn -k und den oberen Gewinn 6+9/(6+k). Mit unterer Masse 9/[9+(6+k)^2] gelten die Momente und die Insolvenzwahrscheinlichkeit überschreitet 1/20. Am minimalen k ist die Wahrscheinlichkeit 1/20 erreichbar, denn die Definition enthält den Grenzpunkt.

Für einen unabhängigen Kontrollweg verwende ich zunächst Chebyshev. Da X<=0 das Ereignis |X-6|>=6 impliziert, erhalte ich P(X<=0)<=9/36=1/4. Die einseitige Schranke 1/5 ist kleiner. In der Extremalverteilung prüfe ich außerdem direkt E[(X-6)^2]=(1/5)*36+(4/5)*(3/2)^2=9. Beide Momentenprüfungen stimmen überein; eine angenommene Normalverteilung wäre dagegen ein zusätzliches Modell und keine Garantie aus diesen Angaben.

Für den Mittelwert nutze ich die Unabhängigkeit genau an der Varianzstelle. Sein Erwartungswert bleibt 6, seine Varianz ist 9/n. Cantelli ergibt P(Mittelwert<=0)<=1/(1+4*n). Die Forderung höchstens 1/100 verlangt n>=99/4, also mindestens 25 Unternehmen. Bei n=24 ist die Schranke 1/97 zu groß, bei n=25 ist sie 1/101. Das ist die kleinste Zahl, die diese Schranke zertifiziert; ich behaupte damit keine exakte kleinste Zahl unter allen möglichen unabhängig identisch verteilten Ausgangsgesetzen.

Zur Schärfe unterscheide ich die Verteilungsklassen. Über alle Gesetze eines Mittelwerts mit diesen zwei Momenten ist Cantelli scharf. Unter n>=2 unabhängigen identisch verteilten nichtkonstanten Gewinnen wäre Gleichheit jedoch nur möglich, wenn der Mittelwert genau zwei Werte hätte. Zwei verschiedene Punkte u<v im Träger des Einzelgewinns erzeugen im Träger der Summe mindestens die drei verschiedenen Punkte n*u, (n-1)*u+v und n*v. Das widerspricht der nötigen Zweipunktstruktur. Der Momentenbeweis allein liefert deshalb keine Schärfe innerhalb der unabhängigen Klasse. Bei perfekt gemeinsamen Gewinnen X_i=X ist der Mittelwert sogar gleich X und seine Varianz 9; die Verkleinerung auf 9/n fällt vollständig weg.

General pattern: Ich suche ein nichtnegatives Polynom, das den Ereignisindikator dominiert und dessen Erwartung aus den bekannten Momenten berechenbar ist. Ein optimiertes verschobenes Quadrat liefert eine einseitige Schranke; seine Gleichheitsbedingungen entdecken die Extremalverteilung. Offene Ereignisgrenzen können ein Maximum in ein bloßes Supremum verwandeln. Zusätzliche Unabhängigkeit verändert die Varianz und die zulässige Extremalstruktur zugleich.
reference_answer:
Die größte Wahrscheinlichkeit von X<=0 ist 1/5. Cantelli folgt aus dem optimierten Zertifikat (Z-b)^2/(a+b)^2 mit Z=X-6, a=6 und b=3/2. Die Verteilung X=0 mit Masse 1/5 und X=15/2 mit Masse 4/5 erreicht die Schranke und hat exakt die geforderten Momente.

Für X<0 bleibt das Supremum 1/5, es wird aber nicht erreicht. Mit epsilon>0, a=6+epsilon, unterem Wert -epsilon, oberem Wert 6+9/a und unterer Masse 9/(9+a^2) nähern sich zulässige Verteilungen diesem Supremum.

Die kleinste garantierende Reserve ist k=3*sqrt(19)-6. Die gewöhnliche Chebyshev-Schranke bei k=0 ist 1/4 statt 1/5.

Für unabhängige identisch verteilte Gewinne garantiert Cantelli mit n=25 die gewünschte Wahrscheinlichkeit, denn die Schranke ist 1/(1+4*n). Die Schranke ist in dieser engeren Klasse für n>=2 nicht erreichbar: Gleichheit verlangt einen Zweipunkt-Mittelwert, während eine unabhängige nichtdegenerierte Summe mindestens drei Trägerpunkte besitzt. Bei perfekt gemeinsamen Gewinnen bleibt die Varianz des Mittelwerts 9.

problem: A device fails independently each period with probability0.2. Let T be the number of periods until the first failure. Compute the probability it lasts more than3 periods, its expected lifetime, and explain the memoryless property.
thinking:
Survival beyond3 requires three consecutive nonfailures, so P(T>3)=0.8³=64/125.

The geometric waiting time has mean1/p=5 periods when T counts the failure period. Its memoryless property follows from P(T>s+t|T>s)=0.8^t: surviving s periods does not change the chance of surviving t more.

This assumption is strong in economics and reliability: aging devices usually have duration-dependent hazards, while a constant independent failure probability imposes a flat hazard each period.

As a check, the survival probabilities form a geometric sequence with ratio0.8. Summing P(T>k) for k≥0 gives1/(1−0.8)=5, the same expected duration.

General pattern: A constant discrete hazard generates a geometric duration distribution. Its survival function decays geometrically, its expected duration is the reciprocal hazard, and memorylessness follows by cancellation of survival terms.
reference_answer: P(T>3)=64/125. Expected lifetime E[T]=5 periods.

problem: Je veux vérifier qu'il n'y a pas d'arbitrage dans ce marché à deux états. Un actif sans risque paie(1,1) et coûte10/11, donc son rendement brut est11/10. L'actif X paie(2,1) et coûte14/11; Y paie(1,3) et coûte2. Un nouvel actif Z paie(3,4) mais ne coûte que3. Trouve les prix d'état et probabilités risque-neutres implicites, puis construis un arbitrage si le prix de Z est incohérent.
thinking:
Je traite les prix comme des produits scalaires entre prix d'état et paiements contingents. Si qU et qD sont les prix aujourd'hui d'une unité versée dans chaque état, l'actif sans risque impose qU+qD=10/11. Les actifs X et Y donnent2qU+qD=14/11 et qU+3qD=2; la première équation avec l'actif sans risque donne qU=4/11 et qD=6/11, ce que Y confirme.

Les deux prix d'état sont positifs, donc ils définissent l'absence d'arbitrage pour les actifs répliqués. En les divisant par le prix de l'actif sans risque, j'obtiens les probabilités risque-neutres2/5 et3/5; elles somment à1. Le prix sans arbitrage de Z devrait être3(4/11)+4(6/11)=36/11, supérieur à son prix observé3.

La réplication donne le même diagnostic sans invoquer une formule d'espérance. Résoudre2a+b=3 et a+3b=4 donne une unité de X plus une unité de Y pour reproduire Z. J'achète donc Z et vends à découvert X et Y: le paiement futur net est(3,4)−(2,1)−(1,3)=(0,0), tandis que l'encaissement initial est14/11+2−3=3/11>0.

Comme contrôle, le portefeuille de réplication coûte14/11+2=36/11; son écart avec le prix coté de Z est exactement3/11. Les prix d'état positifs valorisent les flux répliqués, et le portefeuille explicite montre le profit immédiat sans risque. Si Z coûtait36/11, ce portefeuille n'aurait aucun surplus initial.

General pattern: Dans un marché complet à deux états, les prix d'état valorisent chaque flux contingent et leur positivité fournit le certificat de non-arbitrage. Un actif coté à un autre prix qu'un portefeuille réplicant crée un arbitrage; les probabilités risque-neutres sont les prix d'état normalisés par le prix du titre sans risque.
reference_answer: Les prix d'état sont qU=4/11 et qD=6/11; les probabilités risque-neutres sont2/5 et3/5. Le prix sans arbitrage de Z est36/11. Acheter Z et vendre X et Y procure3/11 aujourd'hui et un paiement futur nul dans les deux états.

problem: Je veux comparer deux indices de prix quand les quantités changent. Prix initiaux p0=(2,1), prix courants p1=(3,2), panier initial q0=(2,4) et panier courant q1=(3,3). Calculez les indices de Laspeyres, Paasche et Fisher, puis expliquez l'écart entre pondérations.
thinking:
Laspeyres garde le panier initial: p1·q0/p0·q0=(3·2+2·4)/(2·2+1·4)=14/8=7/4. Il mesure le coût actuel du panier de départ.

Paasche garde le panier courant: p1·q1/p0·q1=(3·3+2·3)/(2·3+1·3)=15/9=5/3. Il pèse davantage les biens achetés après substitution vers les prix relativement moins augmentés.

L'indice de Fisher est la moyenne géométrique des deux:√[(7/4)(5/3)]=√(35/12)=√105/6≈1,70783. Il se situe entre1,6667 et1,75; les pondérations symétriques atténuent l'effet de figer entièrement le panier à une seule période.

Comme contrôle, chaque indice égale le rapport de deux dépenses calculées avec le même panier au numérateur et au dénominateur. Laspeyres dépasse Paasche ici; cela est compatible avec une substitution vers le bien dont le prix relatif augmente moins, sans suffire à identifier les préférences à lui seul.

General pattern: Laspeyres fixe les quantités de base, Paasche fixe les quantités courantes, et Fisher combine leurs rapports par moyenne géométrique. La divergence signale que le panier choisi modifie la mesure de l'évolution du coût de la vie.
