problem: Un test médical a une sensibilité de90% et une spécificité de95%. La maladie touche1% de la population. Après un résultat positif, quelle est la probabilité d'être malade ? Expliquez pourquoi elle n'est pas proche de90%.
thinking:
Je calcule les probabilités conjointes avant de conditionner. Malade et positif vaut0,01·0,90=0,009; sain et positif vaut0,99·0,05=0,0495.

Bayes donne P(malade|positif)=0,009/(0,009+0,0495)=2/13, soit environ6,92%. Les faux positifs sont plus nombreux que les vrais positifs parce que la population saine est très large.

La sensibilité de90% est P(positif|malade), pas P(malade|positif). Inverser ces conditionnelles ignore le taux de base et confond la performance parmi les malades avec la composition des résultats positifs.

Comme contrôle, sur10 000 personnes,100 sont malades et90 testent positives; parmi9 900 personnes saines,495 testent faussement positives. Donc90/(90+495)=2/13.

General pattern: La valeur prédictive d'un test dépend du taux de base autant que de sa sensibilité et de sa spécificité. Calculer les masses conjointes empêche d'inverser les conditionnelles.
reference_answer: P(malade sachant positif)=2/13≈6,92%.

problem: Comment comparer deux loteries quand l'une a une meilleure moyenne mais que leurs distributions se croisent? A paie0 ou10 avec probabilité1/2 chacun; B paie4 ou8 avec probabilité1/2 chacun. Compare leurs espérances, détermine si B domine A au premier ou au second ordre, et justifie le critère intégral qui permet de conclure pour tout décideur croissant et averse au risque.
thinking:
Je commence par les fonctions de répartition. A a une masse en0 puis une en10; B a ses masses en4 et8. Les moyennes sont5 pour A et6 pour B. B ne domine pas A au premier ordre: entre0 et4, la fonction de répartition de A vaut1/2 tandis que celle de B vaut0; entre8 et10, c'est l'inverse.

Pour l'ordre deux, j'intègre la différence FB−FA depuis moins l'infini. Elle vaut0 jusqu'à0, descend linéairement à−2 entre0 et4, reste−2 jusqu'à8, puis remonte linéairement à−1 entre8 et10. Au-delà de10, les deux répartitions sont égales et l'intégrale reste−1. Elle ne devient jamais positive, donc B domine A au second ordre.

Ce critère relie directement la distribution à l'utilité. Pour toute utilité croissante et concave, l'intégrale cumulative de FB−FA non positive implique E[u(B)]≥E[u(A)]. Le croisement interdit la conclusion pour tous les décideurs croissants, mais l'ordre deux suffit lorsque l'aversion au risque ajoute la concavité.

Comme contrôle, l'intégrale finale vaut E[A]−E[B]=5−6=−1, ce qui correspond au segment constant après le plus grand paiement. La courbe intégrée est non positive à chaque point de rupture; entre ces points elle est linéaire ou constante, donc elle ne peut cacher un dépassement positif. La moyenne et le critère intégral racontent ainsi la même comparaison sous deux formes.

General pattern: La dominance du premier ordre compare les fonctions de répartition point par point; la dominance du second ordre compare leurs intégrales cumulées. Lorsque les CDF se croisent, une moyenne supérieure ne suffit pas, mais une aire cumulative partout favorable garantit un choix pour toute préférence croissante et averse au risque.
reference_answer: E[A]=5 et E[B]=6. Les CDF se croisent, donc B ne domine pas A au premier ordre. L'intégrale de FB−FA vaut0 avant0,−2 à4,−2 à8 et−1 à10; elle reste non positive et constante ensuite. B domine donc A au second ordre et est préféré par tout décideur croissant et averse au risque.

problem:
Kannst du meine Unsicherheitsrechnung überprüfen? Ich habe n zeitlich aufeinanderfolgende Einkommensmessungen gemittelt und die Varianz durch n geteilt. Die einzelnen Messungen haben zwar dieselbe Varianz, sind aber stark abhängig. Hilft eine längere Reihe immer?

Y_i=mu+e_i für i=1,...,n, mit n>=2. Der Fehlervektor ist gemeinsam normalverteilt, hat Mittelwert0 und bekannte Kovarianz Cov(e_i,e_j)=sigma2*alpha^abs(i-j), wobei sigma2>0 und-1<alpha<1. sigma2 ist die feste marginale Varianz, nicht die Innovationsvarianz. Betrachte lineare unverzerrte Schätzer sum_i w_i*Y_i mit sum_i w_i=1.

Leite die Varianz des einfachen Mittels her, ohne die Kovarianzen zu streichen. Finde alle Gewichte des eindeutigen varianzminimalen linearen unverzerrten Schätzers und seine Varianz für jedes n. Nutze die tridiagonale Inverse der Korrelationsmatrix und verifiziere ihre Struktur. Beweise globale Minimalität durch eine unabhängige orthogonale Varianzzerlegung.

Für n=4,alpha=1/2, gib die optimalen Gewichte, die Varianzen des optimalen und einfachen Mittels, ihre Differenz und die falsche Unabhängigkeitsrechnung. Vergleiche bei festem alpha die asymptotische Präzision der beiden Mittel. Was passiert für alpha gegen1 bei festem n?

Untersuche außerdem eine andere Folge von Modellen: alpha_n=1-delta/n mit festem delta>0 und n>delta, weiterhin mit derselben marginalen Varianz sigma2. Berechne die Grenzvarianz des optimalen Schätzers und entscheide, ob er konsistent für mu ist. Für delta=2 berechne auch die Grenzvarianz des einfachen Mittels über ein Doppelintegral und ihre Differenz zur optimalen. Setze r=exp(-2), eine deklarierte Konstante, um dieses Ergebnis anzugeben. Verwechsle die feste-alpha-Grenze nicht mit der zunehmenden Persistenz.
thinking:
Vor der Mittelbildung sollte ich die vollständige Kovarianz zählen. Beim Abstand k gibt es n-k Paare und jede Kovarianz tritt zweimal auf. Daher Var(Mittel)=sigma2*[n+2*sum_{k=1}^{n-1}(n-k)*alpha^k]/n^2. Die Formel sigma2/n gilt nur bei alpha=0; gleiche marginale Varianzen erzeugen keine Unabhängigkeit. Negative alpha kann die Varianz verkleinern, positive alpha vergrößert sie.

Für die Matrixstruktur schreibe ich Gamma=sigma2*C mit C_ij=alpha^abs(i-j). C^(-1) ist1/(1-alpha^2) mal eine tridiagonale Matrix mit Enddiagonalen1, inneren Diagonalen1+alpha^2 und Nachbardiagonalen-alpha. Bei einem inneren Produkt mit C löschen sich die drei geometrischen Terme außerhalb der Diagonale; auf der Diagonale bleibt1-alpha^2. An den Enden löschen sich zwei Terme. Damit ist die behauptete Inverse überprüfbar, ohne eine große dichte Matrix symbolisch zu invertieren.

Für die optimalen Gewichte erinnere ich mich an die GLS-Normalisierung: w=C^(-1)*1/[1'*C^(-1)*1]. Die Endzeilensummen der Inversen sind1/(1+alpha), die inneren(1-alpha)/(1+alpha). Mit D=2+(n-2)*(1-alpha)=n*(1-alpha)+2*alpha erhalten die beiden Endmessungen Gewicht1/D und jede innere Gewicht(1-alpha)/D. Die Summe ist1, und Var(GLS)=sigma2*(1+alpha)/D. Bei n=2 gibt es keine inneren Messungen; die Formel liefert beide Gewichte1/2.

Für einen unabhängigen Optimalitätsbeweis nehme ich beliebige unverzerrte Gewichte w+h, also1'*h=0. Der GLS-Vektor erfüllt Gamma*w=Var(GLS)*1. Folglich Var((w+h)'Y)=Var(w'Y)+h'*Gamma*h, weil der Kreuzterm2*h'*Gamma*w verschwindet. Gamma ist für|alpha|<1 positiv definit, deshalb ist der Zusatz strikt positiv für h!=0. Das beweist globale Minimalität und Eindeutigkeit, nicht nur eine notwendige Ableitungsbedingung.

Für die Zahlen n=4,alpha=1/2 ist D=3. Die Gewichte sind(1/3,1/6,1/6,1/3) und die optimale Varianz sigma2/2. Die einfache Mittelvarianz ist sigma2*[4+2*(3/2+1/2+1/8)]/16=33*sigma2/64. Der Überschuss beträgt sigma2/64. Die naive Rechnung sigma2/4 unterschätzt bereits die optimale Varianz um die Hälfte. Endmessungen bekommen mehr Gewicht, weil innere Messungen von zwei benachbarten Seiten redundante Information enthalten.

Für festes alpha und n gegen unendlich ist n*Var(GLS) gegen sigma2*(1+alpha)/(1-alpha). Dieselbe Grenze ergibt sich beim einfachen Mittel aus der konvergenten geometrischen Kovarianzsumme:2*sum_{k>=1}alpha^k=2*alpha/(1-alpha); die Randkorrektur verschwindet nach Division durch n. Beide Schätzer sind dann konsistent und asymptotisch gleich präzise, auch wenn GLS bei endlichem n besser ist. Dieser Grenzübergang hält alpha wirklich fest.

Für alpha gegen1 bei festem n ist D gegen2 und Var(GLS) gegen sigma2. Die Gewichte gehen gegen1/2 an jedem Ende und0 im Inneren. Auch das einfache Mittel hat Grenzvarianz sigma2, weil alle Kovarianzen gegen dieselbe marginale Varianz gehen. Bei alpha=1 wäre die Matrix singulär; die Grenzgewichte sind keine Behauptung eines eindeutigen GLS-Schätzers an dieser ausgeschlossenen Grenze.

Für zunehmende Persistenz alpha_n=1-delta/n gilt D=delta+2-2*delta/n, also Var(GLS) gegen2*sigma2/(delta+2)>0. Der Fehler bleibt normalverteilt mit einer positiven Grenzvarianz, sodass für jeden festen kleinen Abstand die Überschreitungswahrscheinlichkeit nicht gegen0 geht. Der Schätzer ist daher nicht konsistent. Eine Reihe mit immer stärkerer Abhängigkeit liefert nicht dieselbe wachsende unabhängige Information wie die feste-alpha-Folge.

Für die einfache Mittelvarianz bei delta=2 nutze ich eine Riemannsumme: alpha_n^abs(i-j) geht bei skalierten Zeitabständen zu exp(-2*abs(t-u)). Die Grenzvarianz ist sigma2*Integral_0^1 Integral_0^1 exp(-2*abs(t-u)) dt du=2*sigma2*Integral_0^1(1-z)*exp(-2*z) dz=sigma2*(1+r)/2. Die GLS-Grenze ist sigma2/2, also bleibt eine positive Differenz sigma2*r/2. Die Randgewichte besitzen hier nicht verschwindende Masse; die feste-alpha-Aussage asymptotisch gleicher Präzision gilt deshalb nicht.

General pattern: ich bestimme Information aus der gesamten Kovarianzstruktur, nicht aus der Zahl der Zeilen. Eine tridiagonale Inverse entdeckt die optimalen Randgewichte, und orthogonale Varianzzerlegung prüft sie global. Grenzaussagen brauchen eine festgelegte Modellfolge: feste Korrelation und gegen1 steigende Persistenz können entgegengesetzte Konsistenzresultate liefern.
reference_answer:
Setze D=n*(1-alpha)+2*alpha. GLS gibt jeder Endmessung Gewicht1/D und jeder inneren(1-alpha)/D; seine Varianz ist sigma2*(1+alpha)/D. Jede andere unverzerrte Gewichtung fügt den strikt positiven Term h'*Gamma*h hinzu.

Für n=4,alpha=1/2 sind die Gewichte(1/3,1/6,1/6,1/3), Var(GLS)=sigma2/2 und Var(Mittel)=33*sigma2/64, mit Differenz sigma2/64. Die falsche Unabhängigkeitsrechnung liefert sigma2/4.

Bei festem alpha haben beide asymptotisch Varianz sigma2*(1+alpha)/[n*(1-alpha)] und sind konsistent. Bei alpha gegen1 und festem n gehen ihre Varianzen gegen sigma2.

Für alpha_n=1-delta/n hat GLS positive Grenzvarianz2*sigma2/(delta+2) und ist nicht konsistent. Bei delta=2 hat das einfache Mittel Grenzvarianz sigma2*(1+r)/2, GLS sigma2/2; der verbleibende Unterschied ist sigma2*r/2.

problem: A consumer chooses x and y with utility U=xy, prices px=2 and py=1, and income100. Find the demands and show how expenditure shares follow from homogeneity.
thinking:
Before solving derivatives, degree-two utility makes the marginal conditions transparent: MUx/MUy=y/x=px/py=2, so y=2x. The budget2x+y=100 gives x=25,y=50.

Each good receives half the budget: expenditure on x is50 and on y is50. The first-order conditions verify equal expenditure shares for this symmetric Cobb-Douglas representation.

Utility is strictly quasi-concave on positive bundles, so the tangency plus budget identifies the unique optimum. Scaling income scales both demands proportionally while leaving expenditure shares unchanged.

General pattern: homogeneous Cobb-Douglas preferences imply constant budget shares. Use the marginal-rate-of-substitution condition for the quantity ratio, then the budget for scale.
reference_answer: x*=25 and y*=50; each good receives half of income.

problem: Não percebo por que um projeto que cria riqueza pode tornar inviável a divisão igual. Duas pessoas podem conservar os capitais(C1,C2) ou investi-los num projeto com produção certa Y. A produção substitui os capitais investidos, não é somada novamente a eles. As receitas finais R1,R2 são não negativas, com R1+R2<=Y; permitimos descartar produção. Cada pessoa tem utilidade sqrt(Ri), e só participa se não ficar pior do que conservando o seu capital. Uma melhoria de Pareto exige ainda que pelo menos uma fique estritamente melhor. Para Y=250, analisa primeiro(C1,C2)=(100,50) e depois(150,50). Calcula a riqueza criada, toda a região de participação, a sua fronteira eficiente, e o máximo da soma das utilidades com e sem participação obrigatória. Generaliza a C1>=C2>0 e a qualquer Y>=0: identifica quando o projeto admite uma melhoria de Pareto e quando a divisão igual é implementável. Prova os resultados sem testar repartições sucessivas.
thinking:
Antes de repartir, devo evitar contar o capital duas vezes. A riqueza nova é Y-(C1+C2), porque investir substitui a opção de conservar os capitais. Para a produção250, os ganhos agregados são100 no caso(100,50) e50 no caso(150,50). Um ganho agregado positivo mostra que alguma compensação é possível, mas não prova que qualquer divisão escolhida respeite a participação.

Para a participação, a raiz quadrada é estritamente crescente: sqrt(Ri)>=sqrt(Ci) equivale a Ri>=Ci. Logo a região admissível é R1>=C1,R2>=C2,R1+R2<=Y. Existe se e só se Y>=C1+C2. Quando Y é maior, forma um triângulo com vértices(C1,C2),(Y-C2,C2),(C1,Y-C1). A melhoria estrita de Pareto exclui apenas o ponto inicial(C1,C2) dessa região. Se Y=C1+C2, só resta esse ponto e ninguém melhora estritamente.

Para eficiência, devo distinguir participação de utilização completa da produção. Se R1+R2<Y, posso aumentar uma receita sem reduzir a outra; a alocação não é eficiente. Se R1+R2=Y, aumentar uma receita obriga a reduzir a outra, e ambas as utilidades são crescentes. Assim a fronteira eficiente dentro da região de participação é R2=Y-R1, com R1 em[C1,Y-C2]. Não preciso procurar alocações uma a uma para provar esta fronteira.

Para Bentham sem participação, a desigualdade de Cauchy dá sqrt(R1)+sqrt(R2)<=sqrt(2*(R1+R2))<=sqrt(2*Y). A igualdade exige usar toda a produção e R1=R2=Y/2. Com Y=250, o máximo é a divisão(125,125), de utilidade total sqrt(500)=10*sqrt(5), nos dois casos. No caso inicial(150,50), porém,125<150: o primeiro indivíduo recusa. Um máximo social sem restrições pode estar fora do conjunto de contratos voluntários.

Para o máximo com participação, reduzo o problema à receita r=R1 no intervalo[C1,Y-C2]. A função F(r)=sqrt(r)+sqrt(Y-r) tem derivada1/[2*sqrt(r)]-1/[2*sqrt(Y-r)], positiva antes de Y/2 e negativa depois. Por estrita concavidade, o ótimo é a projeção de Y/2 no intervalo admissível. Como C1>=C2 e Y>=C1+C2, o limite superior Y-C2 nunca fica abaixo de Y/2. Portanto R1*=max(C1,Y/2),R2*=Y-R1*. A participação do indivíduo inicialmente mais rico é a única restrição que pode impedir a igualdade.

No caso(100,50), a região é R1>=100,R2>=50,R1+R2<=250, com vértices(100,50),(200,50),(100,150). A fronteira eficiente vai de(100,150) a(200,50). Como125 pertence a[100,200], o máximo voluntário é(125,125), que melhora ambos. No caso(150,50), os vértices são(150,50),(200,50),(150,100), e a fronteira vai de(150,100) a(200,50). A projeção dá(150,100), de utilidade total5*sqrt(6)+10; o primeiro fica indiferente e o segundo melhora.

Para os limiares gerais, uma melhoria de Pareto existe exatamente quando Y>C1+C2. A igualdade voluntária exige Y/2>=C1 e Y/2>=C2, equivalente a Y>=2*C1 sob a ordem assumida. No intervalo C1+C2<=Y<2*C1, o máximo condicionado é(C1,Y-C1); para Y>=2*C1 é(Y/2,Y/2). Em Y=C1+C2, o projeto não melhora ninguém; em Y=2*C1, as duas fórmulas coincidem. No exemplo, os limiares de igualdade são200 e300, embora a produção seja250 em ambos.

Para um controlo independente, as alocações ótimas usam exatamente250 e respeitam as duas reservas. Os ganhos de receitas são(25,75) no primeiro caso e(0,50) no segundo, somando as riquezas novas100 e50. Além disso, a utilidade marginal do primeiro no ponto(150,100) é1/[2*sqrt(150)], menor que1/[2*sqrt(100)]. Transferir receita do primeiro para o segundo aumentaria a soma das utilidades, mas violaria a participação do primeiro; transferir no sentido permitido diminuiria essa soma. Isto confirma o máximo de fronteira sem reutilizar a desigualdade de Cauchy.

General pattern: devo separar riqueza criada, participação e igualdade. A monotonia transforma reservas de utilidade em limites de receitas; uma desigualdade de concavidade identifica o máximo livre. Projetar esse máximo no intervalo viável dá o contrato voluntário e os limiares, sem enumerar repartições.
reference_answer:
Com capitais(100,50), o projeto cria100. A região de participação é R1>=100,R2>=50,R1+R2<=250; a fronteira eficiente é R1+R2=250 com R1 em[100,200]. O máximo livre e o voluntário são(125,125), com utilidade total10*sqrt(5).

Com capitais(150,50), cria50. A região exige R1>=150,R2>=50; a fronteira tem R1 em[150,200]. O máximo livre(125,125) é recusado; o voluntário é(150,100), com utilidade total5*sqrt(6)+10.

Em geral, há melhoria de Pareto se e só se Y>C1+C2. Para Y>=C1+C2, o máximo voluntário é(max(C1,Y/2),Y-max(C1,Y/2)). A igualdade é implementável se e só se Y>=2*C1. A prova usa monotonia, utilização completa da produção e projeção do máximo estritamente côncavo.

problem:
Help me understand the difference between an action and a strategy. Each player can choose0 or1, but someone gave each player four pure strategies such as "choose the opposite of the other player's action". Can I really use that rule when I cannot see the action?

Player1 receives payoff1 when the two actions match and-1 when they differ. Player2 receives the negative of that payoff. All payoffs and rules are common knowledge. Compare three games: simultaneous choices; player1 chooses first and player2 observes the choice; player1 chooses first but player2 does not observe it, with its two possible decision nodes in a single information set. Randomizations in the simultaneous and unobserved games are private and independent; there is no mediator or common random signal.

Give the number of pure strategies for each player in each game, without listing all strategy combinations. Derive all equilibrium results: Nash for simultaneous and unobserved play, subgame-perfect for observed play. For mixing probabilities r=P(a1=1),s=P(a2=1), derive the unobserved expected payoff and prove the equilibrium analytically. Explain which games have complete information and which have perfect information under their extensive-form representation. Finally distinguish an observed response map from an infeasible rule conditioning on unseen actions, and say why reversing the sequential order while revealing the first action transfers the advantage to the new second mover.
thinking:
Before counting strategies, I should count information sets rather than terminal nodes. In simultaneous play each player makes one binary choice, so each has2 pure strategies. In observed sequential play, player1 still has2, while player2 has two separate information sets and must specify a binary response at each:2^2=4 pure strategies. In unobserved sequential play those two decision nodes are one information set, so player2 must use the same action rule at both and again has only2 pure strategies. A contingent response needs observable histories.

For the unobserved game, a pure player2 strategy cannot choose0 after one hidden action and1 after the other. The player only has one information set, and an admissible mixed rule uses the same probability s at both nodes. With private independent mixing, matching has probability r*s+(1-r)*(1-s). Player1's expected payoff is2 times that probability minus1=(2*r-1)*(2*s-1). The simultaneous game has the same strategic payoff expression despite a different physical timing description.

To solve without checking many profiles, I use the affine best responses. If s>1/2, player1 maximizes payoff at r=1; if s<1/2, at r=0. If r>1/2, player2 minimizes player1's payoff at s=0; if r<1/2, at s=1. These strict responses cannot be mutually consistent away from the midpoint. At r=s=1/2 both are indifferent, and neither unilateral deviation changes the zero expected payoff. Thus the unique mixed equilibrium in both games is independent fair randomization, with no pure equilibrium.

For an independent minimax check, the worst payoff against a fixed r is -abs(2*r-1), obtained by choosing an endpoint s with the opposite sign. Its maximum is0, attained only at r=1/2. Symmetrically, player2 can cap the value at0 only with s=1/2. This confirms both equilibrium mixing probabilities and the zero value by a different route from reciprocal best responses.

For observed sequential play, player2 knows the actual a1 and chooses a2=1-a1, giving itself1 instead of-1. This response is uniquely optimal at both decision nodes, including whichever node the initial strategy does not reach. Player1 then receives-1 after either action, so any initial randomization r in[0,1] is optimal. All subgame-perfect outcomes therefore give payoffs(-1,1), with player2's same uniquely optimal contingent map and arbitrary player1 mixing. A Nash analysis checking only the reached node could retain a noncredible off-path response, so I need the subgame-perfect condition.

For the information distinction, every game has complete information because payoff functions and rules are known; no unknown type changes payoffs. Only the observed sequential game has perfect information: each decision information set is a singleton and past actions are known. The unobserved sequential game has imperfect information, and the standard extensive-form representation of simultaneous choice also hides the first modeled action from the second chooser. Knowledge of payoffs does not reveal an opponent's current action.

For the tempting rule, choosing the opposite is implementable by player2 only in the observed game. In the other two games it is not an admissible unilateral strategy, because it gives different choices at histories the player cannot distinguish. Player1 also cannot condition its first move on a later observed move that has not happened. A pure strategy is a complete feasible action plan over the player's information sets, not an arbitrary mapping from another person's realized action.

For the order reversal, if player2 moves first and player1 observes, the new second mover chooses to match. Player1 then gets1 and player2 gets-1, regardless of the initial action. The second-mover information changes the game value from0 to its own favorable extreme. Mere sequential timing without revelation leaves value0, so timing and observability are separate primitives that must be stated before defining strategy sets.

General pattern: I define strategies on information sets before calculating equilibrium. Unseen histories impose identical behavior, while visible histories allow contingent responses. Bilinear mixing payoffs and minimax bounds avoid profile enumeration; backward induction then exposes how observation, rather than the word sequential alone, changes strategic advantage.
reference_answer:
Pure-strategy counts are(2,2) for simultaneous play,(2,4) for observed sequential play, and(2,2) for unobserved sequential play. A response cannot differ across nodes in one information set.

The simultaneous and unobserved expected payoff is(2*r-1)*(2*s-1). Their unique equilibrium has r=s=1/2 and payoffs(0,0). In observed play, player2 uniquely chooses1-a1 at each node; any player1 mixing is optimal and every subgame-perfect outcome gives(-1,1).

All three games have complete information. Only observed sequential play has perfect information. Reversing the observed order lets player1 match, yielding(1,-1). A rule depending on unseen or future actions is not an admissible strategy.

problem: Explain why the square root of x squared is absolute value of x, not always x; answer with a counterexample.
thinking: The principal square root is nonnegative; a negative input demonstrates the sign issue.
reference_answer: Because a square root is nonnegative, √((-3)²)=√9=3, whereas −3 is not 3; therefore √(x²)=|x|.

problem:
Je pensais que décaler un impôt ne changeait rien si sa valeur actualisée était identique. Est-ce encore vrai quand le ménage ne peut pas emprunter autant qu'il veut ? Peux-tu montrer exactement quand cette neutralité revient ?

Il y a deux dates0 et1. Un ménage a revenus exogènes(1,4) et utilité U=c0*c1, avec c0,c1>0. Il peut épargner s, ou emprunter si s<0, au facteur d'intérêt brut2. Sa limite d'emprunt est s>=-b, où b>=0. Ses budgets sont c0=1-T0-s et c1=4-T1+2*s. Le marché de capitaux extérieur est parfaitement élastique au facteur2; il n'y a ni incertitude ni autres frais. Les impôts sont forfaitaires et connus à la date0.

Le gouvernement finance une dépense identique1/2 à la date0. Dans le régime E, il prélève(T0,T1)=(1/2,0). Dans le régime D, il emprunte1/2 sur ce marché à la date0 et prélève(0,1) à la date1 pour rembourser. Le bénéfice éventuel de la dépense publique est identique et omis de U. Le gouvernement a accès au crédit indépendamment de la limite privée b.

Compare les valeurs actualisées des impôts et établis la contrainte de ressources intertemporelle commune. Trouve l'allocation optimale avec emprunt privé illimité et l'emprunt requis dans chacun des régimes. Avec b fini, trouve toutes les allocations et utilités optimales pour chaque régime ainsi que les seuils où la limite cesse de lier. Donne des expressions exactes de U_D-U_E dans tous les intervalles de b, et justifie le classement par un carré.

Au cas b=0, donne les consommations, utilités, épargne et recettes gouvernementales. À partir de quel b les allocations et utilités des deux régimes deviennent-elles identiques, et les emprunts privés deviennent-ils alors identiques ? Explique le rôle des contraintes de financement plutôt que d'attribuer l'écart à une variation de ressources publiques ou au taux d'intérêt.
thinking:
Avant de comparer les dates, je vérifie les deux budgets publics. E collecte1/2 immédiatement. D emprunte1/2 puis rembourse1 à la date1; sa recette1 a valeur actualisée1/2 au facteur2. La dépense et le taux d'intérêt sont les mêmes. En éliminant l'épargne des budgets privés,2*c0+c1=2*(1-T0)+4-T1=5 dans les deux régimes. La richesse après impôt est donc identique en valeur actualisée.

Pour l'optimum sans limite privée, je remplace c1 par5-2*c0. L'utilité vaut5*c0-2*c0^2=25/8-2*(c0-5/4)^2. Le maximum unique est(c0,c1)=(5/4,5/2), de valeur25/8. Mais l'épargne nécessaire dépend du calendrier: s_E=1/2-5/4=-3/4, tandis que s_D=1-5/4=-1/4. Une même allocation réelle n'implique pas les mêmes transactions financières avant impôt.

Pour la contrainte de crédit, dans E le budget de date0 donne c0<=1/2+b; dans D il donne c0<=1+b. Les deux problèmes partagent la même parabole, croissante jusqu'à5/4 et décroissante ensuite. Ainsi c0_E=min(5/4,1/2+b) et c0_D=min(5/4,1+b), avec c1=5-2*c0. Le maximum est global, les consommations restent positives, et aucune recherche parmi des montants d'emprunt n'est nécessaire.

Pour les branches actives, E donne(c0,c1)=(1/2+b,4-2*b),s=-b et U_E=2+3*b-2*b^2 jusqu'à b=3/4. Au-delà, il atteint le premier optimum et s=-3/4. D donne(1+b,3-2*b),s=-b et U_D=3+b-2*b^2 jusqu'à b=1/4; au-delà, il atteint le même optimum et s=-1/4. Les formules se rejoignent à chaque seuil. À un seuil, la borne est atteinte mais n'entraîne plus de perte d'utilité.

Pour le classement exact, si0<=b<=1/4, la différence est U_D-U_E=1-2*b>0. Si1/4<=b<=3/4, D atteint25/8 tandis que E reste contraint; la différence est25/8-(2+3*b-2*b^2)=2*(b-3/4)^2. Elle est positive avant3/4 et nulle au seuil. Si b>=3/4, les deux utilités sont25/8. Les valeurs de différence coïncident en b=1/4: elles valent1/2. C'est une preuve globale par distance au sommet, pas une comparaison des taux moyens de taxe.

Pour le cas sans emprunt, b=0 force s=0 dans les deux régimes. E donne(1/2,4),U=2 et recettes publiques(1/2,0). D donne(1,3),U=3 et recettes(0,1), plus la dette publique1/2 initiale remboursée à1. Le ménage reporte la même charge actualisée mais peut conserver davantage de consommation à la date0, où son arbitrage était bloqué. La variation n'est pas une création de richesse:2*(1/2)+4=2*1+3=5.

Pour une vérification de la perte, le sommet commun donne25/8-U_E=2*(3/4-b)^2 sur sa branche contrainte et25/8-U_D=2*(1/4-b)^2 sur la sienne. Leur différence reproduit1-2*b quand les deux sont contraints. Cette seconde route montre pourquoi D approche plus tôt l'allocation optimale: son plafond de consommation présente est plus proche du sommet, et non parce que son revenu actualisé est supérieur.

Pour le retour à la neutralité, b>=3/4 permet les deux emprunts requis; les allocations et utilités deviennent identiques. Les emprunts restent différents,3/4 contre1/4, car l'emprunt privé préfinance l'impôt immédiat dans E tandis que la dette publique le fait dans D. La valeur actualisée commune est nécessaire à la neutralité dans ce modèle, mais sa traduction en choix suppose aussi que le ménage puisse accéder aux mêmes allocations intertemporelles.

General pattern: j'élimine d'abord les flux financiers pour comparer les ressources, puis je garde les plafonds de financement qui survivent à cette élimination. Un changement de date fiscale peut remplacer un crédit privé inaccessible. Le carré de l'utilité sur la ressource commune donne les seuils de neutralité et les écarts de bien-être sans confondre allocations réelles et emprunts.
reference_answer:
Les deux impôts valent1/2 à la date0 et donnent la même ressource2*c0+c1=5. L'optimum libre est(5/4,5/2),U=25/8, mais exige s_E=-3/4 et s_D=-1/4.

Avec limite b, c0_E=min(5/4,1/2+b) et c0_D=min(5/4,1+b), puis c1=5-2*c0. E devient libre à b=3/4 et D à b=1/4. La différence U_D-U_E est1-2*b sur[0,1/4],2*(b-3/4)^2 sur[1/4,3/4], puis0. La parabole U=25/8-2*(c0-5/4)^2 prouve ces résultats.

À b=0, E donne(1/2,4),U=2 et D(1,3),U=3; dans les deux cas s=0. Dès b=3/4 les allocations coïncident, mais les emprunts privés restent3/4 et1/4. Le calendrier modifie l'accès à la consommation présente sous contrainte de crédit, pas la richesse actualisée.

problem: The sequence F_0=0,F_1=1,F_(n+2)=F_(n+1)+F_n is familiar, but can you derive its generating function and use it to get F_8 without listing all terms?
thinking:
Before solving a recurrence term by term, I encode the whole sequence in F(x)=Σ F_n x^n. Shifting indices gives F(x)−x=x(F(x)) + x²F(x), because the recurrence starts at n=0. Rearranging yields F(x)=x/(1−x−x²). The denominator records the recurrence; the numerator records initial conditions.

To extract F_8 without enumerating earlier terms, factor the denominator as (1−φx)(1−ψx), where φ=(1+√5)/2 and ψ=(1−√5)/2. Partial fractions give F_n=(φ^n−ψ^n)/√5. At n=8 this is21; the radical expression is integral because the conjugate terms cancel irrational parts.

A cheaper exact check uses the recurrence's companion matrix [[1,1],[1,0]]: its eighth power applied to (F_1,F_0) yields (F_9,F_8)=(34,21). This verifies the index convention and catches the common off-by-one error.

General pattern: generating functions turn shifts into multiplication, so a recurrence becomes a rational function. Factor its denominator to expose modes, then use a matrix or recurrence identity as an index check.

problem:
Help me interpret this difference-in-differences estimate. Treated and comparison areas have outcome means 10 and 8 before a policy, then 15 and 10 afterward. What is the estimated effect, and how much failure of parallel trends would it take to reverse its sign?

Treat the four means as exact. Define the conventional difference-in-differences contrast. Then let delta be the amount by which the treated area's untreated change would exceed the comparison area's change. Derive the treatment effect as a function of delta and find the exact range of delta for which the effect is positive. Explain why the observed four means alone do not identify delta, and why a zero pre-period placebo contrast would not prove parallel trends.
thinking:
Before interpreting a before-after change as causal, I remove the common comparison-area movement. The treated change is15-10=5 and the comparison change is10-8=2, so their difference is3. The DiD contrast cancels any additive shock shared by the two areas; it does not cancel a treated-specific change in the untreated counterfactual trend.

I make that missing identifying restriction explicit. If delta is the treated-minus-comparison difference in untreated trends, the observed contrast decomposes as estimated effect plus delta. Therefore the causal effect is3-delta. It is positive exactly when delta<3, zero at3, and negative above3. The sign conclusion is robust to every trend violation smaller than three outcome units in the positive direction, but the four post-policy means do not bound that violation.

The trick is a sensitivity threshold rather than pretending the assumption is testable from this table. Parallel trends sets delta=0 and yields effect3. A zero pre-period placebo contrast checks one historical contrast, but untreated trends after the policy can diverge even when they matched before it. Thus the placebo is diagnostic evidence, not identification by itself.

For an independent check, I write the contrast as (15-10)-(10-8)=15-10-10+8=3. Adding a common post-versus-pre shock to both groups changes each group difference equally and leaves3 unchanged. Adding a treated-specific untreated trend gap delta changes the contrast by delta, recovering effect plus delta and confirming the sign threshold.

General pattern: Difference-in-differences identifies a treatment effect only after a counterfactual trend restriction. Expressing violations as a sensitivity parameter separates the observed contrast from the unobserved assumption and yields an exact robustness threshold without inventing information from the four cell means.
reference_answer: The conventional DiD contrast is (15-10)-(10-8)=3. If delta is the treated-minus-comparison gap in untreated trends, then the treatment effect is3-delta. It is positive for delta<3, zero at3, and negative for delta>3. The observed means identify the contrast but do not identify delta. A zero pre-period placebo is informative but does not prove post-period parallel trends.

problem: 公平なコインを4回投げます。隣り合う結果が異なる箇所の期待個数を、全系列を列挙せずに求めてください。
thinking:
数える量を、各隣接位置で結果が変わるかどうかの指示変数の和として書く。隣接ペアは3つあり、それぞれで異なる確率は1/2なので、期待個数は3/2である。期待値の線形性だけで足せるため、隣の指示変数どうしの独立性は要らない。

確認として、各隣接ペアの一致と不一致は対称で確率1/2ずつである。系列全体の依存関係は分散には影響するが、期待値の和には影響しない。

General pattern: 局所的な変化の総数を指示変数に分解する。各局所確率を足せば期待値が出て、全系列の列挙や指示変数間の独立性は不要である。
reference_answer: 期待される変化箇所数は3/2である。

problem: How can I identify hidden consumer types without searching over many possible mixtures? Each consumer has an unobserved purchase probability P taking exactly two distinct values in(0,1), both with positive population weights. Conditional on P, three purchase decisions are independent Bernoulli(P). We observe only K, the number of purchases, with population probabilities P(K=0)=P(K=3)=7/32 and P(K=1)=P(K=2)=9/32. Identify the two probabilities and their weights up to relabelling. Explain why one or two repeated decisions cannot identify this two-type model in general. Calculate Var(K), compare with a homogeneous Bernoulli model having the same mean, and predict a fourth purchase after observing three purchases. The fourth decision is independent of the earlier ones conditional on the same P.
thinking:
Before fitting a mixture, I should extract moments that remove the binomial sampling layer. Define mj=E[P^j]. Conditional factorial moments give E[K]=3*m1, E[K*(K-1)]=6*m2 and E[K*(K-1)*(K-2)]=6*m3. The observed distribution gives E[K]=3/2, the second factorial moment15/8 and the third21/16. Hence m1=1/2,m2=5/16,m3=7/32. The latent variance m2-m1^2 is1/16>0, so the two types are genuinely different.

A cheaper identification route uses the annihilating polynomial of the two support points. If they are u and v, put S=u+v and B=u*v. Every support point satisfies P^2-S*P+B=0. Taking expectation gives m2-S*m1+B=0; multiplying by P and taking expectation gives m3-S*m2+B*m1=0. Eliminating B yields S=(m3-m1*m2)/(m2-m1^2). The nonzero latent variance is precisely the denominator needed for identification.

For these moments, S=(7/32-5/32)/(1/16)=1 and B=S*m1-m2=3/16. Thus the support points solve z^2-z+3/16=0, giving u=1/4 and v=3/4. From m1=w*u+(1-w)*v=1/2 I obtain w=1/2. Both weights and support points satisfy the stated restrictions. This gives the unique unordered two-point distribution; relabelling types changes no observable quantity.

For a full-distribution check, K=0 has probability[(3/4)^3+(1/4)^3]/2=7/32, and K=3 has the same probability. K=1 has probability(3/2)*[(1/4)*(3/4)^2+(3/4)*(1/4)^2]=9/32, and K=2 also9/32. Matching all four cells confirms the recovered model, rather than checking only its mean.

To show why fewer repetitions fail, one decision identifies only m1. Two decisions identify only m1,m2. Here another admissible two-type distribution puts probability9/25 on P=1/6 and16/25 on P=11/16. Its mean is1/2 and its second moment5/16, but its third moment is161/768 rather than7/32=168/768. Therefore it produces exactly the same one- and two-decision distributions and a different three-decision distribution. An explicit observational-equivalence witness is stronger than merely counting parameters.

For overdispersion, total variance gives Var(K)=E[3*P*(1-P)]+Var(3*P)=3*(m1-m2)+9*(m2-m1^2)=9/8. Equivalently it is3*m1*(1-m1)+6*Var(P)=3/4+3/8. A homogeneous model with probability1/2 would have variance3/4. Conditional independence within a type does not imply unconditional independence: the same latent probability gives positive covariance1/16 between different decisions.

For prediction after three purchases, the posterior high-type weight is[(1/2)*(3/4)^3]/(7/32)=27/28, and the low-type weight is1/28. The next-purchase probability is(27/28)*(3/4)+(1/28)*(1/4)=41/56. As an independent route, m4=[(1/4)^4+(3/4)^4]/2=41/256, so P(fourth purchase | first three purchases)=m4/m3=41/56. Repeated successes change the posterior type composition, rather than the conditional purchase probability of either type.

General pattern: I should transform repeated Bernoulli counts into latent factorial moments, then use a support polynomial instead of mixture-grid search. A positive moment variance identifies its coefficients, and an explicit alternative distribution demonstrates nonidentification with fewer repetitions. Latent heterogeneity creates both overdispersion and history-dependent prediction despite conditional independence.
reference_answer:
The two purchase probabilities are1/4 and3/4, each with weight1/2. Factorial moments identify m1=1/2,m2=5/16,m3=7/32; the support polynomial is z^2-z+3/16. Its roots and the mean identify the mixture up to labels.

Two repeats are insufficient: support1/6,11/16 with weights9/25,16/25 has the same first two moments but a different third. Var(K)=9/8, exceeding the homogeneous value3/4. Three purchases give posterior high-type probability27/28 and fourth-purchase probability41/56.

problem: Je cherche l'estimateur du taux de défaillance avec censure à droite. Quatre durées sont observées: échec à2, échec à3, censure à4, échec à5. Supposons des durées exponentielles indépendantes de taux λ. Écrivez la vraisemblance, trouvez le maximum de vraisemblance et l'information observée au maximum.
thinking:
Chaque échec contribue une densité λ exp(−λt); une observation censurée contribue seulement sa survie exp(−λc). Il y a donc trois échecs et l'exposition totale est2+3+4+5=14. La vraisemblance est proportionnelle à λ³ exp(−14λ), sans traiter la censure comme un échec.

La log-vraisemblance est3 log λ−14λ. Son score vaut3/λ−14 et s'annule à λ_hat=3/14. La dérivée seconde vaut−3/λ²<0, donc ce point intérieur est le maximum unique sur λ>0.

L'information observée est l'opposé de la dérivée seconde, 3/λ². Au maximum elle vaut3/(3/14)²=196/3. L'approximation normale donne Var(λ_hat)≈1/I=3/196 et erreur-type √3/14. Le temps censuré augmente l'exposition mais ne compte pas comme événement.

Comme contrôle, le score à λ_hat est3/(3/14)−14=0. Si l'observation censurée était faussement comptée comme une défaillance, le numérateur deviendrait4 et l'estimateur4/14, révélant directement le biais de codage des événements.

General pattern: Pour une exponentielle avec censure à droite, l'estimateur du taux est nombre d'événements divisé par temps total à risque. La vraisemblance factorise en puissance du taux et exponentielle de l'exposition; la censure contribue du temps, pas un événement.
reference_answer: Vraisemblance proportionnelle à λ³exp(−14λ). Estimateur λ_hat=3/14. Information observée au maximum=196/3; variance asymptotique=3/196 et erreur-type=√3/14.

problem: A firm can invest100 now in a project yielding a certain perpetual cash flow of8 per year, beginning next year. The discount rate is10%. Compute NPV and the break-even perpetual cash flow; explain why timing matters.
thinking:
The present value of the next-year perpetuity is8/0.10=80. Subtracting the immediate investment gives NPV=−20, so the project is rejected at the required return.

A break-even annual flow solves C/0.10=100, giving C=10. The cash flow begins one year from now, which matches the standard perpetuity formula; a payment today would add an undiscounted first cash flow and change value.

The infinite horizon does not make a small annual flow automatically valuable: discounting makes the stream's value finite when the discount rate is positive. The opportunity cost of capital determines whether that value covers100.

As a check, a flow10 has value100 and NPV zero; flow8 is80 and falls short by20. The value difference is20, equal to the present value of the two-unit annual flow gap.

General pattern: Value a level perpetuity from its first payment date and discount rate, then compare present value with the upfront cost. A timing shift changes which perpetuity formula applies.
reference_answer: PV of the project cash flows=80; NPV=−20, so reject. Break-even annual perpetuity is10.

problem:
I don't understand these programme results: A does better in both groups, but its overall success rate is lower. Can you explain the mathematics and tell me what I can actually conclude? This is a hypothetical employment-training dataset. Programme A has20 easier-case participants,18 successful, and80 harder-case participants,32 successful. Programme B has80 easier-case participants,64 successful, and20 harder-case participants,4 successful. There are200 distinct participants, each receiving exactly one programme, and success is binary.

Compute stratum and overall success rates. Derive both versions of a rate-versus-composition decomposition for overall A minus B, using B's composition first and A's composition second. For a common target population with easier-case share w in[0,1], find both standardised rates and their difference; evaluate the pooled population with w=1/2. Does the positive standardised difference establish a causal benefit? No random assignment or conditional exchangeability is given. Let YA,YB be each participant's binary potential success under A and B, with observed success equal to the potential outcome for the programme actually received. Find sharp bounds on the average causal effect E[YA-YB] over these200 people, and construct compatible potential outcomes attaining each endpoint. Explain the extra assumption that would justify a causal interpretation of the standardised comparison. Use identities and bounds rather than enumerating possible datasets.
thinking:
Before interpreting the ranking, I should separate conditional rates from participant weights. For A, the easier rate is18/20=9/10 and the harder rate32/80=2/5. For B, they are64/80=4/5 and4/20=1/5. The within-group A advantages are1/10 and1/5. Easier-case shares are a=1/5 in A and b=4/5 in B. Overall A success is50/100=1/2, while B success is68/100=17/25. The aggregate difference is-9/50 even though both conditional differences are positive.

For the shortcut, I should add and subtract a rate evaluated at a common composition. Write PA=a*pAE+(1-a)*pAH and PB=b*pBE+(1-b)*pBH. Adding and subtracting b*pAE+(1-b)*pAH gives PA-PB=b*(pAE-pBE)+(1-b)*(pAH-pBH)+(a-b)*(pAE-pAH). The rate effect at B weights is(4/5)*(1/10)+(1/5)*(1/5)=3/25. The composition effect using A rates is(-3/5)*(1/2)=-3/10. Their sum is-9/50. This is the composition decomposition, not evidence that the within-group arithmetic was wrong.

For the other reference, I add and subtract a*pBE+(1-a)*pBH instead. The identity becomes PA-PB=a*(pAE-pBE)+(1-a)*(pAH-pBH)+(a-b)*(pBE-pBH). The rate effect is(1/5)*(1/10)+(4/5)*(1/5)=9/50; the composition effect is(-3/5)*(3/5)=-9/25. Again the sum is-9/50. The decomposed contributions depend on the chosen reference; the observed aggregate difference does not. I should not give either contribution a unique causal interpretation merely because the identity is exact.

For a common target mix, standardised rates are PA(w)=2/5+w/2 and PB(w)=1/5+3*w/5. Their difference is1/5-w/10, between1/10 and1/5 for every feasible w. No common composition reverses the sign, because each stratum advantage is positive. The pooled easier share is(20+80)/200=1/2, giving PA=13/20, PB=1/2 and a standardised advantage3/20. Standardisation removes this measured composition imbalance; it does not remove unmeasured selection within either stratum.

For the causal question, I should preserve the missing potential outcomes. Among the100 A participants, the observed sum of YA is50, but their sum of YB can range from0 to100. Among the100 B participants, the observed sum of YB is68, but their sum of YA can range from0 to100. Therefore the total causal difference can be as small as50-100+0-68=-118 and as large as50-0+100-68=82. Dividing by200 gives the sharp interval[-59/100,41/100]. The observed strata do not narrow it without restrictions connecting observed and unobserved responses.

To check sharpness, I construct the endpoints without enumerating assignments. For the lower endpoint, set every A participant's missing YB to1 and every B participant's missing YA to0. Their observed outcomes stay exactly as recorded, while the total effect is-118. For the upper endpoint, set those missing YB to0 and missing YA to1, giving82. Both constructions retain all four observed group success counts. I can also set each person's missing outcome equal to their observed outcome, making every individual effect0. Thus a positive adjusted association is compatible with a negative, positive or zero causal effect.

For an independent check, potential-outcome means satisfy E[YA] in[1/4,3/4] and E[YB] in[17/50,21/25]. Subtracting the extreme feasible means gives1/4-21/25=-59/100 and3/4-17/50=41/100, matching the groupwise construction. Under consistency, positivity in both strata, and conditional exchangeability of programme assignment and potential outcomes given the stratum, the standardised rate difference would identify the average causal effect for the chosen target mix. Those assumptions are additional information, not consequences of this table; the calculated empirical rates also carry sampling uncertainty if used to infer a wider population.

General pattern: I should express aggregate comparisons as conditional rates times weights, then insert a common reference to expose composition. A shared target mix preserves within-stratum dominance but does not establish causation. Missing-potential-outcome bounds and explicit endpoint constructions distinguish exact descriptive identities from unverified identification assumptions.
reference_answer:
Within-group rates are A:(9/10,2/5), B:(4/5,1/5). Overall rates are1/2 and17/25, so A minus B is-9/50. At B's weights, the decomposition is3/25-3/10=-9/50; at A's weights, it is9/50-9/25=-9/50.

At common easier share w, rates are2/5+w/2 and1/5+3*w/5; their difference1/5-w/10 is always positive. At pooled w=1/2, rates are13/20 and1/2, giving3/20.

This adjusted association does not prove a causal benefit. With only binary outcomes and consistency, the sharp average-effect bounds over the200 participants are[-59/100,41/100]. Set missing B outcomes among A participants to1 and missing A outcomes among B participants to0 for the lower endpoint; reverse them for the upper endpoint. Conditional exchangeability given the stratum, together with consistency and positivity, would permit a causal interpretation of the standardised comparison.

problem: A firm faces inverse demand p=50−Q and cost C(Q)=10Q+Q²/2. Find monopoly quantity and profit, and compare them with the efficient quantity.
thinking:
Before applying a markup rule, marginal revenue is50−2Q and marginal cost is10+Q. Equating them gives40=3Q, so Qm=40/3.

Price is50−40/3=110/3. Profit is(p−10)Q−Q²/2, equivalently revenue minus total cost; substituting gives profit800/3.. Efficiency instead equates willingness to pay with marginal cost:50−Q=10+Q, so Q*=20.

The monopoly quantity is below efficient output because marginal revenue lies below demand. The first-order condition is unique since marginal revenue falls and marginal cost rises.

General pattern: monopoly equates marginal revenue and marginal cost; social efficiency equates marginal benefit and marginal cost. Their wedge determines restricted output and deadweight loss.
reference_answer: Qm=40/3, price=110/3, profit=800/3, and efficient output=20.

problem: Pourquoi une hausse du salaire pousse-t-elle une entreprise à substituer du capital au travail? Sa technologie est F(K,L)=(1/(2K)+1/(2L))^(-1). Elle doit produire une unité; le prix du capital est r=1 et le salaire est w=4. Trouve le ratio optimal K/L, les facteurs choisis et le coût minimal. Compare au cas où w=r=1 et relie la réponse à l'élasticité de substitution.
thinking:
Je transforme d'abord la technologie en forme simple: F(K,L)=2KL/(K+L). Ses produits marginaux donnent MPK/MPL=(L/K)². Au minimum de coût intérieur, le taux marginal de substitution technique égale le rapport des prix r/w; ainsi(L/K)²=1/4 et K/L=2. Le travail est devenu relativement cher, donc l'entreprise choisit davantage de capital par unité de travail.

En imposant K=2L et F=1, la production vaut4L/3, donc L=3/4 et K=3/2. Le coût minimal estrK+wL=3/2+4(3/4)=9/2. La technologie est homogène de degré1 et strictement quasi-concave dans les facteurs positifs, donc la condition de tangence et la contrainte de production donnent le minimum global.

À prix égaux r=w=1, le rapport optimal est K/L=1; F(K,K)=K impose K=L=1 pour produire une unité, au coût2. Quand w/r passe de1 à4, le rapport K/L passe de1 à2. La pente logarithmique est ln2/ln4=1/2, exactement l'élasticité de substitution du CES avec exposantρ=−1, soit1/(1−ρ)=1/2.

Comme contrôle indépendant, au panier(3/2,3/4), F=[1/3+2/3]^(-1)=1 et MPK/MPL=(1/2)²=1/4=r/w. Le panier à facteurs égaux qui produirait une unité coûterait5.5 aux nouveaux prix, contre4.5 au panier optimal; la substitution réduit le coût d'une unité malgré le salaire plus élevé.

General pattern: La minimisation de coût égalise le taux marginal de substitution technique au prix relatif des facteurs. Dans une technologie CES, l'élasticité de substitution gouverne la réponse logarithmique du ratio des facteurs au prix relatif; vérifie ensuite le niveau de production et le coût, pas seulement le ratio.
reference_answer: Le ratio optimal est K/L=2. Pour produire une unité, K=3/2 et L=3/4, avec coût minimal9/2. Lorsque les prix sont égaux, K=L=1 et le coût vaut2. Le salaire relatif est multiplié par4 tandis que K/L est multiplié par2, donnant une élasticité de substitution1/2.

problem: If Earth is closer to the Sun in January, why is it winter in the Northern Hemisphere?
thinking: The seasons are mainly caused by Earth's axial tilt, not its changing distance from the Sun.
reference_answer: Seasons are mainly caused by Earth’s tilted axis. In January the Northern Hemisphere tilts away from the Sun, receiving less direct sunlight and shorter days, even though Earth is near its closest orbital point.

problem: Ten observations each have variance4 and common pairwise correlation0.25. Compute the variance of their sample mean and its effective independent sample size. Compare it with the variance under independence.
thinking:
The variance of an average is the sum of all variances and covariances divided by n². Equicorrelation gives Var(mean)=σ²/n·[1+(n−1)ρ]=4/10·[1+9/4]=13/10.

If observations were independent, the variance would be4/10=2/5. Positive dependence therefore raises variance by a factor13/4=3.25.

Define effective sample size by matching the independent formula σ²/n_eff to the actual variance. Then n_eff=4/(13/10)=40/13, about3.08 independent observations despite collecting10 correlated ones.

As a check, the covariance contribution is n(n−1)ρσ² divided by n², equal to9/10; adding the diagonal contribution4/10 gives13/10. The effective size reproduces the same variance exactly.

General pattern: Correlation changes the variance of an average through off-diagonal covariance terms. Effective sample size translates that dependence penalty into an equivalent number of independent observations.
reference_answer: Var(mean)=13/10; under independence it is2/5. Effective sample size=40/13≈3.08.

problem:
Une pratique procure un gain Delta>0. L'enquête survient avec probabilité alpha=1/5; conditionnellement à l'enquête, une sanction intervient avec probabilité beta=3/4. La sanction retire le gain Delta et ajoute une amende F=4. Sans sanction, le gain reste acquis. Calculez le seuil de dissuasion et vérifiez la formule Delta0=alpha*beta*F/(1-alpha*beta*F).

L'autorité peut proposer, lors d'une enquête, un engagement retirant intégralement le gain sans amende. L'entreprise peut refuser et subir alors le procès décrit ci-dessus. Si cette offre est faite avec probabilité x conditionnelle à l'enquête, caractérisez les entreprises qui l'acceptent, le gain espéré et le seuil de dissuasion. Comparez x=0 et x=1 pour Delta=1/2 et Delta=1, en distinguant prévention ex ante et cessation d'une pratique détectée.
thinking:
Avant de calculer, je dois multiplier des probabilités conditionnelles: la sanction totale a probabilité p=alpha*beta=3/20. Le gain espéré est G0=Delta-p*(Delta+F)=(17/20)*Delta-3/5. Ainsi G0<=0 équivaut à Delta<=12/17. L'égalité signifie indifférence, pas abstention certaine sans règle de choix.

Pour contrôler la formule proposée, je garde p symbolique: (1-p)*Delta-p*F=0 donne Delta0=p*F/(1-p). Le dénominateur 1-p*F est incorrect. Avec les valeurs données il proposerait Delta0=3/2; substituer ce nombre dans G0 donne 27/40>0, ce qui réfute directement le prétendu seuil. La comparaison doit utiliser les états de paiement, pas une expression mémorisée.

Pour découvrir la condition de négociation, lors d'une enquête le procès rapporte (1-beta)*Delta-beta*F=Delta/4-3. L'engagement rapporte zéro. Il est donc accepté si Delta<=12, avec indifférence à 12. Au-delà, l'entreprise refuse; la réputation de négociation n'affecte alors pas son gain espéré.

Pour les types qui acceptent, Gx=(1-alpha)*Delta+alpha*(1-x)*[(1-beta)*Delta-beta*F]. En développant, Gx=[1-alpha*(beta+x*(1-beta))]*Delta-alpha*(1-x)*beta*F. La probabilité de cessation après choix de la pratique est alpha*[beta+x*(1-beta)], mais l'amende espérée est réduite par le facteur 1-x. Ces deux effets ne vont pas dans le même sens pour la dissuasion.

Une voie plus courte est de résoudre Gx=0. On obtient Delta0(x)=12*(1-x)/(17-x), dont la dérivée est -192/(17-x)^2<0 sur [0,1]. Ce seuil reste inférieur à 12 et relève donc bien de la branche où l'offre est acceptée. Pour Delta>12, G0 est positif; aucun type oublié de la branche refusant l'offre n'est dissuadé. À x=1, Gx=4*Delta/5>0 pour tout Delta>0: la pratique est parfois arrêtée, mais jamais prévenue par cette seule menace.

Pour vérifier les implications, Delta=1/2 donne G0=-7/40 et G1=2/5: la négociation transforme une pratique dissuadée en pratique profitable. Delta=1 donne G0=1/4 et G1=4/5: la pratique n'est prévenue dans aucun cas. Conditionnellement à son choix, la cessation passe néanmoins de 3/20 à 1/5. Une amélioration du traitement des pratiques effectivement choisies ne prouve donc pas une amélioration du dommage global, car le nombre de pratiques peut changer.

General pattern: je dois reconstruire l'espérance depuis les états, comparer la négociation au véritable gain conditionnel du procès, puis résoudre le seuil dans sa branche valide. Distinguer détection, sanction, cessation et dissuasion évite de confondre effets procéduraux et comportement ex ante.
reference_answer:
Sans négociation, le gain espéré est (17/20)*Delta-3/5; la pratique est non profitable pour Delta<=12/17. La formule générale correcte est alpha*beta*F/(1-alpha*beta), et non celle proposée.

L'engagement est accepté pour Delta<=12. Dans cette branche, le seuil devient 12*(1-x)/(17-x), décroissant jusqu'à zéro. Les types au-dessus de 12 refusent l'offre et restent non dissuadés. À Delta=1/2, négocier systématiquement supprime la dissuasion; à Delta=1, cela améliore la probabilité de cessation de 3/20 à 1/5 sans prévenir la pratique. Les comparaisons suivent des gains conditionnels et ne constituent pas une conclusion universelle sur le dommage total.

problem: A consumer has quasi-linear utility U=x+10√q, where x is a numeraire and q is a good priced at2. Find optimal q and consumer surplus, assuming the consumer can afford the numeraire allocation.
thinking:
The marginal willingness to pay is5/√q. Setting it equal to price2 gives q=25/4. Quasi-linearity makes this quantity choice independent of income, provided the numeraire remains nonnegative.

Inverse demand is p(q)=5/√q. Consumer surplus is the integral from0 to25/4 of p(q)−2, which equals10√q−2q evaluated at the optimum:25/2.

The integral is finite at zero despite inverse demand diverging there, because q to the power−1/2 is integrable. A triangle approximation would be invalid since willingness to pay is curved.

As a check, marginal willingness to pay at q=25/4 is2, matching price; total willingness to pay is10√(25/4)=25, expenditure is2·25/4=25/2, leaving surplus25/2.

General pattern: With quasi-linear utility, set marginal utility of the purchased good equal to its price, then integrate inverse demand for surplus. Income effects vanish while the numeraire constraint remains slack.
reference_answer: Optimal quantity q=25/4. Consumer surplus=25/2.

problem: Deux types de clients ont des valeurs 10 et20, équiprobables. Un monopole choisit une qualité x et un transfert t; l'utilité est θx−t et le coût de qualité est x²/2. Si les deux types reçoivent la même qualité x=1, quel tarif fixe maximal assure la participation des deux et quel profit espéré obtient-on?
thinking:
Avant de maximiser un menu, j'applique la contrainte de participation du type à faible valeur: 10·1−t≥0, donc t≤10. Le type élevé accepte aussi tout tarif t≤20, alors le type faible est contraignant.

Le tarif maximal commun est10. Les deux clients achètent, le coût de qualité est1/2 par client, donc le profit par client est10−1/2=19/2 et le profit espéré par client est aussi19/2. Avec un client tiré uniformément parmi les deux types, le profit total espéré vaut19/2.

Le type haut obtient une rente informationnelle10 sous ce tarif. Un menu séparant les types pourrait modifier qualité et transfert, mais n'est pas demandé; le tarif commun est limité par la participation basse.

General pattern: under a pooling contract, the lowest valuation usually binds participation. Compute the maximal common transfer from that type, then subtract the real resource cost; transfers are not themselves social costs.
reference_answer: The maximal common fee is 10 and expected profit per arriving customer is 19/2.

problem:
Can you explain this apparent contradiction? A randomized job-training programme triples the employment odds in every group, but the overall odds ratio is smaller than three. Does that prove the randomization failed, or that controlling for the group created bias?

Let T be randomized programme assignment, independent of a pre-treatment group Z. Each group has population share1/2. In group Z=0 the employment probabilities are P(Y=1|T=0,Z=0)=1/10 and P(Y=1|T=1,Z=0)=1/4. In group Z=1 they are P(Y=1|T=0,Z=1)=1/2 and P(Y=1|T=1,Z=1)=3/4. Assume consistency and random assignment, so these conditional risks have a causal interpretation for the respective groups. All probabilities are exact population values.

Compute each group's odds ratio, the marginal risks and marginal odds ratio, and the population average treatment effect on the probability scale. Compare the group risk differences and risk ratios. Explain why the difference between conditional and marginal odds ratios need not be confounding.

Generalize: suppose baseline employment risk is a random variable B in (0,1), and treatment multiplies the conditional odds by a common factor rho>1. Derive the treated-risk map f_rho(B). Prove that with equal group composition across assignments, a nonconstant B gives a marginal odds ratio strictly between1 and rho. Find the exact Jensen gap for two baseline values x,y with weights w,1-w, and verify it in the numerical example.

Finally, change the target population so that group0 has share3/4 while the groupwise risks remain unchanged. Standardize both assignments to this same new population. Recompute the marginal odds ratio and average treatment effect. Does a common conditional odds ratio define a population-invariant marginal effect?
thinking:
Before comparing effects, I write odds as probability divided by its complement. In group0, untreated odds are (1/10)/(9/10)=1/9 and treated odds are (1/4)/(3/4)=1/3, so the odds ratio is3. In group1, untreated odds are1 and treated odds3, giving the same ratio3. The risk differences are1/4-1/10=3/20 and3/4-1/2=1/4. The risk ratios are5/2 and3/2. Equal effects on the odds scale do not imply equal effects on the probability or risk-ratio scale.

For the marginal quantities, I use the same group weights in both assignment arms, as randomization requires here. The untreated risk is r0=(1/10+1/2)/2=3/10, and the treated risk is r1=(1/4+3/4)/2=1/2. Their marginal odds ratio is [r1/(1-r1)]/[r0/(1-r0)]=1/(3/7)=7/3, below3. The average treatment effect on employment probability is r1-r0=1/5. Independently, averaging the two group risk differences gives (3/20+1/4)/2=1/5. Probability differences commute with this common-weight averaging, whereas odds transformations do not.

To identify the issue, I distinguish population averaging from confounding. T is independent of Z, so neither arm has an excess of the high-baseline group. Marginal and conditional effects refer to different summaries even under this balanced assignment. The conditional odds ratio3 describes an odds comparison within each group; the marginal ratio7/3 describes the odds of the averaged population risks. Its change is odds-ratio noncollapsibility, not evidence that randomization failed. A conditional and a marginal logistic coefficient would accordingly describe different targets.

For a general pattern, I solve the odds equation rather than memorize the result. If baseline risk is b and the treated risk is f, then f/(1-f)=rho*b/(1-b). Rearrangement gives f_rho(b)=rho*b/[1+(rho-1)*b]. For rho>1, f_rho(b)-b=(rho-1)*b*(1-b)/[1+(rho-1)*b]>0. Its second derivative is -2*rho*(rho-1)/[1+(rho-1)*b]^3<0. I have found the reusable trick: the treatment map is increasing but strictly concave, so averaging its input and averaging its output cannot be interchanged.

To prove the marginal inequality, let mu=E[B]. Common target weights imply r0=mu and r1=E[f_rho(B)]. Since B lies strictly between0 and1, the pointwise gain gives r1>mu. If B is not almost surely constant, strict Jensen gives r1<f_rho(mu). The odds map o(r)=r/(1-r) is strictly increasing, so 1<o(r1)/o(mu)<o(f_rho(mu))/o(mu)=rho. Both bounds are strict under these assumptions. If B is constant, the Jensen gap vanishes and the marginal odds ratio equals rho. I do not claim this strict result for baseline risks at the degenerate endpoints without checking their support separately.

To quantify the loss of collapsibility, I derive the two-point Jensen gap. Set c=rho-1, mu=w*x+(1-w)*y and d_b=1+c*b. The identity f_rho(b)=(rho/c)*(1-1/d_b) converts the gap into an average of reciprocals. Bringing the three rational terms to a common denominator gives f_rho(mu)-[w*f_rho(x)+(1-w)*f_rho(y)]=rho*c*w*(1-w)*(x-y)^2/(d_x*d_y*d_mu). Every factor is positive when rho>1, 0<w<1 and x!=y. Baseline heterogeneity enters through a squared difference, giving an exact version of the curvature argument.

For the numerical check, I set rho=3, x=1/10, y=1/2 and w=1/2. Then mu=3/10 and f_rho(mu)=9/16, whereas the average treated risk is1/2. The gap is1/16. The exact formula independently gives 3*2*(1/4)*(2/5)^2/[(6/5)*2*(8/5)]=1/16. Thus taking the common conditional odds multiplier3 and applying it to the marginal baseline risk would predict treated risk9/16 instead of the true1/2. That incorrect calculation explains the apparent discrepancy directly.

For the new target population, I standardize both assignments to w=3/4 rather than leave their compositions implicit. The untreated risk is(3/4)*(1/10)+(1/4)*(1/2)=1/5, while treated risk is(3/4)*(1/4)+(1/4)*(3/4)=3/8. The marginal odds ratio is[(3/8)/(5/8)]/[(1/5)/(4/5)]=(3/5)/(1/4)=12/5. The average probability effect is3/8-1/5=7/40. Averaging the group differences with the new weights also gives(3/4)*(3/20)+(1/4)*(1/4)=7/40. Both population effects changed despite unchanged groupwise probabilities and the same conditional odds ratio3.

For interpretation, I keep assignment, conditioning and target population separate. Balanced assignment supports causal comparisons; it does not make a nonlinear effect measure collapsible. Standardization specifies which population is being averaged and changes that target deliberately. The examples have beneficial treatment in every group and both populations, so there is no sign reversal to explain. The discrepancy concerns the size and scale of the effect, not an opposite causal conclusion.

General pattern: I derive the probability map implied by a conditional effect measure, then check its curvature before averaging. Common-weight risk differences aggregate linearly; conditional odds multipliers pass through a nonlinear concave map. Jensen's inequality and its exact two-point remainder distinguish noncollapsibility from confounding and show why the target population must be stated explicitly.
reference_answer:
Both group odds ratios are3. In the original population, untreated and treated risks are3/10 and1/2, so the marginal odds ratio is7/3 and the average probability effect is1/5. The group risk differences are3/20 and1/4; their risk ratios are5/2 and3/2.

A common conditional odds multiplier rho induces f_rho(b)=rho*b/[1+(rho-1)*b]. For rho>1 this map is strictly concave and exceeds b on(0,1). Thus a nonconstant baseline risk gives 1<marginal odds ratio<rho by strict Jensen and monotonicity of odds. For two baseline risks, the Jensen gap is rho*(rho-1)*w*(1-w)*(x-y)^2 divided by [1+(rho-1)*x]*[1+(rho-1)*y]*[1+(rho-1)*mu]. Here it equals1/16.

With group0 share3/4, standardized risks become1/5 and3/8, the marginal odds ratio becomes12/5, and the average probability effect is7/40. The changing marginal ratio is compatible with randomization and unchanged conditional effects: it reflects nonlinear averaging and a changed target population, not evidence of confounding.

problem: How many factors of 2 divide 100!? Use a valuation argument rather than factoring 100! itself.
thinking:
Before multiplying factorial terms, I count how often each power of2 appears. Every even integer contributes at least one factor, every multiple of4 contributes one extra, and so on. Thus v₂(100!)=⌊100/2⌋+⌊100/4⌋+⌊100/8⌋+⌊100/16⌋+⌊100/32⌋+⌊100/64⌋=50+25+12+6+3+1=97.

This layered count avoids double-counting: a multiple of8 is counted once at each of the 2,4,8 layers, exactly matching its three factors of2. Higher powers beyond128 contribute nothing because no integer up to100 is divisible by them.

The independent Legendre formula v_p(n!)=Σ⌊n/p^j⌋ gives the same finite sum, stopping when p^j>n. Therefore 100! is divisible by2^97 but not by2^98.

General pattern: count prime factors by nested divisibility layers. Each multiple of p^j contributes one unit at level j, turning a huge product into a short sum of floors.
reference_answer: The exponent is v₂(100!)=97, so 2^97 divides 100! but 2^98 does not.

problem: Eine faire Münze wird zweimal geworfen. A sei das Ereignis „mindestens ein Kopf“, B das Ereignis „der erste Wurf ist Kopf“. Bestimme P(B|A) und erkläre, weshalb 1/2 hier falsch ist.
thinking:
Vor der Bedingung ist P(B)=1/2, aber nach A sind nur HH, HT und TH gleich wahrscheinlich. Davon erfüllen HH und HT das Ereignis B, also P(B|A)=2/3.

Bayes bestätigt es: P(A|B)=1, P(B)=1/2 und P(A)=3/4, daher P(B|A)=P(A|B)P(B)/P(A)=2/3. Die Bedingung entfernt TT und verändert den Grundraum.

Der Fehler 1/2 überträgt eine unbedingte Wahrscheinlichkeit auf einen eingeschränkten Raum. Innerhalb A muss neu normiert werden; zwei der drei verbleibenden Ergebnisse beginnen mit Kopf.

General pattern: bedingte Wahrscheinlichkeiten leben auf dem gefilterten Ereignisraum. Zähle gemeinsame günstige Fälle und dividiere durch die Masse der Bedingung, nicht durch die ursprüngliche Grundmenge.
