problem:
Tenho três sensores, mas não observo diretamente o estado que eles tentam detectar. É possível separar a frequência do estado dos erros dos sensores usando apenas os seus resultados? Quero entender a identificação, não procurar combinações de parâmetros por tentativa.

Um estado latente T vale0 ou1, com P(T=1)=pi em(0,1). Os resultados X1,X2,X3 são binários. Condicionalmente a T, são independentes, com P(Xi=1|T=0)=ai e P(Xi=1|T=1)=bi. Assume0<=ai<bi<=1 para cada sensor; essa orientação define o significado do estado1. Nenhuma observação direta de T está disponível.

As médias observadas são mu=(3/10,7/20,2/5). As covariâncias são c12=9/100,c13=3/50,c23=9/200. O momento central de terceira ordem é m=E[(X1-mu1)*(X2-mu2)*(X3-mu3)]=9/500. São momentos exatos de população.

Derive as identidades dos momentos a partir do modelo e obtenha uma fórmula geral para pi usando m e as três covariâncias positivas. Encontre ai,bi e prove a unicidade dentro do modelo orientado. Verifique os intervalos de probabilidade e reconstrua os momentos.

Calcule P(X1=X2=X3=1) e P(T=1|X1=X2=X3=1). Faça uma verificação independente com odds e razões de verossimilhança. Explique o que acontece se a orientação ai<bi for removida, se uma covariância se anular, ou se m0 com as covariâncias ainda positivas. A compatibilidade dos momentos demonstra, por si só, independência condicional?
thinking:
Antes de inverter os dados, devo separar a variação latente da variação dos sensores. Defino di=bi-ai>0 e h=pi*(1-pi). A média condicional é ai+di*T, logo mui=ai+pi*di. Pela independência condicional, cij=Cov(E[Xi|T],E[Xj|T])=h*di*dj. A dependência marginal pode ser positiva mesmo quando os sensores são independentes depois de fixar o estado.

Para o momento de terceira ordem, posso escrever Xi-mui=di*(T-pi)+ei, onde E[ei|T]=0. A independência condicional anula os produtos que incluem resíduos de sensores diferentes. Assim m=d1*d2*d3*E[(T-pi)^3]=h*(1-2*pi)*d1*d2*d3. Essa identidade usa a hipótese de independência condicional; não devo justificá-la apenas com covariâncias observadas.

Para descobrir uma inversão curta, procuro um quadrado que elimine a frequência latente. Ponho D=c12*c13*c23=h^3*(d1*d2*d3)^2. Então m^2+4*D=h^2*(d1*d2*d3)^2*[(1-2*pi)^2+4*pi*(1-pi)]. O fator entre colchetes é1. Como h e os di são positivos, sqrt(m^2+4*D)=h*d1*d2*d3. Portanto pi=[1-m/sqrt(m^2+4*D)]/2. A orientação positiva escolhe o sinal da raiz sem enumerar soluções.

Para recuperar cada sensor, devo usar os produtos aos pares. Com h conhecido, d1=sqrt(c12*c13/(h*c23)), e as outras duas diferenças vêm das permutações correspondentes. Depois ai=mui-pi*di e bi=mui+(1-pi)*di. Essas fórmulas dão uma única solução orientada quando todas as covariâncias são positivas. Os limites0<=ai<bi<=1 ainda precisam ser verificados: uma inversão algébrica fora deles não seria um modelo de probabilidades válido.

Para os dados fornecidos, D243/1000000 e sqrt(m^2+4*D)=9/250. A razão m sobre essa raiz é1/2, dando pi1/4 e h3/16. As diferenças são d=(4/5,3/5,2/5). As probabilidades no estado0 são a=(1/10,1/5,3/10), e no estado1 são b=(9/10,4/5,7/10). Todas satisfazem os intervalos e a orientação. Substituir em ai+pi*di, h*di*dj e h*(1-2*pi)*d1*d2*d3 reproduz exatamente os momentos observados.

Para a ocorrência conjunta dos três resultados positivos, devo misturar produtos condicionais, não multiplicar as médias marginais. A probabilidade é pi*b1*b2*b3+(1-pi)*a1*a2*a3=(1/4)*(9/10)*(4/5)*(7/10)+(3/4)*(1/10)*(1/5)*(3/10)=261/2000. O termo do estado1 é63/500, então a probabilidade posterior do estado1 é(63/500)/(261/2000)=28/29. O produto das médias3/10*7/20*2/5=21/500 seria incorreto sob uma falsa independência marginal.

Para uma verificação independente, posso atualizar odds em vez de repetir a divisão de probabilidades. As odds prévias são1/3, e as razões de verossimilhança dos três resultados positivos são9,4,7/3. Seu produto com as odds prévias é28. As odds posteriores28 correspondem à probabilidade28/(1+28)=28/29. Esse produto é legítimo condicionalmente a T, exatamente onde foi assumida a independência dos sensores.

Para a ambiguidade de rótulos, remover a orientação permite trocar T por1-T. Isso substitui pi por1-pi e troca ai com bi, preservando toda a distribuição observada. Os dados não escolhem o nome do estado. Se uma covariância se anula, o modelo estritamente orientado com pi em(0,1) deixa de satisfazer suas próprias condições; ao permitir diferenças nulas ou estados degenerados, a fórmula perde denominadores e não garante identificação. Em contraste, m0 com covariâncias positivas impõe pi1/2 nesta classe, não independência marginal.

Para delimitar a conclusão, devo reconstruir a lei binária completa, não só uma estatística selecionada. Médias, segundos momentos brutos e o terceiro momento bruto determinam as probabilidades dos oito resultados por inclusão e exclusão. O modelo recuperado reproduz esses momentos e portanto a lei observada correspondente. Isso demonstra compatibilidade e identificação dentro da classe assumida. Não prova que mecanismos alternativos com dependência condicional sejam impossíveis; essa hipótese continua sendo parte da especificação.

General pattern: devo fatorar covariâncias em uma escala latente e diferenças de resposta, depois procurar uma combinação de momentos que elimine fatores desconhecidos. A identidade quadrática isola a frequência do estado, enquanto raízes positivas e limites de probabilidade verificam os sensores. Uma atualização por odds controla a probabilidade posterior por outra rota. Identificação dentro de um modelo não transforma suas hipóteses em fatos observados.
reference_answer:
Defina di=bi-ai e h=pi*(1-pi). O modelo implica mui=ai+pi*di, cij=h*di*dj e m=h*(1-2*pi)*d1*d2*d3. A identidade m^2+4*c12*c13*c23=h^2*(d1*d2*d3)^2 dá pi=[1-m/sqrt(m^2+4*c12*c13*c23)]/2 sob a orientação di>0.

Os dados identificam pi1/4, a=(1/10,1/5,3/10) e b=(9/10,4/5,7/10). A recuperação dos di por raízes positivas é única, e todos os limites e momentos são satisfeitos. A probabilidade de três positivos é261/2000, com posterior28/29 para o estado1. Odds prévias1/3 vezes razões9,4,7/3 dão odds posteriores28, confirmando o resultado.

Sem orientação, trocar os rótulos preserva a lei observada. Covariâncias nulas invalidam a inversão não degenerada. Um terceiro momento nulo com covariâncias positivas implica pi1/2 nesta classe. Reproduzir a distribuição demonstra compatibilidade com o modelo, não prova a independência condicional fora dele.

problem:
Can you help me interpret this encouragement experiment? The instrumental-variable estimate is positive, but does it tell me how many people benefit, or the average effect for everyone? Please derive what is identified and give sharp bounds for the rest.

A binary randomized encouragement Z is independent of all potential treatment and outcome variables. Treatment is D=D(Z), with D(0),D(1) in{0,1}. Outcomes are binary Y(0),Y(1), with observed Y=Y(D); encouragement has no direct effect on outcome. Maintain treatment monotonicity D(1)>=D(0), allowing always-takers, never-takers and compliers. No assumption of equal effects or individual outcome monotonicity is imposed initially.

Conditional on Z=0, the joint probabilities of(D,Y) are D0,Y0:11/20; D0,Y1:1/5; D1,Y0:1/20; D1,Y1:1/5. Conditional on Z=1 they are D0,Y0:1/5; D0,Y1:1/20; D1,Y0:1/5; D1,Y1:11/20. These are exact population probabilities, not noisy sample frequencies.

Identify the three treatment-type shares, the first stage, reduced-form outcome effect and Wald ratio. Use the full joint tables to identify the compliers' two outcome means and the observed potential-outcome means for the other types. Find the sharp identified set for the population average treatment effect. Then find the sharp range of the fraction of compliers who individually benefit, parameterizing their entire potential-outcome joint table with t=P(Y(0)=1,Y(1)=1|complier). Prove attainability without listing all latent response patterns. Finally add Y(1)>=Y(0) for every person: determine the revised average-effect interval and complier benefit fraction. Explain which conclusions use this additional assumption.
thinking:
Before dividing outcomes by a first stage, I should identify who can change treatment. Under treatment monotonicity, the treated share at Z=0 is exactly the always-taker mass1/4, and the untreated share at Z=1 is the never-taker mass1/4. The remaining1/2 are compliers. The first stage is3/4-1/4=1/2. Outcome means are2/5 and3/5, so the reduced-form effect is1/5 and the Wald ratio2/5. Exclusion and randomization make the outcome difference the complier mass times its average effect; dividing isolates that local average, not the population average.

To extract more information, I subtract the cells for the same received treatment across encouragement arms. Treated successes increase from1/5 to11/20, adding7/20 of population mass; dividing by complier mass1/2 gives E[Y(1)|C]=7/10. Untreated successes decrease from1/5 to1/20, removing3/20; dividing gives E[Y(0)|C]=3/10. Their difference2/5 independently verifies the Wald ratio. Always-takers' observed treated mean is(1/5)/(1/4)=4/5, and never-takers' observed untreated mean is(1/20)/(1/4)=1/5.

For the population effect, the missing quantities are not sampling errors. Let x=E[Y(0)|always] and y=E[Y(1)|never], each in[0,1]. The average effect is(1/2)*(2/5)+(1/4)*(4/5-x)+(1/4)*(y-1/5)=7/20+(y-x)/4. Therefore its identified set is[1/10,3/5]. Treating the IV value2/5 as everyone's effect would replace two genuinely unobserved means by an unsupported homogeneity assumption.

To prove sharpness, I hold the observed always-taker Y(1) mean4/5 and never-taker Y(0) mean1/5 fixed. Any chosen x,y in[0,1] can be assigned to their missing binary outcomes, for example independently within each type, without changing any observed cell. At x=1,y=0 the average effect is1/10; at x=0,y=1 it is3/5. Mixing these latent constructions continuously fills the interval and preserves the observed tables. The bound is thus attainable, not merely an algebraic outer range.

For who benefits among compliers, I need the joint distribution of their two potential outcomes. With t=P(Y(0)=1,Y(1)=1|C), rows Y(0)=0,1 and columns Y(1)=0,1 give [[t,7/10-t],[3/10-t,t]]. Nonnegativity requires0<=t<=3/10. Every such table has the same marginals3/10 and7/10 and hence the same observables. The benefit fraction is7/10-t, ranging from2/5 to7/10; the harmed fraction is3/10-t, ranging from0 to3/10. The local average2/5 is benefit fraction minus harmed fraction, not generally the benefit fraction alone.

To check the coupling bound independently, the intersection probability t is at most the smaller marginal3/10 and at least max(0,3/10+7/10-1)=0. These Frechet bounds reproduce the same interval. At t=0,70% of compliers benefit and30% are harmed. At t=3/10,40% benefit and none are harmed, with30% always successful and30% never successful. Both extreme joint laws yield exactly the same observed marginal outcomes, so even perfect experimental tables cannot distinguish these cross-world patterns.

For the added individual outcome monotonicity, complier harm must be zero. This forces t=3/10 and makes the complier benefit fraction exactly2/5. It also restricts x<=4/5 for always-takers and y>=1/5 for never-takers. Hence every type has a nonnegative effect and the population interval narrows to[1/5,3/5]. The lower endpoint sets x=4/5,y=1/5, while the upper still sets x=0,y=1. Binary couplings with the specified ordered marginals exist throughout: put common success probability in the(1,1) cell and the remaining success increment in(0,1). This proves the revised bounds are sharp under the stronger assumption.

For a complete observation check, at Z=0 the always-taker treated-success mass is(1/4)*(4/5)=1/5, while untreated-success mass is(1/4)*(1/5)+(1/2)*(3/10)=1/5. At Z=1, treated-success mass is1/5+(1/2)*(7/10)=11/20, and untreated-success mass remains1/20. Treatment-type totals supply the complementary failure cells. Neither t nor the missing means x,y enters these observed probabilities, precisely locating the remaining identification gaps.

General pattern: I separate treatment-type mixtures before interpreting an IV ratio. Cell differences recover complier marginals, while missing type outcomes and cross-world couplings remain free. Probability nonnegativity gives bounds; explicit latent constructions prove sharpness. Treatment monotonicity and outcome monotonicity are different assumptions, and only the latter turns a binary average effect into the fraction who benefit.
reference_answer:
Always-takers, never-takers and compliers have shares(1/4,1/4,1/2). The first stage is1/2, reduced-form effect1/5 and Wald/LATE2/5. Complier outcome means are(3/10,7/10); always-takers' Y(1) mean is4/5 and never-takers' Y(0) mean1/5.

The sharp population average-effect interval is[1/10,3/5], because ATE=7/20+(y-x)/4 for unobserved means x,y in[0,1]. The complier potential-outcome table is [[t,7/10-t],[3/10-t,t]], with t in[0,3/10]. Thus the benefit fraction ranges over[2/5,7/10], although the average remains2/5.

Adding individual outcome monotonicity forces t=3/10, identifies the complier benefit fraction2/5, and narrows population ATE to[1/5,3/5]. Constructing the missing outcomes within each type proves both sets of bounds attainable. These last conclusions require the extra outcome assumption, not merely treatment monotonicity.

problem:
Can a small increase in rivals' capacity cause a large price drop? Help me solve the global pricing problem rather than trusting one first-order condition.

In a hypothetical market, demand at price p>=0 is D(p)=max(0,20-p). A dominant firm with constant marginal cost2 commits to p and serves residual demand. A competitive fringe has aggregate real cost CF(q)=4*q+q^2/2 and a capacity K>=0, so its supply is qF(p)=min(K,max(0,p-4)). Only prices where demand can absorb the fringe's supply are feasible. The dominant quantity is qD=D(p)-qF>=0 and its profit is(p-2)*qD. Capacity is given; do not subtract an investment cost.

Find every globally optimal price and resulting quantities as a function of K. Distinguish inactive, responsive and capacity-bound fringe regimes; do not extrapolate a stationary price beyond its valid branch. Locate the exact capacity where the optimal policy switches, including any tie, and show whether dominant profit and price are continuous there.

At that switch, compute consumer surplus, fringe profit and real welfare under each optimal price. Compare with efficient production, prove the direction and magnitude of the welfare jump, and check the accounts independently. Explain why the fringe earns a scarcity rent under the high-price policy and why increasing capacity need not change price smoothly.
thinking:
Before optimizing, I should keep the fringe's two kinks. Below p4 it is inactive, between4 and4+K it responds with qF=p-4, and above4+K it supplies K. Residual demand has a different slope on each branch. With no fringe, profit is(p-2)*(20-p), whose vertex11 lies outside p<=4; the branch maximum is32 at p4. Prices below cost cannot beat a positive-profit candidate, and any zero-demand feasible price gives zero profit.

A cheaper route is to complete each positive-demand branch into a square. With a responsive fringe, qD=24-2*p and profit=50-2*(p-7)^2; this branch requires4<=p<=4+K and p<=12. With a binding capacity, qD=20-K-p and profit=(18-K)^2/4-(p-(11-K/2))^2, requiring p>=4+K and p<=20-K. The candidate pL=7 needs K>=3. The capacity-branch vertex pH=11-K/2 needs K<=14/3. A vertex outside its interval is not a candidate for that interval's global maximum.

For K<3, the responsive branch increases up to its endpoint4+K. The capacity branch still increases there because its vertex lies above the endpoint; its admissible vertex therefore dominates the endpoint and the inactive-fringe branch. Thus the high-price policy is globally optimal. For3<=K<=14/3, both vertices are admissible: their profits are50 and(18-K)^2/4. Their equality gives Kc=18-10*sqrt(2), which lies strictly between3 and14/3. The high-price vertex wins below Kc and the responsive vertex wins above it.

For larger K, I must still exclude a remote capacity-branch maximum. When14/3<K<=8, the capacity vertex is below its branch, so that branch decreases from p=4+K. Its endpoint profit equals the responsive-branch value there and is at most50, strictly below it once K>14/3. For K>8, the binding-capacity branch cannot have positive feasible residual demand at all. The feasible responsive branch still contains7, and the inactive branch reaches only32. This completes the global comparison for all K, rather than stopping after comparing two interior roots.

For the policy map, if K<Kc then p=11-K/2, qF=K and qD=(18-K)/2. If K>Kc then p=7, qF=3 and qD=10. At K=Kc both prices are globally optimal and no other price ties, since both relevant squares are strict. The high price there is2+5*sqrt(2), with qD=5*sqrt(2) and qF=18-10*sqrt(2). Its total output is18-5*sqrt(2). The low price gives total output13. A small capacity increase through Kc selects a discrete change of residual-demand branch.

For continuity, optimized dominant profit is(18-K)^2/4 below Kc and50 above it, with value50 under either policy at the switch. It is continuous, although its left derivative at Kc is-5*sqrt(2) and its right derivative is0. Optimal price falls from2+5*sqrt(2) to7, a drop5*(sqrt(2)-1)>0. A continuous optimized value does not require a continuous maximizing action, especially when two separated maxima exchange their ordering.

For the low-price welfare accounts at Kc, market output13 gives CS=13^2/2=169/2. Fringe supply3 has cost12+9/2, so its profit7*3-12-9/2=9/2. Dominant profit is50. Real welfare is gross benefit20*Q-Q^2/2 minus2*qD and CF(qF), hence139. The profit-plus-surplus ledger gives169/2+50+9/2=139. Capacity exceeds3 here, so fringe marginal cost7 equals price and its capacity is slack.

For the high-price accounts, let r=sqrt(2), Kc=18-10*r and pH=2+5*r. The capacity binds and fringe profit is(pH-4)*Kc-Kc^2/2=290*r-398. Its final-unit marginal cost is4+Kc=22-10*r, below pH by15*r-20>0. That positive gap is the capacity scarcity rent per extra marginal unit; it is not an extra resource cost. Consumer surplus is(18-5*r)^2/2=187-90*r. Adding it to dominant profit50 and fringe profit yields W_H=200*r-161.

For the independent efficiency check, the cheaper dominant technology can produce all efficient output: maximizing18*Q-Q^2/2 gives Q*=18 and W*=162, with no fringe production. For any actual qF and Q, the welfare loss is(18-Q)^2/2+2*qF+qF^2/2. The first term is lost total-output surplus; the other terms are extra real costs from using the more expensive fringe. At the low policy this is25/2+6+9/2=23, giving139. At the high policy it is25+2*Kc+Kc^2/2=323-200*r, giving200*r-161. Both match the transfer ledgers.

For the welfare jump, W_L-W_H=300-200*sqrt(2)>0. Consumer surplus rises by90*sqrt(2)-205/2, while dominant profit is unchanged and fringe profit falls from290*sqrt(2)-398 to9/2. Their changes sum to the same welfare gain. At exactly Kc, welfare depends on which optimal dominant price is selected; profit maximization alone does not resolve that tie. The high-price regime induces costly fringe production and lower total output despite the fringe's capacity being fully utilized.

General pattern: I should identify residual-demand slopes, certify branch maxima and compare their values globally. A capacity kink can create separated local maxima and a discontinuous policy switch while optimized profit stays continuous. Scarcity rents belong in the transfer ledger, while welfare subtracts actual production costs. A completed output-loss square independently checks both equilibria and distinguishes the quantity distortion from the allocation of production.
reference_answer:
Let Kc=18-10*sqrt(2). For K<Kc the unique optimum is p=11-K/2, qF=K, qD=(18-K)/2. For K>Kc it is p7,qF3,qD10. At Kc both policies are optimal, with dominant profit50; no other price ties. Optimized profit is continuous, but price drops by5*(sqrt(2)-1) when the selected optimum switches to the low-price branch.

At the tie, the low policy gives CS169/2, fringe profit9/2 and welfare139. The high policy gives CS187-90*sqrt(2), fringe profit290*sqrt(2)-398 and welfare200*sqrt(2)-161. Switching low raises welfare300-200*sqrt(2).

Efficient production uses only the dominant technology, Q18 and W162. The loss formula(18-Q)^2/2+2*qF+qF^2/2 confirms both welfare accounts. Global optimality follows from branch-valid completed squares, not a single first-order condition.

problem: How many independent observations are needed to estimate a population mean with known standard deviation12, a 95% normal-approximation margin of error no greater than3, using z=1.96? Show why the final sample size must be rounded upward.
thinking:
The margin condition is1.96·12/√n≤3. Squaring positive sides gives n≥(1.96·12/3)^2=38416/625=61.4656.

Since n counts observations and the inequality is a minimum precision requirement, the smallest feasible integer is the ceiling:62. Rounding to61 would violate the target even though it is numerically close.

At n=62 the margin is about2.987, below3; at n=61 it is about3.011, above3. The integer boundary check confirms the ceiling operation rather than ordinary nearest-integer rounding.

As a check, doubling the target margin would divide required sample size by four, because margin varies as1/√n. The noninteger threshold61.4656 scales quadratically with the desired precision.

General pattern: For a known-variance normal margin, required sample size is the squared ratio of critical value times standard deviation to target error. Always round upward to preserve the inequality.
reference_answer: The minimum sample size is n=62.

problem: A firm chooses outputs x and y with revenue 12x+8y and cost x²+2y², subject to x+y=4 and x,y≥0. Find its profit-maximizing mix and profit.
thinking:
Before solving two unconstrained FOCs, substitute y=4−x. Profit becomes 12x+8(4−x)−x²−2(4−x)², a concave quadratic on [0,4].

Its derivative is 20−6x, so x=10/3 and y=2/3. The second derivative −6 proves a global maximum; the solution lies inside the feasible interval.

Profit is 12·10/3+8·2/3−(10/3)²−2(2/3)²=100/3. The tangency condition equates net marginal returns: 12−2x=8−4y, which gives the same mix with x+y=4.

General pattern: eliminate a linear constraint first, then use concavity and boundary checks to turn a stationary point into a global solution.
reference_answer: The optimal mix is (x,y)=(10/3,2/3), with profit 100/3.

problem: An approximate IV variance formula is σ²/[n Var(Z) π₁²], where π₁ is the first-stage effect. Take σ²=4, n=1000, Var(Z)=1/4, and π₁=0.1. Compute the variance, then recompute it if the first stage doubles.
thinking:
Substituting gives4/[1000·(1/4)·0.1²]=4/2.5=1.6. The first-stage coefficient is squared in the denominator, so doubling it multiplies the information term by four.

At π₁=0.2 the variance is4/[1000·(1/4)·0.2²]=0.4, one quarter of1.6. The standard error halves, from√1.6 to√0.4, because uncertainty scales inversely with the magnitude of the first stage.

This approximation isolates the weak-instrument channel while holding sample size, instrument variation, and structural noise fixed. It does not by itself describe finite-sample bias or guarantee valid normal confidence intervals when π₁ is near zero.

As a check, n Var(Z)π₁² rises from2.5 to10 when π₁ doubles, exactly fourfold; its reciprocal variance therefore falls from1.6 to0.4.

General pattern: IV precision depends quadratically on first-stage strength. A weak instrument amplifies variance sharply, so relevance is both an identification condition and a precision condition.
reference_answer: Approximate variance is1.6 at π₁=0.1 and0.4 at π₁=0.2; doubling the first stage quarters variance.

problem: The risk-free return is2%, the market's expected return is8%, and a stock has beta1.5. Use the CAPM to find its required expected return. If its forecast return is13%, compute Jensen's alpha.
thinking:
CAPM prices only systematic risk: required return is r_f+β(E[r_m]−r_f)=2+1.5(8−2)=11%.

The forecast exceeds that benchmark by13−11=2 percentage points, so Jensen's alpha is2%. It is abnormal performance relative to the stock's market exposure, conditional on CAPM being the correct pricing model.

Beta scales the market risk premium, not the market return itself. Multiplying1.5 by8% and then adding the risk-free rate would double-count the safe component.

As a check, beta one would imply the market return8%; beta zero would imply2%. The linear formula gives11% at beta1.5, exactly halfway between those values and beyond the market by half a premium.

General pattern: CAPM required return is the risk-free rate plus beta times the market risk premium. Alpha is forecast or realized return minus this risk-adjusted benchmark.
reference_answer: CAPM required return=11%. Jensen's alpha=2 percentage points.

problem: Un monopole de coût marginal 2 vend sur deux segments séparables avec demandes qA=max(0,10-pA) et qB=max(0,6-pB). Comparez la tarification uniforme pA=pB et la discrimination du troisième degré. Calculez les quantités, profits, surplus des consommateurs et surplus total. La discrimination améliore-t-elle nécessairement le bien-être si la quantité totale ne change pas? Donnez aussi le résultat sous discrimination parfaite du premier degré avec extraction intégrale du surplus.
thinking:
Avant de résoudre le prix uniforme, je dois garder le seuil de demande du second segment. Pour 0<=p<=6, la quantité totale est 16-2*p et le profit est (p-2)*(16-2*p)=18-2*(p-5)^2. Son maximum est 18 à p=5. Pour 6<=p<=10, seul A achète et le profit est (p-2)*(10-p)=16-(p-6)^2, au plus 16. Au-delà de 10 le profit est nul. Le maximum global uniforme est donc p=5, avec (qA,qB)=(5,1).

Pour la discrimination du troisième degré, les profits sont séparables. Les conditions 10-2*qA-2=0 et 6-2*qB-2=0 donnent qA=4,qB=2, avec prix 6 et 4. Les profits sont 16 et 4, donc total 20. La quantité totale reste 6, comme sous prix uniforme, mais une unité passe du segment A au segment B.

Pour évaluer les ressources, le surplus total est W=8*qA-qA^2/2+4*qB-qB^2/2. Au prix uniforme, W=31 et CS=(5^2+1^2)/2=13; ajouter profit 18 vérifie 31. Avec discrimination, W=30 et CS=(4^2+2^2)/2=10; ajouter profit 20 vérifie 30. Le gain privé 2 s'accompagne d'une perte sociale 1.

Pour découvrir pourquoi la quantité totale ne suffit pas, je minimise la perte à total 6 fixé. En posant qB=6-qA, le surplus devient 31-(qA-5)^2. Le prix uniforme répartit donc efficacement cette quantité entre segments, car leurs bénéfices marginaux sont égaux à 5. La discrimination choisit qA=4 et perd exactement 1. La conclusion suit d'un carré complété, sans énumérer des allocations.

Pour la discrimination parfaite, le vendeur peut extraire chaque disposition marginale à payer. Il produit jusqu'au coût marginal: qA=8,qB=4, donnant W=8^2/2+4^2/2=40. Tout ce surplus est capté comme profit et CS=0 selon l'hypothèse d'extraction intégrale. Le bien-être et sa répartition doivent rester distincts.

Un contrôle indépendant emploie le déficit quadratique à l'optimum efficace. La perte sous prix uniforme est ((8-5)^2+(4-1)^2)/2=9, donc W=40-9=31. Avec discrimination elle est ((8-4)^2+(4-2)^2)/2=10, donc W=30. Les deux méthodes concordent et montrent que le déplacement inter-segments peut compter autant que le volume total.

General pattern: je dois traiter les seuils de demande avant de comparer les politiques de prix. À volume total identique, l'allocation entre segments peut modifier le bien-être. Un carré complété sépare cette perte réelle du transfert de surplus vers le vendeur.
reference_answer:
Le prix uniforme optimal est 5, avec quantités (5,1), profit 18, surplus consommateur 13 et bien-être 31. La discrimination du troisième degré choisit prix (6,4), quantités (4,2), profit 20, surplus consommateur 10 et bien-être 30.

Les deux politiques vendent 6 unités, mais la discrimination dégrade leur allocation: à ce volume W=31-(qA-5)^2. La discrimination parfaite produit (8,4), atteint le bien-être 40 et l'extrait entièrement comme profit sous l'hypothèse donnée.

problem: Parmi 11 entiers, montre qu'il y en a deux dont la différence est divisible par 10. Je cherche l'idée structurelle, pas un examen de toutes les paires.
thinking:
Avant de comparer des paires, je partitionne les entiers par leur reste modulo10. Il n'existe que10 classes de restes pour11 objets. Le principe des tiroirs force deux entiers dans la même classe.

S'ils ont le même reste r, ils s'écrivent10a+r et10b+r; leur différence est10(a−b), donc divisible par10. La preuve utilise seulement la structure du quotient Z/10Z, pas la taille des entiers.

La borne est exacte: les dix nombres0 à9 occupent chacun une classe distincte et aucune paire n'a une différence divisible par10. Ajouter un onzième entier déclenche nécessairement une collision de classe.

General pattern: remplacer les valeurs par leurs classes d'équivalence, puis comparer nombre d'objets et nombre de classes. Une collision dans le quotient devient une relation de divisibilité dans les entiers.
reference_answer: Deux des 11 entiers ont nécessairement la même classe modulo 10; leur différence est donc divisible par 10.

problem: A map sends the unit square by the matrix [[2,1],[1,2]]. I need its area factor and orientation, plus the image area of the triangle with vertices (0,0),(1,0),(0,1). Can the determinant answer all three?
thinking:
Before transforming the vertices, I should use the determinant as the signed area multiplier. The matrix determinant is 4−1=3, positive, so areas triple and orientation is preserved. This is the exterior-product trick: the determinant measures how the map acts on an oriented area element.

The unit square therefore maps to a parallelogram of area3. The original triangle has area1/2, hence its image has area3/2. This conclusion needs no coordinate-by-coordinate polygon reconstruction because a linear map scales every planar area by the same determinant magnitude.

As an independent check, the image basis vectors are (2,1) and (1,2); the parallelogram area is |2·2−1·1|=3. The triangle is half that parallelogram. Positivity of the determinant also agrees with the preserved orientation.

General pattern: for a linear map, determinant is the signed volume scale. Compute it once, then transfer all areas or volumes uniformly; use a transformed basis parallelepiped as a geometric check.
reference_answer: The area factor is 3, orientation is preserved, and the triangle image has area 3/2.

problem: Two firms choose quantities under p=1-q1-q2. Firm1 has zero cost. Firm2 privately observes a unit cost that is0 or1/3 with probability1/2 each. Find Bayesian Cournot quantities and expected profits. Then suppose firm2's realised cost is publicly revealed before quantities are chosen. Compare expected profits, consumer surplus and resource welfare under revelation. Use equality of expected total quantities and a variance identity to explain the consumer result. Check the high-cost profit directly from price minus unit cost; clarify which Cournot profit identity holds for firm1 in expectation rather than in every realised state.
thinking:
Before replacing a private cost by its average, I should solve the type-contingent response. Let qL,qH denote firm2's quantities and q1 the uninformed firm's fixed quantity. Conditions are2*q1+(qL+qH)/2=1,2*qL+q1=1 and2*qH+q1=2/3. They give q1=7/18,qL=11/36,qH=5/36. Strict own concavity verifies each response; both types produce positive quantities.

For profits, each informed type satisfies p-cost=its own quantity, so profits are qL^2 and qH^2. In the high state, price is1-7/18-5/36=17/36 and unit cost1/3=12/36; the margin is5/36, giving profit25/1296. Expected firm2 profit is(121+25)/2592=73/1296. Cost must be subtracted from the whole price, not from a price numerator before division.

For the uninformed firm, its expected first-order condition implies E[p]=q1, hence expected profit q1^2=49/324. State profits are instead(11/36)*(7/18)=77/648 and(17/36)*(7/18)=119/648. Their average is49/324, but neither state profit equals q1^2. The markup identity follows the information set under which the firm optimises.

With public revelation, the low-cost state has quantities (1/3,1/3) and the high-cost state (4/9,1/9). Expected profits are25/162 for firm1 and5/81 for firm2. Their increases are1/324 and7/1296. Ex ante both firms benefit from public information here; that does not by itself establish a truthful disclosure mechanism. The high-cost type's profit falls from25/1296 under secrecy to1/81 after revelation, while the low-cost type gains.

For consumer surplus, total output is25/36 or19/36 under private information and2/3 or5/9 after revelation. Both means are11/18. The private-information variance is1/144, and the public-information variance1/324. Since consumer surplus is Q^2/2, equal means make its expected change half the variance change: (1/2)*(1/324-1/144)=-5/2592. Expected consumer surplus falls from493/2592 to61/324 despite unchanged mean output.

To combine welfare, add producer profits to consumer surplus because costs are already subtracted in profits. Private-information welfare is1031/2592; public-information welfare is131/324=1048/2592. The gain17/2592 equals the profit increase1/324+7/1296 minus the consumer loss5/2592. Lower output variance hurts consumers for this convex surplus function but does not offset the producer gains.

An independent primitive check computes W=Q-Q^2/2-c2*q2 in each state and averages with equal weights. It gives the same welfare values, so neither the unit-cost accounting nor the informational profit identity has introduced an extra transfer or omitted real production cost. The variance route explains the consumer comparison without another long expansion of both squares.

General pattern: I should condition informed actions on types and apply first-order identities at the correct information set. Equal mean quantities allow a variance decomposition of expected surplus. Ex ante information value and each realised type's disclosure incentive are separate questions.
reference_answer:
Private-information quantities are q1=7/18,qL=11/36,qH=5/36; expected profits are49/324 and73/1296. Public revelation raises them to25/162 and5/81, gains1/324 and7/1296.

Mean output stays11/18, but its variance falls, reducing expected consumer surplus by5/2592. Resource welfare rises by17/2592 to131/324. Firm1's profit identity q1^2 holds in expectation; high-type firm2 profit is exactly(17/36-1/3)*(5/36)=25/1296.

problem: Comment résoudre ce problème de bénévolat quand chacun connaît seulement son propre coût? Trois personnes choisissent simultanément de participer ou non. Le projet est réalisé dès qu'une personne participe, et procure à chacune un bénéfice1. Chaque participant paie son propre coût Ci, indépendamment du nombre de participants; les coûts sont indépendants et uniformes sur[0,1], et chacun observe seulement le sien. Trouve l'équilibre bayésien symétrique en stratégies de seuil, la probabilité d'échec, le coût total espéré et la somme des gains espérés. Compare avec un planificateur connaissant les trois coûts, qui peut désigner un seul participant. Explique la généralisation de l'équation de seuil à n personnes, sans supposer que tous les équilibres sont symétriques.
thinking:
Avant de rendre les stratégies aléatoires, je dois conditionner sur mon coût. Participer garantit le bénéfice1 et me coûte c. Ne pas participer donne le bénéfice1 seulement si au moins un autre participe. La différence de gains est donc P(aucun autre ne participe)-c. Elle décroît strictement en c, ce qui découvre directement une stratégie de seuil plutôt qu'une liste de réponses par type.

Pour un seuil commun tau, une personne participe avec probabilité tau puisque son coût est uniforme. L'indépendance donne P(aucun des deux autres ne participe)=(1-tau)^2. La condition d'indifférence au seuil est tau=(1-tau)^2, donc tau^2-3*tau+1=0. La seule racine dans[0,1] est tau=(3-sqrt(5))/2; l'autre dépasse1. Le gain de participation est positif en dessous du seuil et négatif au-dessus, ce qui vérifie tous les types sauf l'indifférence de probabilité nulle au seuil.

Pour prouver l'unicité symétrique autrement, la fonction(1-tau)^2-tau décroît strictement sur[0,1], vaut1 à0 et -1 à1. Elle possède donc exactement un zéro admissible. Cette preuve porte sur l'équilibre symétrique; elle ne permet pas d'écarter des équilibres asymétriques, par exemple un participant toujours désigné et les autres abstentionnistes, à des types indifférents de probabilité nulle près.

Pour la probabilité d'échec, les trois coûts doivent dépasser le seuil: P(echec)=(1-tau)^3. L'équation du seuil donne(1-tau)^3=tau*(1-tau)=sqrt(5)-2. La probabilité de réalisation vaut3-sqrt(5). J'utilise le polynôme minimal de tau pour réduire les puissances, plutôt que développer des radicaux de plus en plus longs.

Pour le coût espéré, chaque personne paie Ci uniquement quand Ci<=tau, donc E[Ci*indicator(Ci<=tau)]=integral de0 àtau de c=tau^2/2. Le coût total espéré est3*tau^2/2=(21-9*sqrt(5))/4. Les trois bénéfices valent au total3 en cas de réalisation. La somme des gains espérés est3*(3-sqrt(5))-(21-9*sqrt(5))/4=(15-3*sqrt(5))/4. La contribution propre d'un participant n'est pas remboursée quand un autre participe aussi.

Pour le planificateur informé, le bénéfice total3 dépasse toujours le plus petit coût, qui appartient à[0,1]. Il réalise donc toujours le projet et choisit la personne au coût minimal. La survie de ce minimum est P(min Ci>x)=(1-x)^3 sur[0,1]; son espérance est integral de0 à1 de(1-x)^3=1/4. Le surplus informé est3-1/4=11/4. L'écart avec l'équilibre symétrique est(3*sqrt(5)-4)/4, strictement positif.

Pour une vérification indépendante des gains individuels, un type c<=tau obtient1-c, tandis qu'un type c>tau obtient1-(1-tau)^2=1-tau. L'intégrale des gains sur les types est tau-tau^2/2+(1-tau)^2=1-tau+tau^2/2. Trois fois cette expression se simplifie en(15-3*sqrt(5))/4 grâce à tau^2=3*tau-1. Elle coïncide avec bénéfices moins coûts.

Pour n personnes, le même argument donne tau_n=(1-tau_n)^(n-1), avec un unique seuil symétrique dans(0,1) pour n>=2. L'échec vaut(1-tau_n)^n=tau_n*(1-tau_n). Si tau_n restait supérieur à une constante positive sur une sous-suite, le membre droit de l'équation du seuil tendrait vers0, contradiction; donc tau_n tend vers0 et la probabilité d'échec aussi. Une moindre participation individuelle peut accompagner une réalisation presque certaine dans un grand groupe.

General pattern: je dois transformer l'incitation privée en différence de gains conditionnelle, puis exploiter l'indépendance pour fermer l'équation du seuil. Le polynôme minimal réduit les moments; la survie d'un minimum calcule le coût informé. Un équilibre symétrique unique n'est pas une preuve d'unicité parmi toutes les stratégies asymétriques.
reference_answer:
Le seuil symétrique est tau=(3-sqrt(5))/2, solution admissible de tau=(1-tau)^2. L'échec a probabilité sqrt(5)-2, le coût total espéré vaut(21-9*sqrt(5))/4 et le surplus espéré(15-3*sqrt(5))/4.

Le planificateur réalise toujours le projet avec le coût minimal, d'espérance1/4, donc atteint11/4; le gain par rapport à l'équilibre symétrique est(3*sqrt(5)-4)/4. Avec n personnes, tau_n=(1-tau_n)^(n-1) et l'échec vaut tau_n*(1-tau_n), qui tend vers0. L'unicité établie est seulement symétrique.

problem: A graph has vertices of degrees 1,2,3,4,5. Is that degree sequence possible for a simple graph? Find the contradiction without trying to draw candidate graphs.
thinking:
Before applying a realization algorithm, use the handshake parity invariant. The degree sum is1+2+3+4+5=15, which is odd. Every edge contributes2 to the sum, so no graph can have this degree sequence.

This obstruction is decisive regardless of how edges might be arranged. A graphical-sequence algorithm would eventually reject it, but parity detects impossibility immediately.

A quick repair check shows why parity matters: changing any one degree by1 could make the sum even, though that alone would not guarantee graphicality. Parity is necessary, not sufficient, for a degree sequence to exist.

General pattern: test global invariants before constructing a combinatorial object. Parity can rule out an entire family of candidate structures at zero search cost.
reference_answer: No. The degree sum is 15, but every graph has an even degree sum.

problem:
Does fixing the final price really reproduce integration if the retailer also chooses sales effort? First audit a no-effort claim. Demand is q=max(0,1-p), production cost is c=1/5, and a monopolist retailer buys at wholesale price w. Under ordinary sequential wholesale pricing, its outside profit is1/25 and the upstream outside profit is2/25. Impose a resale-price ceiling p<=3/5 and restrict w to[1/5,3/5], with no fixed payment. Determine the retailer's chosen price, its profit and the wholesale-price interval making both firms weakly prefer this arrangement to their outside profits. The source suggests the retailer strictly gains whenever w<3/5: is that correct?

Now consider a different, explicit effort model, with outside profit0 and acceptance at indifference. Demand is q=max(0,1+e-p), where the retailer chooses effort e>=0 and pays the real cost e^2. Production still costs1/5 per unit; the upstream firm has no effort cost. First find the globally optimal integrated price, effort, quantity and profit. A binding resale-price contract then fixes that integrated price, but lets the upstream firm choose w between c and that price, with no fixed fee. The retailer chooses effort after accepting. Find the upstream optimum and resulting effort, quantity and both profits. Calculate real welfare, using gross consumer benefit(1+e)*q-q^2/2 and subtracting production and effort costs. Finally, use a two-part tariff with w=c and nonnegative fixed fee F to reproduce the integrated outcome; find all participation-compatible fees and the upstream-optimal one. Prove the optima analytically and explain the missing marginal incentive.
thinking:
Before judging the no-effort claim, I should compare profit with the stated outside option. The retailer's unconstrained price is(1+w)/2, at least3/5 on the specified wholesale interval. Thus it chooses the ceiling p=3/5 and sells2/5. Its profit is(3/5-w)*(2/5), and the upstream firm's is(w-1/5)*(2/5). Retailer participation requires(3/5-w)*(2/5)>=1/25, hence w<=1/2. Upstream participation requires(w-1/5)*(2/5)>=2/25, hence w>=2/5. Both weakly gain exactly for w in[2/5,1/2], and both strictly gain in its interior.

For the source claim, w<3/5 ensures only a positive retail margin, not a profit above1/25. For example w=11/20 gives retail profit(1/20)*(2/5)=1/50, below the outside profit. The correct strict-gain bound is w<1/2. At the two participation endpoints, profits are(2/25,2/25) for w=2/5 and(3/25,1/25) for w=1/2, written upstream then retailer. They always sum to the integrated no-effort profit4/25. This independent budget identity confirms the gain is a redistribution within the channel, not an extra production cost.

For the effort model, I should change variables from price to quantity before optimising. With positive sales, p=1+e-q. Integrated profit is(4/5)*q+e*q-q^2-e^2. Completing the effort square gives(4/5)*q-3*q^2/4-(e-q/2)^2. Completing the remaining quantity square gives16/75-(3/4)*(q-8/15)^2-(e-q/2)^2. Therefore the unique global optimum has q=8/15,e=4/15 and p=1+4/15-8/15=11/15, with profit16/75. The nonnegative quantity, effort and price constraints are satisfied. Zero sales give at most0, so they cannot improve on this positive optimum.

For the fixed resale price, denote P=11/15 and the retail margin M=P-w>=0. The retailer's effort objective is M*(1+e-P)-e^2. Completing the square, or differentiating, gives e=M/2 uniquely. Its quantity is1-P+M/2=19/30-w/2. This is positive throughout w in[1/5,P]. Retail profit after effort is M*(1-P)+M^2/4>=0, so the specified zero-outside-option retailer accepts, including the zero-margin endpoint.

For the upstream optimum without a fixed fee, its profit is(w-1/5)*(19/30-w/2). This concave quadratic equals32/225-(w-11/15)^2/2. Hence the unique optimum on the wholesale interval is w=P=11/15. Retail margin and effort become0, quantity falls to1-P=4/15, upstream profit is32/225 and retail profit0. The final price equals the integrated price, but effort and sales do not. Extracting the whole per-unit margin removes the retailer's incentive to expand demand.

For real welfare, I should return to primitives rather than count wholesale payments. W=(1+e)*q-q^2/2-(1/5)*q-e^2=(4/5)*q+e*q-q^2/2-e^2. At the integrated effort choice(q,e)=(8/15,4/15), this gives16/45. At the resale-price-only outcome(4/15,0), it gives8/45. Consumer surplus is q^2/2 in either case:128/225? I should square carefully: at q=8/15 it is32/225, and at q=4/15 it is8/225. Adding channel profits16/75=48/225 or32/225 gives80/225=16/45 or40/225=8/45, independently verifying both welfare values.

For restoring the incentive, wholesale price w=c leaves the retailer the same marginal return as the integrated firm. Its objective before any fixed fee is precisely the integrated profit, so it chooses q=8/15,e=4/15,p=11/15. A fixed fee F is sunk when it chooses price and effort, and therefore does not alter these first-order conditions. The retailer participates exactly when16/75-F>=0. Every F in[0,16/75] is compatible with its zero outside option; upstream profit is F and retail profit16/75-F. The upstream optimum is F=16/75, extracting all profit while preserving the marginal effort incentive.

For the contractual distinction, the no-effort audit used the positive separated outside profits stated there; the effort extension deliberately used outside profit0. I should not transfer a participation bound between these different benchmarks. In both, the principle is the same: a level payment must leave sufficient profit for acceptance, while a per-unit margin shapes subsequent choices. A fixed final price controls one choice but cannot by itself make a retailer with zero sales margin supply costly effort.

General pattern: I should separate positive margins from participation gains and distinguish price control from incentive alignment. Quantity substitution and completed squares certify joint optima; wholesale margins determine effort, whereas a sunk fixed fee can redistribute profit without changing that marginal reward. Welfare counts gross benefit minus real costs, with internal payments cancelling.
reference_answer:
Without effort, the retailer chooses p=3/5 and sells2/5. Its profit is(3/5-w)*2/5, so it strictly improves on1/25 exactly when w<1/2, not whenever w<3/5. Both firms weakly gain for w in[2/5,1/2].

With effort, integration uniquely gives p=11/15,e=4/15,q=8/15, profit16/75 and welfare16/45. Under a contract fixing that price, retailer effort is(11/15-w)/2. The upstream optimum is w=11/15, giving effort0, quantity4/15, upstream profit32/225, retail profit0 and welfare8/45. Fixing price therefore does not reproduce integration.

A two-part tariff with w=1/5 restores the integrated choices. All fees F in[0,16/75] satisfy participation; the upstream-optimal fee is16/75. The fixed fee extracts profit while leaving the retailer's marginal sales-effort incentive intact. Completed-square identities prove the global optima, and consumer surplus plus channel profit independently verifies welfare.

problem:
A tariff raises government revenue, so a colleague says the larger the tariff the better. Can you compare the revenue and national-welfare optima for a small country and a country that affects the world price?

Domestic inverse demand is p_D=20-Q_D and inverse domestic supply is p_S=Q_S, with quantities nonnegative. Tariff revenue is rebated lump-sum to domestic residents. Under free trade, a small country faces fixed world price6. With a per-unit tariff t>=0 and positive imports, its domestic price is6+t. Under the large-country case, foreign inverse export supply is p_W=4+M, where M is imports; domestic arbitrage gives p_D=p_W+t. For each case solve market clearing, including the prohibitive-tariff boundary where imports vanish.

Derive tariff revenue and national welfare as functions of t, treating tariff receipts as a domestic transfer and payments to foreign exporters as a national outflow. Find the revenue-maximizing tariff and the welfare-maximizing tariff in each case. At t=2 compare prices, imports, revenue and welfare across the two country sizes. For the large country also evaluate the welfare optimum and prove it is globally optimal on the feasible tariff interval. Explain precisely why the small-country and large-country answers differ.
thinking:
Before optimizing policy, I solve market clearing. Domestic net import demand is Q_D-Q_S=(20-p)-p=20-2p. A small country therefore imports M=8-2*t while t<4, at domestic price6+t; for t>=4 imports are zero and the domestic price is the autarky price10. A large country instead satisfies M=20-2*(4+M+t), hence M=4-2*t/3 for0<=t<6. Its prices are p_W=8-2*t/3 and p_D=8+t/3. At t>=6 imports vanish; the domestic price is the autarky price10 and the foreign price is4. A higher tariff changes neither price nor trade.

For the small country, tariff revenue is t*(8-2*t). Domestic consumer and producer surplus sum to their free-trade value116 minus the real distortion t^2, so national welfare is116-t^2 on0<=t<=4. Revenue is a concave quadratic maximized at t=2, yielding8; welfare is maximized at free trade t=0. At t=4 trade is zero and welfare100, consistent with the formula. A tariff transfers part of surplus to residents but creates a triangular production-consumption loss.

For the large country I keep the foreign price endogenous. Domestic surplus plus tariff receipts is(20-p_D)^2/2+p_D^2/2+t*M. Substituting market clearing gives104+8*t/3-5*t^2/9, a strictly concave quadratic. Its derivative is8/3-10*t/9, so the unique welfare maximum on[0,6] is t=12/5. Revenue t*(4-2*t/3) is separately maximized at t=3. The revenue peak is not the welfare peak because a higher tariff changes both import volume and the price paid to foreign suppliers.

At t=2, the small country has domestic price8, world price6, imports4, revenue8 and welfare112. The large country has world price20/3, domestic price26/3, imports8/3 and revenue16/3. Its welfare is964/9. The price wedge raises the domestic price less in the large country because part of the tariff is absorbed by a fall in the foreign price.

At the large-country welfare optimum t=12/5, imports are12/5, world price32/5 and domestic price44/5. Revenue is144/25 and welfare536/5, compared with104 under free trade. Global optimality follows from the negative quadratic coefficient-5/9 and the interior derivative root. The small-country national optimum remains zero tariff because it cannot improve its terms of trade; the large country can transfer part of the tariff burden to foreign exporters. That strategic gain is a transfer across borders, not a disappearance of resource costs.

General pattern: I solve the equilibrium price first, then separate domestic surplus, fiscal transfers and foreign payments. A tariff’s revenue peak does not generally maximize national welfare. Market power changes the price paid abroad and creates a terms-of-trade motive absent for a price-taking country.
reference_answer:
For a small country with positive imports, M=8-2*t and p=6+t,0<=t<=4. Revenue is t*(8-2*t), maximized at t=2 with8. National welfare is116-t^2, maximized at t=0; at t=2 it is112. For t>=4 imports are zero.

For the large country, M=4-2*t/3, p_W=8-2*t/3 and p_D=8+t/3 for0<=t<=6. Revenue is t*(4-2*t/3), maximized at t=3. National welfare is104+8*t/3-5*t^2/9, maximized at t=12/5 with value536/5. At that optimum M=12/5, p_W=32/5, p_D=44/5 and revenue144/25.

At t=2, the large country has M=8/3, prices(p_D,p_W)=(26/3,20/3), revenue16/3 and welfare964/9. Its ability to lower the foreign price creates a terms-of-trade gain; the small country cannot do so.

problem:
How can I regulate this service without pretending subsidies are free? I found two prices that cover costs, and I don't know which one is sensible. Please connect the algebra to the welfare decision.

Inverse demand is p=a-b*q, with b>0 and s=a-c>0. Operating costs are c*q+F, with c>=0 and an avoidable real fixed cost F>=0. Shutdown incurs no costs and gives welfare0. A regulator can require a uniform price p>=c, hence an output q in(0,s/b], and provide a lump-sum operating subsidy S>=0. Firm participation requires (p-c)*q-F+S>=0; at equality it operates. The regulator chooses the minimum subsidy satisfying participation. Every unit of subsidy creates an additional real funding loss lambda>=0, beyond the fixed cost already counted. Subsidy payments themselves are transfers.

Derive the efficient output if funding has no excess cost, the operating threshold, and all positive-output break-even roots without subsidy. Explain why the larger root is the best break-even allocation and when no break-even service exists despite positive real gains from operating.

Then solve the regulator's global problem for all F>=0 and lambda>=0. Identify the threshold where subsidy use begins, the optimal subsidized output, and the shutdown threshold. Check regime boundaries and indifference. A local first-order condition is insufficient because the required subsidy is a positive-part function and shutdown is available.

At a12,c2,b1 and lambda1, compare the optimal policy for F16 and F30. For F16 compute both break-even quantities, the monopoly outcome, the efficient marginal-cost outcome and the policy's funding-adjusted welfare. For F30 give the optimal price, subsidy, real welfare and funding-adjusted welfare. Verify resource welfare by consumer surplus plus net firm profit minus subsidy before applying the excess funding loss. No grid over prices is needed.
thinking:
Before pricing, I should separate operating revenue, real surplus and financing. At quantity q, the variable-cost margin revenue is R(q)=q*(s-b*q). Real welfare is W(q)=s*q-b*q^2/2-F when the service operates. Participation requires S(q)=max(0,F-R(q)). Funding-adjusted welfare is J(q)=W(q)-lambda*S(q). The fixed cost F is already a real resource cost; subtracting the subsidy itself from W again would count its financing transfer twice.

For the no-funding-cost benchmark, completing the square gives W(q)=s^2/(2*b)-F-(b/2)*(q-s/b)^2. Efficient output is qE=s/b at price c. Operating is strictly better than shutdown if F<s^2/(2*b), equally good at equality, and worse above it. Marginal-cost pricing needs subsidy F. This subsidy does not change W when lambda0, but its excess funding loss matters when lambda>0.

For break-even prices, I should solve R(q)=F rather than divide by q before checking its domain. The two roots are q_minus=(s-sqrt(s^2-4*b*F))/(2*b) and q_plus=(s+sqrt(s^2-4*b*F))/(2*b), existing when F<=M=s^2/(4*b). For0<F<M both are positive. At F0, the lower root0 is not an operating average-cost price; only the positive upper root is relevant. At FM the roots coalesce at the monopoly quantity s/(2*b). Above M no output can cover the fixed cost without subsidy.

For the welfare ranking, W is increasing throughout0<=q<=s/b. Thus among nonnegative-profit unsubsidized outputs, the largest feasible output q_plus maximizes welfare. At either positive break-even root, F=s*q-b*q^2, so W=b*q^2/2, exactly consumer surplus because net firm profit is0. The larger root therefore dominates the smaller one. If M<F<s^2/(2*b), no unsubsidized service is viable even though real operating gains are positive. Private cost recovery and social viability use different thresholds.

For a subsidized output, I can temporarily use S=F-R(q). Its adjusted objective becomes J_sub=(1+lambda)*s*q-(1/2+lambda)*b*q^2-(1+lambda)*F. The completed square peaks at qL=(1+lambda)*s/[(1+2*lambda)*b]. The associated revenue is FL=R(qL)=s^2*lambda*(1+lambda)/[b*(1+2*lambda)^2]. Its global peak value is (1+lambda)*[FO-F], where FO=s^2*(1+lambda)/[2*b*(1+2*lambda)]. This branch calculation is valid only where the required subsidy is nonnegative.

For a small fixed cost, F<=FL, the unsubsidized upper root satisfies q_plus>=qL. Between break-even roots, J=W and increases toward q_plus. Above q_plus, the subsidized quadratic is already decreasing because its peak qL lies below the join. Below the lower root, real welfare is smaller and a positive funding loss cannot improve it. Hence the global optimum is q_plus with subsidy0. For lambda0, FL0, so this regime contains only F0 and gives q_plus=qE.

For a larger viable cost, FL<F<FO, qL lies on the subsidized branch and the optimum is qL with S=F-FL. If break-even outputs still exist, the right subsidy region begins below qL, and the concave subsidized branch improves from its join to its peak. If F>M, every output needs subsidy and the same quadratic certificate applies directly. No unsubsidized output can beat the peak. The peak's value is positive exactly when F<FO, establishing both optimal output and operation rather than assuming the service must run.

For the shutdown boundary, F>FO makes every feasible operating allocation worse than0, so shutdown is optimal. At FFO the subsidized output qL and shutdown both give0. The inequalities FL<M<FO<=s^2/(2*b) hold for finite lambda>0; for lambda0, FL0 and FO equals the efficient threshold. At FFL the two output formulas coincide, the subsidy is0 and both objective formulas agree. As lambda grows, qL tends toward the monopoly quantity and FO tends toward the largest privately recoverable fixed cost M.

For the first numerical case, s10, M25, FL200/9 and FO100/3. Since F16<200/9, the optimal policy uses no subsidy. Its break-even roots are2 and8, at prices10 and4. Their real and adjusted welfare values are2 and32. The regulator chooses q8,p4. The monopoly instead chooses q5,p7, earning9; consumer surplus25/2 and welfare43/2. Efficient marginal-cost output10 needs subsidy16, has real welfare34, but adjusted welfare34-16=18. Costly financing makes this higher-output alternative worse than the break-even policy32.

For the second numerical case, F30>M25 but F30<FO100/3, so a subsidized service is optimal. Output is qL20/3, price16/3, margin revenue200/9 and subsidy70/9. Real welfare is10*(20/3)-(20/3)^2/2-30=130/9. Funding-adjusted welfare is130/9-70/9=20/3>0. Marginal-cost output10 would need subsidy30 and yield real welfare20 but adjusted welfare-10. The optimal subsidy supports operation while avoiding the excessively costly full-output policy.

For an independent resource check, I should use consumer surplus CS=b*q^2/2 and firm profit including the subsidy pi_net=R(q)-F+S. Their sum minus subsidy is CS+pi_net-S=W. At F16,q8 this gives32+0-0=32. At F30,q20/3 it gives200/9+0-70/9=130/9. Only afterward do I subtract lambda*S to obtain20/3. The transfer correction and the excess funding loss are different terms, so this route checks the accounting as well as the output calculation.

General pattern: I should solve cost recovery through the revenue parabola, choose the high-output break-even root by welfare monotonicity, and handle the positive-part subsidy at its joins. A completed square certifies the subsidized optimum; comparing its value with shutdown gives the operating threshold. Marginal-cost pricing, average-cost recovery and funding-adjusted welfare are distinct decisions, connected by participation and real-resource accounting.
reference_answer:
Put M=s^2/(4*b), FL=s^2*lambda*(1+lambda)/[b*(1+2*lambda)^2], and FO=s^2*(1+lambda)/[2*b*(1+2*lambda)]. Break-even outputs exist only for F<=M. Their roots are(s±sqrt(s^2-4*b*F))/(2*b); the positive upper root maximizes unsubsidized welfare. The zero lower root at F0 is not an operating price.

For F<=FL, choose the upper root with subsidy0. For FL<F<FO, choose qL=(1+lambda)*s/[(1+2*lambda)*b] and subsidy F-FL. For F>FO, shut down. At FFO, shutdown and operating at qL tie. Without excess funding cost, efficient output is s/b and the operating threshold is s^2/(2*b).

At a12,c2,b1,lambda1, thresholds are FL200/9 and FO100/3. For F16, the roots2,8 give welfare2,32; choose output8,price4 without subsidy. Monopoly welfare is43/2; marginal-cost real welfare34 becomes18 after funding losses. For F30, choose output20/3,price16/3,subsidy70/9,real welfare130/9 and adjusted welfare20/3.

Global optimality follows from welfare monotonicity on the unsubsidized interval, the subsidized completed square and comparison with shutdown. The accounting identity CS+net firm profit-S=W confirms that the subsidy transfer and excess funding loss must be treated separately.

problem: A fair die is rolled once. Find the expected value of (X−3.5)², and explain why this is also the variance without listing six squared deviations.
thinking:
Before expanding around3.5, use symmetry: the die's mean is3.5, so E[(X−3.5)²]=Var(X). For a discrete uniform set1,…,6, the variance formula (n²−1)/12 gives35/12.

I can derive the compact formula by pairing values around the mean: deviations are ±1/2,±3/2,±5/2, so the average squared deviation is [2((1/2)²+(3/2)²+(5/2)²)]/6=(1/4+9/4+25/4)/3=35/12.

The raw-moment check gives E[X²]=91/6 and E[X]²=49/4; their difference is35/12. Centering at the true mean is essential: for any other c, E[(X−c)²]=Var(X)+(c−E[X])².

General pattern: squared error around the mean decomposes into variance plus squared bias. Symmetry or raw moments can compute the variance without treating each outcome as a separate case.

problem: A two-state Markov chain switches states with probability q and stays with probability1−q, where0<q<1. Starting in state 1, find the probability of being in state 1 after n steps without multiplying n matrices.
thinking:
Before iterating a transition matrix, track the signed imbalance d_n=P(state1)−P(state2). A switch reverses the sign and a stay preserves it, so d_(n+1)=(1−2q)d_n.

Initially d_0=1. Hence d_n=(1−2q)^n, while the total probability remains1. Solving the two equations gives P(state1)=[1+(1−2q)^n]/2.

At q=1/2 the imbalance vanishes after one step; at q near0 it decays slowly without sign flips, while q>1/2 makes it alternate. The single eigenmode explains all three regimes.

General pattern: for a symmetric two-state chain, decompose probability into conserved total mass and signed imbalance. The latter is a one-dimensional eigenmode whose power gives the exact transient.

problem: Can you prove my source is reliable? I haven’t shared the source.
thinking: Reliability depends on the source and claim, neither of which is present. Ask for both before judging.
reference_answer: Please share the source and the claim you want checked. I can then look at authorship, evidence, date, and independent confirmation; without them I can’t assess reliability.

problem: Under uncovered interest parity with no risk premium, the domestic nominal interest rate is5%, the foreign rate is3%, and the current exchange rate is1.20 domestic currency per unit of foreign currency. Compute expected percentage depreciation of the domestic currency and the implied expected future exchange rate.
thinking:
UIP equates the domestic return to the foreign return plus expected domestic-currency depreciation. Thus the exact expected depreciation is1.05/1.03−1=2/103, about1.94%; the interest-differential approximation is2%.

Applying the gross-return ratio gives E[S_next]=1.20·1.05/1.03=126/103, about1.2233 domestic currency per foreign unit. A higher quote means the domestic currency is expected to weaken.

The conclusion depends on the quote convention and zero risk premium. Reversing the exchange-rate quote reverses the currency interpretation, so I keep units attached to the ratio.

As a check, a domestic deposit grows by1.05 while the foreign deposit converted at the expected future rate grows by1.03·1.02=1.0506, close but not exactly equal because exact UIP multiplies gross returns rather than adding rates.

General pattern: Uncovered interest parity links the interest differential to expected currency movement, subject to quote convention and risk premium. Exact gross-return parity distinguishes multiplicative from approximate additive rates.
reference_answer: Exact expected depreciation is2/103≈1.94%; the expected future rate is126/103≈1.2233 domestic per foreign unit.

problem:
I estimated different cross-price effects for two goods. Does that mean the demand system cannot come from a utility function? Please check whether changing the value of the consumer's endowment could explain the asymmetry.

A price-taking consumer has utility u(x,y)=x^(1/3)*y^(2/3), x,y>=0, and fixed physical endowment omega=(1,1). At positive prices p1,p2, it can sell the endowment and buy a basket with wealth m=p1+p2; there is initially no cash transfer. The prices are exogenous to this individual problem, not claimed to clear an entire exchange economy. Define Marshallian demand f(p,m) with money wealth held fixed, and gross endowment-financed demand d(p)=f(p,p dot omega).

Derive both demands globally. At prices(1,1), calculate the Jacobian D of d with respect to prices, the money-income derivative g of f, and the consumer's net trade vector. Derive the compensated substitution matrix S using a price change plus the extra cash needed to keep utility fixed while the physical endowment remains unchanged. Explain the correct chain-rule adjustment to D, and check symmetry, negative semidefiniteness and the price null direction. Do not apply a fixed-money-income identity without accounting for endowment revaluation.

Then change prices to(8,1). Find the uncompensated basket and the ratio of its utility to the original level. Find the exact expenditure needed to retain original utility, the additional cash transfer after accounting for the new endowment value, and the compensated basket. A negative transfer means money can be withdrawn while preserving original utility. Check the matrix through Hicksian demand derivatives and the finite compensation through an independent utility calculation.
thinking:
Before testing symmetry, I should specify what is held fixed. For fixed money wealth m>0, maximizing log u=(1/3)*log x+(2/3)*log y subject to p1*x+p2*y<=m gives f1=m/(3*p1),f2=2*m/(3*p2). The log objective is strictly concave on the positive orthant, tends to minus infinity at either axis, and the budget set is bounded. The interior first-order conditions therefore give the unique global demand. With the endowment, substitute m=p1+p2 only after deriving this fixed-income system.

For gross endowment-financed demand, d1=(p1+p2)/(3*p1) and d2=2*(p1+p2)/(3*p2). At prices(1,1), wealth2 and demand(2/3,4/3), so net trade z=d-omega=(-1/3,1/3). The consumer is a net seller of good1 and a net buyer of good2. The total price Jacobian is D=[[-1/3,1/3],[2/3,-2/3]], while the fixed-money-income derivative is g=(1/3,2/3). D12 differs from D21 even though the utility function has been explicitly rationalized.

A cheaper route to the correction uses the chain rule. Let Mp be the price Jacobian of f at fixed m. Since endowment wealth changes by omega dot dp, D=Mp+g*omega^T. To retain utility, total spending must instead change by d dot dp. Thus the extra cash required after endowment revaluation changes by z dot dp=(d-omega) dot dp. Compensated demand derivatives are S=D+g*z^T=Mp+g*d^T. The endowment adjustment uses net trade, not gross consumption, when it starts from the already endowment-adjusted Jacobian D.

For the numerical matrix, g*z^T=[[-1/9,1/9],[-2/9,2/9]]. Adding this to D gives S=[[-4/9,4/9],[4/9,-4/9]]. It is symmetric and S*(1,1)^T=0. For any real direction v=(v1,v2), v^T*S*v=-(4/9)*(v1-v2)^2<=0. This quadratic-form check proves negative semidefiniteness globally across directions without testing many price vectors. Its eigenvalues are0 and-8/9. The correct substitution matrix, rather than the gross price Jacobian, carries the compensated symmetry restriction.

For an independent dual route, fixed-income indirect utility is proportional to m/(p1^(1/3)*p2^(2/3)). Relative to the original attained utility at prices(1,1) and wealth2, the expenditure function is e(p,u0)=2*p1^(1/3)*p2^(2/3). Hicksian demands are h1=(2/3)*p1^(-2/3)*p2^(2/3) and h2=(4/3)*p1^(1/3)*p2^(-1/3). Differentiating them at(1,1) gives exactly S. Equivalently they are the first derivatives of e, so S is its symmetric Hessian. This validates the chain-rule correction through the dual cost-minimization problem.

For the finite price change without compensation, the new endowment wealth is8+1=9. Marshallian demand is x=9/(3*8)=3/8 and y=2*9/3=6. The indirect utility ratio is(9/2)/8^(1/3)=9/4>1. Despite the price increase of good1, this consumer becomes better off because it was a net seller at the original prices and its asset wealth rises. A price increase need not have the fixed-income welfare effect when the endowment finances consumption.

For exact compensation at the new prices, required expenditure is e((8,1),u0)=2*8^(1/3)=4. The additional cash transfer is T=required spending-new endowment wealth=4-9=-5. Withdrawing5 leaves the required wealth4. The compensated basket is x=4/(3*8)=1/6 and y=2*4/3=8/3. Calling this an extra positive compensation would confuse the expenditure increase from2 to4 with the larger endowment revaluation from2 to9.

For an independent finite utility check, cube the utility to remove fractional powers: u^3=x*y^2. At the original basket, this is(2/3)*(4/3)^2=32/27. At the compensated basket it is(1/6)*(8/3)^2=32/27, proving exact utility preservation. At the uncompensated basket it is(3/8)*6^2=27/2. The ratio of these cubes is(27/2)/(32/27)=729/64=(9/4)^3, independently confirming the utility ratio. The compensated budget is8*(1/6)+8/3=4, agreeing with the dual expenditure calculation.

For the local transfer check, along p1=k,p2=1, extra cash is T(k)=2*k^(1/3)-(k+1). Its derivative at k1 is2/3-1=-1/3, equal to the original net trade in good1. The second price's local transfer derivative is4/3-1=1/3, equal to its net purchase. This envelope identity checks the compensation signs and shows why adding g*d^T directly to the gross D would double count endowment income.

General pattern: I should distinguish fixed-money demand derivatives from derivatives that already include asset revaluation. The chain rule adds the endowment-income term; compensation then adjusts for net trade to recover the symmetric substitution matrix. Dual expenditure derivatives and a quadratic-form certificate independently test rational demand restrictions. Finite welfare comparisons require subtracting the new endowment value from required spending, so maintaining utility can call for a withdrawal rather than a payment.
reference_answer:
Fixed-income demand is(m/(3*p1),2*m/(3*p2)); endowment-financed demand uses m=p1+p2. At prices(1,1), demand is(2/3,4/3), net trade(-1/3,1/3), income derivative(1/3,2/3), and D=[[-1/3,1/3],[2/3,-2/3]]. Its asymmetric cross effects do not invalidate rational preferences.

The compensated matrix is S=D+g*(d-omega)^T=[[-4/9,4/9],[4/9,-4/9]]. It is symmetric, has the price null direction, and satisfies v^T*S*v=-(4/9)*(v1-v2)^2. Hicksian derivatives independently reproduce it.

At prices(8,1), the uncompensated basket is(3/8,6), with utility ratio9/4. Required spending for old utility is4, but the endowment is worth9, so the extra transfer is-5. The compensated basket(1/6,8/3) has the same utility cube32/27 as the original basket and costs4. This verifies the welfare calculation exactly.

problem:
Can you help me check this derivation? The correction writes one monopoly condition as 4-6*q2+4*q1=0, but then claims q1=q2=2/5. I want a structural check of the sign, not just the final numbers.

Consumers have quasilinear utility in a numeraire plus V(q1,q2)=5*(q1+q2)-(3*q1^2+4*q1*q2+3*q2^2)/2. Quantities are nonnegative, marginal costs of both goods are1, and numeraire wealth is sufficient for the allocations considered. A single owner can choose any nonnegative quantity vector and charge the associated inverse-demand prices. Its objective is total profit, not social welfare.

First recover inverse and direct demands. Derive the correct monopoly conditions and prove the global optimum using total quantity u=q1+q2 and imbalance d=q1-q2. Explain why the displayed plus sign cannot be correct.

Then consider separate firms choosing prices simultaneously in [1,7/3] each. These explicitly imposed bounds make the direct demand formulas nonnegative at every allowed profile; they do not constrain the single owner's quantity choice. Derive the unique price equilibrium and verify global best responses on these intervals.

Compute prices, quantities, consumer surplus, total profit and total welfare under each ownership regime. Find the globally efficient allocation and the two efficiency ratios. Check the welfare losses using a completed square, and explain why joint ownership internalizes a demand cross effect that separate firms omit.
thinking:
Before solving, I inspect the quadratic matrix A with rows (3,2) and (2,3). Its eigenvalues are5 in the common direction and1 in the difference direction, so it is positive definite. Marginal utility gives p1=5-3*q1-2*q2 and p2=5-2*q1-3*q2. Inverting A yields q1=1-3*p1/5+2*p2/5 and q2=1-3*p2/5+2*p1/5. The positive cross-price derivative2/5 means the products are substitutes. Strict concavity of the consumer objective guarantees the interior demand solution wherever these quantities are nonnegative.

For the sign check, I write total profit from primitives: Pi=(p1-1)*q1+(p2-1)*q2=4*(q1+q2)-3*q1^2-4*q1*q2-3*q2^2. Its derivatives are4-6*q1-4*q2 and4-4*q1-6*q2. Both cross derivatives equal -4, as a single scalar objective requires. The displayed condition with +4*q1 contradicts this gradient and even fails at q1=q2=2/5. The typo is the sign of that cross term; the stated symmetric solution belongs to the correctly differentiated objective.

For a cheaper global proof, I diagonalize with u=q1+q2 and d=q1-q2. Nonnegative quantities mean u>=0 and |d|<=u. The quadratic term q'*A*q=(5*u^2+d^2)/2, so Pi=4*u-(5*u^2+d^2)/2=8/5-(5/2)*(u-4/5)^2-d^2/2. The unique optimum is u=4/5,d=0, giving q1=q2=2/5, prices3 and total profit8/5. This sum-and-difference trick proves symmetry from an explicit imbalance penalty instead of assuming symmetry before optimization. The solution is feasible, and every deviation lowers profit by a sum of nonnegative squares.

For separate price choice, firm i differentiates (p_i-1)*(1-3*p_i/5+2*p_j/5). The derivative is(8-6*p_i+2*p_j)/5 and the second derivative is -6/5. Its best response is r_i=4/3+p_j/3. When p_j ranges from1 to7/3, this response ranges from5/3 to19/9, within the allowed interval. Hence it is a global best response throughout the stated game. Solving the two reactions gives uniquely p1=p2=2, quantities3/5 each and profit3/5 each. At the joint-owner prices3, a separate rival's unconstrained affine reaction would instead be7/3; a monopoly optimum need not be a Nash point for two independent owners.

For surplus, I use the quadratic identity CS=V-p'*q=q'*A*q/2. At symmetric quantities q1=q2=q, this is5*q^2. Thus monopoly consumer surplus is4/5, profit8/5 and welfare12/5. Separate-price consumer surplus is9/5, total profit6/5 and welfare3. Joint ownership raises profit by2/5 but lowers consumer surplus by1, leaving a welfare decline3/5. The cross term in utility is included in CS; adding two isolated own-demand triangles would omit it.

For an independent welfare route, I subtract real costs directly: W=V-(q1+q2)=4*u-(5*u^2+d^2)/4. Its completed square is W=16/5-(5/4)*(u-8/5)^2-d^2/4. The globally efficient vector is therefore q1=q2=4/5, with prices1 and welfare16/5. Both constraints are satisfied. The monopoly welfare loss is(5/4)*(4/5)^2=4/5, while the separate-price loss is(5/4)*(2/5)^2=1/5. These equal16/5-12/5 and16/5-3. The efficiency ratios are3/4 and15/16 respectively.

To connect ownership to the algebra, I compare the gradients of separate quantity profits and total profit. Increasing q1 lowers the price of good2 by2 per unit. The joint owner therefore includes an extra term -2*q2 in its derivative, in addition to the effect on product1 revenue. Separate owners do not receive product2's profit and omit this cross-revenue loss. In the sum-and-difference coordinates, private monopoly profit penalizes quantity twice as strongly as resource welfare does. The common efficient direction is the same, but the privately optimal scale is half the efficient scale.

General pattern: I recover demand from a concave utility before solving firms' objectives. A symmetric quadratic separates into total activity and imbalance, making global optimality and sign errors visible. Joint ownership adds cross-revenue effects; welfare instead cancels payments and counts real costs. Separate completed squares for profit and welfare reveal their distinct optimal scales and provide exact efficiency-loss checks.
reference_answer:
The inverse demands are p_i=5-3*q_i-2*q_j; direct demands are q_i=1-3*p_i/5+2*p_j/5. The correct monopoly conditions both have negative cross terms: 4-6*q_i-4*q_j=0. In u=q1+q2,d=q1-q2 coordinates, profit is8/5-(5/2)*(u-4/5)^2-d^2/2, proving the unique global monopoly choice q_i=2/5 and p_i=3.

Separate firms have best responses p_i=4/3+p_j/3, globally optimal on the stated intervals. Their unique equilibrium has p_i=2 and q_i=3/5.

Monopoly consumer surplus, total profit and welfare are(4/5,8/5,12/5); separate-price values are(9/5,6/5,3). Efficiency gives q_i=4/5, p_i=1 and welfare16/5. Welfare losses are4/5 and1/5, and efficiency ratios3/4 and15/16. The welfare square confirms these values. The correction's plus sign is inconsistent with the gradient; joint ownership internalizes the negative cross-revenue effect.

problem: In a second-price auction with two independent uniform[0,1] values, what is the seller's expected revenue under truthful bidding? Derive it from order statistics rather than simulating bids.
thinking:
Before computing payments, note the winner pays the lower of the two values. For two uniform draws, the expected minimum is∫₀¹P(min>X?); more directly the minimum has density2(1−x), so its mean is∫₀¹2x(1−x)dx=1/3.

Truthful bidding is weakly dominant in a second-price auction, so the allocation goes to the higher value and the payment is the second-highest value, which with two bidders is the minimum. Expected revenue is1/3.

The survival route gives E[min]=∫₀¹P(V1≥t,V2≥t)dt=∫₀¹(1−t)²dt=1/3. This independent tail integral verifies the order-statistic density result.

General pattern: auction revenue in a second-price mechanism is an order statistic. Use the distribution of the payment rank or integrate its survival probability; incentive compatibility identifies the truthful allocation first.
reference_answer: Expected revenue is 1/3.

problem: Help me check a claim: “A negligence rule that induces efficient care must also induce efficient activity.” A risk-neutral actor chooses activity n>=0 and a common care decision for every unit. Gross benefit is B(n)=12*n-n^2. Without care, accident probability per unit is1/2; with care it is1/5 and care costs1 per unit. Each accident causes real harm10. Expected costs add across units.
